ARTIFICIAL CORUSCATIONS MAY ALSO BE PRODUCED BY

Pages 315-315

l coruscations may also be produced by means of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of vitriol and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, in the following manner: Take a glass body capable of holding three quarts; put into this three ounces of oil of vitriol and twelve ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; then warming the mixture a little, throw in, at several times, two ounces <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more of clean iron filings; upon this an ebullition and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> vapours <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> arise; then present a lighted <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> to the mouth of the vessel, and the vapour will take fire, and afford a bright <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FULMINATION">fulmination</a> or flash like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. Applying the candle in this manner several times, the effect will always be the same; and sometimes the fire will fill the whole body of the glass, and even circulate to the bottom of the liquor; at others, it will only reach a little way <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> its neck. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> caution to be used in making this experiment is the making the vapour of a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>: for, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, few vapours will arise; and, if made too hot, they will arise too fast, and will only take fire in the neck of the glass, without any remarkable coruscation. **Corvorant,** formerly written Cormorant. See Pelicanus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Corvus,** the Raven or Crow kind, a genus of birds of the order of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICA">pica</a>. See Ornithology Index. Corvus (Raven), in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the southern hemisphere; whose stars in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue are 7; in Tycho's as many; in the Britannic catalogue 9. Corvus, in Roman antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> engine, or rather gallery, moveable at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> by means of pulleys; chiefly used in boarding the enemy's ships to cover the men. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the corvus was as follows: They erected on the prow of their vessels a round piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> of about a foot and a half diameter, and about 12 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; on the top of which they had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> or pulley. Round this piece of timber they laid a stage or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of boards, four feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and about 18 feet long, which was well framed and fastened with iron. The entrance was long-ways, and it moved about on the above-mentioned upright piece of timber as on a spindle, and could be hoisted up within six feet of the top: about this was a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> knee-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, which was defended with upright bars of iron sharpened at the end, and towards the top there was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, by the help of which and a pulley or tackle, they raised or lowered the engine at pleasure. With this moveable gallery they boarded the enemy's vessels (when they did not oppose side to side).

AUSTONIUS PROPOSES THE SAME

Pages 411-411

s proposes the same means to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a> in the two following verses: Laetè incide notas; arescens <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a> tenebit Semper inaspicuas; prodentur scripta favillis. Epift. xxiii. But it would appear, that the commentators on this poet have mistaken the meaning of the word favilla, which is used here to signify fuligo, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> foot; and in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is often employed by other poets. Columella, speaking of the method of preserving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> from insects with foot, calls it nigra favilla. In another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he mentions the same practice, and says fuliginem que supra focos teftis inhaberet. Other glutinous juices besides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> may be employed for the same purpose, as they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> equally hold fast the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> powder strewed over them. Pliny, therefore, recommends the milky juice of certain plants, and particularly mentions that of lettuce, to produce this effect. It is now well known that several metallic solutions may be employed for a similar purpose, and being exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of certain vapours, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> which are written with them become visible. This effect was perhaps accidentally discovered; but it does not appear to be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. In a book De secretis, compiled by Wecker from Porta, Cardan, and some other old writers, and printed in 1592, there is no mention of it; nor even is it noticed by Canearius in his book de Atramentis, printed in 1619. The first receipt given for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of a sympathetic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> is in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Borel printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1653, where it is called magnetic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which acts at a distance. Beckmann, Hist. of Invent. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, Cipher, and Ink.

something of equal order, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> with another. CO-SECANT

Pages 317-317

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECANT">secant</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> which is the complement of another to 90°. See Geometry.

CO-SINE

Pages 317-317

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">Trigonometry</a>, the sine of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> which is the complement of another to 90°. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>.

CO-TANGENT

Pages 320-320

the tangent of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> which is the complement of another to 90°. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>.

CO-VERSED SINE

Pages 326-326

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, the remaining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the diameter of a circle, after the versed sine is taken from it. See GEOMETRY. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">COVERT</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>.—Femme Covert denotes a woman married, and so covered by, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> under the protection of, her husband.

CONCOU

Pages 99-99

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a name given by the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> to an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, which is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem among them for killing that troublesome sort of worm called the Guinea worm, that breeds in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. They bruise the leaves, and mixing them with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> apply them in form of a cataplasm.

CONCRETE

Pages 99-99

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, signifies a body made up of different principles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any mixed body: thus, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> is a fictitious concrete, mixed together by art; and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a> is a natural concrete, or a mixed body compounded in the bowels of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>.

CONCRETION

Pages 99-99

the uniting several small particles of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> body into sensible masses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> concretes, whereby it becomes so and so figured and determined, and is endowed with such and such properties. CONCRETION is also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> whereby soft bodies are rendered hard; or an insensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the particles of a fluid or soft body, whereby they come to a consistence. It is indifferently used for induration, condensation, congestion, and coagulation.

CONCUBINAGE SOMETIMES

Pages 99-100

E sometimes expresses a criminal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prohibited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> between the two sexes; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it comprehends <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INCEST">incest</a>, and simple fornication. In its more restrained sense, concubinage is used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s and a woman's cohabiting together in the way of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, without having passed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> thereof. Concubinage was anciently tolerated: the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> calls it an allowed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, licita conjunctura. When this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> occurs in the constitutions of the Christian emperors, it signifies what we now call a marriage in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. The concubinage tolerated among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the republic, and of the heathen emperors, was that between persons not capable of contracting marriage together; nor did they even refuse to let inheritances descend to children which sprung from such a tolerated cohabitation. Concubinage between such persons they looked on as a kind of marriage, and even allowed it several privileges; but then this concubinage was confined to a single person, and was of perpetual obligation as much as marriage itself. Hottoman observes, that the Roman laws had allowed of concubinage <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before Julius Caesar made that law whereby every one was allowed to marry as many wives as he pleased. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> tell us, allowed every man two. CONCUBINAGE is also used for a marriage performed with less solemnity than the formal marriage: or a marriage marriage with a woman of inferior condition, and to whom the husband does not convey his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Cujas observes, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> laws allowed a man to espouse, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of concubine, certain persons, such as were esteemed unequal to him, on account of the want of some qualities requisite to sustain the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of marriage. He adds, that though concubinage was beneath marriage, both as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and civil effects; yet was concubinage a reputable title, very different from that of mistresses among us. The commerce was esteemed so lawful, that the concubine might be accused of adultery in the same manner as a wife. This kind of concubinage is still in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in some countries, particularly in Germany, under the title of a half-marriage, morgengabe marriage or marriage with the left-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; alluding to the manner of its being contracted, viz. by the man's giving the woman his left hand instead of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. This is a real marriage, though without solemnity: the parties are both bound forever; though the woman be thus excluded from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of a wife for want of quality or fortune. The children of concubines were not reputed either legitimate or bastards, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> children, and were capable only of donations. They were deemed to retain the low rank of the mother; and were on this ground unqualified for inheriting the effects of the father. Concubinage, in a legal sense, is used as an exception against her that sueth for dower, alleging thereby, that she was not a wife lawfully married to the party, in whose lands she seeks to be endowed, but his concubine.

CONCUBINE

Pages 100-100

a woman whom a person takes to cohabit with him, in the manner, and under the character, of a wife, without being authorized thereto by a legal <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Concubine is also used for a real, legitimate, and only wife, distinguished by no other circumstance but a disparity of birth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> condition between her and the husband. Du Cange observes, that one may gather from several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the epistles of the popes, that they anciently allowed of such concubines. The seventeenth canon of the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a> declares, that he who, with a faithful wife, keeps a concubine, is excommunicated; but that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the concubine served him as a wife, so that he had only one woman, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of concubine, he should not be rejected from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>: which shows that there were legitimate wives under the title of concubines. In effect, the Roman laws did not allow a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to espouse whom he pleased; there was required a kind of parity, or proportion, between the conditions of the contracting parties: but a woman of inferior condition, who could not be espoused as a wife, might be kept as a concubine; and the laws allowed of it, provided the man had no other wife. It is certain the patriarchs had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of wives, and that these did not all hold the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>; some being subservient to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> wife; which were what we call concubines or half-wives. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> prohibited a plurality of concubines, and only had regard to the children issuing from a single concubine, because she might become a legitimate wife. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> had 700 wives and 300 concubines; the Corcupis, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> has sometimes two or three thousand concubines in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. Q. Curtius observes, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> was followed in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> by 365 concubines, all in the equipage of queens.

CONCUPISCIENCE

Pages 100-100

according to divines, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> appetite, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lust after carnal things, inherent in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> ever since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>.

COND

Pages 100-100

Con, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Conn, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifies to guide or conduct a ship in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> course. He that cons her, stands aloft with a compass before him, and gives the word of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> at the helm how he is to steer. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the ship go before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, or, as they call it, betwixt the sheets, the word is either starboard, or port the helm; according as the conder would have the helm put to the right or left side of the ship, upon which the ship always goes the contrary way. If he says, helm amidship, he would have the ship to go right before the wind, or directly between her two sheets. If the ship fail by a wind, or on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> wind, the word is, aloof, keep your <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUFF">luff</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> not off, veer no more, keep her to, touch the wind, have a care of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-latch: all which expressions are of the same import, and imply that the steersman should keep the ship near the wind. On the contrary, if he would have her sail more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, or more before the wind, the word is, ease the helm, no near, bear up. If he cries steady, it means, keep her from going in and out, or making yaws (as they call it), however she fails, whether large or before a wind: and when he would have her go <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as she does, he cries, keep her thus, thus, &c.

Hence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RENNES">Rennes</a>, in Brittany. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 45. Lat. 48. 5. Another Condate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> (Antonia); now thought to be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGLETON">Congleton</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>; others say in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>.

CONDE

Pages 100-104
LEWIS DE BOURBON PRINCE OF, was born at Paris Sept. 7. 1621. He was styled Duke d'Enguien, till he succeeded to the title of Prince of Conde by his father's death in 1646. As he was of a tender and delicate constitution, the prince sent him to the castle of Montrond in Berry, that he might breathe a more pure and salutary air. Here he was educated in his infancy by some experienced and prudent citizens' wives. When he was of a proper age, the prince took upon himself the task of governor, and appointed for his attendant M. de la Bouffieres, a private gentleman, a man of honour, fidelity, and good nature, and who made it a rule to observe inviolably the orders that were given him. Two Jesuits distinguished for their genius and knowledge were also given him for preceptors. He formed him a household of 15 or 20 officers, all men of the greatest virtue and discretion. With these attendants the duke d'Enguien went to settle at Bourges, where he frequented the college of Jesuits. Here, besides the ordinary studies, he was taught ancient and modern history, mathematics, geography, declamation; also riding and dancing, in which last he soon excelled. He made such a surprising progress, that before the age of 13, he defended in public some questions in philosophy with incredible applause. applause. At his return from Montreond, he had for his tutor M. de Merille; a man deeply versed in the knowledge of common law, of ancient and modern laws, of the holy scriptures, and of the mathematics. Under his direction the duke went through that new course with prodigious success. He acquired a critical taste in the arts and sciences, which he retained all his life; he never suffered a day to pass without dedicating two or three hours at least to reading; his thirst for knowledge was universal, and he endeavoured to search every thing to the bottom. His chief inclination, however, lay towards the military art; and at the age of 18 he obtained permission to make his first campaign as a volunteer in the army commanded by M. de la Meilleraye. This campaign was unfortunate; and the duke d'Enguien was only a witness of the marshal's imprudence and disgrace. Nevertheless, in this campaign he laid the foundation of that renown which made him afterwards considered as the greatest general of his age. On his return to Paris, the duke waited upon Cardinal Richelieu at Rueil. That minister was so pleased with his conversation, that he soon after made proposals of an alliance with the prince of Conde, by marrying the duke d'Enguien to Claire Clemence de Maille Breza, the cardinal's niece. The duke consented to this match out of obedience to his father; but the force he put upon himself by yielding to it was so great, that he fell dangerously ill. It was long before he got the better of his distemper; but at length he not only recovered, but became so strong as afterwards to bear the greatest fatigues with ease. The duke made two more campaigns as a volunteer; the one under the marshal de la Meilleraye, the other in the army of Louis XIII. which conquered Roussillon. In 1643, at the age of 22, he obtained from the king, at the persuasion of Cardinal Mazarin, the command of the army destined to cover Champagne and Picardy; which command was confirmed to him after the king's death by the queen regent, Anne of Austria, to whose interest he was strongly devoted. In this station, though he never had been present at any battle, he soon gave such a specimen of his abilities as crowned him with glory. The Spaniards, who threatened France with an invasion, were defeated by him at Rocroi; and this signal victory made him from that time considered as the guardian genius of his country. He next formed the project of besieging Thionville, and proposed it to the council of regency. They consented with fear and distrust; but the duke carried it into execution with such skill, activity, and courage, that he became justly the subject of general admiration. In two months time Thionville surrendered. At length, having covered Alsace and Lorraine from the enterprises of the Imperialists, the duke returned to Paris, where he obtained the government of Champagne, and of the city of Stenai. The three following years were little more than a series of military operations. The three battles of Fribourg, in which the duke d'Enguien triumphed over Velt Marshal count de Mercy, the greatest general in all Germany; the taking of Philippsbourg, and a great number of other places, which rendered him master of the palatinate, and of the whole course of the Rhine; the victory of Norlingue, by which he revenge the vicount du Turenne's defeat at Mariendal; the siege and conquest of Dunkirk, the good and bad success of his arms in Catalonia, where, though he was forced to raise the siege of Lerida, he kept the Spaniards in awe, and cut to pieces their rear guard; these are the principal events which distinguished the campaigns of 1644, 1645, and 1646. The victories of the duke d'Enguien, his great reputation and esteem with the people, began now to give umbrage to Mazarin. The cardinal's dislike to him appeared on the death of the duke de Breze, admiral of France. The prince of Conde earnestly demanded for his son the duke de Breze's places. But Mazarin, afraid of increasing the wealth and power of a prince whom his victories and the love and confidence of the people and the army had already rendered too formidable to him, evaded his request, by persuading the queen to take the admiralty to herself. On the death of his father, the minister's dislike to the young prince of Conde became still more apparent. By the minister's persuasion he had accepted of the command of the army in Catalonia; but, on his arrival at Barcelona, he found neither troops, money, artillery, provisions, nor ammunition. Enraged at this deception, he vented his resentment in bitter complaints and severe threats; but by the resources that he found in this dilemma, the prince added new lustre to his glory. The campaign of 1648 was as glorious to Conde as those which preceded it had been. To disconcert at once the projects of the arch-duke Leopold, the prince resolved to attack him even in the heart of the Low Countries; and notwithstanding the considerable difficulties which he had to surmount, he besieged the important city of Ypres, and took it in sight of all the enemy's forces. Notwithstanding this success, Conde saw himself at the point of experiencing the greatest reverse of fortune. His army was a prey to scarcity, to nakedness, contagious distempers, and desertion. For eight months it received no supply from the minister, but half a muleter. Every thing was supplied by the prince himself; he lavished his money, and borrowed more to supply his troops. When it was represented to him that he was in danger of ruining himself by such an enormous expense, he replied, that "since he every day ventured his life for the service of his country, he could very well sacrifice his fortune to it. Let but the government exist (added he), and I shall want for nothing." The French army having been reinforced by 4000 of the troops of Weimar, Conde attacked the Spaniards advantageously encamped near Lens, and gained a complete victory over them, which disabled them from attempting anything more, and even from supporting themselves. Afterwards he besieged Furnes, the garrison of which, 900 men, surrendered themselves prisoners of war. But the prince was wounded there in the trenches by a musket-shot above the right hip; and the contusion was so great, that he was forced to submit to several incisions. The French court, animated with the victory at Lens, thought this a proper time to take vengeance on the factions which for some time had violently agitated the kingdom; and accordingly imprisoned Broussel and Blanckenil, two of the principal leaders of the country party. This vigorous proceeding, however, occasioned a general revolt. Two hundred thousand men took arms in Paris, barricaded the streets, invested the palais-royal, and demanded the prisoners. It was necessary to release them; but from that time the regal authority was annihilated; the queen was exposed to a thousand insults, and Mazarin dared no longer venture out of the palais-royal. In this embarrassment the queen recalled the prince of Conde, as the only one from whom she could hope for support. He retired to Rueil, whither the regent had gone with the young king and Mazarin. Anne of Austria proposed to him the reducing of Paris by force of arms; but he calmed the resentments of that princess; and instead of being accessory to her vengeance, he directed all his views to pacify the kingdom, and at length brought about an accommodation between the parties, who desired it with equal ardour. But new incidents soon rekindled the combustion. The treachery of Mazarin, and the artifices of the leaders of the country party, occasioned new cabals and fresh troubles. Conde was caressed by the leaders of both parties; but at last, enraged at the arrogance of the malecontents, who every day formed new pretensions, he took part openly with the court, though he thought it ungrateful, and protected the minister, though he did not esteem him. The royal family, the duke of Orleans, Conde, and Mazarin, left Paris privately in the night between the 5th and 6th of January 1646, and went to St Germain. The parliament sent deputies to learn from the queen herself the reasons of her departure, and to beg her to name the citizens whom she suspected, that they might be tried. Mazarin had the imprudence to dismiss them without any answer. Exasperated at this, the people again took up arms in order to defend themselves against the enterprises of the court, who had determined to block up and to starve the capital, in order to suppress the party of malecontents. With 7 or 8000 men, the broken relics of the last campaign, the prince of Conde formed a design of reducing above 500,000 entrenched behind walls. He had neither money nor magazines; he saw himself in the depth of a most severe winter; nevertheless he triumphed over Paris, and this great success completed his glory. It did him so much the more honour, as during the siege he constantly defeated the troops of the malecontents; he prevailed on the army that marched to their assistance under Turenne, to abandon that general; he flopped the progress of the duke de Longueville, who had caused an insurrection in Normandy; and got the start of the Spaniards, who were advancing to give him battle. Condi de Retz, coadjutor of Paris, and afterwards cardinal, was the life and soul of the revolters, and directed all their motions. He had taken Catiline for his model; and was equally intrepid and capable of the greatest actions; of an exalted genius, but governed by his ambition. He distinguished his hatred to Mazarin by arming the malecontents; and he himself raised at his own expense a regiment which he called the regiment of Corinth; as soon as this corps took the field during the blockade of Paris, it was defeated and dispersed. This check was called the first to the Corinthians. The peace was signed at St Germain; but neither party carried its point, and scarce anyone but Conde acquired glory by this war. After the conclusion of the treaty, the prince repaired to the capital, and traversed all the streets in his coach alone. All persons of any consequence paid their compliments to him, and the parliament sent a solemn deputation to thank him for the peace to which he had so powerfully contributed. The people, however, made loud complaints on account of the king's absence (for the court was not yet returned to Paris), and the malecontents gave reason to apprehend a new insurrection. Conde encouraged the king and queen to return; and at length brought them to Paris, amidst the acclamations and blessings of the public. The important service which Conde had just done the court entitled him to the acknowledgments of the queen, and especially of Mazarin; but the dark soul of that cardinal only remembered it to punish a too fortunate and too powerful protector. He privately swore the prince's destruction; at least that he should give the whole kingdom a pattern of submission and dependence on his will. However, not to excite the public indignation, he still kept up appearances with the prince, while he secretly spread about him distrusts, suspicions, snares of every kind, and the most heinous calumnies. The ungrateful minister deceived the prince by making him the most flattering proposals; and with the most alluring promises which he always found means to avoid fulfilling. The enraged prince despised the minister, and treated him with disdain. After this they were reconciled again only to be again at variance. Each of them in their turn courted the country party, in order to make it subservient to their designs. At last Mazarin thought of an expedient, which but too effectually answered his purpose, of making an irreconcilable quarrel between that party and the prince. Among the malecontents the marquis de la Boulaié, a man of an infamous character, had obtained the confidence of the party by false appearances of hatred to the cardinal, but secretly kept up a correspondence with him. It is pretended that he made him an offer of privately killing Conde. Mazarin was charmed with the proposal; yet he only required Boulaié to exhibit all the proofs of an afflatusion, and to act in such a manner that everything might concur to render the country party suspected of that crime. He was punctually obeyed; the coach was stopped; some pistols were fired at it; by which two of the footmen were dangerously wounded; and, after that shameful exploit, la Boulaié took refuge in the hotel of the duke of Beaufort, who was the hero of the party, in order no doubt to countenance the prince's suspicion of the malecontents. Luckily Conde was not in his coach when it was stopped; the cardinal had spread the report of his intended afflatusion; and in concert with the queen and the prince he had prevailed to have the coach sent away empty, to prove the reality of the attempt. Mazarin counterfeited a zeal for the prince's life; he furiously declaimed against the malecontents, who, he pretended, had made an attempt on a life so precious to the state; and he inflamed Conde's resentment against the duke of Beaufort. Conde. Beaufert and the coadjutor, whom he supposed to be the authors of this heinous outrage. The prince was so strongly prejudiced, that he refused to hear them when they appeared before him to justify themselves. He demanded justice against them of the king; he formally accused them before the parliament, and remained inflexible in spite of the pains which the leaders of the party took to demonstrate to him that he had been imposed upon. However, the affair was brought before the parliament; the accused defended themselves, and the coadjutor, who had discovered the cardinal's secret, unmasked him to well, that the prince agreed to a private negociation with the malecontents; he required nothing more than the coadjutor's leaving Paris, but with the rank of ambassador to Rome or Vienna. That prelate would have consented to it, to satisfy Conde, if Mazarin, some days after, had not given him the choice of any recompense, in order to engage his concurrence in the prince's destruction. Affairs were now in such a dangerous situation, that the cardinal saw clearly it was necessary to hasten to the winding up of the plot. Master of the queen's mind, which he guided as he pleased; and sure of having inflamed against Conde all the resentment of the malecontents; he fought and obtained, by means of the duchess Chevreuse, the support of that powerful faction, which connected itself the more readily with him, in hopes that the prince's fall would soon enable it to crush without difficulty the cardinal himself. The coadjutor had private conferences with the queen and the minister. Conde had notice of it; and in order to discover if it were true, he endeavoured to surmise it from Mazarin's own mouth. "Cardinal (said he, one day), it is publicly reported that you have nightly meetings with the coadjutor, disguised like a trooper." He accompanied this speech with a quick and penetrating look: but the cardinal, who was a perfect master of dissimulation, answered him in such a free, artless-like manner, that he entirely removed Conde's apprehensions; and he slighted the information he had received, of the plot forming against him. Mazarin wanted nothing but the support of the duke of Orleans; and at last found means, by the duchess Chevreuse, to inflame the jealousy of that fickle and inconstant prince, and to engage him to consent to the imprisonment of Conde. Having thus united all parties, and fearing no other obstacle, this ungrateful and pernicious minister made preparations for privately arresting the prince: the order for it was signed January 18th 1650. Conde having that day repaired as usual to the palais-royal, to assist at council with the prince of Conti and the duke of Longueville, the queen gave orders to arrest them all three, and convey them without any noise to the castle of Vincennes. She was instantly obeyed, and the princes were strictly guarded in that prison. In this unexpected reverse of fortune, the fortitude and greatness of Conde's mind appeared only the more remarkable. Confined with the other two princes in the tower of Vincennes, where neither supper, furniture, nor beds, were provided, he contented himself with two new laid eggs, and threw himself in his clothes, on a truss of straw, where he slept 12 hours without waking. He still retained his cheerfulness, and dedicated the greatest part of his time to reading, the rest to conversation, playing at battle-lover and shuttlecock, to bodily exercises, and the cultivation of flowers. Mazarin triumphed at the disgrace of the princes, procribed all those who were attached to Conde, and behaved in the most insolent and arbitrary manner. The prince's friends, however, notwithstanding their being strictly watched, found means to keep up a punctual correspondence with him. They made various attempts to release him: they raised troops; in particular, the dukes of Bouillon and Rochefoucault, and the vicount de Turenne. The princes of Conde engaged the province of Guienne to declare in his favour; he made war, in order to force the court to release him; at length the partizans of the prince signed a treaty with the Spaniards, to labour in concert for his enlargement. But all these efforts would, perhaps, have been ineffectual, if other more powerful resources had not been employed. In that gallant and warlike age, every thing was managed by the passions and intrigues of five or six women, who possessed the confidence of the leaders of the state, and of the various parties. The princesses of Mantua, wife to one of the sons of the elector Palatine, king of Bohemia, principally directed the councils in the party of the princes. She found means to reconcile the duke of Orleans, the coadjutor, and the malecontents, with the friends of the prince, and united their efforts against the cardinal. The parliament, on the other side, loudly demanded the release of the prisoners. All the orders of the state united in soliciting it, inasmuch that the queen was at last prevailed on to give her consent. At this news, Mazarin was so confounded, that he fled in the disguise of a trooper, and arrived at the gates of Richlieu, where a body of horse waited for him. The parliament, informed by the queen of his flight, thundered forth an arrêt, by which he was obliged to leave the kingdom, with his family and foreign servants, in the space of 15 days, under the penalty of being exposed to a criminal prosecution. The queen desired to follow him with the king; but the nobles and burghers invested the palais royal, and prevented the execution of this project, which would have kindled a civil war. Mazarin, therefore, perceiving that it was impossible for the queen to join him, determined to go himself to restore the princes to their liberty, and to get the start of the deputies who were coming to acquaint them with it. On his arrival at Havre, he informed the princes that they were free; he entreated Conde's friendship; and was so abject as to prostrate himself at the feet of him whom he had so basely oppressed. Conde gave him a polite reception, and spoke to him in a free and cheerful tone; but tired with the mean submissions which the cardinal lavished upon him, he left him without making any promise, and set out on his return to Paris, which he entered as it were in triumph, amidst the acclamations of all orders of men, and the demonstrations of a most sincere and general joy. After this a civil war ensued, in which the prince of Conde sided with the malecontents. Being pressed by the king's army, he retired into the suburbs of St Anthony, where he behaved with the utmost bravery; when the citizens opened their gates and received received him in; and a peace ensued soon after. His hatred of the cardinal, however, made him quit Paris, and take refuge among the Spaniards, who made him generalissimo of their forces; and he took Rocroi. The peace of the Pyrenees restored him to his country; and he again signalized himself at the head of the king's armies. Being afflicted with the gout, he refused the command of the army in 1676, and retired to Chantilly, where he was as much esteemed for the virtues of peace, as he had been before for his military talents. He died in 1686, at Fontainebleau. Conde, a town of the French Netherlands, in the province of Hainault, with the title of a principality, and a castle. It is one of the strongest towns in this country, and seated near the confluence of the rivers Hulst and Scheldt. It was taken by the allies in 1793, and retaken by the French in 1794. Its name by the convention was changed to Nord Libre. E. Long. 3° 39'. N. Lat. 50° 27'. Condé, a town of France, in the department of Calvados, which carries on a considerable trade; seated on the river Nereau, 15 miles west of Paris. W. Long. 0° 37'. N. Lat. 48° 50'.

CONDEMNATION

Pages 104-104

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of giving judgment, passing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pronouncing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> against a person who is thus subjected to some penalty or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, either in respect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, reputation, or fortune.

CONDENSATION

Pages 104-104

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> whereby a body is rendered more dense, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and heavy. The word is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> applied to the conversion of vapour into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> naturally in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>. The way in which vapour commonly condenses, is by the application of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> substance. On touching it, the vapour parts with its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> which it had before absorbed; and on doing so, it immediately loses the proper characteristics of vapour, and becomes water. But though this is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and usual way in which we observe vapour to be condensed, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> certainly proceeds after another method; since we often observe the vapours most plentifully condensed when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> is really warmer than at other times. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Cloud, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">Evaporation</a>, &c.

CONDENSER

Pages 104-104

a pneumatic engine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> syringe, with which a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> may be crowded into a given space; so that sometimes ten atmospheres, or ten times as much air as there is at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the same space, under the usual pressure, may be thrown in by means of it, and its effects prevented by valves properly disposed. It consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, wherein is a moveable piston; which being drawn out, the air rushes into the cylinder through a hole provided for purpose; and when the piston is again forced into the cylinder, the air is driven into the receiver through an orifice, furnished with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALVE">valve</a> to hinder its getting out. The receiver or vessel containing the condensed air, should be made very strong, to bear the force of the air's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> thus increased; for which reason they are generally made of brass; its orifice is fitted with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> screw to receive the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> screw at the end of the condenser. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> glass be used for a condenser, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not suffer so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of condensation; but the experiment will be more entertaining, since the subject may be viewed in the condensed air.

CONDITION

Pages 104-104

in the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a clause of obligation stipulated as an article of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>; or in a donation of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>, legacy, &c., in which last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> a donee does not lose his donative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with any dishonest or impossible conditions.

CONDITIONAL

Pages 104-104

something not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, but subject to conditions. CONDITIONAL Conjunctions, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, are those which serve to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> conditional; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, unless, provided, &c. CONDITIONAL Propositions, in Logic, such as consist of two parts connected together by a conditional particle. CONDITIONAL Syllogism, a syllogism where the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> is a conditional proposition. Thus, If there is a God, he ought to be worshipped. But there is a God; Therefore he ought to be worshipped.

CONDIVICNUM

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Namnetes, in Armorica. Now Nantes in Brittany, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, from its name Civitas Namnetum. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 30'. Lat. 47° 15'.

CONDOM

Pages 104-104

a town of Gascony in France, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Condomeois, with a bishop's see. It is but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the trade is very small. It is seated on the river Gelisse, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 22'. N. Lat. 44'.

CONDORCET

Pages 104-106

John-Antony Nicholas Cartat, marquis of, a French writer, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> character of considerable eminence, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family from the principality of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, and born at Ribemont in Picardy, in 1743. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Navarre, where he was distinguished at an early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for his strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physics and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. On his entrance into public life, he established a friendly intercourse with Voltaire, D'Alembert, and other literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, who professed opinions analogous to his own, and formed a very powerful party among the French literati, whose united efforts to propagate their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and politics, have been applauded <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> condemned, according to the principles of their different judges. Condorcet first attracted the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the public as a mathematician, obtaining their approbation for his treatise on integral calculations, which he composed at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 22. In the year 1767, his solution of the problem of the Three Bodies made its appearance, and in the following year the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">Analysis</a>." In the year 1769 he was received a member of the Academy of Sciences, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of which were greatly enriched by him with different papers on the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> branches of mathematical science. His justly merited reputation pointed him out as a fit person to cooperate with D'Alembert and Bossut, in afflicting M. Turgot, that celebrated minister and able financier, with arithmetical calculations. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he laboured indefatigably in the study of politics and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, and defended, in an anonymous publication, the feet of philosophers to which he had attached himself, from Condorcet, an attack made upon them in the Trois Siecles; and replied to M. Necker's essay on Corn Laws. He was appointed secretary to the Academy of Sciences in the year 1773, when he employed much of his time in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> eulogies on such of its deceased members as Fontenelle had passed over in silence. Like D'Alembert and some others, Condorcet having united in himself the characters of an elegant writer and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of profound research, was admitted into the French academy in 1783, when he pronounced an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> on the influence of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, which was ordered to be printed. From the time of D'Alembert's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened this year, he filled the station of secretary to that academy, rendering his name conspicuous by the publication of eulogies on different eminent characters. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> on D'Alembert, to whom he was most sincerely attached, is a very elaborate performance, notwithstanding of which it is deemed by judges as a candid account of the genuine merits of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. His encomium bestowed on that very able mathematician Euler, furnished him with a favourable opportunity of giving a circumstantial account of the specific improvements and inventions conferred on a peculiar branch of science by the labours of an individual; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> in a biographical writer which Condorcet appears to have possessed in an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. His eulogy on the minister Turgot was read with avidity, and admired by all those who approved of Turgot's plans of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and system of finance. In the year 1787 he gave the public his "Life of Voltaire," which was highly elaborate, and replete with lofty panegyric, on the merits of which mankind were consequently much divided, according to their sentiments of that author's philosophy. The last of his biographical works was an eulogy on the celebrated Dr Franklin, published in 1792, all of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be read with some degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> by those who are inimical to the school of philosophy to which he belonged. The memorable event of the French revolution, which the writings of Condorcet and his associates unquestionably accelerated, naturally interested his feelings, and called forth his exertions. But the conduct of the political parties and their leaders, during this tumultuous period, is painted in colours so diametrically opposite to each other, that a proper estimate of it is scarcely possible. In this part of Condorcet's life, therefore, we must confine ourselves to such facts as are universally acknowledged, leaving it to our readers to draw inferences for themselves. At an early period he employed his talents to promote those reforms, (for such they appeared in his judgment) which were to pave the way to a new order of things. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled "La Bibliothèque de l'Homme Public," to contain an analysis of the writings of the most eminent politicians, was chiefly conducted by him, as was also a newspaper called "La Chronique de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>," filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a> against royalty. He had likewise a share in the "Journal de Paris," a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> conducted on similar principles. About the time, when the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> fled to Varennes he proposed a paper called "Le Républicain," the obvious intention of which is clearly deducible from its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. He was an indefatigable member of the Jacobin club, and spoke frequently, though not forcibly, in it. He was chosen a representative for Paris when Condorcet's constituent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> was dissolved, and followed the general political course of the Brissotine party. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for public instruction was now to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> his abilities, which he finished in two elaborate memoirs, allowed to contain some exalted and enlarged ideas, but perhaps rather extensive to be reduced to practice. He was likewise author of the manifesto addressed to the European powers by the people of France, on the approach of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSTULATION">expostulation</a> to the king while he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the assembly, which some have considered as by far too severe, and destitute of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> to which the sovereign is entitled. When the king was insulted by the populace at the Tuileries, in being offered the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, it is said that he vindicated their proceedings. We are also informed, that while he was degrading royalty in this manner, he was secretly soliciting the office of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the dauphin; a proposition which the king utterly rejected, on account of his avowed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>. Attempts have been made to fix upon his character the most abominable ingratitude, by making him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de la Rochefoucault, to whom he was under the strongest obligations, and from whose family he had received a most accomplished wife with a fortune; but we sincerely hope that this calumny entirely originated from the malevolence of party spirit. When the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the king came to be agitated, Condorcet gave it as his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that he could not be brought to judgment in a legal manner; yet it must be confessed that his conduct in regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, was rather of an ambiguous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and betrayed that timidity and want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> which formed the most prominent features of his political <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. The judgment of Madame Roland concerning the moral <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of this wonderful man has all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of impartiality. "The genius of Condorcet," says that lady, "is equal to the comprehension of the greatest truths; but he has no other characteristic besides fear. It may be said of his understanding, combined with his person, that it is a fine essence absorbed in cotton. The timidity which forms the basis of his character, and which he displays even in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, does not result from his frame alone, but seems to be inherent in his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and his talents furnish him with no means of subduing it. Thus, after having deduced a principle or demonstrated a fact in the assembly, he would give a vote decidedly opposite, overawed by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of the tribunes, armed with insults, and lavished of menaces. The properest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for him was the secretariatship of the academy. Such men should be employed to write, but never permitted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>." The Girondist party, after the execution of the king, employed him to frame a new constitution, the plan of which was presented to the convention, and obtained their approbation. It was not thus esteemed by the people at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; and it has, perhaps not without reason, been considered as "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of metaphysical absurdities." During the violent struggle between the Girondist and Mountain parties, Condorcet took no decided part with either, which seems to have been owing to the native timidity of his mind, and his abhorrence of the state of public affairs. He was not comprehended among the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those who were sacrificed with their leader Brissot; but having employed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> against the victorious party, Condorcet, he fell under the invincible displeasure of that inhuman, blood-thirsty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, Robespierre, who issued a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> against him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, 1793. He found means to effect his escape from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a>, and during <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months concealed himself in Paris. Dreading at length that the tyrant would order a domiciliary visit for the purpose of discovering the place of his retreat, he passed through the barriers without being taken notice of, and went to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a person in whom he could confide, on the plain of Mont-Rouge, who unfortunately for Condorcet was at that time in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. He was of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of passing two dreary nights in the open fields, a melancholy prey to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. On the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he obtained an interview with his friend, who unhappily durst not venture to afford him shelter under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, so that he was once more compelled to wander in the fields. Worn out at length by hunger and fatigue, and life being no longer supportable without sustenance, he applied at a public house for an omelette, which he devoured with greediness. His cadaverous appearance and uncommonly keen appetite, roused the suspicion of a municipal officer who happened to be present, and by whom he was interrogated. The ambiguity and hesitation which characterized his answers, made the officer conclude that it would be proper to apprehend him. He was accordingly confined to a dungeon, to be next day conducted to Paris, but his melancholy fate rendered such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> unnecessary. He was found dead in the morning; and as it was generally understood that he constantly carried with him a dose of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, to this cause his melancholy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXIT">exit</a> was very properly ascribed. Thus terminated the career of Condorcet on the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, 1794, who for many years sustained a brilliant and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> reputation in the republic of letters. His manners were replete with urbanity, and as well qualified to please in company as could be expected in a man who was conceived as destitute of a heart. He was certainly blest with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> felicity, and had one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> by his wife. Soon after his death appeared his "sketch of a historical draught of the progress of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind," a methodical performance, and evincing the profoundest research, in which he strongly recommends his favourite idea of gradually bringing human nature to a state of perfection, by considering what man has been, now is, and may be. This treatise will no doubt be viewed by some as rather fanciful, but it is clearly the effort of a very superior genius, and must be peculiarly interesting to the feeling man, when it is known that it was composed while its author was in circumstances of danger and distress. The idea of man's progressive advancement towards perfection and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, inspired him with consolation under his complicated misfortunes. Besides the works which we have enumerated in this sketch of his life, he published "letters to the King of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>," with whom he kept up a correspondence, as well as with Catharine, empress of Russia. A treatise on calculation, and an elementary treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, were left behind him in manuscript. Although he was an enemy to revealed religion, he was certainly a man of virtue and integrity; yet all his philosophy could never inspire him with that heroic fortitude and contempt of death in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> cause, for which the sincere votaries of Christian conformity have ever been so conspicuous.

CONDORMIENNES

Pages 106-106

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sectaries, who take their name from lying all together, men and women, young and old. They arose in the 13th century, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>; where they are said to have worshipped an image of Lucifer, and to have received answers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> from him.

CONDRIEU

Pages 106-106

a town of Lyonnais in France, remarkable for its excellent wines. It is seated at the foot of a hill near the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 33'. N. Lat. 45° 28'.

CONDUCTOR

Pages 106-106

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> which serves to conduct the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> in the operation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and in laying up sinuses and fistulas.

CONDUCTORS

Pages 106-106

in electrical experiments, are those bodies that receive and communicate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>; and those that repel it are called non-conductors. See Electricity.

CONDUIT

Pages 106-106

a canal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pipe for the conveyance of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or other fluid. There are several subterraneous conduits through which the waters <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> that form <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> conduits for water are made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, potter's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, &c. CONDYLOID and CORONOID processes. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CONDURUSII

Pages 106-106

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>, originally Germans, dwelling about the Maese. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is now called Condroz, in the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, between Luxemburg and the Maese.

CONDYLOMA

Pages 106-106

in Medicine, a tubercle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> callosus eminence, which arises in the folds of the anus; or rather a swelling or hardening of the wrinkles of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>.

CONDYLUS

Pages 106-106

a name given by anatomists to a knot in any of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, formed by the epiphysis of a bone.

CONESSI

Pages 106-107

CONESSI, a sort of bark of a tree, which grows on the Coromandel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> in the East Indies. It is recommended in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Dr Monro, in the Medical Essays, as a specific in diarrhoeas. It is to be finely pulverized, and made into an electuary with syrup of oranges. The bark should be fresh, and the electuary new made every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day, otherwise it loses its astringent but grateful bitterness on the palate, and its proper effects on the intestines.

CONFARREATION

Pages 107-107

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, used in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of persons whose children were destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the priesthood. Confarreation was the most sacred of the three modes of contracting marriage among that people; and consisted, according to Servius, in this, that the pontifex maximus and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMEN">flamen</a> dialis joined and contracted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and woman, by making them eat of the same cake of salted <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> far, signifying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flour. Ulpian says, it consisted in the offering up of some pure wheaten bread; rehearsing, withal, a certain formula, in presence of ten witnesses. Dionysius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a> adds, that the husband and wife did eat of the same wheaten bread, and threw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> on the victims.

CONFECTION

Pages 107-107

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, signifies, in general, anything prepared with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; in particular it imports something preserved, especially dry substances. It also signifies a liquid <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> soft electuary, of which there are various sorts directed in dispensaries. See PHARMACY.

CONFECTOR

Pages 107-107

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a sort of gladiator, hired to fight in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> against beasts; thence also denominated bestiarus. The confessors were thus called a conficiendi bestiae, from their dispatching and killing beasts. The Greeks called them μαχηται, q. d. daring, rash, desperates; whence the Latins borrowed the appellations parabola and parabolarii. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were sometimes condemned to this sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>.

CONFECTS

Pages 107-107

a denomination given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, herbs, roots, &c., when boiled <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prepared with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, to dispose them to keep, and render them more agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>.

CONFEDERACY

Pages 107-107

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is when two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more persons combine to do any damage to another, or to commit any unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. Confederacy is punishable, though nothing be put in execution; but then it must have these four incidents; 1. That it be declared by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of prosecution, as by making of bonds or promises to one another; 2. That it be malicious, as for unjust <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>; 3. That it be false, i.e. against the innocent; and, lastly, That it be out of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> voluntary. CONFERVA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CONFESSION

Pages 107-107

among divines, the verbal acknowledgment which a Christian makes of his sins. Among the Jews it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, on the annual feast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> to make confession of sins to God in the name of the whole people; besides this general confession, the Jews were enjoined, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> their sins were a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, to make confession of them to God; but violations of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> table were to be acknowledged to their brethren. The confessions of the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were all voluntary, and not imposed on them by any laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; yet private confession was not only allowed, but encouraged. The Roman church requires confession not only as a duty, but has advanced it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a sacrament: this confession is made to the priest, and is private and auricular; and the priest is not to reveal them under pain of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. CONFESSION OF <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in any church.

CONFESSIONAL

Pages 107-107
or CONFESSIONARY, a place in churches under the great altar, where the bodies of deceased saints, martyrs, and confessors, were deposited. This word is also used by the Romanists for a desk in the church where the confessor takes the confessions of the penitents.

CONFESSIONER

Pages 107-107

a Christian who has made a solemn and resolute profession of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and has endured torments in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> saint is called a confessor, to distinguish him from the roll of dignified saints; such as apostles, martyrs, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, we frequently find the word confessors used for martyrs: in after-times, it was confined to those who, after having been tormented by the tyrants, were permitted to live and die in peace. And at last it was also used for those who, after having lived a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, died under an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of sanctity. According to St Cyprian, he who presented himself to torture, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even to martyrdom, without being called to it, was not called a confessor but a profissor: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any out of a want of courage abandoned his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and became a voluntary exile for the sake of the faith, he was called ex terris. Confessor is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who has a power to hear sinners in the sacrament of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, and to give them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTION">absolution</a>. The church calls him in Latin confessorius, to distinguish him from confessor, which is a name consecrated to saints. The confessors of the kings of France, from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Henry IV. have been constantly Jesuits: before him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a> and Cordeliers shared the office between them. The confessors of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> have also, ordinarily, been Dominicans and Cordeliers; but the later emperors have all taken Jesuits.

CONFIGURATION

Pages 107-107

the outward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> which bounds bodies, and gives them their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance; being that which, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, constitutes the specific <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between bodies.

CONFIRMATION

Pages 107-108
