in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of laying on of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, for the conveyance of the Holy Ghost. The antiquity of this ceremony is, by all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, carried as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as the apostles, and founded upon their example and practice. In the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, it used to be given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> immediately after <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the bishop happened to be present at the solemnity. Among the Greeks, and throughout the East, it still accompanies baptism; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> make it a distinct independent sacrament. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> years is the stated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for confirmation; however, they are sometimes confirmed before, and sometimes after, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The person to be confirmed has a godfather and godmother appointed him, as in baptism. The order of confirmation in the church of England does not determine the precise age of the persons to be confirmed.

CONFISSIO

Pages 108-108

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the adjudication of goods <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> effects to the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>; as the bodies and effects of criminals, traitors, &c.

CONFLAGRATION

Pages 108-108

the general <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. This word is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> applied to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> or catastrophe of our world, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is to be changed by fire, as formerly it was by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Pythagoreans, Platonists, Epicureans, and Stoics, appear to have had a notion of the conflagration; though whence they should derive it, unless from the sacred books, is difficult to conceive; except, perhaps, from the Phoenicians, who themselves had it from the Jews. Seneca says expressly, *Tempus advenire quo fidera fidelibus incurrent, et omni flagrante materia uno igne, quicquid nunc ex depesto lucet, ardebit.* This general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> the Stoics call *exvagatio, eccypatrois.* Mention of the conflagration is also made in the books of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIBYLS">Sibyls</a>, Sophocles, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, Ovid, Lucan, &c. Dr. Burnet, after F. Tachard and others, relates that the Siamese believe that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> at last be parched up with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> melted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> whole surface reduced to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, and then consumed with fire. And the Brahmins of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a> do not only hold that the world shall be destroyed by fire, but also that a new earth shall be made out of the cinders of the old. Various are the sentiments of authors on the subject of the conflagration; the cause whence it is to arise, and the effects it is to produce. Divines ordinarily account for it metaphysically; and will have it take its rise from a miracle, as a fire from heaven. Philosophers contend for its being produced from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> causes; and will have it effected according to the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>. Some think an eruption of the central fire sufficient for the purpose, and add, that this may be occasioned several ways, viz. either by having its intensity increased; which again may be effected either by being driven into less space by the encroachments of the superficial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, or by an increase of the inflammability of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> whereon it is fed; or by having the resistance of the imprisoning earth weakened, which may happen either from the diminution of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, by the consumption of its central Confluent parts, or by weakening the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> of the constituent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> by the excess or the defect of moisture. Others look for the cause of the conflagration in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and suppose, that some of the meteors there engendered in unusual quantities, and exploded with unusual vehemence, from the concurrence of various circumstances, may effect it, without seeking any further. The astrologers account for it from a conjunction of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> in the sign Cancer; as the deluge, say they, was occasioned by their conjunction in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPRICORN">Capricorn</a>. Lastly, others have recourse to a fill more effectual and flaming machine, and conclude the world is to undergo its conflagration from the near approach of a comet in its return from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>.

CONFLUENT

Pages 108-108

among physicians, &c. an appellation given to that kind of Small-fox wherein the pustules run into each other.

CONFLUENTES

Pages 108-108

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> and Moselle, supposed to be one of the 50 forts erected by Drusus on the Rhine, in Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>: Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COBLENZ">Coblenz</a>, a town of Triers. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 15. N. Lat. 50. 30.

CONFORMATION

Pages 108-108

in Medicine, that make and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body which is peculiar to every individual. Hence a mala conformatio signifies some fault in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a>; whereby a person comes into the world crooked, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with some of the viscera or cavities unduly framed or proportioned. Many are subject to incurable asthmas, from a too small capacity of the thorax, and the like vicious conformations.

CONFORMITY

Pages 108-108

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, is the congruency <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> relation of agreement between one thing and another; as between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> and the thing measured, the object and the understanding, the thing and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> thereof, &c.

CONFRONTATION

Pages 108-108

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of bringing two persons in presence of each other, to discover the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of some fact which they relate differently. The word is chiefly used in criminal matters, where the witnesses are confronted with the accused, the accused with one another, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the witnesses with one another.

CONFUCIUS

Pages 108-110
or Cong-fu-tse, the most eminent, and most justly venerated of all the philosophers of China, a descendant of the imperial family of the dynasty of Chang, was born in the kingdom of Lu, now called the province of Chang-tong, about 550 years before the commencement of the Christian era. This makes him to have been contemporary with Pythagoras and Solon, and prior to the days of Socrates. He gave striking proofs of very uncommon talents at an early period of life, which were cultivated and improved with great assiduity under the tuition of the ablest masters. Scarcely had he attained to the years of maturity, when he evinced himself acquainted with all the literature of that period, professing, in particular, a comprehensive knowledge of the canonical and classical books, ascribed to the legislators Yao and Chun, which the Chinese emphatically denominate the five volumes, Confucius, as containing the essence of all their science and morality. Nature had bestowed upon him a most amiable temper, and his moral deportment was altogether unexceptionable. He acquired a distinguished reputation for humility, sincerity, the government of his appetites, a disinterested heart, and a sovereign contempt of wealth. These rare qualities pointed him out as a proper person to fill offices of importance and trust in the government of his country, which he did with honour to himself and advantage to the empire. These public stations afforded him excellent opportunities of estimating with accuracy the true state of morals among his countrymen, which at this time were dilute and vicious in the extreme. He conceived the godlike idea of attempting a general reformation both in morals and in politics, and his efforts for some time were attended with such remarkable effects, that he inspired his countrymen with a just veneration for his excellent character, and gratitude for his exertions, being raised to a station of the last importance in the kingdom of Lu. Here his counsels and advice were productive of the most beneficial consequences, in establishing good order, the due exercise of justice, concord, and decorum through the whole kingdom. As it thus very naturally became an object of admiration, so, likewise, neighbouring princes beheld with envy, its growing happiness and prosperity; to destroy which, they contrived a fatal and effectual expedient. The king of Ts'ing being apprehensive, that if the king of Lu continued to be directed by the wisdom and sound policy of Confucius, he would soon become by far too powerful, sent him and his nobility a present of the most beautiful young women, trained up from their infancy in all the arts of seduction, who were but too successful in plunging the whole court into voluptuousness and dissipation. This demolished in a short time, the whole of that beautiful fabric which had been erected by Confucius. Finding it a hopeless attempt to stem the universal torrent of corruption and depravity, he resolved to exert his talents in some distant kingdom, in the philanthropic cause of moral reformation, in hopes of better success. But he had the mortification to discover, that vice was everywhere triumphant, while virtue, that darling of his soul, was compelled to hide her head. This induced him to adopt the more humble, although not the less interesting employment, of a teacher of youth, in which he made great and rapid progress. About 600 of his scholars were sent into different parts of the empire, to carry on his favourite work of moral reformation. Among his disciples, 72 were remarkably distinguished above the rest for their mental acquisitions, and 10 others were deemed superior, even to these, as having a thorough comprehension of their master's whole system. These were divided by him into four classes; the first being destined to the study of the moral virtues; the second to the arts of logic and public speaking; the third class studied jurisprudence and the duties of the civil magistrate; and public speaking, or the delivery of popular discourses on moral topics. Indefatigable, however, as his labours were, the task was too mighty to be accomplished by human exertions. During his last illness, he declared to his pupils, that the grief of his mind occasioned by the profligacy of human nature was become insupportable; and in a melancholy voice, he exclaimed "Immensely mountain, how art thou fallen? The grand machine is demolished, and the wise and the virtuous are no more. The kings will not follow my maxims; I am no longer useful on earth; it is, therefore, time that I should quit it." On uttering these words he was seized with lethargy, which brought him to the grave. He finished his honourable career in the 72nd year of his age, in his native kingdom, to which he had returned in company with his disciples. It is frequently the fate of illustrious characters, never to be properly valued till they are cut off by death, which was the case with Confucius. The whole empire of China bewailed the loss of him, and erected innumerable edifices to perpetuate his memory, adorned with such honourable inscriptions as the following: "To the great master;" "To the chief doctor;" "To the saint;" "To the wife king of literature;" "To the instructor of emperors and kings." All his descendants, even to the present day, enjoy the honourable title and office of mandarins, and are exempted from the payment of taxes to the emperor, as well as the princes of the blood. The man who applies for the title of doctor, must previously have made a present to a mandarin descended in a direct line from Confucius. The writings of this great man are esteemed by the Chinese as of the highest authority, next to the five volumes, to which he modestly acknowledges himself to have been much indebted. His works are, 1. The Tseu-bio; "The Grand Science, or School of Adults," chiefly intended for the information of princes and magistrates, recommending the duties of self-government, and uniform obedience to the laws of right reason. 2. The Chong-yong, or "Immutable Medium," in which he shows its importance in the government of the passions by a variety of examples, and points out the method of arriving at perfection in virtue. 3. Lung-yun, or moral and sententious discourses, which exhibit a lively picture of the opinions, conduct, and maxims of Confucius and his followers. 4. Meng-tse, the book of Mencius, which derived its name from one of that great philosopher's disciples. These are all deservedly esteemed by the Chinese, being held next in importance to the five volumes. 5. The Hsiau-king, or dissertation on the duty and respect which children owe their parents; and, 6. The Syau-bio, or science for children, being a judicious collection of moral sentences from ancient and modern writers. If a fair and impartial estimate of the religion of Confucius be made, it cannot be viewed in any other light than as uncorrupted deism, although he has sometimes been accused of befriending and secretly propagating atheistical sentiments; but such an accusation is as cruel as it is unjust, since the purity of his moral precepts, and the acknowledged rectitude of his whole deportment, are utterly incompatible with such a supposition. He considered the Tyen or Deity as the purest and most perfect essence, principle, and source of all things in the boundless universe, who is absolutely independent, omnipotent, the governor and guardian of every thing; possessed of infinite wisdom which nothing can deceive; holy, without partiality, of unlimited goodness and justice. We are at a loss to form any adequate opinion of his sentiments relative to the soul of man and the doctrine of futurity, having no well authenticated data, on which to proceed. His morality is in many instances superior to that of Greece and Rome, Confusion, and yields to none upon earth, except to that of divine revelation. The religion of Confucius, notwithstanding the estimation in which he is held, is adopted as a model by none of his countrymen, the literati excepted. Their prevailing system is a medley of pagan idolatry and the fabulous superstition of the Indians, introduced into China by Fo, in the first century of the Christian era.

CONFUSION

Pages 110-110

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is opposed to order, in a perturbation whereof confusion consists: e.g., when things <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> do not precede, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> do not follow, &c. In a logical sense, confusion is opposed to distinctness or perspicuity: and may happen even in words, as when misconceived or misapplied; or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, as when the idea of any thing presents something along with it, which does not properly belong to that thing. See IDEA and NOTION. In a physical sense, confusion is a sort of union or mixture by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTIGUITY">contiguity</a>. Such is that between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> of contrary nature, as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, &c. CONFUSION in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a method of suspending and extinguishing obligations. For the illustration of this see LAW <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>. CONFUSION of Tongues, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of mankind, is a memorable event, which happened in the one hundred and first year according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, and the four hundred and first year by the Samaritan, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, at the overthrow of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a>; and which was providentially brought about in order to facilitate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of mankind and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Until this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> there had been one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, which formed a bond of union that prevented the separation of mankind into distinct nations; and some have supposed, that the tower of Babel was erected as a kind of fortress, by which the people intended to defend themselves against that separation which <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a> had projected. There has been a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> as to the nature of this confusion, and the manner in which it was effected. Some learned men, prepossessed with the notion that all the different idioms now in the world did at first arise from one original language to which they may be reduced, and that the variety among them is no more than must naturally have happened in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> course of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by the mere separation of the builders of Babel, have maintained, that there were no new languages formed at the confusion; but, that this event was accomplished by creating a misunderstanding and variance among the builders without any immediate influence on their language. But this opinion, advanced by Le Clerc, &c. seems to be directly contrary to the obvious meaning of the word בָּבֶל, בָּבֶל, "lip," used by the sacred historian.—Others have imagined, that this was brought about by a temporary confusion of their speech, or rather of their apprehensions, causing them, whilst they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> together and spoke the same language, to understand the words differently. Scaliger is of this opinion. Others, again, account for this event by the privation of all language, and by supposing that mankind were under a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of associating together, and of imposing new names on things by common consent. Another opinion affirms the confusion to such an indistinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of the original language which they spoke before, as made them speak it very differently; so that Confusion, by the various inflexions, terminations, and pronunciations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> dialects, they could no more understand one another, than they who understand Latin can understand those who speak French, Italian, or Spanish, though all these languages arise out of it. This opinion is adopted by Calaubon, and by Bishop Patrick in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> in loc. and is certainly much more probable than either of the former. And Mr Shuckford maintains, that the confusion arose from small beginnings, by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of new words in either of the three families of Shem, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAM">Ham</a>, and Japhet, which might contribute to separate them from one another: and that in each family new differences of speech might gradually arise, so that each of these families went on to divide and subdivide among themselves. Others, again, as Mr Jof Mede and Dr Wotton, &c., not satisfied with either of the foregoing methods of accounting for the diversity of languages among mankind, have recourse to an extraordinary interposition of divine power, by which new languages were framed and communicated to different families by a supernatural infusion or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>; which languages have been the roots and originals from which the several dialects that are, or have been, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be spoken, as long as this earth shall last, have arisen, and to which they may with ease be reduced. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of languages thus introduced, many opinions have been adopted. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> there were no more than there were nations or heads of nations, then the number would be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> for Japhet, four for Ham, and five for Shem; but if there were as many as there were families, which is the more probable opinion, their number cannot be certainly assigned. However, the Hebrews fancy they were 70, because the descendants from the sons of Noah, enumerated <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a> x., were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> so many. Allowing, then, the languages of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> families to have been fundamentally different from each other, the sub languages and dialects within each branch would probably have had a mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a>, greater or less as they settled nearer or farther from each other. But whichever of these hypotheses is adopted, the primary object of the confusion at Babel was the separation and dispersion of mankind. Dr Bryant, in the third volume of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">Analysis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, has advanced a singular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, both with respect to the confusion of tongues and the dispersion. He supposes that the confusion of language was local and partial, and limited to Babel only. By וַיִּבְאֹר, Gen. xi. 1. and 8. which our translators render the whole earth, he understands every region; and by the same words in ver. 9, the whole region or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. This confusion was occasioned, as he supposes, by a labial failure; so that the people could not articulate. Thus their speech was confounded, but not altered; for as soon as they separated, they recovered their true tenor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>, and the language of the earth continued for some ages nearly the same. The interviews between the Hebrews and other nations, recorded in Scripture, were conducted without an interpreter; and he farther observes, that the various languages which subsist at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> retain sufficient relation to show, that they were once dialects from the same matrix, and that their variety was the effect of time. See DISPERSION.

CONFUTATION

Pages 110-111

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, &c., a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>, wherein the orator seconds his own arguments and strengthens his cause, by refelling and destroying the opposite arguments of the antagonist. This is done by denying what is apparently false, by detecting some flaw in the reasoning of the adverse party, by granting their argument, and showing its invalidity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> retorting it upon the adversary.

CONGE

Pages 111-111

in the French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a license, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> permission, granted by a superior to an inferior, which gives him a dispensation from some duty to which he was before obliged. A woman cannot oblige herself without the conge or license of her husband; a monk cannot go out of his convent, without the conge of his superiors. Conges d'elire, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> policy, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s permission <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of a vacancy, to choose a bishop; or to an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, or priory, of his own foundation, to choose their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a>. The king of England, as sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of all archbishoprics, bishoprics, and other ecclesiastical benefices, had of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> time free appointment of all ecclesiastical dignities, whensoever they chanced to be void; investing them first per baculum et annulum, and afterwards by his letters patent; and in course of time he made the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> over to others, under certain forms and limitations, as that they should at every vacation, before they choose, demand the king's conge d'elire, and after the election crave his royal assent, &c. Conge, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a mould in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> round, or a cavetto, which serves to separate two members from one another; such as that which joins the shaft of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> to the cincture, called also apophyse. Conges are also rings or ferrets formerly used in the extremities of wooden pillars, to keep them from splitting, afterwards imitated in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>.

CONGELATION

Pages 111-114

signifies the passing of any body from a fluid to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> state: so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is thus applicable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> when they resume their solid form after being heated, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> when it freezes, to wax, spermaceti, &c., when they become solid after having been rendered fluid by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; and in general to all processes, where the whole substance of the fluid is converted into a solid: but it differs from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a>; because in the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, though the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> passes from a fluid to a solid state, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of liquid is always left, so that the term congelation is never applied in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. The process of congelation in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> depends upon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least is accompanied with, the emission of heat, as has been evinced by experiments made not only on water, but on spermaceti, wax, &c., for in all of these, though the thermometer immersed in them while fluid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to descend gradually till a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, yet it was as constantly observed to remain <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>, or even to ascend while the congelation went on. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>. It is not known whether all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> are naturally capable of congelation or not; though we are certain that there are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> differences among them in this respect. The most difficult of all those of which the congelation has been actually attained is quicksilver. This was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> thought capable of resisting any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> whatever; and it is only within a few years that its congelation by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> means was known, and still more lately that some climates were found to be so severe as to congeal this fluid by the cold of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. The congelation of quicksilver was first ascertained by M. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Braun, professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>. He had been employed in making thermometrical experiments, not with a view to make the discovery he actually did, but to see how many degrees of cold he could produce. An excellent opportunity for this occurred on the 14th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1759, when the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> stood naturally at —34°, which is now known to be only five or six degrees above its point of congelation. M. Braun, having determined to avail himself of this great degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> cold, prepared a freezing mixture of nitric acid and pounded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, by means of which his thermometer was reduced to —69°. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> of the quicksilver had now really congealed; yet so far was M. Braun from entertaining any suspicion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, that he had almost desisted from further attempts, being satisfied with having so far exceeded all the philosophers who went before him. Animated, however, by the hopes of producing a still greater degree of cold, he renewed the experiment; but having expended all his pounded ice, he was obliged to substitute snow in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. With this fresh mixture the mercury sunk to —100°, 240°, and 352°. He then supposed that the thermometer was broken; but on taking it out to observe whether it was so or not, he found the quicksilver fixed, and continuing so for 12 minutes. On repeating the same experiment with another thermometer which had been graduated no lower than —120°, all the mercury sunk into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, and became solid as before, not beginning to reascend till after a still longer <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Hence the professor concluded that the quicksilver was really frozen, and prepared for making a decisive experiment. This was accomplished on the 25th of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> of the thermometer broken as soon as the metal was congealed. The mercury was now converted into a solid and shining metallic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, which extended under the strokes of a pebble, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> rather inferior to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and yielding a dull <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> like that metal. Professor Æpinus made similar experiments at the same time, employing both thermometers and tubes of a larger bore: in which last he remarked, that the quicksilver fell feebly on being frozen, affuming a concave surface, and likewise that the congealed pieces sunk in fluid mercury. The fact being thus established, and fluidity no longer to be considered as an essential <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of quicksilver, M. Braun communicated an account of his experiments to the Peterburg Academy, on the 6th of September 1760; of which a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> extract was inserted in the Philosophical Transactions, vol. iii., p. 156. Five years afterwards he published another treatise on the same subject, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Supplement to his former dissertation. In these he declared, that, since his former publication, he had never suffered any winter to elapse without repeating the experiment of congealing quicksilver, and never failed of success when the natural cold was of a sufficient strength for the purpose. This degree of natural cold he supposes to be —10° of Fahrenheit, though some commencement The commencement of the congelation might be perceived when the temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> was as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as +2°. The results of all his experiments were, that with the above-mentioned frigorific mixtures, and once with rectified spirits and snow, when the natural cold was at 28°, he congealed the quicksilver, and discovered that it is a real metal which melts with a very small degree of heat. Not perceiving, however, the necessary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> in freezing, he, in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, as well as in the former, confounded its point of congelation with that of its greatest contraction in freezing, and thus marked the former a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> too low; though the point of congelation was very uncertain according to him, various difficulties having occurred to his attempts of finding the greatest point of contraction while freezing. The experiments of M. Braun were not repeated by any person till the year 1774, when Mr. John Frederic Blumenbach, then a student of physic at Göttingen, performed them to more advantage than it appears M. Braun had ever done. He was encouraged to make the attempt by the excessive cold of the winter that year. "I put (says he), at five in the evening of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 11th, three drachms of quicksilver into a small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-glass, and covered it with a mixture of snow and Egyptian sal-ammoniac. This mixture was put loose into the glass, so that the quicksilver lay perfectly free, being only covered with it as by pieces of ice; the whole, together with the glass, weighed somewhat above an ounce. It was hung out at a window in such a position as to expose it freely to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west; and two drachms more of sal-ammoniac mixed with the snow on which it stood. The snow and sal-ammoniac, in the open air, soon froze into a mass like ice; no sensible change, however, appeared in the quicksilver that evening; but at one in the morning it was found frozen solid. It had divided into two large and four smaller pieces: one of the former was hemispherical, the other cylindrical, each seemingly rather above a drachm in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; the four small bits might amount to half a scruple. They were all with their flat side frozen hard to the glass, and nowhere immediately touched by the mixture; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> was a dull <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> with a bluish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, like <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, very different from the natural appearance of quicksilver. Next morning, about eleven o'clock, I found that the larger hemisphere began to melt, perhaps because it was most exposed to the air, and not so near as the others to the sal-ammoniac mixture which lay beneath. In this state it resembled an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMALGAM">amalgam</a>, sinking to that side on which the glass was inclined; but without quitting the surface of the glass, to which it was yet firmly congealed: the five other pieces had not yet undergone any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>, but remained frozen hard. Toward eight o'clock the cylindrical piece began to soften in the same manner, and the other four soon followed. About eight they fell from the surface of the glass, and divided into many fluid shining globules, which were soon lost in the interstices of the frozen mixture, and reunited in part at the bottom, being now exactly like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> quicksilver." At the time this experiment was made, the thermometer stood at —10° in the open air. The circumstances attending this experiment are still unaccountable; for, in the first place, the natural cold was scarcely sufficient, along with that of the artificial mixture, which produces 32° more, to have congealed the quicksilver; which yet appears to have been very effectually done by the length of time it continued solid. 2. It is not easy to account for the length of time required for congealing the quicksilver in this experiment, since other frigorific mixtures begin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> almost immediately; and, 3. There was not at last even the appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, which consists in a solution of the snow, and not in its freezing into a mass. "The whole experiment (says Dr. Blagden) remains involved in such obscurity, that some persons have supposed the quicksilver itself was not frozen, but only covered over with ice; to which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, however, there are great objections. It is worthy of remark, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOTTINGEN">Gottingen</a>, though situated in the same latitude as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and enjoying a temperate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> in general, becomes subject at times to a great severity of cold. This of 11th of January 1774 is one instance: I find others there where the thermometer sunk to —12°, —16°, or —19°; and at Cattlenburg, a small town about two German miles distant, to —30°. By watching such extraordinary occasions, experiments on the freezing of quicksilver might easily be performed in many places, where the possibility of them is at present little suspected. The cold observed at Glasgow in 1780 would have been fully sufficient for that purpose." In consequence of the publication of M. Braun's Experiments, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> desired their late Secretary Dr Maty to make the necessary application to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, in order to repeat the experiment in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Mr. Hutchins, who was then at London, and going out with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> as governor of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a> fort, offered to undertake the experiments, and executed them very completely, freezing quicksilver twice in the months of January and February 1775. The account of his success was read before the Royal Society at the commencement of the severest winter that had been known for many years in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and at this time the experiment was repeated by two gentlemen of different countries. One was Dr Lambert Bicker, secretary to the Batavian society at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>; who, on the 28th of January 1776, at eight in the morning, made an experiment to try how low he could bring the thermometer by artificial cold, the temperature of the atmosphere being then +20°. He could not, however, bring it lower than —94°, at which point it stood immovable; and on breaking the thermometer, part of the quicksilver was found to have lost its fluidity, and was thickened to the consistence of an amalgam. It fell out of the tube in little bits, which bore to be flattened by pressure, without running into globules like the inner fluid part. The experiment was repeated next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, when the thermometer stood at +8°, but the mercury would not then defend below —80°; and as the thermometer was not broken, it could not be known whether the mercury had congealed or not. All that could be inferred from these experiments therefore was, that the congealing point of mercury was not below —94° of Fahrenheit's thermometer. The other who attempted the congelation of this fluid was the late Dr. Anthony Fothergill; but it could not be determined whether... whether he succeeded or not. An account of his experiment is inserted in the Philosophical Transactions, vol. lxvi. No other attempts were made to congeal quicksilver until the year 1781, when Mr. Hutchins resumed the subject with great success, informing that from his experiments the freezing point of mercury is now almost as well settled as that of water. Preceding philosophers, indeed, had not been altogether inattentive to this subject. Professor Braun himself had taken great pains to investigate it; but for want of paying the requisite <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the contraction of the fluid mercury by cold and that of the congealing metal by freezing, he could determine nothing certain concerning it. Others declared it as their opinion, that nothing certain could be determined by merely freezing mercury in a thermometer filled with that fluid. Mr. Cavendish and Dr. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> first suggested the proper method of obviating the difficulties on this subject. Dr. Black, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Mr. Hutchins, dated October 5, 1779, gave the following directions for making the experiment with accuracy: "Provide a few wide and short tubes of thin glass, sealed at one end and open at the other; the wideness of these tubes may be from half to three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an inch, and the length of them about three inches. Put an inch or an inch and a half depth of mercury into one of these tubes, and plunging the bulb of the thermometer into the mercury, set the tube with the mercury and the thermometer in it into a freezing mixture, which should be made for this purpose in a common tumbler or water glass: and, N.B., in making a freezing mixture with snow and nitric acid, the quantity of the acid should never be so great as to dissolve the whole of the snow, and only enough to reduce it to the consistence of panada. When the mercury in the wide tube is thus set in the freezing mixture, it must be stirred gently and frequently with the bulb of the thermometer; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the cold be sufficiently strong, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> congeal by becoming thick like an amalgam. As soon as this is observed, the thermometer should be examined without lifting it out of the congealing mercury; and I have no doubt that in every experiment thus made, with the same mercury, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> will always point to the same degree, provided it has been made and graduated with accuracy." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> recommended by Mr. Cavendish, and which Mr. Hutchins made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, consisted of a small mercurial thermometer, the bulb of which reaches about 2½ inches below the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, and was inclosed in a glass <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> swelled at the bottom into a ball, which when used was filled with quicksilver, so that the bulb of the thermometer was entirely covered with it. If this cylinder be immersed in a freezing mixture till great part of the quicksilver in it is frozen, it is evident that the degree shown at that time by the inclosed thermometer is the precise point at which mercury freezes; for as in this case the ball of the thermometer must be surrounded for some time with quicksilver, part of which is actually frozen, it seems impossible that the thermometer should be sensibly above that point; and while any of the quicksilver in the cylinder remains fluid, it is impossible that it should sink sensibly below it. The diameter of the bulb of the thermometer was rather less than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch, that of the swelled part of the cylinder two-thirds; and as it was easy to keep the thermometer constantly in the middle of the cylinder, the thickness of quicksilver between it and the glass could never be much less than the fifth part of an inch. The bulb of the thermometer was purposely made as small as it conveniently could, in order to leave a sufficient space between it and the cylinder, without making the swelled part larger than necessary, which would have caused more difficulty in freezing the mercury in it. The first experiment with this apparatus was made on the 15th of December 1781; the thermometer had stood the evening before at —18°. A bottle of spiritus nitri fortis was put on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-top, in order to cool it to the same temperature. The thermometers made use of had been hung up in the open air for three weeks, to compare their scales. On the morning of the experiment they were about 23° below zero.—In making it, the thermometer of the apparatus was suspended in the bulb of the cylinder by means of some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> worsted wound about the upper part of its stem, to a sufficient thickness to fill the upper part of its orifice; and a space of near half an inch was left empty between the quicksilver and worsted. The apparatus was placed in the open air, on the top of the fort, with only a few deer skins sewed together for a shelter; the snow lay 18 inches deep on the works, and the apparatus was sunk into the snow, in order to bring it sooner to the temperature of the air. The instruments were afterwards placed in three fresh freezing mixtures, in hopes of being able by their means to produce a greater degree of cold, but without effect; nor was any greater cold produced by adding more nitric acid. The mercury, however, was very completely frozen, that in the thermometer descending to —448°. On plunging the mercury into the freezing mixture, it descended in less than one minute to 40° below zero. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> experiment was made the day following; and the same quantity of quicksilver employed that had been used in the former. As too small a quantity of the freezing mixture, however, had been originally made, it was necessary to add more during the operation of congelation; by which means the spirit of nitre, in pouring it upon the snow, sometimes touched the bulb of the thermometer, and instantly raised it much higher; nor did the mercury ever descend below 206°, which was not half as far as it had done the day before, though the temperature of the atmosphere had been this day at —34° before the commencement of the operation. That in the apparatus, however, sunk to —95°. The apparatus was taken out of the mixture for half a minute, in order to examine whether the mercury was perfectly congealed or not, and during that time it showed no sign of liquefaction. The third experiment was made the same day, and with the freezing mixture used in the last. By it the point of congelation was determined to be not below 40°. The fourth experiment was made January 7th 1782; and and in it he observed, that the mercury in the apparatus thermometer, after standing at 42 and 41½ for a considerable time, fell to 77, not gradually, but at once as a weight falls. In the fifth experiment the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> was excessively severe, so that it ought to have frozen the metal in the open air; but this did not then happen. At the time of making the fifth experiment, the quicksilver in the open air stood at 44 below 0; and Mr Hutchins resolved to make use of this opportunity to observe how far it was possible to make it descend by means of cold, observing the degrees at the same time with a spirit thermometer made by Nairne and Blount, with which he had been furnished by the Royal Society in 1773. In this, however, he did not succeed; for the mercury never fell below 438, nor the standard 48. It stood at 27½ at the beginning of the experiment. The reason of this was supposed to be, that the atmosphere was too cold for making this kind of experiment, by reason of its freezing the thread of quicksilver in the stem of the thermometer, so that it became incapable of contraction along with that in the bulb. In other experiments, though the metal in the bulb became solid, yet that in the stem always remained fluid; and thus was enabled to subside to a great degree by the diminution of bulk in the solid mercury. That this was really the case, appeared from the quicksilver falling at once from —86 to —434, when the cold of the freezing mixture diminished, and the temperature of the air becoming about the same time somewhat milder, melted the congealed part in the stem, which thus had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to descend to that point. In this experiment, also, the mixtures were made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> quantity to those of the former; these being only in common tumblers, but the mixtures for this experiment in pint-basons. It was observed that they liquefied faster than in other experiments. He had usually made them of the consistence of pap; but though he added snow at different times, it had very little effect in augmenting the cold, but rather decreased it. The congealed pieces of the metal fell to the bottom, as might naturally have been expected from its great contraction in becoming solid. From this experiment Mr Hutchins concluded, that the nearer the temperature of the atmosphere approached to the congealing point of mercury (so that a great degree of cold might be communicated to the bulb of a thermometer, and yet the quicksilver in the tube remain fluid), he might make the experiment of ascertaining the greatest contraction of mercury to more advantage. With this view, he made another experiment, when the temperature of some of his thermometers stood as low as —37°; and after an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>'s attendance, he perceived the mercury had fallen to 1367; but the thermometer unluckily was broken, and its bulb thrown away with the mixture. Professor Braun had likewise observed, that his thermometers were always broken when the mercury descended below 600. The eighth experiment was made with a view to try whether quicksilver would congeal when in contact with the freezing mixture. For this purpose, he did not use the apparatus provided for other experiments, but filled a galipot made of flint <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> (as being thinner than the common fort), containing about an ounce, half full of quicksilver, into which he inserted a mercurial thermometer, employing another as an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a>. Thus he hoped to determine exactly when the quicksilver was congealed, as he had free access to it at all times, which was not the case when it was inclosed in the cylindrical glass, the worsted wound round the tube of the thermometer to exclude the air being equally effectual in excluding any instrument from being introduced to touch the quicksilver. He then made a kind of skewer, with a flat blunt point, of dried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>-wood, on account of its lightness, which he found would remain in the gelatinous freezing mixture at any depth he chose; but, when inserted into the quicksilver, the great difference betwixt the specific gravity of it and that ponderous fluid, made it always rebound upward; and by the degree of resistance, he could always know whether it proceeded from fluid or solid metal. At this time, however, the experiment did not succeed; but, at another <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, having employed about ¼ lbs of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of metal, and let it remain a considerable time immersed in the same mixture which had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> now been supposed to fail, he found that part of it was congealed; and, on pouring off the fluid part, no less than two-thirds remained fixed at the bottom.

CONGERIES

Pages 121-121

a Latin word, sometimes used in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> for a collection <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> heap of several particles of bodies united into one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> or aggregate.

CONGESTION

Pages 121-121

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> collection of humours, crowded together and hardened in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body, and there forming a preternatural tumor. Congestion is effected by little and little; in which it differs from defluxion, which is more sudden.

CONGIARIUM

Pages 121-126

CONGIARIUM, CONGIARY, among medalists, a gift <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> donative represented on a medal. The word comes from the Latin *congius*; because the first presents made to the people of Rome consisted in wine and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which were measured out to them in *congi*. The congiary was properly a present made by the emperors to the people of Rome. Those made to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were not called *congiaries* but *donatives*. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGEND">legend</a> on medals representing *congiaries*, i.e., *Congiarium* or *Liberalitas*. Tiberius gave a congiary of three hundred pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to each citizen; Caligula twice gave three hundred sesterces a head; Nero, whose congiaries are the first that we find represented on medals, gave four hundred. *CONGIUS*, a liquid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, containing the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHORA">amphora</a>, or the fourth of the urna, or six sextarii. The *congius* in English measure contains 2,070.676 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> inches; that is, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> pints, 4,942 fluid inches. *CONLOBATE GLAND*. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. *CONGLOMERATE GLAND*. See Anatomy Index. *CONGLOMERATE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">Flowers</a>*, those growing on a branching foot-stalk, to which they are irregularly but closely connected. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of inflorescence, as Linnaeus terms it, is opposed to that in which the flowers are irregularly and loosely supported on their foot-stalks, hence termed a *diffuse panicle* *. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is exemplified in several of the grasses, particularly in some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the *poa*, *festuca gralis*, and *agrostis*. *CONGLUTINATION*, the glueing or fastening any two bodies together by the introduction of a third, whose parts are unctuous and tenacious, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>. See *Glue*. *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>*, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the river Zair, or Zarib, which divides it from Loanga; on the south by the river Danda, which separates it from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a>; on the east by the kingdoms of Fungono and Metamba, and the burnt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, those of crystal or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> petre and silver, or (according to Anthony Cavazzi, a traveller into those parts) by the mountains of Coanza, Berbela, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mountains of Chilandria or Aquilonia; and on the west by that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a> called the *Ethiopic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>*, or the *sea of Congo*. According to these limits, Congo Proper extends about three degrees from north to south; lying between the line and 18° S. Lat.; but widens in its breadth inland, by the course of the river Zair, which runs winding above two degrees more to the north. Its length from east to west is very uncertain, as no observations have been taken of the exact situation of those mountains which bound it. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this kingdom affords but few interesting particulars. Before its discovery by the Portuguese, the history is altogether uncertain and fabulous, as the inhabitants were totally unacquainted with letters and learning. So little were they acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, that it is said they did not even distinguish between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night; much less could they compute their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by moons or years; and therefore could remember past transactions only by saying they happened in such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s reign. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was discovered by the Portuguese in 1484. The discoverer was named Diego Cam, an Congo expert and bold soldier. He was very well received by the natives, and sent some of his men with presents to the king; but they being detained by unexpected accidents beyond the promised time of their return, Cam was obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> away without them, the Portugese took with him four young Congolese as hostages for the safety of his countrymen. These he taught the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, in which they made such progress that King John was highly pleased, and sent them back next year to Congo with rich presents; charging them to exhort their monarch, in his name, to become a convert to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and to permit it to be propagated through his dominions. A firm <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> was concluded between the two monarchs, which continues to this day, though not without some interruptions, to which the Portuguese themselves have given occasion more than the natives. Any particular account we have of this kingdom, rests almost entirely on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of Anthony Cavazzi, the traveller above mentioned. He was a capu-Congo chin friar, a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, and was sent missionary into those parts de propaganda fide, in the year 1654, and arrived at Congo the same year. During his stay there, his zeal to make converts made him travel through all these different kingdoms; and the credit he gained, as well as the great employments he was intrusted with, gave him an opportunity of informing himself of every thing relating to them with great exactness. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and situation, however, he could not possibly ascertain, for want of instruments; nor hath this defect been since supplied. According to him the dominions of Congo extended a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> further eastward and southwards before the introduction of Christianity than afterwards; a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the states that were under the Congolese monarchs, either as subjects, or tributary, having withdrawn their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> out of dislike to them on that account. Not content with opposing the officers and troops that came annually to raise the tribute imposed by the king, they made such frequent and powerful incursions into his dominions, that they obliged him to draw his forces nearer the centre of Congo to prevent an invasion; by which means the kingdom, from an extent of 600 leagues, was reduced to less than one half. Congo Proper being situated within the torrid zone, is liable to excessive heats; as it lies on the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> side of the equinoctial, the seasons are of course opposite to ours. They reckon only two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> seasons, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and winter; the former begins in October, and continues till February or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>; during which time the sun's rays dart with such force, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> appears to an European to be in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>. The excessive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, however, is mitigated by the equal length of the days and nights, as well as by the winds, breezes, rains, and dews. The winter takes up the other part of the year; and is said by the natives to be proportionally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, though to an European it would appear hot. These two seasons they divide into six lesser ones, viz. Maflanza, Neasu, Ecundi, Quitombo, Quibilo, and Qitibangala. Maflanza begins with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of October, which is the beginning of their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. The rains begin to fall at that time, and continue during the next two and sometimes three months. When this happens, the low lands are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> overflowed with extraordinary floods, and all their corn carried off. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of this kind is commonly followed by a famine; for the lazy inhabitants take no care to lay up any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, although such misfortunes happen very frequently. This first season they reckon commences at the time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> begin to spring. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> season, Neafu, begins about the end of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, when the produce of their lands has arrived at its full height, and wants but a few days of being ripened for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. This first crop is no sooner gathered in, than they sow their fields afresh, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> commonly yielding them two harvests. The third and fourth seasons, called Ecundi and Quitombo, are frequently blended together towards the middle of March, when the more gentle rains begin to fall, and continue till the month of May. These two seasons are distinguished by the greater or lesser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> that falls during that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>. During the rest of the time, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is either very clear, hot, and dry; or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> being overcharged with electric <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, burst out into the most terrible thunders and lightnings, without yielding the least drop of rain, though they seem loaded with it. The two last, viz. the Quibiso and Quibangala, make up their short winter, which consists not in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a> or snow, but in dry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLASTING">blasting</a> winds, which strip the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> of all its verdure, till the next Massanze begins to restore them to their former bloom. They now divide their year into twelve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> months, and begin it in September. They have also weeks consisting of four days only, the last of which is their Sabbath; and on it they religiously abstain from every kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. This practice, the compilers of the Universal History conjecture to have arisen from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> laziness for which this people, and indeed all the African nations, are so remarkable. To this shameful indolence also is to be ascribed the little produce they reap from their lands, while the Portuguese settled among them, who are at more pains in the cultivation of theirs, enjoy all manner of plenty. The natives, however, had rather run the risk of the most terrible famines, than be at the tenth part of the labour they see the Portuguese take. They seem to think it below them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> any other exercises than those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>, hunting, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a>, &c.; the rest of their time they spend in smoking, and downright idleness, committing the laborious part of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> affairs to their slaves, or, in want of them, to their wives. Nothing is more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> than to see these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> creatures toiling in the fields and woods with a child tied to their backs, and fainting under their excessive labour and heavy burdens, or (which is still worse) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> and thirst. What is yet more surprisingly shameful is, that though they have plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals which they might easily make use of for cultivating their grounds, and for other laborious services, and though they see the Portuguese do it every day to great advantage; yet they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> rather see their tender females sink under their toil and labour, than be at the trouble of breeding up any of these useful creatures to their affluence. The ground produces variety of grain, but no corn or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> except what is cultivated by the Portuguese. Their maize, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> wheat, grows very strong, and is well laden. This being well ground, they make vegetables into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, or boil with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> into a kind of pap. Of produced in this they have four kinds; one of which, resembling Congo, what we call French wheat, is produced in plenty, and makes some amends for the want of industry in the people. They cultivate also a variety of the peas and bean kind: but what they chiefly live upon, as most suitable to their lazy disposition, is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, like our filberts, which fall to the ground of themselves, and are to be found everywhere; every nut that falls to the ground producing a new shrub next year. They have scarcely any fruit-trees but what have been brought hither by the Portuguese. They have various sorts of palm-trees, useful both by their fruit, leaves, and their juice, which is easily converted into wine; also by affording a kind of oil with which they dress their victuals, though the Europeans use it only to burn in their lamps. They have also a vast number of plants and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, which it would be impossible to describe or enumerate. Wheat is the only thing that the ground will not produce. It pushes forth, indeed, the straw and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>; the former of which grows <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> enough we are told, to hide a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> on horseback, but the latter is empty, without one grain fit for use. Father Labat, however, who had lived a considerable time in some of the American <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, where he had observed the same thing, tells us, that he had the curiosity to examine those ears more carefully, and had found some few grains; and that, having sowed them afresh, they produced very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ears, full of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> heavy grain. Whence he conjectures, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the Portuguese had tried the same experiment in their African settlements, it might perhaps have been attended with the same success. In the low lands the grass grows so high, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, hazardous and thick, that it becomes one of the most dangerous travelling receptacles for wild beasts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, and other venomous insects: on this account travelling is exceedingly hazardous, as there are few beaten <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> in the whole country, and travellers are obliged to march over it through vast plains, in continual danger of being devoured or flung to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; to say nothing of the manifold diseases produced by the unwholesome dews with which the grass is covered during some part of the day. The only method of guarding against all these evils effectually, is by setting fire to the grass in the hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, when it is quite parched by the heat of the sun: but even this cannot be done without the greatest danger; because both the wild beasts and venomous reptiles, being roused out of their places of retirement, will fly furiously at those who happen to be in the way. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> there is no possibility of escaping, but by climbing up the highest trees, or defending one's self with fire-arms or other weapons. In such emergencies, the natives have a much better chance than the Europeans; the former being able to climb trees with surprising swiftness; while the latter must be assisted with rope-ladders, which they commonly cause their blacks to carry about with them, and to go up and fall to one of the branches. The flowers are here exceedingly beautiful and numerous. Almost every field and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> yields a multitude of nobler flowers. nobler prospect than the European gardens can boast of, notwithstanding the pains bestowed on their cultivation. The flowers are remarkable, not only for the prodigious variety of their colours, but the vast quantity of heads which grow upon one stalk. In the daytime, indeed, they seem to have lost their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> fragrance; that being in some measure exhaled by the heat of the sun; but this is amply compensated after its setting, and more especially a little before its rising, when their sweetness is again condensed, and revived by the coldness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> of the night, after which they exhale their various refreshing scents in a much higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> than ours. The lilies, which there grow naturally in the fields, valleys, and woods, excel those of our gardens, not only in their extreme whiteness, but much more in a delightful fragrance, without offending the head, as the European lilies do by their faintest sweetness. The tulips which there grow wild, though generally called Peric, have something to surprisingly charming in the variety and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of their colours, that they dazzle the eyes of an intense beholder: neither do their flowers grow singly as with us, but ten or twelve upon one stalk; and with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> advantage, that they diffuse a very reviving and agreeable sweetness, and continue much longer in their full bloom. Of the same nature are their tuberose, hyacinths, and other native flowers; which spring up in vast groups of 100 and 200 from one root, though somewhat smaller than ours; some of them finely variegated, and all of them yielding an agreeable smell. The roses, jessamines, and other exotics brought hither from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, come up likewise in great perfection, but require a constant supply of water, and diligent attendance, to prevent them from degenerating. The American jessamine, in particular, instead of single flowers, will grow up by dozens in a bunch; some of them of an exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and others of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the most vivid fire. A vast variety of animals of different kinds are found in the kingdom of Congo; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which is the elephant. This creature is mostly found in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bamba, which abounds with woods, pasture, and plenty of water; the elephants delighting much to bathe themselves during the heat of the day. They commonly go in troops of a hundred or more; and some of them are of such a monstrous size, that we are told the print of their hoof hath measured four, nay seven, spans in diameter.
