From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of their tails, and that of some other animals, the natives, especially the women, weave themselves collars, bracelets, girdles, &c. with variety of devices and figures, which denote their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and are in such esteem, that the hair of two elephants tails is sufficient to buy a slave. The reason of this is, that the natives have not the art of taming them, but are obliged to send some of the bravest and stoutest men to hunt them in the woods; which is not done without great labour and danger, they being here exceedingly fierce. The most common way of hunting them is by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> deep holes in the ground, the top of which they cover with branches and leaves, as is practised in most parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Lions, leopards, tigers, wolves, and other beasts of prey, abound here in great plenty, and do much damage. Here are also a vast variety of monkeys of all sizes and shapes. The zebra, well known for its extreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and swiftness, is also met with in this country. They have also a variety of buffaloes and wild asses; but the dante seems to be an animal peculiar to this kingdom. It is shaped and coloured much like an ox, though not so large. Its skin is commonly bought by the Portuguese, and sent into Germany to be tanned and made into targets, which are then called dantes. The natives make use of their raw hide dried to make their shields; which are so tough that no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> or dart can pierce them; and they are also large enough to cover the whole body. The creature is vastly swift; and when wounded, will follow the scent or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> with such fury, that the hunter is obliged to climb up a tree with all possible speed; and this retreat he always takes care to secure before he ventures to fire. The wounded beast finding its enemy out of its reach, stays for him at the foot of the tree, and will not stir from it; of which the hunter taking the advantage, dispatches it with repeated shots. The forests of Congo also swarm with wild dogs, who, like the wolves, prey upon the tame cattle, and are so fierce that they will attack armed men. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are exceeding keen and sharp; they never bark, but make a dreadful howling when famished or in pursuit of their prey. This country also abounds with all the different birds, kinds of birds that are to be found in other warm climates. One fort, which they call birds of mercy, is greatly esteemed, inasmuch that persons of the highest rank have from time immemorial taken the greatest delight in keeping them in cages and aviaries for the sake of their surprising <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, as the Congolese are superstitious to the last degree, there are several kinds of birds which they look upon as ominous, and are so terrified at the sight or hearing of them, that if they were going to enter upon every momentous an expedition, if they were met in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, or going to engage an enemy with ever so great an advantage, the flight or cry of such birds would throw them into a general panic, and disperse them in the utmost haste and confusion. The most dreadful of the ominous kind are the crows, ravens, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATS">bats</a>, and owls. The great owl is the most terrible of all, and to him they give the name of karian pemba, by which words they likewise denote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>. Fishes of different kinds abound on the coasts of Congo in great numbers; but the inland parts are infested with such numbers of serpents, scorpions, and other venomous insects, as are perhaps sufficient to overbalance every natural advantage we have yet mentioned. The most pernicious and dangerous kind are the ants; Ants very of which they reckon no less than six several species of dangerous different colours and sizes; all of them formidable on account of their prodigious numbers, and the mischief they do not only to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the earth, but to men and beasts; whom they will surround in the night time, and devour even to the very bone. It is a common practice, we are told, to condemn persons guilty of some atrocious crimes to be stripped naked, tied hand and foot, and thrown into a hole where these insects swarm; where they are sure to be devoured by them in less than 24 hours to the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. But criminals are not the only persons who are in danger from the the jaws of these little devouring insects. People may be attacked by them, as we have already hinted, in the night-time, and while they are sleeping in their beds. This obliges the natives to be careful where they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and to kindle a small fire, or at least to have a circle of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> hot embers round their beds. This caution is still more necessary in the country villages and hamlets, where persons are otherwise in danger of being attacked by millions of them in the dead of the night. In such a case the only expedient to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> one's self is to jump up as soon as one feels the bite, to bath them off with all possible speed, and then at once to set the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> on fire. The danger is still greater in travelling through the country, where a person is often obliged to take up his lodging on the bare ground; and may be overtaken during the heat of the day with such profound <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, as not to be awakened by these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> animals till they have made their way through the skin; and in such a case nothing will prevent their devouring a man alive, though there were ever so many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to assist him: in such incredible quantities do these creatures abound, notwithstanding the great numbers of monkeys who are continually ferreting the ants out of their retreats, and feed upon them with the utmost avidity. This can only be ascribed to the natural laziness and indolence of the inhabitants; which is such, that they not only neglect to rid their lands of them by proper cultivation, but will suffer their houses, nay, even their very churches, to be undermined by them. Another kind of these destructive <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> lie so thick upon the paths and highways, that a person cannot walk without treading upon, and having his legs and thighs almost devoured by them. A third sort of a white and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> colour, but very small, will gnaw their way through the hardest wood, penetrate into a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, and in a little while devour all the clothes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and every thing that is in it. A fourth sort, small and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, leave a most intolerable stench upon every thing they touch or crawl over, whether clothes or household stuff, which are not easily sweetened again; or if they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over victuals, they are entirely spoiled. A fifth sort harbour chiefly on the leaves and branches of trees; and if a man chance to climb up thither to save himself from a wild beast, he is so tormented by them, that nothing but the fear of the jaws of the one could make him endure the stings of the other. A sixth sort is of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> kind; and is probably one of the former kinds, that live wholly under ground, till nature furnishes them with wings. After this, they rise in such swarms as darken the air, and would make terrible havoc among all kinds of vegetables, did not the natives come out against them in whole companies, and by dint of flaps, and other flat weapons, knock them down by myriads, and then laying them in heaps, set fire to their wings, which half broil them for food. Amidst all this variety of pernicious insects, however, they have one species of a more friendly and profitable kind, viz. the industrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEE">bee</a>, which furnishes the inhabitants with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and wax in such plenty, that there is scarce a holm very low tree, cleft of a rock, or chop of the earth, in which their combs are not found in great quantities. With respect to the populousness of the kingdom of Congo, some authors, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> either from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> conjecture, or at best precarious inferences, have represented it as thinly peopled. The accounts of the missionaries and Portuguese, however, are directly opposite to these. They found the country for the most part covered with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, and these swarming with inhabitants; the cities well filled with people, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, which is said to contain above 50,000 souls. The provinces, though not equally populous, yet in the whole make up such an amount as plainly proves, that what is wanting in the one is amply made up by the other. We are told that the duchy of Bamba is still able to raise 200,000 fighting men, and was formerly in a condition to raise double that number; and that the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the king of Congo, in the year 1665, consisted of 900,000 fighting men, who were attended by an infinite number of women, children, and slaves. The numbers of the Congolese will appear the more credible, when we consider the extreme fecundity of their women, the hardiness with which they bring up their children, and the stoutness and healthiness of their men. In some villages, if the missionaries are to be credited, the number of children is so great, that a father will part with one or two, for any commodity he wants, or even for some trifling bauble he fancies; so that the number of slaves they fell abroad seldom amounts, communibus annis, to less than 15,000 or 16,000. There is scarcely a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> on earth that have a higher <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of themselves or their country than the Congolese, or that is more hardened against all conviction to the contrary, from reason, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, or the most impartial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with other countries in Europe or Asia. Indeed it is impossible they should think otherwise, when it is one of the fundamentals of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, that the rest of the world was the work of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, but that the kingdom of Congo, in its full and ancient extent, was the handywork of the Supreme <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">Architect</a>; and must of course have vast prerogatives and advantages over all others. When told of the magnificence of the European and Asiatic courts, their immense revenues, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of their palaces and edifices, the richness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of their subjects, the great progress they have made in the arts and sciences to which their country is wholly a stranger, they coolly answer, that all this comes vastly short of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and splendour of the kings and kingdom of Congo; and that there can be but one Congo in the world, to the happiness of whose monarch and people all the rest were created to contribute, and to whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> the sea and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> pay their constant tribute of zimbis (or shells, which are their current <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>); whilst other princes must condescend to enrich themselves by digging through rocks and mountains, to come at the excrements of the earth, so they flyle <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver which are in such request among other nations. Accordingly, they imagine, that the nations which come to traffic with them, are forced to that fervent employment by their poverty and the badness of their country, rather than induced to it by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> or avarice; whilst they themselves can indulge their natural indolence or sloth, though attended with the most pinching poverty, rather than disgrace the dignity of their blood by the least effort of industry, which, how laudable and beneficial soever, is looked upon by them as only a lesser degree of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. But though they generally esteem it so much below their dignity to apply to any useful useful work, they think it no disgrace to beg or steal. With respect to the first, they are said to be the most shameless and importunate beggars in the world. They will take no denial, spare no crouching, lying, prayers, to obtain what they want, nor curies and ill language when sent away without it. With regard to the last, they deem no theft unlawful or scandalous, except it be committed in a private manner, without the knowledge of the person wronged. It is esteemed a piece of bravery and gallantry to wrench any thing from another by violence; and this kind of theft is so common, not only among the vulgar, but also among the great ones, that they make no scruple, in their travels from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> not only upon all the provisions they meet with in towns and villages, but upon every thing else that falls in their way. These violences oblige the poor people to conceal the few valuables they have, in some secret place out of the knowledge and reach of those harpies; and they think themselves well off if they can escape a severe bastinadoing, or other cruel usage, frequently inflicted upon them, in order to make them discover the place of their concealment. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of the natives, both men and women, is black, though not in the same degree; some being of a much deeper black than others. Their hair is black and finely curled; some have it also of a dark <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> colour; their eyes are mostly of a lively black; but some are of a dark sea-colour. They have neither flat noses nor thick lips like the Nubians and other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>. Their stature is mostly of the middle size; and, excepting their black complexion, they much resemble the Portuguese. In their temper they are mistrustful, envious, jealous, and treacherous; and where they once take a dislike or affront, will spare no pains, and stick at no means, however base, to be avenged of, and crush their enemy under their feet. There is no such thing among them as natural affection. A husband, if a Heathen, may take as many wives as he pleases; and if a Christian, may have any number of concubines, whom he may divorce at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, or even sell them though with child. So little regard have they for their children, that there is scarce one among them who will not sell a son or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, or perhaps both, for a piece of cloth, a collar or girdle of coral or beads, and often for a bottle of wine or brandy. The religion of the Congoese in many parts is downright idolatry, accompanied with the most ridiculous superstitions, and the most absurd and detestable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> invented by their gangas or priests; and even in those parts where Christianity is professed, it is so darkened by superstitions of one kind or other, that we may justly question whether the people are any gainers by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of this kingdom is monarchical, and as despotic as any in Asia or Africa. The kings are the sole proprietors of all the lands within their dominions; and these they can dispose of to whom they please, upon condition they pay a certain tribute out of them; upon failure of the payment of which, or any other neglect, they turn them out. Even the princes of the blood are subjected to the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; so that there is no person of any rank or quality whatever that can bequeath a foot of land to his heirs or successors; and when these owners under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> die, the lands immediately return to it again, whether they were in their possession, or had been left to ever so many tenants under them; so that it entirely depends on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> whether these lands shall be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the same, or be disposed into other hands. The Portuguese, however, since their settling in these parts, have prevailed upon the monarchs to permit the heirs and successors to continue in the quiet possession of such lands, in order to avoid the confusions, or even rebellions, which the alienation and deprival of them frequently occasioned, and to oblige the tenants of them to pay their tribute more exactly and readily than they did before. St Salvador is the chief place of trade in this country belonging to the Portuguese and other Europeans. There are thought to be about 4000 of them settled here, who trade with most parts of the kingdom. The chief commodities they bring hither are either the product of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> or European <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. The former consist chiefly of grains, fruits, plants, &c.; the latter of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> carpets, English cloth, and other stuffs; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> vessels, some kinds of blue earthen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, rings, and ornaments of gold, silver, and other baser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>; coral, glass-beads, bugles, and other trinkets; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> stuffs made of cotton, woollen, and linen, for clothing; and a great variety of tools and other utensils. In return for these, they carry off a great number of slaves, amounting to 15,000 or 16,000 annually, as we have already observed. Formerly they used also to carry away elephants' teeth, furs, and other commodities of the country; but these branches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> are now greatly decayed, and the slave-trade is what the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> principally depend on. Congo, a term applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> of the second quality.

CONGREGATION

Pages 126-127

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, united to as to constitute a body. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is principally used for assemblies of cardinals appointed by the pope, and distributed into several chambers, for the discharge of certain functions and jurisdictions, after the manner of our offices and courts. The first is the congregation of the holy office, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, that of jurisdiction over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and regulars; the third, that of councils; this has power to interpret the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>; the fourth, that of customs, ceremonies, precedencies, canonizations, called the congregation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>; the fifth, that of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s fabric, which takes cognizance of all causes relating to piety and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> whereof is due to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Peter; the sixth, that of waters, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>; the seventh, of fountains and streets; the eighth, that of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a>, which examines the books to be printed or corrected; the ninth, that of the council of state, for the management of the territories belonging to the pope and church (see CAMERLINGO); the tenth, de bono regimen; of which two last the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>-nephew is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; the eleventh, that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; the twelfth, that of bishops, wherein those who are to be promoted to bishoprics in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> are examined; this is held before the pope; the thirteenth, that of consistorial matters; the chief whereof is the cardinal-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>; the fourteenth, a congregation for propagating the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> (see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">COLLEGE</a>); and the fifteenth, that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> immunity, for settling suits against churchmen. There is also a congrega- Congregation of alms, which takes care of every thing that relates to the subordination of Rome and the state of the church. Congregation is also used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> cantoned out of this or that order; and making, as it were, an inferior order, or a subdivision of the order itself. Such are the congregations of the oratory, and those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLUNY">Cluny</a>, &c. among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>. The word is also used for assemblies of pious persons in manner of fraternities, frequent among the Jesuits in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Virgin, &c. It is likewise applied to the audience in a church, particularly as consisting of the inhabitants of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>.

CONGREGATIONALISTS

Pages 127-127

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> who reject all church-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, except that of a single <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of one pastor.

CONGRESS

Pages 127-127

in a judicial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> made by appointment of a judge before surgeons and matrons, in order to prove whether <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> be impotent, before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> is passed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> solicited upon such a complaint. Neither the civil nor canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> makes any mention of the trial of virility by congress. It had its origin in France from the boldness of a young fellow, who, in open <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, having been hard pressed by his wife, demanded the congress. The judge, surprised with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of the demand, found it could not be denied, as being the surest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> could admit of. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it became a branch in the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, and was authorized by decrees and arrests. It obtained for about 120 years; and was annulled by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in 1677, as being found precarious; some having failed under the experiment out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and shame, which is found to have the same effect with actual impotency.

CONGREVE

Pages 127-128

WILLIAM, a younger <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>. His father was employed in the stewardship of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> estate of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLINGTON">Burlington</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, where he resided many years; and our author was born there in 1672. Mr Congreve entered into the Middle-Temple when he came to England, and began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but his bias was toward polite literature and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. His first performance was a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a>, entitled, Incognita, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> and Duty reconciled. He soon after began his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of the Old Bachelor; which was the amusement of some leisure hours during a slow <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> from a fit of illness soon after his return to England; yet was in itself so perfect, that Mr Dryden, on its being shown to him, declared he had never in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> seen such a first play. When brought on the stage in 1693, it met with such universal approbation, that Mr Congreve, though he was but 19 years old at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> it, became now considered as a prop to the declining stage, and a rising genius in dramatic poetry. The next year he produced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a> Dealer; which, for what reason is not obvious, did not meet with so much success as the former. The merit of his first play, however Congreve, had obtained him the favour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>, and some peculiar mark of distinction from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; on whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of this year, he wrote a very elegant elegiac pastoral. In 1695, when Betterton opened the new <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s-Inn fields, Mr Congreve joining with him, gave him his comedy of Love for Love, with which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> opened their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>, and which met with such success, that they immediately offered the author a share in the management of the house, on condition of his furnishing them with one play yearly. This offer he accepted; but whether through indolence, or that correctness which he looked upon as necessary to his works, his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">Mourning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">Bride</a> did not come out till 1697, nor his Way of the World till two years after that. The indifferent success this last mentioned play, though an exceeding good one, met with from the public, completed that disgust to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> contest with Jeremy Collier, who had attacked the immorality of the English stage, and more especially some of his pieces, had begun, and he determined never more to write for the stage. However, though he quitted dramatic writing, he did not lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> entirely; but occasionally wrote many little pieces both in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, all of which stand on the records of literary fame. It is very possible, however, that he might not so soon have given way to this disgust, had not the easiness of his circumstances rendered any subservience to the opinions and caprices of the town absolutely unnecessary to him. For his abilities having very early in life raised him to the acquaintance of the earl of Halifax, who was then the Mecenas of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; that nobleman, desirous of raising to promising a genius above the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of too hasty productions, made him one of the commissioners for licensing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HACKNEY">hackney</a>-coaches; or, according to Coxeter, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the wine-licence. He soon after bestowed on him a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the pipe-office; and not long after gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> in the customs worth 600l. per annum. In the year 1718, he was appointed secretary of Jamaica; so that the whole of his income towards the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his life was upwards of 1200l. a-year. The greatest part of the last 20 years of his life was spent in ease and retirement; and he either did not, or affected not to give himself any trouble about reputation. Yet some part of that conduct might proceed from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>; to which purpose, T. Gibber, in his Lives of the Poets, vol. iv. p. 93. relates the following anecdote of him: "When the celebrated Voltaire was in England, he waited upon Mr Congreve, and paid some compliments upon the merit and reputation of his works. Congreve thanked him; but at the same time told that ingenious foreigner, that he did not choose to be considered as an author, but only as a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> expected to be visited. Voltaire answered, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had never been anything but a private gentleman, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> he had never been troubled with that visit." He observes, in his own account of the transaction, that he was not a little disgusted with so unbecoming a piece of vanity. Towards the close of his life he was much afflicted with the gout; and making a tour to Bath for the benefit <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRUITY">Congruity</a>, next of the waters, was unfortunately overturned in his chariot; by which, it is supposed, he got some inward bruise, as he ever after complained of a pain in his side; and, on his return to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> gradually declining in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, till the 19th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1729, when he died, aged 57; and, on the 26th following, was buried in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, the pall being supported by persons of the first distinction.

CONGRUITY

Pages 128-130

a suitableness <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> relation of agreement between things. The terms congruity and propriety are not applicable to any single object: they imply a plurality, and obviously signify a particular relation between different objects. Thus we currently say, that a decent garb is suitable or proper for a judge; modest behaviour for a young woman; and a lofty style for an epic poem: and on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, that it is unsuitable or incongruous to see a little woman sunk in an overgrown farthingale, a coat richly embroidered covering coarse and dirty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> subject in an elevated style, an elevated subject in a mean style, a first minister <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> his wife's flouncing, or a reverend prelate in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> sleeves dancing a hornpipe. The perception we have of this relation, which seems peculiar to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, cannot proceed from any other cause, but from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of congruity or propriety; for supposing us destitute of that sense, the terms would be to us unintelligible. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that congruity or propriety, wherever perceived, is agreeable; and that incongruity, or impropriety, wherever perceived, is disagreeable. The only difficulty is, to ascertain what are the particular objects that in conjunction suggest these relations; for there are many objects that do not: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, for example, viewed in conjunction with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, or a man viewed in conjunction with a mountain, suggest not either congruity or incongruity. It seems <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to infer, what <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found true by induction, that we never perceive congruity or incongruity but among things that are connected together by some relation; such as a man and his actions, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and his accessories, a subject and its ornaments. We are indeed so framed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, as among things so connected, to require a certain suitableness or correspondence, termed congruity or propriety; and to be displeased when we find the opposite relation of incongruity or impropriety. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> things connected be the subject of congruity, it is reasonable before hand to expect, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of congruity should be required proportioned to the degree of the connexion. And upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> we find this to hold in fact: where the relation is intimate, as between a cause and its effect, a whole and its parts, we require the strictest congruity; but where the relation is slight, or accidental, as among things jumbled together in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, we require little or no congruity: the strictest propriety is required in behaviour and manner of living; because a man is connected with these by the relation of cause and effect: the relation between an edifice and the ground it stands upon, is of the most intimate kind: and therefore the situation of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> ought to be lofty; its relation to neighbouring hills, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, plains, being that of propinquity only, demands but a small share of congruity; among members of the same club, Congruity, the congruity ought to be considerable, as well as among things placed for show in the same niche: among passengers in a stage <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, we require very little congruity; and less still at a public spectacle. Congruity is so nearly allied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, as <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> to be held a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of it; and yet they differ so essentially as never to coincide: beauty, like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, is placed upon a single subject; congruity upon a plurality: further, a thing beautiful in itself, may, with relation to other things, produce the strongest sense of incongruity. Congruity and propriety are commonly reckoned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms; but they are distinguishable, and the precise meaning of each must be ascertained. Congruity is the genus of which propriety is a species; for we call nothing propriety, but that congruity or suitableness which ought to subsist between sensible beings and their thoughts, words, and actions. In order to give a full view of these secondary relations, we shall trace them through some of the most considerable primary relations. The relation of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> to the whole, being extremely intimate, demands the utmost degree of congruity; even the slightest deviation is difficult. Examples of congruity and incongruity are furnished in plenty by the relation between a subject and its ornaments. A literary performance intended merely for amusement, is susceptible of much ornament, as well as a music-room or a play-house; for in gaiety, the mind hath a peculiar relish for show and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a>. The most gorgeous apparel, however improper in tragedy, is not unsuitable to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, an opera, in its present form, is a mighty fine thing; but as it deviates from nature in its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> circumstances, we look not for nature or propriety in those which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a>. On the other hand, a serious and important subject admits not much ornament; nor a subject that of itself is extremely beautiful; and a subject that fills the mind with its loftiness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, appears best in a dress altogether plain. To a person of a mean appearance, gorgeous apparel is unsuitable; which, besides the incongruity, has a bad effect; for by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> it shows the meanness of appearance in the strongest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Sweetness of look and manner requires simplicity of dress, joined with the greatest elegance. A stately and majestic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> requires sumptuous apparel, which ought not to be gaudy, nor crowded with little ornaments. A woman of consummate beauty can bear to be highly adorned, and yet shows best in a plain dress: For loveliness Needs not the foreign aid of ornament, But is when unadorn'd, adorn'd the most. Thomson's Autumn, 208. Congruity regulates not only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ornament, but also the kind. The ornaments that embellish a dancing room ought to be all of them gay. No picture is proper for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> but what has <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> for its subject. All the ornaments upon a shield ought to relate to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, with great judgment, confines the carvings upon the shield of Æneas to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>: but this beauty is overlooked by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>; for the bulk of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> Congruity, ture upon the shield of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>, is of the arts of peace in general, and of joy and festivity in particular: the author of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELEMACHUS">Telemachus</a> betrays the same inattention, in describing that young <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>. In judging of propriety with regard to ornaments, we must attend, not only to the nature of the subject that is to be adorned, but also to the circumstances in which it is placed: the ornaments that are proper for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, will appear not altogether so decent at public worship; and the same person ought to dress differently for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> feast and for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>. Nothing is more intimately related to a man, than his sentiments, words, and actions; and therefore we require here the strictest conformity. When we find what we thus require, we have a lively sense of propriety: when we find the contrary, our sense of impropriety is not less lively. Hence the universal distaste of affectation, which consists in making a show of greater delicacy and refinement than is suited either to the character or circumstance of the person. Congruity and propriety, wherever perceived, appear agreeable; and every agreeable object produces in the mind a pleasant <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>: incongruity and impropriety, on the other hand, are disagreeable; and of course produce painful emotions. These emotions, whether pleasant or painful, sometimes vanish without any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; but more frequently occasion other emotions, which we proceed to exemplify. When any flight incongruity is perceived in an accidental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of persons or things, as of passengers in a stage-coach, or of individuals dining at an ordinary; the painful emotion of incongruity, after a momentary existence, vanishes without producing any effect. But this is not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of propriety and impropriety: voluntary acts, whether words or deeds, are imputed to the author; when proper, we reward him with our esteem; when improper, we punish him with our contempt. Let us suppose, for example, a generous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> suited to the character of the author, which raises him in and in every spectator the pleasant emotion of propriety; this emotion generates in the author both self-esteem and joy; the former when he considers the relation to the action, and the latter when he considers the good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that others will entertain of him: the same emotion of propriety produceth in the spectators esteem for the author of the action; and when they think of themselves, it also produceth, by means of contrast, an emotion of humility. To discover the effects of an unfavourable action, we must invert each of these circumstances: the painful emotion of impropriety generates in the author of the action both humility and shame; the former when he considers his relation to the action, and the latter when he considers what others will think of him: the same emotion of impropriety produceth in the spectators contempt for the author of the action; and it also produceth, by means of contrast, when they think of themselves, an emotion of self-esteem. Here then are many different emotions, derived from the same action, considered in different views by different persons; a machine provided with many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, and not a little complicated. Propriety of action, it would seem, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> favourite of nature, when such care and solicitude is bestowed upon it. It is not left to our own choice; but, like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, is required at our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and, like justice, is enforced by natural rewards and punishments: a man cannot, with impunity, do anything unbecoming or improper; he suffers the chastisement of contempt inflicted by others, and of shame inflicted by himself. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> so complicated, and so singular, ought to rouse our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>: for nature doth nothing in vain; and we may conclude with great certainty, that this curious branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> is intended for some valuable purpose. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> impropriety is punished with contempt and indignation, which are vented against the offender by corresponding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> expressions; nor is even the slightest impropriety suffered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> without some degree of contempt. But there are improprieties, of the slightest kind, that provoke <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>; of which we have examples without end, in the blunders and absurdities of our own species: such improprieties receive a different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, as will appear by what follows. The emotions of contempt and of laughter occasioned by an impropriety of this kind, uniting intimately in the mind of the spectator, are expressed externally by a peculiar sort of laugh, termed a laugh of derision or scorn. An impropriety that thus moves not only contempt, but laughter, is distinguished by the epithet of ridiculous; and a laugh of derision or scorn is the punishment provided for it by nature. Nor ought it to escape observation, that we are so fond of inflicting this punishment, as sometimes to exert it even against creatures of an inferior species; witness a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">turkey</a>-cock swelling with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, and strutting with displayed feathers; a ridiculous object, which in a gay mood is apt to provoke a laugh of derision. We must not expect, that these different improprieties are separated by distinct boundaries; for of improprieties, from the slightest to the most gross, from the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RISIBLE">risible</a> to the most serious, there are degrees without end. Hence it is, that in viewing some unbecoming actions, too risible for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, and too serious for derision, the spectator feels a sort of mixed emotion, partaking both of derision and of anger; which accounts for an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with respect to the impropriety of some actions, that we know not whether to laugh or be angry. It cannot fail to be observed, that in the case of a risible impropriety, which is always flight, the contempt we have for the offender is extremely faint, though derision, its gratification, is extremely pleasant. This disproportion between a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> and its gratification, seems not conformable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> of nature. In looking about for a solution, we must reflect upon what is laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> above, that an improper action not only moves our contempt for the author, but also, by means of contrast, swells the good opinion we have of ourselves. This contributes, more than any other article, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> we have in ridiculing follies and absurdities; and accordingly, it is well known, that they who put the greatest value upon themselves are the most prone to laugh at others. Pride, which is a vivid passion, pleasant in itself, and not less so in its gratification, would singly be sufficient to account for the pleasure of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>, without borrowing any aid from contempt. Hence appears the reason of a noted observation, That we are the most disposed to ridicule the Congruity, the blunders and absurdities of others, when we are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> spirits; for in high spirits, self-conceit displays itself with more than ordinary vigour. With regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> causes of congruity and impropriety; one, regarding congruity, is pretty obvious, that the sense of congruity, as one principle of the fine arts, contributes in a remarkable degree to our entertainment. Congruity, indeed, with respect to quantity coincides with proportion: when the parts of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> are nicely adjusted to each other, it may be said indifferently, that it is agreeable by the congruity of its parts, or by the proportion of its parts. But propriety, which regards voluntary agents only, can never be the same with proportion: a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> nose is disproportional, but cannot be termed improper. In some instances, it is true, impropriety coincides with disproportion in the same subject, but never in the same respect; for example, a very little man buckled to a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">toledo</a>: considering the man and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> with respect to size, we perceive a disproportion; considering the sword as the choice of the man, we perceive an impropriety. The sense of impropriety with respect to mistakes, blunders, and absurdities, is happily contrived for the good of mankind. In the spectators, it is productive of mirth and laughter, excellent recreation in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> from business. But this is a trifle in respect of what follows. It is painful to be the subject of ridicule; and to punish with ridicule the man who is guilty of an absurdity, tends to put him more upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> coming. Thus even the most innocent blunder is not committed with impunity; because, were errors licensed where they do not hurt, inattention would grow into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and be the occasion of much hurt. The final cause of propriety as to moral duties, is of all the most illustrious. To have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> notion of it, the moral duties that respect others must be distinguished from those that respect ourselves. Fidelity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, and the forbearing injury, are examples of the first sort; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, firmness of mind, are examples of the other: the former are <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> duties by the sense of justice; the latter by the sense of propriety. Here is a final cause of the sense of propriety, that must rouse our attention. It is undoubtedly the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of every man, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> his behaviour to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his nature, and to the station allotted him by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>; for such rational conduct contributes in every respect to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, by preserving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, by procuring plenty, by gaining the esteem of others, and, which of all is the greatest blessing, by gaining a justly-founded self-esteem. But in a matter so essential to our well-being, even self-interest is not relied on: the powerful authority of duty is superadded to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of interest. The God of nature, in all things essential to our happiness, hath observed one uniform method: to keep us steady in our conduct, he hath fortified us with natural laws and principles, which prevent many aberrations, that would daily happen were we totally surrendered to so fallible a guide as human reason. Propriety cannot rightly be considered in another light, than as the natural <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> that regulates our conduct with respect to ourselves; as justice is the natural law that regulates our conduct with respect to others. We call propriety a law, not less than justice; because both are equally rules of conduct that ought to be obeyed: propriety includes this obligation; for to say an action is proper, is, in other words, to say, that it ought to be performed; and to say it is improper, is, in other words, to say that it ought to be borne. It is this very character of ought and should that makes justice a law to us; and the same character is applicable to propriety, though perhaps more faintly than to justice: but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is in degree only, not in kind; and we ought, without hesitation or reluctance, to submit equally to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of both. But it must, in the next place, be observed, that to the sense of propriety, as well as of justice, are annexed the sanctions of rewards and punishments; which evidently prove the one to be a law as well as the other. The satisfaction a man hath in doing his duty, joined with the esteem and good will of others, is the reward that belongs to both equally. The punishments also, though not the same, are nearly allied; and differ in degree more than in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Disobedience to the law of justice, is punished with remorse; disobedience to the law of propriety, with shame, which is remorse in a lower degree. Every transgression of the law of justice raises indignation in the beholder; and so doth every flagrant transgression of the law of propriety. Slighter improprieties receive a milder punishment: they are always rebuked with some degree of contempt, and frequently with derision. In general, it is true, that the rewards and punishments annexed to the sense of propriety, are slighter in degree than those annexed to the sense of justice: which is wisely ordered, because duty to others is still more essential to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> than duty to ourselves; for society could not subsist a moment were individuals not protected from the headstrong and turbulent passion of their neighbours.

CONI

a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a territory of that name, with a good citadel. The town being divided into two factions, it surrendered to the French in 1641; but was restored to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy soon after. It is seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Grelle and Stura. Its trade is considerable, being the repository of all merchandise from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a> and Nice, destined for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> and Germany. It contains about 10,000 people besides the garrison. It was taken by the French in April 1796. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 45. N. Lat. 44. 30.

Of the Conic Sections. Let \( D \) meet \( P \) in \( Y \), draw \( GH \) perpendicular to \( LK \) meeting \( PL \) in \( N \), and \( PI \) in \( Z \), and draw \( YV \) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to \( GN \) meeting \( LP \) in \( V \). Because \( EY \parallel QZ \) are parallel, also \( VY \parallel LQ \). \[ Pp : pE :: (QP : QY ::) LP : LV; \] now \( LP \) being the parameter, we have, as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">Case</a> II. Prop. I. \[ DE^2 : GE^2 :: LV : LN :: QY : QZ; \] but wherever the point \( G \) be taken in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> \( PGI \), \( QY \) is greater than \( QZ \), therefore also \( DE^2 \) is greater than \( GE^2 \); thus the arch \( PGI \) falls wholly within the conic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTION">section</a>. Let the ordinate \( DE \) now meet the other arch \( PGI \) anywhere in \( g \); draw \( g \) perpendicular to \( LK \) meeting \( LP \) in \( n \), and \( IP \) in \( z \), then it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> in like manner appear that \[ dE^2 : gE^2 :: LV : Ln :: QY : Qz; \] and since in this case \( QY \) is less than \( Qz \), therefore \( dE^2 \) is less than \( gE^2 \); hence the arch \( PGI \) is wholly without the conic section. Prop. IV. The chord of the circle of curvature which is drawn from the point of contact through the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of a parabola is equal to that which is cut off from the diameter; and half the radius of the circle is a third <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the perpendicular from the focus upon the tangent, and the distance of the point of contact from the focus. Let \( PL \) be the chord cut off from the diameter, and \( PHF \) the chord passing through \( F \) the focus; draw \( PM \) the diameter of the circle, join \( HL, HM \), and draw \( FK \) perpendicular to the tangent at \( P \). Because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> \( PFH, PL \) make equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with the tangent at \( P \) (3. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> I.), the angles \( PHL, PLH \) are equal (32. 3. E.), hence \( PH = PL \). Secondly, the triangles \( FKP, PHM \), being manifestly similar, \[ FK : FP :: PH : PL, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> \( \frac{4}{3} FP : PM, \] hence \( FK : FP :: FP : \frac{3}{4} PM, or \( \frac{3}{4} \) the radius. Cor. 1. Hence the radius is equal to \( \frac{2FP^2}{FK} \). Cor. 2. The radius is also equal to \( \frac{2FK^3}{AF^2} \), where \( AF \) is the distance of the focus from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERTEX">vertex</a> of the parabola; for \( FP = \frac{FK^2}{AF} \) (11. Part I.) Cor. 3. Hence also the radius is equal to \( \frac{\frac{3}{4} LFP^3}{FK^3} \), where \( L \) denotes the parameter of the axis, for \( \frac{2FP^2}{FK} = \frac{2AF \cdot FP^3}{AF \cdot FP \cdot FK} = \frac{\frac{3}{4} LFP^3}{FK^3} \). Prop. V. The radius of the circle of curvature at the vertex of any diameter of an ellipse, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPERBOLA">hyperbola</a>, is Fig. 92. a third proportional to the perpendicular drawn from the centre upon the tangent, and half the conjugate diameter; and the chord which is drawn from the point of contact through the focus is a third proportional to the transverse axis, and conjugate diameter. Let \( PL \) be the chord cut off from the diameter, and \( PHF \) the chord passing through \( F \) the focus; draw \( PM \) the diameter of the circle, and from the centre \( O \) draw \( OR \) perpendicular to \( PL \), which will bisect \( PL \) in \( R \); join \( HM \), and draw the conjugate diameter \( QG \) meeting \( PH \) in \( N \) and \( PM \) in \( S \), then \( PS \) is equal to the perpendicular from the centre \( C \) upon the tangent. The triangles \( PSC, PRO \) are similar, therefore, \[ PS : PC :: PR : PO, \] but \( PC : CQ :: CQ : PR \) (Def. of param., therefore \( PS : CQ :: CQ : PO \). Secondly, the triangles \( PSN, PHM \) are similar, therefore \( PN : PS :: PM : PH \); but \( PS : CQ :: (CQ : PO ::) Qg : PM \), therefore \( PN : CQ :: Qg : PH \), or, since \( PN = AC \) (18. Part II. and 25. Part III.), \( <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">Aa</a> : Qg :: Qg : PH \). Cor. 1. Hence the radius of curvature is equal to \( \frac{CQ^2}{PS} \), and the chord passing through the focus is equal to \( \frac{2CQ^2}{AC} \). Cor. 2. The radius of curvature is also equal to \( \frac{CQ^2}{AC \cdot BC} \) for \( PS = \frac{AC \cdot BC}{CQ} \) (14. Part II. and 23. Part III.). Cor. 3. Draw \( FK \) from the focus perpendicular to the tangent, and let \( L \) denote the parameter of the transverse axis; the radius of curvature is also equal to \( \frac{\frac{3}{4} L \times FP^3}{FK^3} \). For the triangles \( PFK, NPS \) are manifestly similar, therefore \[ FK : FP :: PS : PN, or AC :: BC : CQ; \] hence \( CQ = \frac{FP}{FK} \times BC \), and \( \frac{CQ^3}{AC \cdot BC} = \frac{FP^3}{FK^3} \times \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{FP^3}{FK^3} \times \frac{3}{4} L \). This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> for the radius of curvature is the same for all the three conic sections.

CONICHTHYODONTES

Pages 160-187

CONICHTHYODONTES, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Plectronitæ, in *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>*, a name by which the fossil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of fishes are sometimes distinguished. **Coniferæ**, in *<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>*, an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> in the *Fragmenta methodi naturalis* of Linnaeus, containing the following genera, viz. cupressus, ephedra, equidium, juniperus, pinus, taxus, thuja. See *Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*. **Coniferous trees**, such as bear hard dry feed-vessels of a conical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; consisting of several woody parts, being mostly scaly, adhering closely together, and separating when ripe. **Conimbrica**, in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSITANIA">Lusitania</a>, on the south side of the river Monde; from the ruins of which arose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>, in its neighbourhood, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 5'. N. Lat. 40° 16'. **Coningseck**, a town of Swabia in Germany, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, 20 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>. E. Long. 9° 20'. N. Lat. 47° 50'. **Conjoint**, in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies united or connected. **Conjoint Degrees**, in *Music*, two notes which follow each other immediately in the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, as ut and re. **Conjoint Tetrachords**, two tetrachords, or fourths, where the same chord is the highest of one and the lowest of the other. **Conissalæ**, an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in natural history, signifying a clas of fossils, which were said to be naturally and essentially compounded, not inflammable, nor soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, found in detached masses, and formed of crystalline <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> debased by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. It included sand and gritty substances. **Conjugate Diameter**, or *Axis of an Ellipse*, the shortest of the two diameters, or that bisecting the axis. **Conjugation**, in *<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>*, a regular distribution of the several inflections of verbs in their different voices, moods, tenses, numbers, and persons, so as to distinguish them from one another. See *Grammar and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a>*. **Conium <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HEMLOCK">hemlock</a>**. See *Botany Index*. **Conjunct**, in a general sense, signifies joined, concurrent, or united. **Conjunct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">Rights</a>**, in *Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>*, such as are granted to two or more persons. See *Law Index*. **Conjunct, or Confidant Persons**, in *Scots Law*, such as are about the person of another, or employed by him. See *Law Index*. **Conjunction**, in *<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>*, the meeting of two or more stars or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>. **Conjunction**, in *Grammar*, an indeclinable word or particle, which serves to join words and sentences together, and thereby shows their relation or dependence upon one another. See *Grammar*. **Conjuration**, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> words, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, or ceremonies, whereby evil spirits, tempests, &c., are supposed to be raised, or driven away. The Romish priests pretend to expel devils, by preparing holy water in a particular manner, and sprinkling it over the possessed, with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of conjurations and exorcisms. Some authors make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between conjuration and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">witchcraft</a> to consist in this; that the former effects its end by prayers and invocation of God's name, &c. to compel the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> to do what is desired; so that the conjurer is supposed to be at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the devil, and that evil spirit to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> merely out of constraint; whereas the latter attains its end by an immediate application to the devil himself: and the devil's complaisance is supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> between them, so that the devil and the witch have a good understanding together. Both these, again, differ from enchantment and sorcery; in that these latter operate secretly and slowly by spells, charms, &c. without ever calling on the devil, or having any conference with him. **Conn.** See *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONNECTICUT">Connecticut</a>*. **Connacht**, one of the four provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, bounded on the east by that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, on the west by the ocean, on the north and north-west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ocean and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster, and on the south and east by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>. It is about 130 miles in length, and 84 in breadth. It has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHANNON">Shannon</a>. It has several convenient bays and creeks, and is fertile in many places. It had several dangerous bogs, overrun with woods, which are now in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> cleared away. This province produces abundance of cattle, sheep, deer, hawks, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; but the inhabitants being lazy, it is the least cultivated of all the four provinces. It contains 1 archbishopric, 5 bishoprics, 6 counties, 7 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 8 places of trade, 10 boroughs that send members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, 47,256 houses, 24 old castles, besides fortresses that have been erected of late, and 330 parishes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALWAY">Galway</a>. **Connarus, Ceylon <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUMACH">sumach</a>**. See *Botany Index*. **Connecticut**, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river in New England, which gives name to one of the five colonies of that province (see the next article). It rises in a swamp on the height of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, in N. Lat. 45° 10'. W. Long. 71°. After a sleepy course of eight or ten miles, it tumbles over four separate falls, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> west keeps <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> under the hills which form the northern boundary of the vale through which it runs. The Ammonoosuck and Iseel rivers, two principal branches of Connecticut river, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into it from the east, between the latitudes 44° and 45°. Between the towns of Walpole on the east, and Westminister on the west side of the river, are the great falls. The whole river, comprehended between two rocks scarcely 30 feet asunder, flows with amazing rapidity into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> basin below. Over these falls, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> 160 feet in length was built in 1784, under which the highest floods may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> without detriment. This is the first bridge that was ever erected over this noble river. Above Deerfield in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASSACHUSETTS">Massachusetts</a> it receives Deerfield river from the west, and Miller's river from the east, after which it turns westerly in a sinuous course to Fighting-falls, and a little after tumbles over Deerfield falls, which are impassable by boats. At <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> in Connecticut it receives Farmington river from the west, and at Hartford meets the tide. From Hartford it passes on in a crooked course, until it falls into Long <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> between Saybrook and Lyme. The length of this river, in a straight line, is nearly 300 miles. Its general course is several degrees west of south. It is from 80 to 100 rods wide, 130 miles from... Connecticut from its mouth. At its mouth is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of sand which considerably obstructs the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. Ten feet water at full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> is found on this bar, and the same depth to Middleton. The distance of the bar from this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, as the river runs, is 36 miles. Above Middleton are several shoals which stretch quite across the river. Only six feet water is found on the shoal at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tide, and here the tide ebbs and flows but about eight inches. About three miles below Middleton the river is contracted to about 40 rods in breadth by two high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Almost everywhere else the banks are low, and spread into fine extensive meadows. In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> floods, which generally happen in May, these meadows are covered with water. At Hartford the water sometimes rises 20 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> surface of the river, and having all to pass through the above-mentioned strait, it is sometimes two or three weeks before it returns to its usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>. These floods add nothing to the depth of water on the bar at the mouth of the river; this bar lying too far off in the sound to be affected by them. On this beautiful river, whose banks are settled almost to its source, are many pleasant, neat, well-built towns. On its western <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, from its mouth northward, are the towns of Saybrook, Haddam, Middleton, Weathersfield, Hartford, Windsor, and Suffield, in Connecticut; West Springfield, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HATFIELD">Hatfield</a>, and Deerfield, in Massachusetts; Guilford, Brattleborough, in which is Fort Dummer, Westminster, Windsor, Hartford, Fairlee, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWBURY">Newbury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, and many others in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VERMONT">Vermont</a>. Crossing the river into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_HAMPSHIRE">New <a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, and travelling on the eastern bank, you pass through Woodbury nearly opposite to Brunswick, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, the Coos <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, Lyman, Orford, Lyme, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, in which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARTMOUTH">Dartmouth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, Lebanon, Cornish, Chesterfield, and many others in New Hampshire; Sunderland, Hadley, Springfield, Long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">Meadow</a>, in Massachusetts; and in Connecticut, Enfield, East Windsor, East Hartford, Glastenbury, East Haddam, and Lyme. This river is navigable to Hartford, upwards of 50 miles from its mouth, and the produce of the country for 200 miles above is brought thither in boats. The boats which are used in this business are flat-bottomed, long and narrow, for the convenience of going up stream, and of so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> a make as to be portable in carts. They are taken out of the river at three different carrying-places, all of which make 15 miles. Sturgeon, salmon, and shad, are caught in plenty in their season, from the mouth of the river upwards, excepting sturgeon, which do not ascend the upper falls; besides a variety of small fish, such as pike, carp, perch, &c. From this river are employed three brigs of 180 tons each, in the European trade; and about 60 sail from 60 to 150 tons, in the West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> trade; besides a few fishermen, and 40 or 50 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COASTING">coasting</a> vessels.
