Lineal consanguinity is that which subsists between persons of whom one is descended in a direct line from the other; as between John Stiles (the progenitor in the table of consanguinity) and his father, grandfather, great grandfather, and so upwards in the direct ascending line; or between John Stiles and his son, grandson, great grandson, and so downwards in the direct descending line. Every generation, in this direct lineal consanguinity, constitutes a different degree, reckoning either upwards or downwards: the father of John Stiles is related to him in the first degree, and so likewise is his son; his grand sire and grandson in the second; his great grand sire and great-grandson in the third. This is the only natural way of reckoning the degrees in the direct line; and therefore universally obtains, as well in the civil and canon, as in the common law. The doctrine of lineal consanguinity is sufficiently plain and obvious; but it is, at the first view, astonishing to consider the number of lineal ancestors which every man has, within no very great number of degrees; and so many different bloods is a man said to contain in his veins, as he hath lineal ancestors. Of these he hath two in the first ascending degree; his own parents; he hath four in the second; the parents of his father, and the parents of his mother; he hath eight in the third, the parents of his two grandfathers; and of his two grandmothers; and by the same rule of progression, he hath 128 in the seventh; 1024 in the tenth; and at the 20th degree, or the distance of 20 generations, every man hath above a million of ancestors, as common arithmetic will demonstrate (A). This lineal consanguinity, we may observe, falls strictly within the definition of *vinculum personarum ab eodem filiis descendentium*; since lineal relations are such as descend one from the other, and both of course from the same common ancestor. Collateral kindred answers to the same description: collateral (A) This will seem surprising to those who are unacquainted with the increasing power of progressive numbers; but is palpably evident from the following table of a geometrical progression, in which the first term is 2, and the denominator also 2: or, to speak more intelligibly, it is evident, for that each of us has two ancestors. collateral relations agreeing with the lineal in this, that they descend from the same stock or ancestor; but differing in this, that they do not descend the one from the other. Collateral kinsmen, then, are such as lineally spring from one and the same ancestor, who is the first, or "root," "the fiper," "trunk," or common flock, from whence these relations are branched out. As if John Stiles hath two sons, who have each a numerous issue: both these issues are lineally descended from John Stiles as their common ancestor; and they are collateral kinsmen to each other, because they are all descended from this common ancestor, and all have a portion of his blood in their veins, which denominates them consanguineous. We must be careful to remember, that the very being of collateral consanguinity consists in this descent from one and the same common ancestor. Thus Titus and his brother are related; why? because both are derived from one father: Titus and his first cousin are related; why? because both descend from the same grandfather; and his second cousin's claim to consanguinity is this, that they are both derived from one and the same great-grandfather. In short, as many ancestors as a man has, so many common stocks he has from which collateral kinsmen may be derived. And as we are taught by holy writ, that there is one couple of common ancestors belonging to us all, from whom the whole race of mankind is descended, the obvious and undeniable consequence is, that all men are in some degree related to one another. For, in deed, if we only suppose each couple of our ancestors to have left, one with another, two children; and each of those children to have left, on an average, two more (and without such a supposition the human species must be daily diminishing); we shall find that all of us have now subsisting near 270 millions of kindred in the 13th degree, at the same distance from the several common ancestors as we ourselves are; besides those that are one or two degrees nearer to or farther from the common stock, who may amount to as many more (b). And if this calculation should appear incompatible with the number of inhabitants on the earth; it is because, by intermarriages among the several descendants from the same ancestor, a hundred or a thousand modes of consanguinity may be consolidated in one person; or he may be related to us a hundred or a thousand different ways. The method of computing these degrees in the canon law, which we have adopted, is as follows. We begin at the common ancestor, and reckon downwards; and in whatsoever degree the two persons, or the most remote of them, is distant from the common ancestor, that is the degree in which they are related to each other. Thus, Titus and his brother are related in the first degree; for from the father to each of them is counted only one: Titus and his nephew are related in the second degree; for the nephew is two degrees removed from the common ancestor, viz. his own grandfather, the father of Titus: or (to give a more illustrious instance from the English annals) | Degree | Number of Ancestors | |--------|---------------------| | 1 | 2 | | 2 | 4 | | 3 | 8 | | 4 | 16 | | 5 | 32 | | 6 | 64 | | 7 | 128 | | 8 | 256 | | 9 | 512 | | 10 | 1024 | | 11 | 2048 | | 12 | 4096 | | 13 | 8192 | | 14 | 16384 | | 15 | 32768 | | 16 | 65536 | | 17 | 131072 | | 18 | 262144 | | 19 | 524288 | | 20 | 1048576 | A shorter way of finding the number of ancestors at any given degree, is by squaring the number of ancestors at half that number of degrees. Thus 16, the number of ancestors at 4 degrees, is the square of 4; the number of ancestors at 256 is the square of 16; 65536 of 256; and the number of ancestors at 40 degrees would be the square of 1,048,576, or upwards of a million of millions. (b) This will swell more considerably than the former calculation: for here, though the first term is but 1, the denominator is 4; that is, there is one kinsman (a brother) in the first degree, who makes, together with the propotius, the two defendants from the first couple of ancestors; and in every other degree, the number of kindred must be the quadruple of those in the degree which immediately precedes it. For since each couple of ancestors King Henry VII, who flew Richard III in the battle of Bosworth, was related to that prince in the fifth degree. Let the propotius, therefore, in the table of consanguinity, represent King Richard III and the clas marked e, King Henry VII. Now their common stock or ancestor was King Edward III, the abatus in the same table: from him to Edmund duke of York, the proavus, is one degree; to Richard earl of Cambridge, the avus, two; to Richard duke of York, the pater, three; to King Richard III, the propotius, four; and from King Edward III to John of Gaunt (a) is one degree; to John earl of Somerset (b) two; to John duke of Somerset (c) three; to Margaret countess of Richmond (d) four; to King Henry VII (e) five. Which last-mentioned prince, being the farthest removed from the common stock, gives the denomination to the degree of kindred in the canon and municipal law. Though according to the computation of the civilians (who count upwards from either of the persons related, to the common stock, and then downwards again to the other; reckoning a degree for each person both ascending and descending) these two princes were related in the ninth degree; for from King Richard III, to Richard duke of York is one degree; to Richard earl of Cambridge two; to Edmund duke of York three; to King Edward III, the common ancestor, four; to John of Gaunt five; to John earl of Somerset six; to John duke of Somerset seven; to Margaret countess of Richmond eight; to King Henry VII nine. See the Table of Consanguinity (Plate CLXIV.), wherein all the degrees of collateral kindred to the propotius are computed, as far as the tenth of the civilians and the seventh of the canons inclusive; the former being distinguished by the numeral letters, the latter by the common ciphers. Consanguinity and Affinity, degrees of, forbidden in marriage. See Marriage, and Law Index. Consanguinity and Affinity, an objection against a judge or a witness. See Law Index. Conscience, a secret testimony of the soul, whereby it gives its approbation to things that are naturally good, and condemns those that are evil. See Moral Philosophy. A man of integrity will never listen to any reason, or give way to any measure, or be misled by any inducement, against conscience.—The inhabitants of a great town offered Marshal de Turenne 100,000 crowns, upon condition he would take another road, and not march his troops their way. He answered them, "As your town is not in the road I intend to march, I cannot accept the money you offer me."—The earl of Derby, in the reign of Edward III, making a descent ancestors has two descendants who increase in a duplicate ratio, it will follow, that the ratio in which all the descendants increase downwards, must be double to that in which the ancestors increase upwards: but we have seen, that the ancestors increase in a duplicate ratio: therefore the descendants must increase in a double duplicate; that is, in a quadruple ratio. | Collateral Degrees | Number of Kindred | |-------------------|------------------| | 1 | 1 | | 2 | 4 | | 3 | 16 | | 4 | 64 | | 5 | 256 | | 6 | 1024 | | 7 | 4096 | | 8 | 16384 | | 9 | 65536 | | 10 | 262144 | | 11 | 1048576 | | 12 | 4194304 | | 13 | 16777216 | | 14 | 67108864 | | 15 | 268435456 | | 16 | 1073741824 | | 17 | 4294967296 | | 18 | 17179569184 | | 19 | 68719476736 | | 20 | 274877906944 | This calculation may also be formed by a more compendious process, viz. by squaring the couples, or half the number of ancestors, at any given degree; which will furnish us with the number of kindred we have in the same degree, at equal distance with ourselves from the common stock, besides those at unequal distances. Thus in the tenth lineal degree, the number of ancestors is 1024; its half, or the couples, amount to 512; the number of kindred in the tenth collateral degree amounts therefore to 262144, or the square of 512. And if we will be at the trouble to recollect the state of the several families within our own knowledge, and observe how far they agree with this account; that is, whether, on an average, every man has not one brother or sister, four first-cousins, fifteen second-cousins, and so on, we shall find, that the present calculation is very far from being overcharged. Conscience, scent in Guienne, carried by florm the town of Ber- gerac, and gave it up to be plundered. A Welch knight happened by chance to light upon the receiver's office. He found there such a quantity of money that he thought himself obliged to acquaint his gene- ral with it, imagining that so great a booty naturally belonged to him. But he was agreeably surprifed when the earl told him, with a pleafant countenance, that he wished him joy of his good fortune; and that he did not make the keeping of his word to depend upon the great or little value of the thing he had pro- mifed.—In the fiefge of Falifci by Camillus general of the Romans, the schoolmaster of the town, who had the children of the senators under his care, led them abroad under the pretext of recreation, and carried them to the Roman camp, faying to Camillus, that by this artifice he had delivered Falifci into his hands. Camillus, abhorring this treachery, obferved, "That there were laws for war as well as for peace; and that the Romans were taught to make war with inte- grity not lefs than with courage." He ordered the schoolmaster to be stripped, his hands to be bound be- hind his back, and to be delivered to the boys to be lashed back into the town. The Falerians, formerly obftinate in refiftance, struck with an act of justice fo illuftrious, delivered themfelves up to the Romans; convinced that they would be far better to have the Romans for their allies than their enemies. It is a faying, That no man ever offended his own confince, but firft or laft it was revenged upon him. The power of confinfe indeed has been remarked in all ages, and the examples of it upon record are immu- erable. The following is related by Mr Fordyce, in his Dialogues on Education*, as a real occurrence which happened in a neihbouring fteate not many years ago. A jeweller, a man of good character and confiderable wealth, having occasion in the way of his business to travel at fome diftance from the place of his abode, took along with him a fervant, in order to take care of his portmanteau. He had with him fome of his beft jewels, and a large fum of money, to which his fervant was likewife privy. The matter having oc- casion to dismount on the road, the fervant watching his opportunity, took a pistol from his master's saddle and fhot him dead on the spot; then rifed him of his jewels and money, and hanging a large fone to his neck, he threw him into the nearest canal. With this booty he made off to a diftant part of the country, where he had reafon to believe that neither he nor his mafter were known. There he began to trade in a very low way at firft, that his obfcurity might screen him from observation, and in the course of a good many years seemed to rife, by the natural progres of business, into wealth and confideration; fo that his good fortune appeared at once the effect and reward of induftry and virtue. Of thofe he counterfeited the appearance fo well, that he grew into great credit, married into a good family, and by laying out his hid- den stores difcreetly, as he faw occasion, and joining to all an univerfal affability, he was admitted to a share of the government of the town, and rofe from one poft to another, till at length he was chofen chief magiftrate. In this office he maintained a fair cha- racter, and continued to fill it with no small applaule, both as a governor and a judge; till one day as he sat on the bench with fome of his brethren, a criminal Confince. was brought before him who was accused of murder- ing his mafter. The evidence came out full, the jury brought in their verdict that the prifoner was guilty, and the whole assembly waited the fentence of the pre- ident of the court (which he happened to be that day) with great fulpenfe. Meanwhile he appeared to be in unusual disorder and agitation of mind, and his colour changed often; at length he arose from his seat, and coming down from the bench, placed him- self juft by the unfortunate man at the bar. "You fee before you (faid he, addrefling himfelf to thofe who had fat on the bench with him), a striking in- stance of the juft rewards of heaven, which this day, after 30 years concealment, prefents to you a greater criminal than the man juft now found guilty." Then he made an ample confeflion of his guilt, and of all its aggravations. "Nor can I feel (continued he) any relief from the agonies of an awakened confinfe, but by requiring that juftice be forthwith done againft me in the moft public and folemn manner." We may eafily fuppofe the amazement of all the assembly, and efpecially of his fellow-judges. However, they pro- ceeded, upon this confeflion, to paft fentence upon him, and he died with all the symptoms of a penitent mind. Courts of Confince, are courts for recovery of small debts, constituted by act of parliament in Lon- don, Westminster, &c. and other populous and trading diftricts. CONSCIOUSNESS. Metaphysicians, in lieu of the word confinfe, which feems appropriated to theo- logical or moral matters, ordinarily ufe that of con- ficiofnefs; whereby they mean an inner feniment of a thing, whereof one may have a clear and diftinct no- tion. In this fenfe they fay that we do not know our own foul, nor are affured of the exiftence of our own thoughts, otherwife than by felf-conficfionefs. See Metaphysics.

CONSCRIPT

Pages 191-191

in Roman antiquity, an appellation given to the senators of Rome, who were called con- script fathers, on account of their names being all en- tered in one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>.

CONSECRATION

Pages 192-192

among medallists, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his translation into heaven and reception among the gods. On medals the consecration is thus represented: on one side is the emperor's head, crowned with laurel, sometimes veiled; and the inscription gives him the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of divus: on the reverse is a temple, a bustum, an altar, or an eagle taking its flight towards heaven, either from off the altar, or from a cipus: at other times the emperor is seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, borne up by the eagle; the inscription always, consecratio. These are the usual symbols: yet on the reverse of that of Antoninus is the Antonine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>. In the apotheosis of empresses, instead of an eagle there is a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>. As to the honours rendered these princes after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, they were explained by the words consecratio, pater, divus, and dea. Sometimes around the temple or altar are put, memoriae felicis, or memoriae aeternae: for princesses, perpetuas, and fidelibus recepta: on the one side of the head, dea, or &c.

CONSENT

Pages 192-192

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes much the same with ASSENT. Consent of Parts, in the animal economy, an agreement <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sympathy, whereby when one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is immediately affected, another at a distance becomes affected in the same manner. This mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> or consent is supposed to be effected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the nerves, and their artful distribution and ramification throughout the body. The effect is so sensible as even to come under the physician's cognizance: thus, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in the bladder, by vellicating the fibres there, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> pain and draw them so much into spasms, as to affect the coats of the bowels, in the same manner, by the intermediation of nervous threads, and make a colic there; and also extend their twitches sometimes as far as the stomach, and occasion grievous vomitings; the remedy, therefore, in such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, is to regard the part originally affected, how remote and grievous forever may be the consequences and symptoms in other places. The fifth conjugation of nerves branched to the parts of the eye, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, those of the mouth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, precordia, and parts adjacent, &c. is supposed by naturalists to be the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of that particular and extraordinary consent between those parts. Hence it is, that a savoury thing seen or smelled excites the appetite, and affects the glands and parts of the mouth; that a shameful thing seen or heard affects the cheeks with blushes: on the contrary, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it pleases, it affects the precordia, and excites the muscles of the mouth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>; if it grieves, it affects the glands of the eyes, so as to occasion tears, and the muscles of the face, putting them into an aspect of crying. Dr Willis, quoted by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a>, imputes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of killing, and its effects, to this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of nerves; which being branched both to the lips and the genital parts, when the former are affected an irritation is occasioned in the latter. See SYMPATHY.

CONSENTES

Pages 192-192

the name which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> gave to the 12 superior gods, the Dii majorum gentium. The word signifies as much as consentientes; that is, who consented to the deliberations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. They were twelve in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, whose name Ennius has briefly expressed in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, Juno, Vesta, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, Cerer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, Venus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, Mercurius, Jovis, Neptunus, Vulcanus, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>.

CONSEQUENCE

Pages 192-192

in Logic, the conclusion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> what results from reason or argument. See CONCLUSION. The consequence is that other proposition in which the extremes or premises of a syllogism are joined, or separated; and is gained from what was asserted in the premises. This word, in a more restrained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is used for the relation or connection between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, whereof one is inferred from the other.

CONSEQUENT

Pages 192-192

something deduced <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gathered from a former argumentation. But, in a more precise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, it is used for the proposition which contains the conclusion, considered in itself, without any regard to the antecedent: in which sense the consequent may be true, though the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> be false. See the preceding article.

CONSERVATOR

Pages 192-194

an officer ordained for the security and preservation of the privileges of some cities and communities, having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to judge of and determine the differences among them. In most catholic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> there are two conservators; the conservator of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> privileges, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those granted by kings; and the conservator of apostolical privileges, or those granted by the pope. The first takes cognizance of personal and mixed causes between the regents, students, &c. and the latter of spiritual matters between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>. Anciently there were appointed conservators of treaties of peace between princes; which conservators became judges of the infractions made on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, and were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with procuring satisfaction to be made. These were usually the feudatories of the several powers. In lieu of conservators, princes now have recourse to other indifferent princes to guarantee their treaties. Conservator of Scots Privileges at Campvere, is an officer belonging to the royal boroughs of Scotland, who takes care of the mercantile affairs of Scotland, agreeable to the staple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> between them and the States-General. Conservator of the Peace, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> English customs, was a person who had an especial <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, by virtue of his office, to see the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s peace kept. Till the erection of justices of the peace by King Edward III., there were several persons who by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> were interested in keeping the peace: some having that charge as incident to other offices; and others simply, or of itself, called cyfoedos, or conservators of the peace. The chamberlain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a> is still a conservator. Conservator servator in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; and petty constables are, by the common law, conservators, &c., in the first fense, within their own jurisdiction; so are also the coroner and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> within their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The king is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> conservator of the peace within all his dominions: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, lord marshal, lord high <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a>, all the justices of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of king's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, by their office, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the rolls, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, are general conservators of the peace through the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and may commit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAKERS">breakers</a> of the peace, and bind them in recognizances to keep it. Conservator of the Truce, and Safe Conducts, was an officer appointed in every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port, under the king's letters patent. His charge was to inquire of all offenses committed against the king's truce, and safe conducts upon the main sea, out of the franchises of the cinque-ports, as the admirals were wont to do, and such other things as are declared anno 3 Hen. V. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 6. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSERVATORIOS">Conservatorios</a>, are musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> established for the instruction of children in the profession of music. There are four of these at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, designed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of girls, and three at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, for the education of boys. It has been suggested that the operation of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASTRATION">castration</a> was performed in the conservatories; but the practice is absolutely prohibited: and the young castrati are brought from Lucia in Puglia: but before that operation is performed, their voices are tried in a conservatorio. The scholars of the Venetian conservatories have been chiefly celebrated for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and neatness of execution; and those of Naples have had the reputation of being the first contrapuntists, or composers, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSERVATORY">Conservatory</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> sometimes used for a greenhouse or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICE_HOUSE"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Conserve, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a form of medicine contrived to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, herbs, roots, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of several simples, as near as possible, to what they are when fresh gathered. See Pharmacy. Consignment, in Law, the depositing any sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, bills, papers, or commodities, in good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; either by appointment of a court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, in order to be delivered to the persons to whom they are adjudged; or voluntarily, in order to their being returned to the persons they belong to, or sent to the places they are designed for. Consignment of Goods, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, is the delivering or making them over to another; thus, goods are said to be consigned to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a>, when they are sent to him to be sold, &c.; or when a factor lends back goods to his principal, they are said to be consigned to him. Consistence, in Physics, that state of a body wherein its component particles are so connected or entangled among themselves, as not to separate or recede from each other. It differs from continuity in this, that it implies a regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> or rest, which continuity does not, it being sufficient to denominate a thing continuous that its parts are contiguous to each other. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSISTENTES">Consistentes</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a kind of penitents who were allowed to assist at prayers, but who could not be admitted to receive the sacrament. Consistory (Consistorium), signifies as much as praetorium, a tribunal: it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used for a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>-house of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> persons, or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of justice in the spiritual court; a session or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of prelates. And every archbishop and bishop of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> hath a consistory court held before his chancellor or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> church, or other convenient place of his diocese, for ecclesiastical causes. The bishop's chancellor is the judge of this court, supposed to be skilled in the civil and canon law; and in places of the diocese far remote from the bishop's consistory, the bishop appoints a commissary to judge in all causes within a certain district, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> to enter his decrees, &c. Consistory, at Rome, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of cardinals, or the pope's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and council, before whom judiciary causes are pleaded. Du Cange derives the word from consistorium; i.e. locus ubi consistorium; used chiefly for a vestibule, gallery, or anti-chamber, where the courtiers wait for admission: and called a consistorium multitudine. The consistory is the first court, or tribunal of Rome: it never meets but when the pope pleases to convocate it: the pope presides in it in person, mounted on a magnificent throne, and habited in his pontificalia; on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and priests, and on the left the cardinal-deacons. The place where it is held, is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in the apostolical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, where princes and ambassadors of kings are received. The other prelates, protonotaries, auditors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTA">rota</a>, and other officers, are seated on the steps of the throne: the courtiers sit on the ground; ambassadors on the right, and confessorial and fiscal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> behind the cardinals. Besides the public consistory, there is also a private one, held in a retired chamber, called the chamber of popes; the pope's throne here being only raised two steps high. Nobody is here admitted but the cardinals, whose opinions are collected, and called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>. Here are first proposed and passed all bulls for bishoprics, abbeys, &c. Hence bishopricks and abbeys are said to be consistorial benefices; in regard they must be proposed in the consistory, the annates be paid to the pope, and his bulls taken. Anciently they were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a>; but by the concordat, which abolishes elections, they are appointed to be collated by the pope alone, on the nomination of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. Consistory was also the name of a court under Constantine, where he sat in person, and heard causes: the members of this court were called comites. Consistory is also used among the reformed, for a council or assembly of ministers and elders, to regulate their affairs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, &c. Consistory, or Court Christian, in the English laws, is a council of ecclesiastical persons, or the place of justice in an ecclesiastical or spiritual court. Every archbishop and bishop has a consistory-court, held before his chancellor or commissary, either in his cathedral, in some chapel, aisle, or portico, belonging thereto; or in some other convenient place of his diocese, for ecclesiastical causes. The spiritual court was anciently, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Saxons, joined with the county or hundred court; and the original of the consistory court, as divided from those courts, is found in a law of the conqueror. Consolation conqueror, quoted by Lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>. From this court there lies an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the archbishop of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> respectively.

CONSOLATION

Pages 194-194

one of the places in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, wherein the orator endeavours to abate and moderate the grief <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> concern of another.

CONSOLE

Pages 194-194

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, an ornament cut upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, which has a projection, and on occasion serves to support little cornices, figures, busts, and vases.

CONSOLIDATION

Pages 194-194

in Medicine, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of uniting broken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the lips of wounds, by means of consolidating remedies, as they are called; which cleansing with a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and force, taking corruption out of the wounds, and preserving the temperature of the parts, cause the nourishment to be fitly applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> affected. Among the many influences of the consolidating power of blood and raw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, we have a very remarkable one in Bartholomew's Medical Observations. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> being condemned to have his nose cut off by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> executioner, the friends, who were to be present, provided a new loaf of warm <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, which was cut in the middle, and the nose received in it as it fell from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>; the nose was after this nicely placed on the face again; and being sewed on, the whole in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> consolidated, and left no other marks of the ignominy than the scar round the whole nose, and the traces of the stitches.

CONSONANT

Pages 194-194

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> that cannot be sounded without some single <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> vowel before or after it; as b, c, d, &c.

CONSPIRACY

Pages 194-194

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies an agreement between two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more, falsely to indict, or procure to be indicted, an innocent person, of felony. CONSPIRATORS are, by statute, defined to be such as bind themselves by oath, covenant, or other <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>, to assist one another falsely and maliciously to indict persons, or falsely to maintain pleas. Conspirators in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, are those that plot against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>.

CONSTABLE

Pages 194-196

according to some, is a Saxon word, compounded of coning, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>," and fleple which signifies the "stay <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> support of the king." But as we borrowed the name as well as the office of Constable from the French, Sir William Blackstone is rather inclined to deduce it, with Sir Henry Spelman and Dr Cowell, from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; wherein it is plainly derived from the Latin comes flabuli, an officer well known in the empire; so called, because, like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> constable of France, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> constable of England, he was to regulate all matters of chivalry, tilts, tournaments, and feats of arms, which were performed on horseback.—The Lord High Constable of England is the seventh great officer of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and he, with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> marshal of England, were formerly judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> Constable, of chivalry, called in King Henry IV's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CURIA">Curia</a> Militaris, and now the court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. It is the fountain of the martial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and anciently was held in the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. The power of the lord high constable was formerly so great, and of which so improper a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> was made, that so early as the 13th of King Richard II., a statute passed for regulating and abridging the same, together with the power of the earl marshal of England; and by this statute, no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> could be tried by them or their courts, that could be tried by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law of the realm. The office of constable existed before the conquest. After the conquest, the office went with inheritance, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> of the manors of Harlefield, Newman, and Whitenhurst, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> serjeanty in the family of the Bohuns earl of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, and afterwards in the line of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a> as heirs-general to them; but in 1521, this great office became forfeited to the king in the person of Edward Stafford <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, who was that year attainted for high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>; and in consideration of its extensive power, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> authority, both in time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and peace, it has never been granted to any person, otherwise than by baec vice, and that to attend at a coronation, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>. In France, the same office was also suppressed about a century after by an edict of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII.; though it has been exercised, in the command of the Marshals, by the first officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Lord high constable of Scotland was an office of great antiquity and dignity. The first upon record is Hugo de Morville in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. He had two grand prerogatives, viz. First, the keeping of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, which the king, at his promotion, when he wears fealty, delivers to him naked. Hence the badge of the constable is a naked sword.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">Second</a>, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and unlimited command of the king's armies while in the field, in the absence of the king; but this command does not extend to castles and garrisons. He was likewise judge of all crimes committed within two leagues of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which precinct was called the Chalmer of Peace; though his jurisdiction came at last to be exercised only as to crimes during the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, which some extended likewise to all general conventions. This office was conferred heritably upon the noble family of Errol, by King Robert Bruce; and with them it still remains, being expressly referred by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of union. Inferior Constables. From the great office of high constable is derived that inferior order, since called the constables of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> and franchises; these were first ordained in the 13th year of Edward I., by the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>; which, for the conservation of the peace, and view of armour, appointed that two constables should be chosen in every hundred and franchise. These are what we now call constabularii capitales, or high constables; because continuance of time, and increase of people, &c. have occasioned others of like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, but inferior authority, in every town, called petty constables, or sub-constabularii, first instituted about the reign of Edward III. The former, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> high constables, are appointed at the court-leets of the franchise or hundred over which they preside; or, in default of that, by the justices at their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-leetions; and are removable by Constable, by the same authority that appoints them. The petty constables have two offices united in them, the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and the other modern. Their ancient office is that of head-borough, tithing-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, or borstholder; which is as ancient as the time of King Alfred: their more modern office is that of constable merely; which was appointed so lately as the reign of Edward III., in order to assist the high-constable. And in general the ancient head-boroughs, tithing-men, and borstholders, were made use of to serve as petty constables; though not so generally, but that in many places they still continue distinct officers from the constables. They are all chosen by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> at the court-leet; or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> no court-leet be held, are appointed by two justices of the peace. The general duty of all constables, both high and petty, as well as of the other officers, is to keep the king's peace in their several districts; and to that purpose they are armed with very large powers of arresting and imprisoning, of breaking open houses, and the like: of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of which powers, conferring what manner of men are for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> put upon these offices, it is perhaps very well that they are generally kept in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>. One of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> duties arising from the statute of Winchester, which appoints them, is to keep watch and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> in their respective jurisdictions. Ward, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, or custodia, is chiefly intended of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>-time, in order to apprehend rioters, and robbers on the highways; the manner of doing which is left to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the justices of the peace and the constable: the hundred being, however, liable for all the robberies committed therein by day-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, for having kept negligent guard. Watch is properly applicable to the night only (being called among the Saxons wach't or waftir); and it begins when ward ends, and ends when that begins: for, by the statute of Winchester, in walled <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> the gates shall be closed from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-falling to sun-rising; and watch shall be kept in every borough and town, especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season, to apprehend all rogues, vagabonds, and night-walkers, and make them give an account of themselves. The constable may appoint watchmen at his discretion, regulated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and these, being his deputies, have, for the time being, the authority of their principal. There are also constables denominated from particular places, as constable of the Tower, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> castle, of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> castle, of the castle of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAERNARVON">Caernarvon</a> and many other of the castles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>; whose office is the same with that of the castellani, or governors of castles. Constables of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of London is divided into 26 wards, and the wards into precincts, in each of which is a constable. They are nominated by the inhabitants of each precinct on St Thomas's day, and confirmed, or otherwise, at the court of wardmote. After <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, they are sworn into their offices at a court of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>, on the next Monday after Twelfth day. Such as are chosen into the office, are obliged to place the king's arms, and the arms of the city, over their doors; and if they reside in alleys, at the ends of such alleys toward the streets, to signify that a constable lives there, and that they may be the more easily found when wanted. Constables to Justices of the Peace, in Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a> are the proper officers for executing their orders. They have powers to suppress tumults, and to apprehend delinquents and those who can give no good account of themselves, and carry them to the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Constance, a strong town of Germany, in the circle of Swabia, with a bishop's see, whose bishop is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire. It has a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and several fine structures, as well sacred as profane. It carries on a great trade, and is well fortified: and though it pretends to be an imperial town, the Austrians keep a garrison here. It is famous for a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> held here in 1514, when there were three popes; but they were all deposed, and Martin V. was elected in their room. The council caused Jerom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a> and John Hus to be burnt, though the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Sigismund had given them a safe conduct; in pursuance of this maxim, "that no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> is to be kept with heretics." They likewise condemned the doctrine of Wickliff, and ordered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> to be burned 40 years after he was dead. However, the inhabitants now are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. It is seated on a lake of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 10. N. Lat. 47. 38. Constance, one of the most considerable and beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, which separates it from Swabia, except that part where the city of Constance is seated on its side. It is divided into three parts; the upper or largest part is called Boden see, the middle Bodmer see, and the lower part Zeller see. The first is 37 miles long, and its greatest breadth 15 miles. It is deeper in summer than in winter. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">Constancy</a>, in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes immutability, or inviability.—In ethics, or when applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> implies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> or steadfastness, particularly under sufferings and the trials of adversity. It was the saying of a heathen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, That there cannot be imagined upon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> a spectacle more worthy the regard of the Creator intent on his works, than a brave man superior to his sufferings. Nothing indeed can be more noble or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> than to have courage enough to execute the commands of reason and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>; to maintain the dignity of our nature, and the station assigned us; and to be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against poverty, pain, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> itself, so far as not to do anything that is scandalous or sinful to avoid them. To be thus, is to be great above <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> or fortune. This argues the foul of a heavenly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, and is worthy the offspring of the Deity. Of this virtue the following example, related in English <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, is here selected, as superior perhaps, all circumstances considered, to any other upon record. Sir William Askew of Kelvay, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, had several daughters. His second, named <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, had received a genteel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; which, with an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> and good understanding, rendered her a very proper person to be at the head of a family. Her father, regardless of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>'s inclination and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, obliged her to marry a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who had nothing to recommend him but his fortune, and who was a most bigotted Papist. No sooner was he convinced of his wife's regard for the doctrines of the reformation from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>, than, by the instigation of his priests, Constancy, priests, he violently drove her from his house, though she had borne him two children, and her conduct was unexceptionable. Abandoned by her husband, she came up to London, in order to procure a divorce, and to make herself known to that part of the court who either professed or were favourers of Protestantism; but as Henry VIII., with consent of parliament, had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> enacted the law of the six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the bloody statute, she was cruelly betrayed by her own husband; and, upon his information, taken into custody, and examined concerning her faith. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> above mentioned denounced death against all those who should deny the doctrine of transubstantiation; or, that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and wine made use of in the sacrament was not converted after consecration into the real body and blood of Christ; or, maintain the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of receiving the sacrament in both kinds; or affirm, that it was lawful for priests to marry; that the vows of celibacy might be broken; that private masses were of no avail; and that auricular confession to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> was not necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>. Upon these articles she was examined by the inquisitor, a priest, the lord-mayor of London, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>; and to all their queries gave proper and pertinent answers; but not being such as they approved, she was sent back to prison, where she remained eleven days to ruminate alone on her alarming situation, and was denied the small consolation of a friendly visit. The king's council being at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, she was once more examined by Chancellor Wriothesley, Gardiner bishop of Winchester, Dr. Cox, and Dr. Robinson; but not being able to convince her of supposed errors, she was sent to the Tower. Mr. Strype, from an authentic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, gives us the following short account of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, which may not, perhaps, be unentertaining or useless to the reader: "Sir Martin Bowes (lord mayor) fitting with the council, as most meet for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and feeling her stand upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and death, I pray you, quoth he, my lords, give me leave to talk to this woman? Leave was granted. Lord Mayor. Thou foolish woman, sayest thou that the priest cannot make the holy body of Christ? A. Askew. I say so, my lord: for I have read that God made man; but that man made God I never read; nor I suppose ever shall read it. Lord Mayor. No! Thou foolish woman, after the words of consecration, is it not the Lord's body? A. Askew. No: it is but consecrated bread, or sacramental bread. Lord Mayor. What if a mouse eat it after consecration; what shall become of this mouse? what sayest thou, thou foolish woman? A. Askew. What shall become of her, say you, my lord? Lord Mayor. I say, that the mouse is damned. A. Askew. Alack, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> mouse!" Perceiving that some could not keep in their laughing, the council proceeded to the butchery and slaughter that they intended before they came there.—It was strongly suspected that Mrs Askew was favoured by some ladies of high <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>; and that she carried on a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> correspondence with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>. So that the chancellor Wriothesley, hoping that he might discover something that would afford <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of impeachment against that princess, the earl of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol10.html#article-HERTFORD">Hertford</a>, or his countess, who all favoured reformation, ordered her to be put to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a>; but her fortitude in suffering, and her resolution not to betray her friends, was proof against that diabolical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. Not a groan, not a word, could be extorted from her. The chancellor, provoked with what he called her obstinacy, augmented her tortures with his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and with unheard-of violence: but her courage and constancy were invincible; and these barbarians gained nothing by their cruelties but everlasting disgrace and infamy. As soon as she was taken from the rack, she fainted away; but being recovered, she was condemned to the flames. Her bones were dislocated in such a manner, that they were forced to carry her in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> to the place of execution. While she was at the stake, letters were brought her from the lord chancellor, offering her the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> if she would recant. But she refused to look at them; telling the messenger, that "she came not thither to deny her Lord and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>." The same letters were also tendered to three other persons condemned to the same fate; and who, animated by her example, refused to accept them. Whereupon the lord-mayor commanded the fire to be kindled; and with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> ignorance cried out, Fiat justitia, "Let justice take its course." The faggots being lighted, she commended her <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> with the utmost composure, into the hands of her Maker; and, like the great founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> she professed, expired, praying for her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 16, 1546, about the 25th year of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

CONSTANTIA

Pages 196-197

a district at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, consisting of two farms, which produce the well-known wine so much prized in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and known by the name of Cape <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Constantia wine. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is situated at the distance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half from Alphen, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> formed by and nearly under the ridge of hills, which comes from Meutzenmountain, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> where it strikes off towards Houtbay. One of these farms is called Little Constantia. Here the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> Constantia wine is made. The other produces the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. According to M. de la Cail's account, not more than 60 fuggars of red, and 90 of the white, Constantia wine are made, each fuggar being reckoned at 600 French pints, or about 150 Swedish cans; so that the whole produce amounts to 22,500 cans. As the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> are used to keep one-third of this for themselves, the remainder is always bespoken by the Europeans <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before it is made. At the Cape this wine is seldom seen at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, partly because it is dear, and partly because it is the produce of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The red Constantia wine sells for about 60 dollars the half a wine; but the white is usually to be purchased at a more reasonable rate. The genuine Constantia wine is undeniably a very racy and delicate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESSERT">dessert</a> wine, and has something peculiarly agreeable in the flavour of it. That its superiority, however, is not owing to anything peculiar in the manner of preparing it, seems extremely probable; for then, without doubt, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> more of it would be made. In fact, Dr. Sparmann informs us, that the genuine wine can only be produced from particular soils. The districts that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> next to these yield merely the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> Cape wine, notwithstanding that they have been planted with vine stocks taken from this, as well as with some brought from the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, whence it is supposed that the true Constantia first originally comes; nay, even though all the vineyards about Constantia seem to have the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. We have instances at the Cape, as well as in Europe, that good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> sometimes produce a bad wine; while, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, bad grapes <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> yield a good sort of wine: therefore, towards making wine of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, besides finer materials, there must be certain conditions and circumstances, which, by a diligent and rational <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, might probably be explored to the great benefit of mankind. Such as are apprised in what quantities Constantia wine is consumed in Europe, will perhaps think the above calculation of the produce too limited. This, however, Dr. Sparrmann affirms us, is by no means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; the overplus being the produce of avarice, which, goaded on by the desire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>, will always <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> upon some method of satisfying the demands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and sensuality. The votaries of these, accustomed to be put off with empty sounds, do not seldom drink with the highest relish an imaginary Constantia, with which, however, this liquor has nothing in common besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> name. It is therefore advisable, even at the Cape itself, to take care, that whilst one has a genuine sample given one to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, one is not made to pay for a made-up red Constantia, which otherwise is in general sold for half the price. The rich quality of this wine, is, according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>, owing partly to the situation and soil, and partly to the care in the manufacture; for ripe fruit only is used, and always entirely freed from the stalks.

CONSTANTINA

Pages 197-197

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a small territory of the same name, with a castle seated on a mountain. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 35. N. Lat. 27. 40.

CONSTANTINE

Pages 197-198
emperor of the East in 1002, left the care of the empire to his wife Helena, who loaded the people with taxes, and sold all the offices in church and state to the highest bidders; while the emperor employed himself in reading, writing, and the fine arts, till he became as good an architect and painter as he was a bad prince; he wrote several biographical and geographical works, which would have done honour to his name, if he had not neglected his duty to compose them. He died in 959. Constantine Dracopius, the son of Emmanuel Palaeologus, was placed on the throne by Sultan Amurath in 1448. But Mahomet II., his successor, refusing to dethrone him, laid siege to Constantinople by sea and land, and took it by assault in 1453; after it had held out 58 days. The unfortunate emperor seeing the Turks enter the breaches, threw himself into the midst of the enemy, and was cut to pieces; the children of the imperial house were massacred by the soldiers; and the women referred to gratify the lust of the conqueror; and thus terminated the dynasty of the Constantines, 1123 years after its establishment at Constantinople. Constantine Robert, a learned physician, born at Caen, taught polite literature in that city; and acquired great reputation by his skill in the Greek language, in history, and in medicine. He died in 1603, aged 103. He wrote a dictionary in Greek and Latin, and other works, which are esteemed.

CONSTANTINOPLE

Pages 198-220

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Byzantium in Thrace. It was enlarged and beautified by the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, in the year 330. At the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he transferred thither the seat of the empire; and this removal is generally thought to have been one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> causes of the sudden decline of the western empire after this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. In the year 332, the Sarmatians implored Constantine's affiance against the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, who had made an irruption into their territories, and destroyed everything with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The emperor readily granted their request, and gained a complete victory. Near 100,000 of the enemy perished, either in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> after it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this overthrow, the Goths were obliged to sue for peace; but the ungrateful Sarmatians no sooner found themselves delivered from their enemies, than they turned their arms against their benefactor, and ravaged the provinces of Moesia and Thrace. The emperor, receiving intelligence of this treachery, returned with incredible expedition, cut great numbers of them in pieces, and obliged the rest to submit to what terms he was pleased to impose. Constantine seems to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> very highly respected, even by far distant nations. In 333, according to Eusebius, ambassadors arrived at Constantinople from the Blemyes, Indians, Ethiopians, and Persians, courting his friendship. They were received in a most obliging manner; and learning from the ambassadors of Sapor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, that there were great numbers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s dominions, Constantine wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> in their behalf to the Persian monarch. Next year, the Sarmatians being again attacked by the Goths, found themselves obliged to set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and arm their slaves against them. By this means they indeed overcame the Goths; but the victorious slaves <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> their arms against their masters, drove them out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. This misfortune obliged them, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 300,000, to apply for relief to the Roman emperor, who incorporated with his legions such as were capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; and gave settlements to the rest in Thrace, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>, Macedon, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. This was the last remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of Constantine the Great. He died on May 15, 337, having divided the empire among his children and nephews, Constantine in the following manner. Constantine, his eldest son, had <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; Constantius, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, had <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; and Constans, the youngest, Illyricum, Italy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. To his nearest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, Phewel Dalmatius, he gave Thrace, Macedon, and divided Achaia; and to King Annibalianus, his other nephew, son of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, Pontus, Cappadocia, and the city of Cesarea, which he desired might be the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. After the death of Constantine, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> proclaimed his three sons emperors, without any notice of his two nephews, who were soon after murdered, with Julius Constantius the late emperors <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, and all their friends and adherents, and two Thus the family of Constantine was at once reduced nephews, to his three sons, and two nephews <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLUS">Gallus</a> and Julian, the sons of Julius Constantius; and of these the former owed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to a malady, from which no one thought he could recover; and the latter to his infancy, being then at most about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The three brothers divided among themselves the dominions of the deceased princes; but did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> agree together. In 340, Constantine having in vain solicited Constans to yield <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Italy to him, raised a considerable army; and under pretence of marching to the assistance of his brother Constantius, who was then at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Persians, made himself master of several places in Italy. Hereupon Constans detached part of his army against him; and Constantine, being drawn into an ambuscade near Aquileia, was cut off with his whole forces. His body was thrown into the river Adra; but being afterwards discovered, was sent to Constantinople, and interred there near the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of his father. By the defeat and death of his brother, Constans remained sole master of all the western part of the empire, in the quiet possession of which he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the year 350. This year Magnentius, the son of one Magnus-Magnus, a native of Germany, finding Constans deposed revolts spilted by the army on account of his indolence and inactivity, resolved to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> him, and let up for him. Having found means to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officers of the army to his designs, he seized on the Imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUTUN">Autun</a>, and distributed among the populace what sums he found there; which induced not only the city, but the neighbouring country, to espouse his cause. But Constans being informed of what had passed, and finding himself unable to resist the usurper, fled towards Spain. He was overtaken, however, by Gaio, whom Magnentius had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> after him with a chosen body of troops, and despatched with many wounds, at Helena, a small village situated near the foot of the Pyrenees. Thus Constantius acquired a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the whole Roman empire; though one-half of it was seized by Magnentius after the murder of Constans. The former had been engaged in a war with the Persians, in which little advantage was gained on either side; but the Persians now giving no more disturbance, the emperor marched against the usurpers in the west. Besides Magnentius, there were at that time two other pretenders to the western empire. Veteranio, general of the foot in Pannonia, had, on the first news of the empire, the death of Constans, caused himself to be proclaimed emperor by the legions under his command. He was a native of Upper Maesia, and advanced in years when he usurped the sovereignty; but so illiterate, that he then first learned to read. The third pretender was Flavius Popilius Nepotianus, son of Europia, the sister of Constantine the Great. Having assembled a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of gladiators and men of desperate fortunes, he assumed the purple on the 3rd of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 350, and in that attire presented himself before the gates of Rome. The prefect Anicetus, who commanded there for Magnentius, fell out against him with a body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who were soon driven back into the city. Soon Nepotianus made himself master of the city itself, which he filled with blood and slaughter. Magnentius being informed of what had happened, sent against this new competitor his chief favourite and prime minister Marcellinus. Nepotianus received him with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; a bloody battle ensued between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of Magnentius and the Romans who had espoused the cause of Nepotianus; but the latter being betrayed by a senator, named Heraclitus, his men were put to flight, and he himself killed, after having enjoyed the sovereignty only 28 days. Marcellinus ordered his head to be carried on the point of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a> through the principal streets of the city; put to death all those who had declared for him; and under pretence of preventing disturbances, commanded a general massacre of all the relations of Constantine. Soon after, Magnentius himself came to Rome, to make the necessary preparations for resisting Constantius, who was exerting himself to the utmost in order to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the death of his brother. In the city he behaved most tyrannically, putting to death many persons of distinction, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> their estates; and obliged the rest to contribute half of what they were worth towards the expense of the war. Having by this means raised great sums, he assembled a mighty army composed of Romans, Germans, Gauls, Franks, Britons, Spaniards, &c. At the same time, however, dreading the uncertain issues of war, he dispatched ambassadors to Constantius with proposals of accommodation.
