in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the name of a certificate which the clerk of the pipe and auditors of the exchequer make at the request of any person who intends to plead <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> move in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> for the discharge of any thing; and the effect of it is, the certifying what does confirme upon record touching the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in question. A constat is held to be superior to a certificate; because this may err or fail in its contents; that cannot, as certifying nothing but what is evident upon record. Also the exemplification under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the enrolment of any letters patent is called a constat.

CONSTELLATION

Pages 221-221

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a system of several stars that are seen in the heavens near to one another. Astronomers not only mark out the stars, but, that they may better bring them into order, they distinguish them by their situation and position in respect to each other; and therefore they distribute them into asterisms <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>, allowing several stars to make up one constellation: and for the better distinguishing and observing them, they reduce the constellations to the forms of animals, as men, bulls, bears, &c.; or to the images of some things known, as of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>, &c.; or give them the names of those whole memories, in consideration of some notable exploit, they had a mind to transmit to future ages. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the stars by images and figures is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, and seems to be as old as astronomy itself: for in the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> book of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORION">Orion</a>, Arcturus, and the Pleiades, are mentioned; and we meet with the names of many of the constellations in the writings of the first poets, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, in their division of the firmament, took in only so much as came under their notice, distributing it into 48 constellations; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> astronomers comprehend the whole starry firmament, dividing it into three regions. See Astronomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CONSTERNATION is defined by ethical writers to be an excess of horror, owing to the ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of our admiration and fear: or such an immoderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fear as confounds the faculties, and incapacitates a person for consultation and execution.

CONSTIPATION

Pages 221-221

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the belly, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> coliciveness. See Costiveness.

CONSTITUENT PART

Pages 221-221

in Physiology, an essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of any thing, differing little from what is otherwise called element <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> principle.

CONSTITUTION

Pages 221-221

in a physical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies the particular temperature of the body. It is curious to observe, says Dr Percival, the revolution which hath taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, within this century, in the constitutions of the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Inflammatory diseases more rarely occur, and, in general, are much less rapid and violent in their progress than formerly (a); nor do they admit of the same antiphlogistic method of cure that was practised with success 100 years ago. The experienced Sydenham makes 40 ounces of blood the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> to be drawn in the acute rheumatism; whereas this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, as it now appears in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not bear above half that evacuation. Vernal intermittents are frequently cured by a vomit and the bark, without venefiction; which is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that at present they are accompanied with fewer symptoms of inflammation than they were wont to be. This advantageous change, however, is more than counterbalanced by the introduction of a numerous class of nervous ailments, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> unknown to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>; but which now prevail universally, and are complicated with almost every other distemper. The bodies of men are enfeebled and enervated; and it is not uncommon to observe very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRRITABILITY">irritability</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance of great strength and robustness. The hypochondria, palus, cachexies, dropsies, and all those diseases which arise from laxity and debility, are in our days endemic everywhere; and the hysterics, which used to be peculiar to the women, as the name itself indicates, now attack both sexes indiscriminately. It is evident that so great a revolution could not be effected without a concurrence of many causes; but amongst these (according to Dr Percival), the present general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> * holds the first and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> * See Tea <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> place may perhaps be allowed to excess in spirituous liquors. This pernicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, in many instances at least, owes its rise to the former, which, by the lowness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> of spirits it occasions, renders it almost necessary to have recourse to something cordial and exhilarating. And hence proceed those odious and disgraceful habits of intemperance, with which many of the softer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> are now, alas! chargeable.

CONSTITUTION ALSO

Pages 221-221

N also denotes an ordinance, decision, regulation, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, made by authority of any superior, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> or civil. Apotropical Constitutions, a collection of regulations attributed to the Apostles, and supposed to have been collected by St Clement, whose name they likewise bear. It is the general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, however, that they are spurious, and that St Clement had no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in them. They appeared first in the 4th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, but have been much changed and corrupted since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They are divided into eight books, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of rules and precepts, relating to the duties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and particularly the ceremonies and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Mr Whiston, in opposition to the general opinion, affirms them to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sacred writings, dictated by the Apostles in their meetings, and written <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from their own mouth by St Clement; and intended as a supplement to the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, or rather as a system of Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and polity. The reason why the Constitutions are suspected by the orthodox, and perhaps the reason also why their genuineness is defended by Mr Whiston, is, that they seem to favour Arianism.

CONSTRUCTION

Pages 222-222

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNTAX">syntax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the arranging and connecting the words of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> according to the rules of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. See Grammar and Language. The construction is generally more simple, easy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> tongues than in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>: we have very few of those inversions which occasion so much embarrassment and obscurity in the Latin; our thoughts are usually delivered in the same order wherein the imagination conceives them: the nominative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, for instance, always precedes the verb, and the verb goes before the oblique <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> it governs. The Greeks and Latins, M. St Evremont observes, usually end their periods, where, in good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and reason, they should have begun; and the elegance of their language consists, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, in this capricious arrangement, or rather in this transposal and disorder of the words. See Language. CONSTRUCTION of Statutes, among lawyers. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CONSTRUCTOR

Pages 221-221

an appellation given to several muscles, (a) The decrease in the violence of inflammatory diseases may perhaps in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> be ascribed to the present improved method of treating them. Moderate evacuations, cool <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, acidulent diet, and the liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of saline and antimonial medicines, are better adapted to check the progress of fevers, than copious bleedings, stimulating purgatives, and profuse sweats excited by theriaca and mithridate.

CONSUALIA

Pages 222-222

in antiquity, feasts which were held among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the god Confus i.e. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>; different from those other feasts of the same deity called Neptunalia. They were introduced with a magnificent cavalcade, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> on horseback; because Neptune was reputed to have first taught men the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of horses; whence his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Ixius, Eques. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVANDER">Evander</a> is said to have first instituted this feast: it was re-established by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, under the name of Confus; because it was some god under the denomination of Confus that suggested to him the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> of the Sabines. It is said, that it was with a view to this rape that he made that establishment. This, however, is certain, that it was to this feast all his neighbours were invited; when, taking advantage of the solemnities and sacrifices, he seized the women. To draw the greater concourse of people, he gave out, that he had found an altar hid under ground, which he intended to consecrate, with sacrifices to the god to whom it had been originally erected. Those who take upon them to explain the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the heathen <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, say, that the altar hid under ground is a symbol of the secret <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of Romulus to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> his neighbours wives. The confusalia were of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of feasts called sacred; as being consecrated to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>.—Originally they were not distinguished from those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>; whence it is, that Valerius Maximus says, that the rape of the Sabines was effected at the games of the circus. Plutarch observes, that during the days of this solemnity, horses and asses were left at rest, and were dressed up with crowns, &c., on account of its being the feast of Neptunus Eques. Festus says, the cavalcade was performed with mules; it being an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that this was the first animal used to draw the car. Servius gives us to understand, that the confusalia fell on the 13th of August; Plutarch, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Romulus, placed them on the 18th, and the old Roman <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> on the 21st of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>.

CONSUBSTANTIAL

Pages 222-222

in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of like import with co-essential; denoting something of the same substance with another. The orthodox believe the Son of God to be consubstantial with the Father. The term ἁρμονίας, consubstantial, was first adopted by the fathers of the councils of Antioch and Nice, to express the orthodox doctrine more precisely, and to serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> and precaution against the errors and subtleties of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>; who owned every thing excepting the consubstantiality. The Arians allowed, that the word was God, as having been made God; but they denied that he was the same God, and of the same substance with the Father: accordingly they exerted themselves to the utmost to abolish the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the word. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine used all his authority with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> to have it expunged out of the symbols; but it still maintained itself, and is at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, as it was then, the distinguishing criterion between an Athanasian and an Arian. Sandius <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, that the word consubstantial was unknown till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice; but it is certain it had been before propounded to the council of Antioch, wherein Paulus Samotracenus had been condemned; though it had there the fortune to be rejected. Curcellius, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, maintains that it was an innovation in doctrine in the council of Nice, to admit an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, the use whereof had been abolished by the council of Antioch. According to St Athanasius, the word consubstantial was only condemned in the council of Antioch, inasmuch as it implied the idea of a pre-existent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the things formed thereof; now, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, it is certain, the Father and the Son are not consubstantial, there having been no pre-existent matter.

CONSUBSTANTIATION

Pages 222-222

a tenet of the Lutheran <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> with regard to the manner of the change made in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and wine in the eucharist. The divines of that profession maintain, that after consecration, the body and blood of our Saviour are substantially present, together with the substance of the bread and wine, which is called consubstantiation, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> impetration.

CONSUL

Pages 222-223

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of the Roman commonwealth, invested with regal authority for the space of one year. They were two in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, called consuls a confundendo, and annually chosen in the Campus Martius. The two first consuls were L. Jun. Brutus, and L. Tarquinius Collatinus, chosen in the year of Rome 244, after the expulsion of the Tarquins. In the first times of the republic the two consuls were always chosen from patrician families <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> noblemen, but the people obtained the privilege in the year of Rome 388, of electing one of the consuls from their own body, and sometimes both were plebeians. The first consul among the plebeians was L. Sextius. It was required that every candidate for the consulship should be 43 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, called legitimum tempus. He was always to appear at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> as a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> without a retinue, Consul. retinue, and it was requisite before he canvassed for the office to have discharged the functions of quaestor, edile, and praetor. Sometimes these qualifications were disregarded. Val. Corvinus was made a consul in his 23rd year, and Scipio in his 24th. Young Marius, Pompey, and Augustus, were also under the proper age, when they were invested with the office, and Pompey had never been quaestor or praetor. The power of the consuls was unbounded, and they knew no superior but the gods and the laws; but after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of their office their conduct was minutely scrutinized by the people, and misbehaviour was often punished by the laws. The badge of their office was the praetexta, a robe fringed with purple, afterwards exchanged for the toga picta or palmata. They were preceded by 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICTORS">lictors</a> carrying the fasces or bundles of sticks, in the middle of which appeared an axe. The axe, as being the characteristic rather of tyranny than of freedom, was taken away from the fasces by Valerius Poplicola, but it was restored by his successor. They took it by turns monthly to be preceded by the lictors while at Rome, lest the appearance of two persons with the badges of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> authority should raise apprehensions in the multitude. While one appeared publicly in state, only a crier walked before the other, and the lictors followed behind without the fasces. Their authority was equal; yet the Valerian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> gave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of priority to the older, and the Julian law to him who had most children; and he was generally called consul <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a>. As their power was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, they presided over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and could convene and dismiss it at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The senators were their counsellors; and among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> the manner of reckoning their years was by the name of the consuls, and by M. Tull. Cicerone et L. Antonio Consulibus, for instance, the year of Rome 689 was always understood. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> lasted from the year of Rome 244 till the 1294, or 541st year of the Christian era. In public assemblies the consuls sat in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> chairs, and held in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> an ivory wand called scipio eburneus, which had an eagle on its top as a sign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and power. When they had drawn by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> the provinces over which they were to preside during their consulship, they went to the capitol to offer their prayers to the gods, and intreat them to protect the republic; after this they departed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> arrayed in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> dress and preceded by the lictors. Sometimes the provinces were assigned them without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> by lot, by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> and appointment of the senators. At their departure they were provided by the state with whatever was requisite during their expedition. In their provinces they were both attended by the 12 lictors, and equally invested with regal authority. They were not permitted to return to Rome without the special command of the senate; and they always remained in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> till the arrival of their successor. At their return they harangued the people, and solemnly protested that they had done nothing against the laws or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but had faithfully and diligently endeavoured to promote the greatness and welfare of the state. No man could be consul two following years; yet this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> was sometimes broken, and we find Marius re-elected consul after the expiration of his office during the Cimbrian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The office of consul, so dignified during the times of the commonwealth, became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> under the emperors, and retained nothing of its authority but the useless ensigns of original dignity. Even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the office, which was originally annual, was reduced to two or three months by J. Caesar; but they who were admitted on the first of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> denominated the year, and were called ordinarii. Their successors during the year were distinguished by the name of suffecti. Tiberius and Claudius abridged the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the consulship; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Commodus made no less than 25 consuls in one year. Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> renewed the original institution, and permitted them to be a whole year in office. Consul, at present, is an officer established by virtue of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and other princes, in all foreign countries of any considerable trade, to facilitate and dispatch business, and protect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. The consuls are to keep up a correspondence with the ministers of England residing in the courts whereon their consulate depends. They are to support the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and the interest of the nation; to dispose of the sums given and the presents made to the lords and principals of places, to obtain their protection, and prevent the insults of the natives on the merchants of the nation.

CONSUMMATION

Pages 223-223

the end, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> completion of any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Thus, we say, the consummation of all things, meaning the end of the world. By the incarnation, all the prophecies are said to be consummated. See Prophecy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">Accomplishment</a>. Consummation of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a>, denotes the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of marriage, which makes its accomplishment; or the most intimate union between the married <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>, &c.

CONSUMPTION

Pages 223-223

in Medicine, a word of very extensive signification, implies all disorders that bring any decay <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> waste upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; but is most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used for the phthisis pulmonalis. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Consumption, in Farriery. See Farriery Index.

CONSUS

Pages 223-223

the pagan god of counsel. He had an altar under ground in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> at Rome, to show that counsel ought to be kept secret. See Consualia.

CONTACT

Pages 223-223

is when one line, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> body, is made to touch another; and the parts that do thus touch are called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or places of contact.

CONTAGION

Pages 223-225

in Physic, the communicating a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> from one body to another. In some diseases it is only effected by an immediate contact <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> touch, as in syphilis; in others it is conveyed by infected clothes; and in others it is supposed to be transmitted through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> at a considerable distance, by means of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> or effluvia arising from the sick, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> and other pestilential disorders, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the air is said to be contagious, though this has been disputed. No attempts which have yet been made to investigate the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of contagion, or to ascertain the properties of contagious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, have proved successful. But from the means which have been effectually employed either to abate its virulence or to destroy it entirely, this matter may be fairly inferred to be of a chemical nature. We have already detailed the effects of the fumes of muriatic acid in purifying the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Dijon, which were successfully used by Morveau in 1773. Pursuing this hint, no doubt, Dr Carmichael Smyth proposed the fumes of nitric acid. This was tried on board different ships at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a> about the year 1796; and being found to answer the purpose of destroying the contagion which then prevailed, Dr Smyth afterwards received a liberal reward from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> for his discovery. These experiments were conducted on board the Union <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> ship by Mr Macnies surgeon of the Discovery, and Mr Baffin surgeon of the Union. The wards at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> were very much crowded with patients; and of 200 sick on board, 150 were in different stages of a malignant, contagious fever, which made a very rapid progress, and produced very fatal effects on the attendants and ship's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. The materials and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> were the following: A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fine sand, two dozen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a> earthen pipkins, as many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-cups, some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> flaps of glass to be used as spatulas, a quantity of concentrated sulphuric acid, and a quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a> (nitrate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>). The process was conducted in the following manner: 1st. All the ports and scuttles were shut up; the sand, previously heated in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> pots, was scooped out into the pipkins with an iron ladle; and in this heated sand, in each pipkin, a small tea-cup was immersed, containing about half an ounce of sulphuric acid, to which, after it had acquired a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, an equal quantity of nitrate of potash in powder was gradually added, and the mixture stirred with a glass spatula till the vapour arose from it in considerable quantity. The pipkins were then carried through the wards by the nurses and convalescents, who kept walking about with them in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, occasionally putting them under the cradles of the sick, and in every corner where any foul air was suspected to lodge. In this manner they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> fumigating, until the whole space between decks, fore and aft, was filled with the vapour, which appeared like a thick haze. The vapour at first excited coughing among the patients, which gradually ceased as it became more generally diffused through the wards: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this effect, however, was to be attributed to the inattention of those who carried the pipkins, in putting them too near the faces of the sick; which caused them to inhale the strong vapour as it immediately issued from the cups. The body-clothes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-clothes of the sick were, as much as possible, exposed to the nitrous vapour during the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUMIGATION">fumigation</a>; and all the foul <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> removed from them was immediately immersed in a tub of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, afterwards carried on deck, rinsed out, and hung up till nearly dry, and then fumigated before it was taken to the wash-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; a precaution extremely necessary in every case of infectious disorder. Proper <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was also paid to cleanliness and ventilation. Three hours were at first found necessary to fumigate the ship. In about an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after, the vapour having entirely subsided, the ports and scuttles were thrown open for the admission of fresh air. It could plainly be perceived that the air of the hospital was greatly sweetened even after this first fumigation. The process was repeated again next morning; and the people employed, being now more expert, finished the whole in about an hour's time. In an hour afterwards, the vapour having entirely subsided, the fresh air was freely admitted into the hospital as before. Fewer pipkins were employed for the evening fumigations than for those of the mornings, as the fresh air could not be admitted so freely after the former as the latter. The pleasing and immediate effect of the fumigation in destroying the offensive and disagreeable smell, arising from so many sick crowded together, was now very perceptible, even to the attendants; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which was, that they began to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> some degree of confidence in its efficacy, and approached the cradles of the infected with less dread of being attacked with the disorder: thus the sick were better attended, and the duty of the hospital was more regularly and more cheerfully performed. From the 26th of November 1795, when the fumigation was first reported to, till the 25th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, not a person on board was attacked with the fever, though, in the three months preceding, more than one third of all the people in the ship had been seized with the distemper, and of these more than one in four were carried off by it; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> is, that the sicknesses and mortality would have gone on, increasing in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of the contagion, and to the increasing despondency of the people, who considered themselves as so many devoted victims. The advantage of the fumigation was not felt by the ship's company and attendants alone, whom it prevented from the baneful effects of the fever: the sick and convalescents derived almost an equal benefit from it. The symptoms of the disease became milder, and lost much of their malignant appearance; and the advantage of a pure and sweet air to convalescents must be obvious. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> confidence is always dangerous. It proved so on the present occasion. On the 17th of December they imagined themselves so secure, that they discontinued the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of fumigating morning and evening, thinking that once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> was sufficient. On the 25th, one of the nurses suffered a flight attack; and on the 26th a marine, who, for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> before, had been in a state of intoxication, was seized with the fever, and died. These two accidents gave immediate alarm; they returned again to the practice of fumigating twice a day; and from that time to the extermination of the disorder, there was not an instance of a person suffering from contagion on board the ship. The success of the experiment was not confined to the Union: the power of the nitrous vapour to destroy contagion was equally displayed on board some Russian ships then in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWNS">Downs</a>. The safety, too, with which it may be employed, in any situation, without inconvenience or risk of fire, is another great recommendation in its favour. It <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be difficult from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> to employ this kind of fumigation. It is only necessary to observe, for the sake of those who may not be versant in chemical pursuits, that the ingredients ought to be pure, and neither metal vessels nor rods should be used. Any kind of metal getting among the ingredients would cause the vapour to be very noxious instead of salutary. The fumes that rise should be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, there is reason to suspect the purity of the ingredients. The importance of this discovery need not be insisted on; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">Contemplation</a>: it is equally applicable to every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of putrid contagion, even to the plague itself. It should therefore be used in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> workhouses; and should be constantly referred to by the proprietors of all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> works, on the first appearance of infectious disease among the people employed in them:—indeed, it should be employed even as a preventive in all situations where a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people, from the nature of their business, are obliged to be crowded together, or where, from local circumstances, there are reasons for suspecting that the purity of the air is injured by noxious exhalations or other causes. If there be any circumstances in which its utility may be called in question, it can only be in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of inflammatory diseases: for, in such, super-oxygenation has been found hurtful.

CONTEMPLATION

Pages 225-225

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the mind, whereby it applies itself to consider and reflect upon the works of God, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, &c.

CONTEMPORARY

Pages 225-225
or CONTEMPORARY, a person or thing that existed in the same age with another. Thus, Socrates, Plato, and Aristophanes, were contemporaries.

CONTEMPT

Pages 225-225

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a disobedience to the rules and orders of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, which hath power to punish such offence; and as this is sometimes a greater, and sometimes a lesser offence, so it is punished with greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, by fine, and sometimes by imprisonment.

CONTENT

Pages 225-225

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> or space included in certain bounds.

CONTESSA

Pages 225-225

a port-town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, situated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the Archipelago, about 200 miles west of Constantinople. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25° O. N. Lat. 41° O.

CONTEXT

Pages 225-225

among divines and critics, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Scripture <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> which lies above the text, before or after it, or both. To take the full and genuine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the text, the context should be regarded.

CONTEXTURE

Pages 225-225

a word frequently used in speaking both of the works of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art; and denoting the disposition and union of the constituent parts with respect to one another.

CONTI

Pages 225-225

a town of Picardy in France, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality. It is seated on the river Seille, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 17' N. Lat. 49° 54'.

CONTIGUOUS

Pages 225-225

a relative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> understood of things disposed so near each other, that they join their surfaces, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> touch. The houses in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome were not contiguous as ours are, but all insulated.

CONTINENCE

Pages 225-227

in Ethics, a moral virtue, by which we resist concupiscence. It should seem that there is this distinction between chastity and continence, in that it requires no effort to be chaste, which results from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; whereas continence appears to be the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a victory gained over ourselves. The verb continere, in the Latin, signifies "to restrain." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, however, is most usually applied to men; as chastity is to women. See CHASTITY. Continence is a virtue that makes but an inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in our days. However, we ought not to lose our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of things, though we have debauched our true relish in our practice: for, after all, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> virtue <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> keep its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the wise and sensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of mankind. And though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> has not made it so scandalous as it ought to be to infame innocent women, and triumph in the filthiness; such actions as we shall relate must be accounted true gallantry, and rise higher in our esteem the farther they are removed from our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. 1. Scipio the younger, when only 24 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was appointed by the Roman republic to the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> against the Spaniards. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and valour would have done <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the most experienced general. Determined to strike an important blow, he formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of besieging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>, then the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Carthaginian empire in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> were so judiciously concerted, and with so much courage and intrepidity pursued, both by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, that notwithstanding a bold and vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, the capital was taken by storm. The plunder was immense. Ten thousand free-men were made prisoners; and above 300 more, of both sexes, were received as hostages. One of the latter, a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> lady, the wife of Mandonius, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Indibilis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Ilergetes, watching her opportunity, came out of the crowd, and throwing herself at the conqueror's feet, conjured him, with tears in her eyes, to recommend to those who had the ladies in their keeping to have regard to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> and birth. Scipio, who did not understand her meaning at first, assured her that he had given orders that they should not want for anything. But the lady replied, "Those conveniences are not what affect us. In the condition to which fortune hath reduced us, with what ought we not to be contented! I have many other apprehensions, when I consider, on one side, the licentiousness of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and on the other, the youth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the princesses which you see here before us; for as to me, my age protects me from all fear in this respect." She had with her the daughters of Indibilis, and several other ladies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, all in the flower of youth, who considered her as their mother. Scipio then comprehending what the subject of her fear was, "My own <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> (says he), and that of the Roman people, are concerned in not suffering that virtue, which ought always to be respected wherever we find it, should be exposed in my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> to a treatment unworthy of it. But you give me a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> for being more strict in my care of it, in the virtuous solicitude you show in thinking only of the preservation of your honour, in the midst of so many other objects of fear." After this conversation, he committed the care of the ladies to some officers of experienced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, strictly commanding that they should treat them with all the respect they could pay to the mothers, wives, and daughters, of their allies and particular friends. It was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before Scipio's integrity and virtue were put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. Being retired in his camp, some of his officers brought him a young virgin of such exquisite beauty, that she drew upon her the eyes and admiration of everybody. The young conqueror started from his seat with confusion and surprise; and, like one thunderstruck, seemed to be robbed of that presence of mind and self-possession so necessary in a general, and for which Continence, which Scipio was remarkably famous. In a few moments, having rallied his straggling spirits, he inquired of the beautiful captive, in the most civil and polite manner, concerning her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, birth, and connections; and finding that she was betrothed to a Celtiberian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> named Allucius, he ordered both him and the captive's parents to be sent for. The Spanish prince no sooner appeared in his presence, than, even before he spoke to the father and mother, he took him aside; and, to remove the anxiety he might be in on account of the young lady, he addressed him in these words: "You and I are young, which admits of my speaking to you with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Those who brought me your future spouse, assured me, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that you loved her with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> tenderness; and her beauty left me no room to doubt it. Upon which reflecting, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, like you, I had thought on making an engagement, and were not wholly engrossed with the affairs of my country, I should desire that so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> and legitimate a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> should find favour, I think myself happy in the present conjuncture to do you this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Though the fortune of war has made me your <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, I desire to be your friend. Here is your wife: take her, and may the gods bless you with her. One thing, however, I would have you be fully assured of, that she has been amongst us as would have been in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of her father and mother. Far be it from Scipio to purchase a loose and momentary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> at the expense of virtue, honour, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of an honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. No; I have kept her for you, in order to make you a present worthy of you and of me. The only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> I require of you for this ineffable gift is, that you would be a friend to the Roman people." Allucius's heart was too full to make him any answer; but throwing himself at the general's feet, he wept aloud. The captive lady fell into the same posture; and remained so, till the father burst out into the following words: "Oh! divine Scipio! the gods have given you more than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> virtue! Oh! glorious leader! Oh! wondrous youth! does not that obliged virgin give you, while she prays to the gods for your prosperity, raptures above all the transports you could have reaped from the possession of her injured person?" The relations of the young lady had brought with them a very considerable sum for her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>; but when they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that she was restored to them in so generous and godlike a manner, they intreated the conqueror, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> earnestness, to accept that sum as a present; and declared, by his complying, that new favour would complete their joy and gratitude. Scipio, not being able to refuse such warm and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> solicitation, told them that he accepted the gift; and ordered it to be laid at his feet; then addressing himself to Allucius, "I add (says he) to the portion which you are to receive from your father-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> this sum; which I desire you to accept as a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>-present." If we consider that Scipio was at this time in the prime of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, unmarried, and under no restraint, we cannot but acknowledge, that the conquest he made of himself was far more glorious than that of the Carthaginian empire: and though his treatment of this captive prince was not more delicate and generous than what might justly be expected from a person endowed with reason and reflection; yet conferring how few there are in his circumstances who would have acted as he did, we cannot but applaud his conduct, and propose him as a suitable example to future ages. Nor was his virtue unrewarded. The young prince, charmed with the liberality and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> of Scipio, went into his country to publish the praises of so generous a victor. He cried out, in the transports of his gratitude, "That there was come into Spain a young <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> like the gods; who conquered all things less by the force of his arms than the charms of his virtue and the greatness of his beneficence." Upon this report all Celtiberia submitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and Allucius returned in a shout to Scipio, at the head of 1400 chosen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, to facilitate his future conquests. To render the marks of his gratitude still more durable, Allucius caused the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> we have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> related to be engraved on a silver shield, which he presented to Scipio, a present infinitely more estimable and glorious than all his treasures and triumphs. The buckler, which Scipio carried with him when he returned to Rome, was lost, in passing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, with part of the baggage. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in that river till the year 1665, when some fishermen found it. It was, before the revolution, in the king of France's cabinet. 2. The circumstance which raises Alexander the Great above many conquerors, and, as it were, above himself, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> he made of his victory after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISSUS">Issus</a>. This is the most beautiful incident in his life. It is the point of view in which it is his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to be considered; and it is impossible for him not to appear truly great in that view. By the victory of Issus he became possessed of the whole Persian empire; not only Syagambis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>'s mother, was his captive, but also his wife and daughters, princesses whose beauty was not to be equalled in all <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Alexander, like Scipio, was in the bloom of life, a conqueror, free, and not yet engaged in matrimony; nevertheless, his camp was to those princesses a sacred <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather a temple, in which their chastity was secured as under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of virtue itself; and so highly revered, that Darius, in his expiring moments, hearing the kind treatment they had met with, could not help lifting up his dying <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> towards heaven, and wishing success to his wife and generous a conqueror, who could govern his passions at so critical a time. Plutarch informs us more particularly, that the princesses lived so retired in the camp, according to their own desire, that they were not seen by any person except their own attendants; nor did any other person dare to approach their apartments. After the first visit, which was a respectful and ceremonious one, Alexander, to avoid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> himself to the dangers of human frailty, made a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> never to visit Darius's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> any more. He himself informs us of this memorable circumstance, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> written by him to Parmenio, in which he commanded him to put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> certain Macedonians who had forced the wives of some foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. In this letter was the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAGRAPH">paragraph</a>: "For as to myself, it will be found that I neither saw nor would see the wife of Darius; and did not suffer any one to speak of her beauty before me." 3. Hecatæus informs us, that Nicocles, king of Salamin, gloried in never having known any woman besides Continence, sides his wife; and was amazed that all other contracts of civil <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> should be treated with due regard, whilst that of marriage, the most sacred and inviolable of obligations, was broken through with impunity; and that men should not blush to commit an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> with respect to their wives, of which, should their wives be guilty, it would throw them into the utmost anguish and fury. 4. Henry VI., king of England, though unhappy in his family and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, was nevertheless possessed of many virtues. He was so remarkable for his chastity, that before his marriage he would not allow any lady of a suspicious character and unguarded conduct to frequent the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>: and having observed one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> some ladies with their bosoms uncovered, he turned away his eyes from the indecent object, and reprimanded them smartly in the simple dialect of the times; "Fy, fy (said he), for shame; forsooth ye be to blame." 5. In the reign of King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., when licentiousness was at its height in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, a yeomen of the guards refused the mistress of a king. The lady, who was dissatisfied with her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> lover, had fixed her eyes upon this man, and thought she had no more to do than speak her pleasure. He got out of her way. He refused to understand her; and when the prelief him further, he said, "I am married." The story reached the king, with all its circumstances; but they who expected an extravagant laugh upon the occasion were disappointed. He sent for the person: he found him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, though reduced to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> station; and "Odds fish, man (says he), though I am not honest enough to be virtuous myself, I value them that are." He gave him an appointment, and respected him for life. 6. In many parts the poorest people are the most virtuous and honest in this respect. In the Swede's dominion, towards the pole, there is no name for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>. They thought it an offence man could not commit against man; and have no word to express it in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The unpolished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>, with these thoughts, is, as a human creature, much more respectable than the gay Briton, whose heart is tainted with vices, and estranged from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> affection; and he is happier. The perfect confidence mutually repaid between him and the honest partner of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, entails a satisfaction even in the lowest poverty. It gilds the humble hearth, and lights the cabin; their homely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> is a sacrifice of thanks, and every breath of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> arises in incense. If <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> be laid upon hand, it is sure affection; and if some infant plays about their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, they look upon him and upon each other with a delight that greatness seldom knows, because it feels distrust.

CONTINENT

Pages 227-227

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> not interrupted by seas, in contradistinction to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, &c. See Geography. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> is said to have been anciently torn from the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and it is an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, which some of our antiquaries still have a regard to, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the continent of France. The world is usually divided into two great continents, the old and the new. Whether there exists in the southern hemisphere another continent, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the whole be only an immense watery region, is a question that for near three centuries has engaged the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the learned as well as the commercial world, and given rise to many interesting voyages and discoveries; concerning which, see the article South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>.

CONTINGENT

Pages 227-227

is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation for the quota that falls to any person upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>. Thus each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Germany in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> is to furnish so many men, so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and munition, for his contingent.

CONTINUED

Pages 227-227
or CONTINUOUS, in a general sense, means incessant, or proceeding without interruption. CONTINUED Fever, is such a one as sometimes remits, but never intermits or goes entirely off till its period. CONTINUED Basso, in Music, thus called, says Rousseau, because it is continued through the whole piece. Its principal use, besides that of regulating the harmony, is to support the voice, and preserve the tone.—They pretend that it was one Ludovico Viana, of whom a treatise still remains, who towards the end of the last century first put the continued bass in practice. CONTINUED Proportion, in Arithmetic, is that where the consequent of the first ratio is the same with the antecedent of the second; as $4:8::8:16$; in contradiction to discrete proportion.

CONTINUITY

Pages 227-227

is defined by some schoolmen the immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> of parts in the same quantum: by others, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of body, whereby its extremities become one; and by others, a state of body resulting from the mutual implication of its parts. There are two kinds of continuity, mathematical and physical. The first is merely imaginary, since it supposes real <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> physical parts where there are none. The other, or physical continuity, is that state of two or more particles, in which their parts are so mutually implicated as to constitute one uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> or continuum.

CONTINUO

Pages 227-227

in Music, signifies the thorough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>, as basso continuo is the continual <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thorough bass, which is sometimes marked in music-books by the letters B. C.

CONTOBABDITES

Pages 227-227

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in the sixth century. Their first leader was Severus of Antioch; who was succeeded by John the grammarian surnamed Philoponus, and one Theodoreus whose followers were also called Theodoriani. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> of them, who were willing to receive a book composed by Theodoreus on the Trinity, made a separate body, and were called Contobaddites, from some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which Nicephorus does not mention; but which must apparently have been the place where they held their assemblies. The Contobaddites allowed of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>; which is the only circumstance given us concerning them.

CONTRACTION

Pages 228-228

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, is the reducing of two syllables into one, as can't for cannot, shouldn't for shouldn't, &c.

CONTRADICTION

Pages 228-228

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> opposition, wherein one thing is found diametrically opposite to another.

CONTRAFISSURE

Pages 228-229

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a kind of fracture, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fissure, in the cranium, which sometimes happens on the side opposite to that which received the blow, or at least at some distance from it.

CONTRAINDICATION

Pages 229-229

in Medicine, is an indication which forbids that to be done which the main scope of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out. Suppose, e.g., in the cure of a disease a vomit were judged proper; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the patient be subject to vomiting of blood, it is a sufficient contraindication as to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a>.

CONTRARIETY

Pages 229-229

an opposition between two things, which imports their being contrary to one another; and consists in this, that one of the terms implies a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a> of the other, either mediately <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> immediately; so that contrariety may be said to be the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>, or opposition of two things, one of which imports the absence of the other, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and hatred. CONTRAST; opposition or dissimilitude of figures, by which one contributes to the visibility or effect of the others. See RESEMBLANCE.

CONTRAST

Pages 229-229

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is to avoid the repetition of the same thing, in order to please by variety.

CONTRATE-WHEEL

Pages 229-229

in watch-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, that next to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> and hoop whereof <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> contrary to those of the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, from whence it takes its name. See WATCH-Making.

CONTRAVALLATION

Pages 229-229
or the Line of CONTRAVALLATION, in Fortification, a trench guarded with a parapet, and usually cut round about a place by the besiegers, to secure themselves on that side, and to stop the ladders of the garrison. See FORTIFICATION.

CONTRAVENTION

Pages 229-229

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s failing to discharge his word, obligation, duty, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the laws or customs of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. CONTRAYERVA. See DORSTENIA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CONTRÉ, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, an appellation given to several bearings, on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the shield contrary and opposite ways: thus we meet with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRE">contre</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>, contre-chevron, contre-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, &c., when there are two ordinaries of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> opposite to each other, so as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> may be opposed to metal, and metallic to colour.

CONTRIBUTION

Pages 229-229

the payment of each person's quota of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> he is to bear in some imposition, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> expense. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINGENT">CONTINGENT</a>, &c.—Contributions are either involuntary, as those of taxes and imposts; or voluntary, as those of expenses for carrying on some undertaking for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>.

CONTRIBUTIONS

Pages 229-229

in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, are impositions paid by frontier countries to secure themselves from being plundered and ruined by the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The peasants till their ground under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of contributions, as securely as in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of profound peace.

CONTRITION

Pages 229-229

in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, a sorrow for our sins, resulting from the reflection of having offended God, from the sole consideration of his goodness, without any regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> due to the triflers, and attended with a sincere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of forsaking them. The word is derived from the Latin contrere, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bruise. CONTROL is properly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> kept of acts, bills, &c., of the officers or commissioners in the revenue, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, &c., in order to perceive the true state thereof, and to certify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and the due keeping of the acts subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>.

CONTROLLER

Pages 229-229

an officer appointed to control <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> oversee the accounts of other officers; and, on occasion, to certify whether or not things have been controlled or examined. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> we have several officers of this name; as controller of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, controller of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, controller of the customs, controller of the mint, &c. CONTROLLER of the Hanaper, an officer who attends the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> daily, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> and in sealt-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, to take all things sealed in leathern bags from the clerks of the hanaper, and to mark the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and effect thereof, and enter them in a book, with all the duties belonging to the king and other officers for the same, and so <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> the clerk of the hanaper with them. CONTROLLER of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">Household</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> officer under the lord <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>. The name of his office comes from the French word contrerouler. His office is to control the accounts and reckonings of the Green Cloth, of which board he is always a member. He carries a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, and is always one of the privy-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. He has 107l. 17s. 6d. a-year <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, and 192l. 25s. 6d. board wages. CONTROLLER of the Pipe, an officer of the exchequer, who makes out a summons twice every year, to levy the farms and debts of the pipe. See PIPE and EXCHEQUER. CONTROLLERS of the Pells, two officers of the exchequer who are the chamberlain's clerks, and keep a control of the pell of receipts and goings out.

CONTUMACY

Pages 229-229

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a refusal to appear in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> when legally summoned, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the disobedience to the rules and orders of a court having power to punish such offence.

CONUS

Pages 233-233

a cone, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>: a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fruit <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scaly seed-vessel, so termed by Tournefort and other botanists. Linnaeus has substituted strobilus in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Conus, the cone-shell, a genus of shells. See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CONVALESCENCE

Pages 230-230

in Medicine, the insensible <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that state in which, after the cure of a disorder, the body which has been reduced, has not yet regained its vigour, but begins to resume its powers. Proper aliments conduce to the re-establishment of the languid faculties; but as the tone of the bowels is weakened, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGESTIVE">digestive</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> is not equal to its office, which is shown by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> sweats over the whole body; and the smallest excess in this respect is oftentimes the occasion of dangerous relapses. A person in this state is like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> relumined, which the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is sufficient to extinguish.

CONVALLARIA

Pages 230-230
or Lily of the Valley, in Botany, a genus of plants, belonging to the hexandria clafs; and in the natural method ranking under Sarmatianaceae. See Botany Index. CONVENARUM urbs, or Lugdunum, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Convenæ, a people of Gallia Narbonensis, at the foot of the Pyrenees. Its origin was owing to the Sertorian war, Pompey compelling the robbers of the Pyrenees and fugitive slaves to settle there, (Pliny). It stood near the head of the Garonne. Now St Bertrand, in Gascony. E. Long. 30. Lat 43 15.

CONVENTICLE

Pages 230-230

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of convent; denoting, properly, a cabal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> secret <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the monks of a convent, to make a brigade or party in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>. From the ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of these assemblies, the word is come into disrepute; and now stands for any mischievous, seditious, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> assembly. F. Doucine observes, the occidentals always esteemed the fifth general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> an unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> conventicle is said, by some, to have been first applied in England to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of Wickliff, and has been since used to signify the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> assemblies of all in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> who do not conform to the established doctrines and worship of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England. By 22 Car. II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 1. it is enacted, That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any persons of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16 years, subjects of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, shall be present at any conventicle, where there are five or more assembled, they shall be fined 5s. for the first offence, and 10s. for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>; and persons preaching incur a penalty of 20l. Also suffering a meeting to be held in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, &c. is liable to 20l. penalty. Justices of peace have power to enter such houses, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> persons assembled, &c. And if they neglect their duty, they shall forfeit too l.
