And if any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a>, &c. know of such meetings, and do not inform a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, &c. he shall forfeit 5l. But the 1st W. and M. cap. 18. ordains, that protestant dissenters shall be exempt from penalties; though, if they meet in a house with the doors locked, barred, or bolted, such dissenters shall have no benefit from 1st W. and M. Officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, &c. present at any conventicle, at which there shall be ten persons, if the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family be not prayed for in express words, shall forfeit 40l. and be disabled (Stat. 10 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, cap. 2.)

CONVENTION

Pages 230-230

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> agreement between two or more parties. CONVENTION is also a name given to an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, or the estates of the realm, held without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s writ. Of this kind was the convention parliament which restored <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. This parliament met above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> before his return, and sat full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months after his restoration, and enacted several laws still in force, which were confirmed by stat. 13 Car. II. c. 7. and c. 14. Such also was the convention of estates in 1688, who upon the retreat of King James II. came to a conclusion that he had abdicated the throne, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of succession devolved to King William and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; whereupon their assembly expired as a convention, and was converted into a parliament. CONVENTION of Estates, in Scotland, was partly of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a parliament; but differing in this, that the former could only lay on taxes, while parliament could both impose taxes and make laws.

CONVENTUAL

Pages 230-230

is particularly used for a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> who actually resides in a convent; in contradistinction to those who are only guests, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> are entertained there, or are in possession of benefices depending on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. See Monk.

CONVENTUS JURIDICI

Pages 230-230

were courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> established in the Roman provinces; with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of jurisdiction, circumscribed and confined within certain limits of district, whither all who were of the resort were to repair for justice. The unaccountable affectation of changing forms of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> into forms of civil courts, proved the ruin of Varus and of three legions in Germany, (Florus). Conventus agere, is to hold a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of justice. CONVERGING or Convergent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">Lines</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, are such as continually approach nearer one another, or whose distances become still less and less. These are opposed to divergent lines, the distances of which become continually greater: those lines which converge one way, diverge the other. Converging Rays, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, those rays that, issuing from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of an object, incline towards another, till at last they meet and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, and then become diverging rays. Converging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">Series</a>, a series of terms or quantities that always decrease the farther they proceed, or which tend to a certain magnitude or limit: in opposition to diverging series, or such as become continually larger and larger.

CONVERSATION

Pages 230-231
or discourse, signifies an interlocution between two, or among more persons: with this distinction, that conversation is used for any general intercourse of sentiments whatever, whereas a discourse means a conversation limited to some particular subject. There is no part, perhaps, of social life, which affords more real satisfaction than those hours which one passes in rational and unreveled conversation. That conversation, however, may answer the ends for which it was designed, the parties who are to join in it must come together with a determined resolution to please, and to be pleased. In the conduct of it, be not eager to interrupt others, or uneasy at being yourself interrupted; since you speak either to amuse or instruct the company, or to receive those benefits from it. Give all, therefore, leave to speak in turn. Hear with patience, and answer with precision. Inattention is ill manners; it shows contempt; and contempt is never forgiven. Trouble not the company with your own private concerns, as you do not love to be troubled with those of others. Yours are as little to them as theirs are to you. You will need no other rule whereby to judge of this matter. Converse, but with dexterity and propriety, that each person may have an opportunity of discoursing on the subject with which he is best acquainted. He will be pleased, and you will be informed. By observing this rule, every one has it in his power to assist in rendering conversation agreeable; since, though he may not choose, or be qualified, to say much himself, he can propose questions to those who are able to answer them. Avoid stories, unless short, pointed, and quite apropos. He who deals in them, says Swift, must either have a very large stock, or a good memory, or must often change his company. Some have a set of them strung together like onions; they take possession of the conversation by an early introduction of one, and then you must have the whole rope; and there is an end of everything else, perhaps, for that meeting, though you may have heard all twenty times before. Talk often, but not long. The talent of haranguing private company is infallible. Senators and barristers are apt to be guilty of this fault; and members who never harangue in the house will often do it out of the house. If the majority of the company be naturally silent, or cautious, the conversation will flag, unless it be often renewed by one among them who can start new subjects. Forbear, however, if possible, to broach a second before the first is out, lest your stock should not last, and you should be obliged to come back to the old barrel. There are those who will repeatedly cross upon and break into the conversation with a fresh topic, till they have touched upon all and exhausted none. Economy here is necessary for most people. Laugh not at your own wit and humour; leave that to the company. When the conversation is flowing in a serious and useful channel, never interrupt it by an ill-timed jest. The stream is scattered, and cannot be again collected. Discourse not in a whisper, or half-voice, to your next neighbour. It is ill-breeding, and, in some degree, a fraud; conversation-stock being, as one has well observed, a joint and common property. In reflections on absent people, go no farther than you would go if they were present. "I resolve (says Bishop Beveridge) never to speak of a man's virtues to his face, nor of his faults behind his back:"—A golden rule! the observation of which would, at one stroke, banish flattery and defamation from the earth.

CONVERSE

Pages 231-231

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>. One proposition is called the converse of another, when, after a conclusion drawn from something supposed in the converse proposition, that conclusion is supposed; and then, that which in the other was supposed, is now drawn as a conclusion from it: thus when two sides of a triangle are equal, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> under these sides are equal; and, on the converse, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> these angles are equal, the two sides are equal.

CONVERSION

Pages 231-231

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, whereby the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of a battalion is turned where the flank was, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the battalion is attacked in the flank. CONVERSION of Equations, the same with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of equations by multiplication. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">ALGEBRA</a>.

CONVERT

Pages 231-231

a person who has undergone a conversion. Convert is chiefly used in respect of changes from one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, to another. Converts with relation to the religion turned to, are denominated apostates with regard to that they have relinquished. The Jews formerly converted to Christianity in England, were called conversos. Henry III. built them a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and allowed them a competent subsistence for their lives; which house was called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOMUS">domus</a> conversorum. But the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> afterwards increasing, they grew a burden to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; upon which they were distributed among the monasteries; and after the expulsion of the Jews under Edward III. the domus conversorum was given for keeping of the rolls.

CONVERTS

Pages 231-231

in a monastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, are lay-frars, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> brothers, admitted for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; without orders, and not allowed to sing in the choir. Till the eleventh century, the word was used for persons who embraced the monkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>; by which they were distinguished from those devoted in their childhood by their parents, called oblati. But in the eleventh century, when they began to receive into monasteries illiterate persons, incapable of being clerks, and only destined for bodily labour, the signification of the word was necessarily changed. F. Mabillon observes, that it was John first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Vallombrosa who first introduced these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-converts, distinguished by their state from the monks of the choir, who were then either clerks or capable of becoming so.

CONVEX

Pages 231-231

an appellation given to the exterior surface of gibbous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> globular bodies; in opposition to the hollow inner surface of such bodies, which is called concave; thus we say, a convex frieze, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENS">lens</a>, mirror, superficies, &c.

CONVEXITY

Pages 231-232

the exterior surface of a convex, i.e. gibbous and globular thing; in opposition to concavity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the inner surface, which is hollow or depressed. See CONCAVE. The word is of particular import in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CATOPTRICS">catoptrics</a> and dioptries: where it is applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a> and lenses. A convex mirror represents its images smaller than the objects; as a concave one represents them larger: a convex mirror reflects the rays from it, diverging; and therefore disperses and weakens their effect: as a concave one reflects them converging; so as they concur Conveyance concur in a point, and have their effect increased; and by how much the mirror is a portion of a smaller sphere, by so much does it diminish the objects, and disperse the rays the more. See Mirror. A convex <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENS">lens</a> is either convex on both sides, called a convexo-convex; or it is plain on one side and convex on the other, called a plano-convex; or concave on one side and convex on the other, called a convexo-concave, or concavo-convex, as the one or the other surface prevails, i.e., as this or that is a portion of a smaller sphere. All convex lenses inflect the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> in their passage, i.e., send them out from their convex surface converging, so as that they concur in a point or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a>. Hence all convex lenses magnify, i.e., represent their images larger than their objects; and this the more as they are portions of smaller spheres.

CONVEYANCE

Pages 232-232

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> that passes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, &c. from one person to another.

CONVICT

Pages 232-232

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a person that is found guilty of an offence by the verdict of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. See the following article.

CONVICTION

Pages 232-232

in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, expresses the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, wherein the sinner becomes sensible of his guilt, of the evil <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of sin, and of the danger of his own ways.

CONVOCATION

Pages 232-233

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the clergy of England, by their representatives, to consult of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> matters. It is held during the session of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and consists of an upper and a lower <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In the upper sit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and in the lower the inferior clergy, who are represented by their proctors; consisting of all the deans and archdeacons, of one proctor for for every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, and two for the clergy of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, in all 143 divines; viz. 22 deans, 53 archdeacons, 24 prebendaries, and 44 proctors of the diocesan clergy. The lower house chooses its prelocutor; whose business it is to take care that the members attend, to collect their debates and votes, and to carry their resolutions to the upper house. The convocation is summoned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s writ, directed to the archbishop of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, requiring him to summon all bishops, deans, archdeacons, &c. The power of the convocation is limited by a statute of Henry VIII. They are not to make any canons <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ecclesiastical laws without the king's license; nor when permitted to make any, can they put them in execution, but under several restrictions. They have the examining and censuring all heretical and schismatical books and persons, &c., but there lies an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the king in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, or to his delegates. The clergy in convocation, and their servants, have the same privileges as members of parliament. Since the year 1665, when the convocation of the clergy gave up the privilege of taxing themselves to the house of commons, they seldom have been allowed to do any business; and are generally prorogued from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time till dissolved, a new one being generally called along with a new parliament. The only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> for giving up the privilege of taxing themselves, was their being allowed to vote at elections for members to the house of commons, which they had not before.

CONVOLUTION

Pages 233-233

a winding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, proper to the trunks of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, as the convolvulus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bindweed; the clusters of vines, bryony, &c.

CONVOLVULUS

Pages 233-233

bindweed: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the pentandra clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 20th order, Campanaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CONVOY

Pages 233-233

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> matters, a body of men that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> any supply of men, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, ammunition, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, conveyed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> into a town, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, or the like, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>.

CONVULSION

Pages 233-233

a preternatural and violent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the membranous and muscular parts of the body. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CONWAY

Pages 233-233

a market-town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAERNARVONSHIRE">Caernarvonshire</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, situated near the mouth of a river of the same name, 15 miles west of St Asaph. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 50' N. Lat. 53° 20'.

CONYZA

Pages 233-233

Ficobane: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the syngenesia clas, ranking under the 49th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CONZA

Pages 233-233

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated on the farther principate, on the river Offanto, 50 miles south-east of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Naples, E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16° 0' N. Lat. 41° 0'. It is the see of an archbishop.

COOK

Pages 233-271

Sir Anthony, descended from Sir Thomas Cook <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayor of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was born in 1506, and supposed to have been educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He was so eminent for his learning, piety, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, that the guardians of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward VI appointed him to be his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> instructor in learning, and to form his manners. He had four daughters; and being resolved to have sons by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, lest he should have none by birth, he taught his daughters those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> by night that he had instilled into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>: he was happy in his endeavours, as they proved learned in Greek and Latin, and equally distinguished by virtue, piety, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>. Mildred was married to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Lord Burleigh; Ann to Sir Nicholas <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, lord keeper of the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> to Sir John Ruffell, son and heir of Francis <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>; and Catharine to Sir Henry Killigrew. He lived in exile during the Marian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>; and returning on the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Elizabeth, spent the rest of his days in peace and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, dying in 1576. Cook, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> James, one of the ablest and most celebrated navigators of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, was the son of James Cook, a labourer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> in husbandry, and supposed to have been a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, and was born on the 27th of October 1728, at the village of Marton in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. He was one of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> children, all of whom are now dead except a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who married a fisherman of Redcar. He received the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of education from the schoolmistress of the village; and afterwards, on his father's removal to Great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AYTON">Ayton</a>, he was put to a day-school, at the expense of Mr Skottow, his father's employer, where he was instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> and in a few of the first rules of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of thirteen he was bound apprentice to Mr W. Sanderon, a haberdasher or shopkeeper at Straiths, about ten miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITBY">Whitby</a>; but some disagreement taking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between him and his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, he indulged his own inclination in binding himself apprentice to Messrs Walkers of Whitby, who had several vessels in the coal trade; and after serving a few years longer in the situation of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sailor, he was at length raised to be mate of one of Mr Walker's ships. During all this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> it is not recollected that he exhibited any thing peculiar either in his abilities or conduct. Early in the year 1755, when hostilities broke out between France and England, Cook entered on board the Eagle of sixty guns, to which vessel Sir Hugh Palliser was soon after appointed, who soon distinguished him as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and diligent seaman; and his promotion was forwarded by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of recommendation which was written by Mr Olbaldeston, member for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCARBOROUGH">Scarborough</a>, at the request of several neighbours, in Mr Cook's favour. On the 15th of May 1759, he was appointed master of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, which soon after sailed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and joined the fleet under Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Saunders at the memorable siege of Quebec. His <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> appears even then to have been very strong; for on Mr Olbaldeston's letter he was appointed master of the Grampus sloop; but the proper master having unexpectedly returned to her, her, the appointment did not take place. Four days after he was made master of the Garland; when upon inquiry it was found that he could not join her, as the vessel had already sailed; and the next day, May 15th 1759, he was made master of the Mercury. On this occasion he was recommended by Captain Palliser to a difficult and dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, viz. to take the foundations of the river St Lawrence, between the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> and the north shore, which he performed in the most complete manner; and soon afterwards he was employed to survey the most dangerous parts of the river below Quebec; these were his first efforts with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>. After this expedition he was appointed, on the 22nd of September, master of the Northumberland, stationed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>, where he first read Euclid, and applied to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> and other branches of science. In the year 1762 he was with the Northumberland, assisting at the recapture of Newfoundland; and in the latter end of the same year he returned to England, and married, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARKING">Barking</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, Miss Elizabeth Batts. Early in 1763, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> (then Captain) Greaves was appointed governor of Newfoundland, Mr Cook went out with him to survey the coasts of that island. At the end of the season he returned to England; but in the beginning of 1764, Sir Hugh Palliser being appointed governor of Newfoundland and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABRADOR">Labrador</a>, Mr Cook accompanied him in the same capacity of surveyor, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANVILLE">Granville</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCHOONER">schooner</a> to attend him on that business; in this situation he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till 1767. While Mr Cook remained on this station, he had an opportunity of exhibiting publicly a specimen of his progress in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of astronomy, in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> printed in the 57th volume of the Philosophical Transactions, entitled "An observation of an eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> at the island of Newfoundland, August 5, 1766, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> of the place of observation deduced from it." Mr Cook's observation was made at one of the Burgeo <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Ray, in N. Lat. 47° 56' 10"; and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of it made by Mr Mitchel, with an observation of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORNBY">Hornby</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, it appeared to have been accurately done; and Mr Cook at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> obtained the character of an able astronomer. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time a spirit for geographical discoveries, which had gradually declined since the beginning of the 18th century, began to discover itself anew. Two voyages of this kind had been performed in the reign of George II., the one under Captain Middleton, the other by Captains Moore and Smyth, with a view to discover a northwest passage through <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> to the East Indies. Two others, under Captains Byron, Wallis, and Carteret, had been undertaken soon after the conclusion of the peace in 1763 by order of his present majesty; and before the return of these navigators, who were ordered to sail round the world, another voyage was resolved upon for astronomical purposes. It having been calculated that a transit of Venus over the sun's disk would happen in 1769, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> memorial to his majesty was presented by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; in which they set forth the great importance of making proper observations on this phenomenon, the regard that had been paid to it by the different courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and intreating, among other things, that a vessel might be fitted out, at the expense of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, for conveying proper persons to some of the Friendly islands, in order to make the necessary observations. This being complied with on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his majesty, Alexander Dalrymple, Esq., an eminent member of the Royal Society, was appointed to take the command of the bark appropriated for the purpose. In the execution of the project, however, an unexpected difficulty occurred. Mr Dalrymple, sensible of the impossibility of guiding a vessel through unknown and dangerous seas without any proper command over the crew, demanded a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREVET">brevet</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> as captain of the vessel, in the same manner as had formerly been granted to Dr Halley in a voyage of discovery made by him. This commission Sir Edward Hawke absolutely refused to sign; declaring, when pressed upon the subject, that he would rather suffer his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to be cut off than trust any of his majesty's ships to a person who had not been properly bred to the service; and in this proceeding he seemed to be justified by the mutinous behaviour of Dr Halley's crew; who, denying the legality of his authority over them, had involved him in a very disagreeable dispute, and which was attended with pernicious consequences. Mr Dalrymple, on the other hand, being equally determined in his refusal to proceed without the authority in question, there was a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for finding out some person of science who might also be free from the objection made by Sir Edward Hawke. Mr Cook therefore was proposed by Mr Stephens; and his recommendation being seconded by Sir Hugh Palliser, he was immediately appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the expedition; and on this occasion was promoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> in his majesty's service. Mr Cook's commission as lieutenant was dated May 25, 1768; a vessel of 370 tons, named the Endeavour, was provided for him; and while the necessary preparations were making for the voyage, Captain Wallis returned. It having been recommended to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> to fix upon a proper place for making the astronomical observations, he had accordingly chosen the island named by him George's Island, but since known by the name of Otaheite; judging also that Port Royal harbour in it would afford an eligible situation. This proposal being accepted, directions for the purpose were accordingly given to Mr Cook, with whom Mr Charles Green was joined in the astronomical part; the latter having been assistant to Dr Bradley in the royal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, and thus judged to be every way qualified for the office. The lieutenant was likewise accompanied by Mr Banks, now Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks, Dr Solander, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the voyage was, as has already been hinted, to make observations on the transit of Venus; but this being done, Mr Cook was directed to make further discoveries in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>; and on the 29th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1768 he set sail on his expedition. An account of the voyage, and the discoveries made during the time of it, is given in the next article; here it is sufficient to observe, that throughout the whole Mr Cook approved himself an able seaman; and from his behaviour both to his own people and to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> nations he occasionally met with, showed a most exact regard to the rules both of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. On his first arrival at Otaheite, the following regulations were drawn up for his people, which he took care should be punctually obeyed: 1. To 1. To endeavour, by every fair means, to cultivate a friendly spirit with the natives, and to treat them with all imaginable humanity. 2. A proper person or persons to be appointed to treat with the natives for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, &c., and no other person belonging to the ship to do so without leave. 3. Every person on shore to attend punctually to his duty, and to pay proper <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to his tools or arms; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> lost through negligence, to have the full value <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> against his pay, with such farther <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted as occasion might require. 4. The same penalty to be inflicted on every one who should embezzle, trade with, or offer to trade with, any part of the ship's stores; and, 5. No <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> to be given in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for anything but provisions. His rigid adherence to these rules was manifested in several instances, particularly by severely punishing the ship's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>, who had threatened the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of a woman, wife to one of the chiefs of the island, for refusing a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a> on the terms he proposed. On erecting their observatory, in order to go through the astronomical operations, an accident happened which had like to have disconcerted the whole scheme. This was the loss of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a>, which had been stolen by some of the natives; but, chiefly through the exertions of Mr Banks, it was recovered, and the observations made accordingly. Scarce was this accomplished, however, before another theft of the natives demanded the most serious consideration of the commander. Some of them taking advantage of the attention of the officers being otherwise engaged, took the opportunity of breaking into one of the store-rooms, and stealing from thence a bag of spike nails of no less than an hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. This was a most important affair; for as those nails were of great estimation among the Indians, the possession of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> must undoubtedly have much lessened their value, and thus rendered provisions of every kind greatly dearer on the island than before. One of the thieves therefore being discovered, was punished with 200 lashes; notwithstanding which he obstinately refused to discover any of his accomplices. Repeated thefts committed afterwards required all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of Mr Cook to conduct himself in a proper manner. After due consideration, he judged it to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of importance to put an end to these practices at once, by doing something which might engage the natives themselves to prevent them for their common interest. This, however, he was not at present able to accomplish; nor indeed did it seem possible to prevent them without using firearms, which from motives of humanity he still determined to avoid. At last, after a stay of three months, when preparing to take his leave, the most disagreeable adventure took place that he had hitherto met with. This was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a> of two of his people, who having married young women of the country, determined to take up their residence in it. Mr Cook was now obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> some of the chiefs, and to inform them that they could not obtain their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> unless the deserters were recovered. This at last produced the desired effect; the deserters were given up, and Mr Cook set sail, along with Tupia (who had formerly been the prime minister to Oberea, a prince of the island) and a boy of 13 years of age, both of whom were desirous of accompanying him to England. While Mr Cook proceeded to visit others of the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> islands, Tupia occasionally served as an interpreter. On his arrival in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, Mr Cook found the people extremely hostile and insolent. At their very first meeting, one of the natives having threatened to dart his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> dead. Another, having carried off Mr Green's hanger was fired at with small shot; and upon his still refusing to restore it, was fired at with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> and killed. This, however, produced very little effect on the rest, who offered to make an attack upon them, till several muskets were fired with small shot, which wounded three or four more. Next day the commander, having determined to force some of the natives on board, in order to conciliate their affections by kind treatment, directed his men to follow two canoes whom he perceived under way before him. One made her escape, but the other, not observing the boats in pursuit, was overtaken; on which the savages plied their oars so briskly, that the ship's boats were not able to keep up with them. Tupia, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> the New Zealanders understood, called to them to return, with assurances that no hurt should be done them; but they continued their flight without minding him. A musket was then fired over their heads with a view to intimidate them, but upon this they prepared to fight; and on the coming up of the boats began the attack with so much vigour, that the lieutenant's people were obliged to fire upon them with ball, by which four out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> that were in the boat were killed, and the other three jumped into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and were taken on board. This part of Mr Cook's conduct seems inconsistent with that humanity for which he was in general so eminently distinguished; he was aware of the censure, and makes the following apology. "These people certainly did not deserve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> for not choosing to confide in my promises, or not consenting to come on board my boat, even if they had apprehended no danger; but the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of my service required me to obtain a knowledge of their country, which I could not otherwise obtain but by forcing into it in an hostile manner, or gaining admission through the confidence and good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the people. I had already tried the power of presents without effect; and I was now prompted by my desire to avoid farther hostilities, to attempt to get some of them on board; the only method we had left of convincing them that we intended them no harm, and had it in our power to contribute to their gratification and convenience. Thus far my intentions certainly were not criminal; and though in the contest, which I had not the least reason to expect, our victory might have been complete without so great an expense of life; yet in such situations, when the command to fire has once been given, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can pretend to restrain its excess, or prescribe its effect." Notwithstanding the disaster <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, to which the three New Zealanders, who were taken on board, had been witnesses, they were soon conciliated, and began to sing with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> that surprised the English gentlemen. They were boys, the oldest about 19 and the youngest about 11; but no kindness which which could be shown them was in any degree effectual to bring about a reconciliation with the rest. On the contrary, having perceived the ship in some distresses, they instantly showed a disposition to make an attack; and from this they were only prevented by the firing of a four-pounder charged with grape-shot. Even this did not produce any permanent effect; another attack was determined upon, and would undoubtedly have been made, had not Tupia informed them, that if they persisted in the attempt, the arms of their adversaries, like <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, would destroy every one of them. This was enforced by the fire of another four-pounder with grape-shot, which spreading wide in the water, terrified them to such a degree that they began to paddle away as fast as possible. Notwithstanding this, however, some intercourse began to take place; but in every instance the New Zealanders manifested their hostility and treachery in such a manner as showed that they were not to be gained by fair means. At last an attempt to carry off Tayeto, Tupia's boy, rendered it absolutely necessary to fire upon them in order to rescue him from certain destruction, some of the savages having got him into a canoe, where they held him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by violence. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this one of the savages was killed on the spot, and several more wounded, by the discharge of muskets from the boats; Tayeto recovered his liberty, jumped into the water, and swam to the ship. Some partial intercourse again took place; but still it appeared that the innate rancour of these savages was not to be subdued by any fair means; and it was only by the powerful arguments of cannon and musketry that they could be kept from attempting to do mischief. From the account of this voyage published by Dr Hawkeworth, indeed, it appears, that a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of savages perished in a manner similar to that above mentioned, and they seem to have manifested a more hostile behaviour than afterwards: on those melancholy occasions, however, it is observed to the honour of Mr Cook, that his humanity was eminently conspicuous beyond that of the common people, who all along showed as much inclination to destroy the Indians as a sportsman does to kill the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> he pursues. While Mr Cook coasted the islands of New Zealand, he was sometimes in the most imminent danger of being shipwrecked. In the latitude of 35° south, and in the midst of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, he met with such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> as he scarce ever experienced before; so that he was no less than three weeks in getting ten leagues to the westward, and two more before he could get 30 leagues farther. Fortunately, however, they were all this time a considerable way from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, otherwise it is probable that the storm must have proved fatal. Mr Cook having spent six months in circumnavigating and fully exploring the islands of New Zealand, he sailed from thence on the 31st of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1770. It must be observed, however, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> hostility manifested by the inhabitants in that part of the island where he first arrived, was not universally diffused, but that a friendly intercourse was for a long time maintained with those about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUEEN_CHARLOTTE_S_SOUND">Queen Charlotte's <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>. From New Zealand he proceeded to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and on the 28th of April came in sight of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOTANY_BAY"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Bay. Here all their endeavours to induce the natives to have any intercourse with them proved ineffectual, though happily there was no blood spilt in any quarrel. During their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> round New Holland, the coasts of which are full of dangerous rocks and shoals, our navigators were brought into a more perilous situation than ever; and from which the escape was so extraordinary, that it deserves a particular relation. This happened on the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1770, as they purposed their course from Trinity Bay, and nearly in the latitude assigned to the islands discovered by Quiros. At that time they had the advantage of a fine breeze and a clear moonlight; and in standing off from fix till near nine o'clock, the ship had deepened her water from 14 to 21 fathoms; but while the navigators were at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, it suddenly shoaled to 12, 10, and 8 fathoms in the space of a few minutes. Every thing was then ready for putting the ship about, when they suddenly got into deep water again, and continued in 20 and 21 fathoms for some time, so that the gentlemen went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> in perfect security. A little before eleven, however, the water shoaled at once from 20 to 17 fathoms; and before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> could be heaved again, the ship struck, and remained immovable, excepting as far as she was heaved up and down, and dashed against the rocks by the surge. The alarm was now universal, and not indeed without the greatest reason. It appeared that the vessel had been lifted over the ledge of a rock, and lay in a hollow within it, where there were in some places from three to four fathoms water, and in others scarcely as many feet: the sheathing boards were disjoined, and floating round the ship in great numbers; and at last the false <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> also was destroyed, while the rock kept grating her bottom with such force as to be heard in the fore store-room. It was now necessary to lighten the ship as much as possible: and this was done with all expedition to the amount of more than 50 tons. In the morning of the 11th of June they discovered the land at about eight leagues distance, without any island between, on which, they could have been sent adrift in the event of the ship going to pieces, so that they might have been carried to the main land by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>. To add to their distresses, the ship drew so much water, that it was with difficulty kept under with three pumps. Lastly, it appeared, that even the rising of the tide, on which they had ultimately depended for relief, was insufficient to answer the purpose as the day tide fell considerably short of that in the night-time. Having therefore lightened the ship till farther, by throwing out everything that could possibly be spared, they waited with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> for the next tide; when, after incredible exertion, the ship righted, and they got her over the ledge of the rock into deep water. By continual labour, however, the men were at last so much exhausted, that they could not stand to the pumps more than five or six minutes at a time; after which they threw themselves flat on the deck, though a stream of water between three and four inches deep ran over it; and in this situation, they lay till others, exhausted as well as themselves, took their places, on which they started up again, and renewed their exertions. In this dreadful extremity, Mr Monkhouse, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDSHIPMAN">midshipman</a>, proposed the expedient of stopping the ship, as it is called, called, by which means he said that he had seen a merchant ship brought from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> to London after she had sprung a leak that admitted more than four feet water in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The expedient being approved of, it was put in execution in the following manner. He took a lower studding-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and having mixed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of oakum and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> together, stitched them down by handfuls as lightly as possible; the whole being afterwards spread over with the dung of the sheep and other filth. The fall was then hauled under the ship's bottom by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> which kept it extended. When it came under the leak, the wool and oakum, with part of the fall, were forced inwards by the pressure of the water, which thus prevented its own ingress in such an effectual manner, that one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>, instead of three, was now sufficient to keep it under. Thus they got the ship into a convenient port on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of New Holland, where they had an opportunity of repairing the injury. Here they discovered that their preservation had not been owing entirely to the expedient above mentioned; for one of the holes was in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> filled up by a piece of rock which had broken off and stuck in it; and this hole was so large, that had it not been filled up in the manner just mentioned, they must undoubtedly have perished notwithstanding all the assistance that could have been derived from the pumps. The dangers they sustained in navigating this coast were innumerable, inasmuch that for very near three months they were obliged to have a man constantly in the chains heaving the lead. They were always entangled among rocks and shoals, which could not have failed to destroy a less experienced navigator; and even Mr Cook, with all his sagacity, could not sometimes have extricated himself, had it not been for the favourable interposition of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> events, which no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> penetration could foresee or have the least dependence upon. Of this we shall only give the following instance. Having at last, as they thought, got safely over the vast reefs of junk rocks with which the coast of New Holland is surrounded, they flattered themselves that all danger was past, and the vast swell of the water convinced them that they were now in the open ocean. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of former dangers, however, induced them frequently to take the precaution of sounding; notwithstanding which, in the latitude of about $14^\circ$ S. they found themselves one morning only about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> distant from the most hideous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAKERS">breakers</a>, though the sea all around was unfathomable. Their situation was rendered the more dreadful by its being a dead calm, at the same time that they were carried towards the rock with such rapidity, that by the time they had got the ship's head turned by means of the boats, she was scarcely 100 yards distant from it. Their only resource then was to tow the ship, if possible, by means of the boats and pinnace, out of a situation to very perilous; but all their efforts would have been unsuccessful, had not a breeze of wind sprung up, which, though too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to have been noticed at any other time, was found to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> their efforts so effectually, that the ship began to move perceptibly from the reef in an oblique <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>: during the time that this breeze lasted, which was not more than ten minutes, they had made a considerable way. A dead calm succeeding, they began to lose ground, and in a little time were driven within 200 yards of the rocks: but fortunately the breeze returned, and lasted ten minutes more; during which time a small opening was perceived in the reef at the distance of about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a mile. The mate being sent out to examine this opening, reported that it was not more than the length of the ship in breadth, but that there was smooth water within. On this it was determined to push into it by all means. The attempt failed of success; as, just when they had brought the ship with great labour to the mouth of the opening, they found a current setting out from it by reason of the tide now beginning to ebb. But though their hopes were disappointed in getting through the opening, they were, by the current setting out from it, driven in a very short time to the distance of a quarter of a mile from the rocks; and by dint of towing and other exertions, they were got by noon to the distance of two miles. This temporary deliverance, however, afforded but small prospect of being ultimately relieved. They had still no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> than of being forced back into their former situation by the return of the tide; but happily they now perceived another opening about a mile to the westward. Mr Hicks the lieutenant being sent to examine this opening, returned with an account of its being narrow and hazardous, but capable of being passed. To this place therefore the ship was directed by every possible means; and a light breeze happening to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up, they fortunately reached it, and were instantly hurried through with great rapidity by the current of the returning tide; which, had it not been for this opening, would undoubtedly have dashed them to pieces against the rocks. From the time they quitted the coast of New Holland till their arrival at Batavia in the island of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, our navigators met with no other danger but what is common in sea-voyages. They were obliged to stay for some time at this place to repair their damages; and on viewing the condition of the ship, found they had more reason than ever to admire the manner in which they had been preserved. Both the false-keel and main-keel were greatly injured; great part of the fleathing was torn off; several of the planks were much damaged, and among these there were two, and half of another, which for six feet in length were not above the eighth part of an inch in thickness, besides being penetrated with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> quite to the timbers. Here the crew were excessively annoyed by sickness, which obliged them to remain much longer than they would otherwise have done: and it is worthy of notice, that every one of the crew was ill excepting the sail-maker, an old man between 70 and 80 years of age, and who was drunk every night. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">Poor</a> Tupia, with his boy Tayeto, fell sacrifices to the unhealthiness of the climate, as well as the surgeon, three seamen, and Mr Green's servant. Nor did the evil stop here; for on their setting out from Batavia, the seeds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> which had been received there broke out in the most violent and fatal manner, inasmuch that in the course of about six weeks there died one of Mr Banks's assistants, by name Mr Sporing, Mr Parkinson his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> painter, Mr Green the astronomer, the boatswain, carpenter, and mate; Mr Monkhouse the midshipman, the corporal of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARINES">marines</a>, two of the 4 H carpenter's Cook's carpenter's crew, and nine seamen. Even the jolly old sail-maker could now hold out no longer; but whether his death might not in some measure be attributed to his being less plentifully supplied with liquors than formerly, might have deserved inquiry. These unfortunate events probably made a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on Mr Cook's mind; and perhaps induced him to direct his attention to those methods of preserving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of seamen which he afterwards put in execution with so much success. After touching at St Helena, they continued their voyage for England, where they arrived on the 11th of June 1771; and on the 29th of August the same year, his majesty testified his approbation of Mr Cook's conduct by appointing him a captain in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. On this occasion Mr Cook wished to have been advanced to the rank of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-captain, which, though not more profitable than the other, is more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>; but this being inconsistent with the rules of preferment in the navy, the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>, at that time at the head of the admiralty, could not agree to it. Captain Cook was not allowed to remain long inactive. The idea of a southern continent had long been entertained, and Mr Dalrymple had renewed the attention of the public towards the question, by his historical collection of voyages to the Pacific ocean, published in two quarto volumes, one in 1770, the other in 1771. To determine the matter finally, Captain Cook was again sent out; and the object of this voyage was not merely to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the question just mentioned, but to extend the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a> of the globe to its utmost limits. That the undertaking might be carried on with the greater advantage, it was determined to employ two ships, on the choice and equipment of which the utmost attention was bestowed. The successful voyage which had already been made in the Endeavour, suggested the idea of that ship being a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> for the two which were to be sent out; and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Lord Sandwich concurring with the general idea, two vessels, constructed by the same person who had built the Endeavour, were purchased for the voyage. These were about 14 or 16 months old at the time they were purchased; and, in the opinion of Captain Cook, were as fit for the purpose as if they had been but newly built. The larger of the two, of 462 tons burden, was named the Resolution; the smaller, of 336 tons, had the name of the Adventure; the complement of men on board the former, of which Captain Cook was commander, being 112; on the latter, commanded by Mr Tobias Furneaux, 81. In their equipment, every article that could be supposed necessary, however much out of the common line, was procured, and every circumstance that could be supposed to contribute to the success of the voyage was attended to in the most scrupulous manner. Besides the usual stores and provisions, all of which were of the best kinds, the ships were furnished with malt, four-kraut, salted cabbage, portable soup, salop, mustard, marmalade of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARROTS">carrots</a>, beer, and infusorial wort. Mr Hodges, an excellent landscape painter, was engaged to make drawings and paintings of such objects as required them. Mr John Reinhold Forster, with his son, were both engaged, in order to explore and collect the natural history of the countries through which they passed; and lastly, that nothing might be wanting to render the voyage as complete as possible, Mr William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> and Mr William Bayley were engaged by the board of longitude to make celestial observations. They were furnished with the best instruments of every kind, and among the rest with four time-pieces; three constructed by Mr Arnold, and one by Mr Kendall on Mr Harrison's principles. At <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a> Captain Cook received his instructions; which were not only to sail round the globe, but to sail round it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> southern latitudes, and to make such traverses as might finally resolve the question concerning the southern continent. In pursuance of these instructions he set sail on the 13th of July 1772, and on the 29th of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> reached the Madeiras. As he proceeded afterwards in his voyage, he made three puncheons of beer from the infusorial wort carried out along with him, and found it excellently to answer the purpose, provided the material could have been kept without <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> in its infusorial state; but as this was found impossible, the expedient seems to have failed. In this voyage, however, the captain used with the greatest success such methods as appeared likely to contribute to the preservation of the health of his men. In rainy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, he took care that the ship should be aired and dried by means of fires made between the decks, the damp places were smoked, and the people were ordered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> their bedding, and wash and dry their clothes, whenever an opportunity offered. Thus he reached the Cape of Good Hope without having a single man sick. Having left it and kept on his course to the southward, he soon began to meet with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and stormy weather, by which he lost almost the whole of his live stock of sheep, hogs, and geese. The bad effects of this stormy weather upon the men were guarded against by an addition to their clothing, and giving them a dram on particular occasions. On the fifth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, being in the latitude of 50° 40', he fell in with islands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, and continued among them in various latitudes till the 17th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1773; when he set sail for New Zealand, which he reached on the 27th. The reception of our navigator by the New Zealanders was now much more friendly than in the former voyage, so that there were no contests with the natives; nor did Captain Cook observe any one of those whom he had seen before, neither was there the smallest remembrance of former hostilities. Having stayed in this country till the 7th of June, our navigators set sail for Otaheite; but during the voyage the crews of both ships were attacked by the scurvy. Those of the Adventure were in a very sickly state; the cook was dead, and 28 of her best men incapable of duty. On board the Resolution matters were much better; and the only reason that could be conjectured for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> was, that the people of the Adventure had been in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of body more inclined to the scurvy than those of the Resolution, and had eaten fewer vegetables. Here it was observed, that the aversion of seamen to a change of diet is so great, that it can only be overcome by the steady and persevering example of a commander. While he remained at New Zealand, the captain had discovered a tree which greatly resembled the American <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> spruce. Persuaded, therefore, that it would be attended with effects equally equally salutary on the health of the people, he employed them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a> beer from it. This was done while they continued at Dufky Bay, in order to supply the want of vegetables, which were not to be procured there; but on removing to Queen Charlotte's Sound, they were more fortunate. Captain Cook himself went to look out for antiscorbutic vegetables; and returned in a very short time with a boat-load of scurvy-grafts, celery, &c. These were boiled with the peas and wheat; and though some of the people disliked them at first, they soon became so sensible of their good effects, that they cheerfully followed the example of the rest: and the freedom of the crew from the scurvy and other distempers was by every one attributed to the New Zealand spruce beer and vegetables. From this time forward the captain had scarce occasion to give orders for gathering vegetables when they came to any land. During this voyage Captain Cook experienced another narrow escape from shipwreck. Being becalmed at the distance of half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from a reef of rocks near Otago Harbour island, it was found necessary to order out the boats to tow off the ships; but this was found impossible. The calm continuing, and the situation of our navigators becoming every moment more dangerous, the captain attempted to get through an opening in the reef which he had judged practicable; but on approaching it, found that there was not sufficient depth of water; at the same time that the draught of the tide through it forced the ship thither in a manner scarce to be resisted. One of the warping <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, with about 400 fathoms of rope, was then ordered out, but did not produce any effect. They were within two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> length of the breakers, and no bottom could be found for casting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>. Having no other resource, however, they did drop an anchor; but before it took hold, the Resolution was in less than three fathoms water, and struck at every fall of the sea, which broke violently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> under her stern, threatening destruction to every one on board. At last the tide ceasing to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in the same direction, the boats were ordered to try to tow off the vessels; in which being assisted by the land-breeze, which fortunately sprung up at that instant, they with much labour succeeded. Having spent a considerable time in the South Sea islands, Captain Cook returned to New Zealand, and from thence set sail for the southern part of the continent of America. Here he explored all the islands in the neighbourhood, and then returned to England, where he arrived in safety on the 30th of July 1774, having been absent three years and 18 days; and in all that time lost only one man, who died of consumption probably begun before he set out on the voyage. The reception our navigator now met with was suited to his merit. He was immediately raised to the rank of post-captain, and soon after unanimously elected a member of the Royal Society; from whom he received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> medal for the best experimental paper that had appeared throughout the year. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of Sir John Pringle, at the delivery of this medal, annually to make an elaborate discourse, containing the history of that part of science for which the medal was given; and, as the subject of Captain Cook's paper (the means of preserving the health of seamen) was analogous to the profession of Sir John Pringle himself as a physician, he had the greater opportunity of displaying his eloquence on the occasion. The speech he made was in the highest degree honourable to Captain Cook. He remarked, that the society had never more meritoriously bestowed the medal than on the person who now received it. "If (says he) Rome decreed the civic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> to him who saved the life of a single citizen, what wreaths are due to the man who, having himself saved many, perpetuates in your transactions the means by which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> may, on the most distant voyages, preserve numbers of her intrepid sons, her mariners; who braving every danger, have so liberally contributed to the fame, to the opulence, and to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> empire of the country?" These honourable testimonies of the public regard, however, Captain Cook did not receive, being already embarked on another voyage, from which he never returned. The third voyage of this celebrated navigator was not undertaken by any express command of his majesty. Captain Cook had already done so much, that it was thought but reasonable he should now spend the remainder of his life in quiet; and in order to enable him to do this in a more comfortable manner, besides his rank of post-captain in the navy, he was also made a captain in Greenwich. Still, however, there were some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> in the science of geography which had very much engaged the attention of the public, and were indeed of such importance as to become a national concern. These were to discover the connection between <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and America, and to determine whether there was not a possibility of shortening the passage to the East Indies by sailing round the northern parts of the continents of Europe and Asia. Many attempts, indeed, had already been made by various navigators of different nations; but all of them had failed, and, what was worse, had left the point still undetermined. An act of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> had been passed in 1745, by which a reward of 20,000l. was held out to the ships of any of his majesty's subjects for accomplishing this important voyage, but without mentioning anything of those belonging to his majesty; and this reward was further confined to the finding out of the north-west passage to the East Indies through Hudson's bay. In the year 1776, however, both the errors just mentioned were corrected. It was now enacted, "That if any ship belonging to any of his majesty's subjects, or to his majesty, shall find out, and fail through, any passage by sea between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, in any direction or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> of the northern hemisphere, to the northward of the 52nd degree of northern latitude; the owners of such ships, if belonging to any of his majesty's subjects, or the commanders, officers, and seamen, of such ship belonging to his majesty, shall receive, as a reward for such discovery, the sum of 20,000l. It was not, as has already been hinted, now deemed proper to solicit Captain Cook to undergo fresh dangers by undertaking a voyage of this kind; nevertheless, as he was universally looked upon to be the fittest person in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> for the purpose, the eyes of every one were tacitly fixed upon him: he was consulted on every thing relating to it, and solicited cited to name the person whom he judged most proper to conduct it. To determine this point, Captain Cook, Sir Hugh Palliser, and Mr. Stephens, were invited to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Lord Sandwich to dinner; where, besides the consideration of the proper officer for conducting the expedition, many things were said concerning the nature of the design. They enlarged upon its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, its consequences to navigation and science, and the completeness it would give to the whole system of discoveries; until at last Captain Cook was so much inflamed by the representation of the importance of the voyage, that he started up, and declared that he would conduct it himself. This was what the parties present had desired, and probably expected; his offer was therefore instantly laid before the king, and Captain Cook appointed commander of the expedition by the 10th of February 1776. At the same time it was agreed, that on his return from the voyage, he should be restored to his place at Greenwich; and if no vacancy occurred during the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, the officer who succeeded him was to reign in his favour. The instructions he now received were, that he should attempt the high latitudes between the continents of Asia and America, and if possible return to England along the northern coasts of Asia and Europe. This was most probably the result of the captain's own deliberations, and what had been suggested by him to Lord Sandwich and other people in power. He was particularly desired to sail first into the Pacific ocean through the chain of newly discovered islands which he had lately visited. After having crossed the equator, and passed into the northern parts of the ocean just mentioned, he was then to hold such a course as might tend to settle many interesting points of geography, and produce some intermediate discoveries, before he arrived at the main <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of operation. With regard to this principal object, he was ordered, immediately on his arrival on the coast of New <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBION">Albion</a>, to proceed northward as far as the latitude of 65 degrees, without losing any time in exploring creeks or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> previous to his arrival in that latitude; and for his further encouragement, the act of 1745, offering a premium for the discovery of the passage, was amended in the manner above mentioned. That nothing might be wanting which could promote the success of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> expedition, Lieutenant Pickering was sent out, in 1776, with directions to explore the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAFFIN_S_BAY">Baffin's bay</a>; and the next year Lieutenant Young was commissioned not only to examine the western parts of that bay, but to endeavour to find a passage on that side from the Atlantic to the Pacific ocean. Nothing, however, was performed by either of these gentlemen which in the least could promote Captain Cook's success.
