The author of animadversions upon Dr Brown's three Essays on the Characteristics, observes, that it is "imprudent, to say no worse, in some sincere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for Christianity, to reject the friendly advice and affluence of so matterly a writer as the lord Shaftesbury, and to give him up to the Deists as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>." But it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of fact, and not considerations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> or imprudence, that must determine the question. In support of his lordship's having been a believer in our holy religion, may be alleged, his Preface to Whichcot's Sermons, and his Letters to a Student at the university: in both which works he constantly expresses himself in such language as seems to indicate that he was really a Christian. And with regard to the letters, it may be remarked, that they were written in 1707, 1708, and 1709, not many years before his lordship's death. Nevertheless, there are in the Characteristics to many sceptical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, that he must be considered as having been a doubter at least, if not an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> unbeliever, with respect to revelation. But if he must be ranked among the Deists, we agree with the observation of one of his biographers; that he is a very different Deist from numbers who have appeared in that character; his general principles being much less exceptionable. The style of Lord Shaftesbury's compositions is also a point upon which various and contradictory sentiments ments have been entertained. But for the fullest and most judicious criticism that has appeared upon that subject, we may refer the reader to Dr Blair's Lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a> and Belles Lettres, vol. i. p. 192, 193, 207, 208, 234, 263, and 396—398. Cooper, Samuel, a very eminent English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> painter, born in 1609, and bred under the care of his uncle John Hopkins. He derived, however, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> excellence from a study of the works of Van Dyck, in whose time he lived; inasmuch that he was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> styled "Vandyck in little." His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> was chiefly confined to the head, in which, with all its dependencies, especially the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, he was inimitable; but if he descended lower his incorrectness was notorious. He died in 1672; and his pieces are universally admired all over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, selling for incredible prices.—He had a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, Alexander, likewise a good miniature painter, who became limner to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> queen of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. Cooper, Thomas, a pious and learned prelate in the reign of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> about the year 1517. He was educated in the school adjoining to Magdalene <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, of which he was a chorister, where also, in 1539, he was elected probationer, and fellow in the following year. About the year 1546, quitting his fellowship, he applied himself to the study of physic, in 1556 took the degree of bachelor in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, and practised as physician at Oxford. Being inclined to the Protestant religion, probably this was only a prudent fulfiling of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> intentions during the popish reign of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; for, on the accession of Elizabeth, he resumed the study of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, became a celebrated preacher, was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Christ-church, and vice-chancellor of the university, having accumulated the degrees of bachelor and doctor in divinity. In 1569 he was made dean of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>; and, the year following, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>: whence, in 1584, he was translated to the see of Winchester, in which city he died on the 29th of April 1594, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> there, on the south side of the choir. The several writers who have mentioned Dr Cooper, unanimously give him the character of an eloquent preacher, a learned divine, and a good man. He had the misfortune, while at Oxford, to marry a lady whose gallantries became notorious: nevertheless he would not be divorced from her; knowing that he could not live without a wife, he did not choose to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> with the scandal of a second marriage."—He wrote, 1. The Epitome of Chronicles from the 17th year after Christ to 1540, and thence after to 1560. 2. Thesaurus linguae Romanae et Britannicae. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, which is an improvement upon Elyot's, was much admired by Queen Elizabeth, who thenceforward determined to promote the author. 3. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> exposition of such chapters of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> as usually are read in the church, at common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, on Sundays throughout the year. 4. An admonition to the people of England. 5. Sermons. Cooper, John Gilbert, a polite writer of the present age, was born in 1723; and was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, whose fortune was injured in the last century by their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>. He resided at Thurgarton priory in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, which was granted by King Henry VIII. to William Cooper, one of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. This mansion Mr Cooper inherited from his father, who in 1639 was high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the county; and transmitted it to his son, who filled the same respectable office in 1783. After passing through Westminster school under Dr John Nicoll, along with the late Lord <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a>, Lord Buckinghamshire, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Johnson, Mr George Ashby, and many other eminent and ingenious men, he became in 1743 a fellow-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of Trinity-college, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and resided there two or three years; but quitted the university on his marriage with Sufanna the daughter of William Wright, Esq.; son to the lord keeper of that name, and recorder of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a> 1729—1763. In the year 1745 he commenced author by the publication of The Power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">Harmony</a>, a poem in 4to; and in 1746 and 1747 he produced several Essays and Poems under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> of Philalethes, in a periodical work called The Museion, published by Mr Dodley. In the same year he came forward as an author, with his name, by a work which received much assistance from his friend the Reverend John Jackson of Leicester, who communicated several learned notes, in which he contrived to manifest his dislike to his formidable antagonist Mr Warburton. It was entitled The Life of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, collected from the Memorabilia of Xenophon, and the Dialogues of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, and illustrated farther by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, Diodorus Siculus, Cicero, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLUS">Proclus</a>, Apuleius, Maximus Tyrius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius, Aulus Gellius, and others, 1749, 8vo. In this work Mr Cooper gave evident marks of superior genius; warm, impetuous, and impatient of restraint. In 1754, Mr Cooper published his Letters on Taste, 8vo; an elegant little volume, on which no small share of his reputation is founded; and in 1755, The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">Tomb</a> of Shakespeare, a Vision, 4to; a decent performance, but in which there is more of wit and application than of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> or genius. In 1756 he assisted Mr Moore, by writing some numbers of the World; and attempted to rouse the indignation of his countrymen against the Hessians, at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> brought over to defend the nation, in a poem called the Genius of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, addressed to Mr Pitt. In 1758, he published Epistles to the Great, from Arisippus in Retirement, 4to; and The Call of Arisippus, Epistle IV. to Mark Akenside, M.D. Also, A Father's Advice to his son, in 4to. In the Annual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">Register</a> of the same year is his Translation of an Epistle from the King of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> to Monseigneur Voltaire. In 1759, he published Ver Vert; or the Nunnery Parrot; an Heroic Poem, in four cantos, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to the Abbots of D***; translated from the French of Monsieur Gresset, 4to; reprinted in the first volume of Dilly's Repository, 1777; and, in 1764, Poems on several subjects, by the Author of the Life of Socrates; with a prefatory Advertisement by Mr Dodley. In this little volume were included all the separate poetical pieces which have been already mentioned, excepting Ver Vert, which is a sprightly composition. Mr Cooper died at his father's house in May Fair, after a long and excruciating illness arising from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, April 14th 1769.

COPAIFERA

Pages 275-276

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>: A genus belonging to the decandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

COPAL

Pages 276-276

improperly called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> copal, is a gum of the resinous kind brought from New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, being the concrete juice of the Rhin Copallinum. It is employed as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>. See Varnishing and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

COPARCENERS

Pages 276-276

(from con and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>/cept, "partner"), <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> PARCENERS; such as have equal portions in the inheritance of their ancestor. Coparceners are so either by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. Coparceners by law, are the issue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>; which, in default of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> or heir, come equally to the lands of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. Coparceners by custom, are those who, by some peculiar custom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, challenge equal parts in such lands; as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, by the custom of gavelkind. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England is not subject to coparcenary.

COPE

Pages 276-276

an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> ornament, usually worn by chanters and subchanters, when they officiate in solemnity. It reaches from the shoulders to the feet. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> called it Phialus.—The word is also used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covering of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, &c. Cope is also the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> or tribute due to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>; of which Manlove <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> thus: Egrets and regrets to the king's highway, The miners have; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> and cope they pay; The thirteenth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of ore within their mine, To the lord for lot, they pay at measuring <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; Sixpence a load for cope the lord demands, And that is paid to the burgomaster's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. This word by doomsday-book, as Mr Hagar hath interpreted it, signifies a hill: and cope is taken for the supreme cover, as the cope of heaven. COPEL. See CUPEL.

COPENHAGEN

Pages 276-276

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, situated on the eastern shore of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, upon a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, not far from the strait called the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° O. N. Lat. 55° 30'. The precise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the foundation of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> is disputed; but the most probable account is, that it took its rise from a castle built on the spot in the year 1168, as a protection against the pirates which at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> swarmed in the Baltic. The conveniency of the situation, and the security afforded by the castle, soon induced a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the inhabitants of Zealand to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> thither: but it was not distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence until 1443, during the reign of Christopher of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>; since which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> it has been gradually enlarged and beautified, and is become the capital of Denmark. Copenhagen is the best built city of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; for although Petersburgh excels it in superb edifices, yet, as it contains no wooden houses, it does not display that striking <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> of meanest and magnificence; but in general exhibits a more equable and uniform appearance. The town is surrounded towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> with regular ramparts and bastions, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> ditch full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and a few outworks; its circumference <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> between four and five miles. The streets are well paved, with a foot-way on each side, but too narrow and inconvenient for general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the buildings are of brick; and a few are of free-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> brought from Germany. The houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> are in general splendid, and constructed in the Italian style of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which was erected by Christian VI. is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pile of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> is of stone, and the wings of brick stuccoed; the suite of apartments is princely; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance is more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> than elegant. The busy spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is visible in this city, which contains about 80,000 inhabitants. The haven is always crowded with merchant ships: and the streets are intersected by broad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, which bring the merchandise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the warehouses that line the quays. This city owes its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> to a dreadful fire in 1728, that destroyed five churches and 67 streets, which have been since rebuilt in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> style. The new part of the town, raised by the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> Frederic V., is extremely beautiful, scarcely inferior to Bath. It consists of an octagon, containing four uniform and elegant buildings of hewn stone, and of four broad streets leading to it in opposite directions. In the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> stands an equestrian statue of Frederic V. in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, as big as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, which cost 80,000l. The Royal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cabinet of Rarities, merits the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of travellers. This collection, which was begun by Frederic III., is deposited in eight apartments, and ranged in the following order: animals, shells, minerals, paintings, antiquities, medals, drestles, arms and implements of the Laplanders. Part of Copenhagen, which is called Christiania, is built upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAK">Amak</a>, which generally attracts the curiosity of foreigners; (see AMAR). From this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, to which the main city is joined by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are supplied with fowl, beef, mutton, venison, corn, and culinary vegetables, which are produced here in the greatest abundance.

COPERNICAN

Pages 276-278

in general, something belonging to Copernicus. Hence Copernican System <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">Hypothesis</a>, that system of the world wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is supposed to revolve in the centre, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, to move in ellipses round him. See Copernicus. Copernicus, Nicolaus, an eminent astronomer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">Thorn</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, Jan. 10, 1472. He was taught the Latin and Greek languages at home; and afterwards sent to Cracovia, where he studied <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and physic. His genius in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was naturally turned to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, which he pursued through all its various branches. He set out for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> when he was 23 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; but staid at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> some time, for the sake of being with the celebrated astronomer of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, Dominicus <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a>: whose conversation, however, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, he affected, not so much as a learner, as an assistant to him in making his observations. From thence he passed to Rome, where he was no sooner arrived than he was considered as not inferior to the famous Regiomontanus; and acquired, in short, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a reputation, that he was chosen professor of mathematics, which he taught for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time with great applause. He also made Copernicus made some astronomical observations there about the year 1500. Returning to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> some years after, he began to apply his vast knowledge in mathematics to correct the system of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> which then prevailed. He set himself to collect all the books which had been written by philosophers and astronomers, and to examine all the various hypotheses they had invented for the solution of the celestial phenomena; to try <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a more symmetrical order and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the parts of the world could not be discovered, and a more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> in its motions established, than what the astronomers of those times so easily admitted. But of all their hypotheses none pleased him so well as the Pythagorean, which made the sun to be the centre of the system, and supposed the earth to move not only round the sun, but round its own axis also. He thought he discerned much beautiful order and proportion in this; and that all that embarrassment and perplexity from epicycles and eccentricities, which attended the Ptolemaic hypothesis, would here be entirely removed. This system, then, he began to consider, and to write upon, when he was about 35 years of age. He employed himself in contemplating the phenomena carefully; in making mathematical calculations; in examining the observations of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and in making new ones of his own; and after more than 20 years chiefly spent in this manner, he brought his scheme to perfection, and established that system of the world which goes by his name, and is now universally received, (see Astronomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>). His system, however, was then looked upon as a most dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>; for which he was thrown into prison by Pope Urban VIII. and not suffered to come out till he had recanted his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; that is, till he had renounced the testimony of his senses. He died the 24th of May 1543, in the 70th year of his age. This extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had been made canon of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a> by his mother's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, Lucas Wazebrodius, who was bishop of that place. He was not only the greatest of astronomers, but a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the Greek and Latin tongues; to all which he joined the greatest piety and innocence of manners. The following is the account of the discoveries of Copernicus by Dr Smith, in his Essays on Philosophical Subjects. "The confusion (says Dr Smith) in which the old hypotheses represented the heavenly bodies, was, as Copernicus himself tells us, what first suggested to him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of forming a new system, that these, the noblest works of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, might no longer appear devoid of that harmony and proportion which discover themselves in her meanest productions. What most of all dissatisfied him was, the notion of the equalizing circle, which, by representing the revolutions of the celestial spheres as equable only when surveyed from a point that was different from their centres, introduced a real inequality into their motions; contrary to that most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, and indeed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> idea, with which all the authors of astronomical systems, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, Eudoxus, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPARCHUS">Hipparchus</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> themselves, had hitherto set out, that the real motions of such beautiful and divine objects must necessarily be perfectly regular, and go on, in a manner as agreeable to the imagination as the objects themselves are to the senses. He began to con- Vol. VI. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. Copernicus, midnight, they appear nearest the earth, are largest, and most sensible to the eye, and seem to revolve backwards in their retrograde <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. To explain these appearances, the system of Ptolemy supposed each of these planets to be at the upper part of their several epicycles in the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and at the lower in the other. But it afforded no satisfactory principle of connection, which could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> the mind easily to conceive how the epicycles of those planets, whose spheres were so distant from the sphere of the sun, should thus, if one may say so, keep time to its motion. The system of Copernicus afforded this easily; and like a more simple machine, without the assistance of epicycles, connected together, by fewer movements, the complex appearances of the heavens. When the superior planets appear nearly in conjunction with the sun, they are then in the side of their orbits, which is almost opposite to, and most distant from, the earth, and therefore appear smallest and least sensible to the eye. But as they then revolve in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> which is almost contrary to that of the earth, they appear to advance forward with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> velocity; as a ship that sails in a contrary direction to another, appears from that other to fail both with its own velocity and the velocity of that from which it is seen. On the contrary, when those planets are in opposition to the sun, they are on the same side of the sun with the earth, are nearest it, most sensible to the eye, and revolve in the same direction with it; but as their revolutions round the sun are slower than that of the earth, they necessarily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> behind by it, and therefore seem to revolve backwards; as a ship which sails slower than another, though it sails in the same direction, appears from that other to fail backwards. After the same manner, by the same annual revolution of the earth, he connected together the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> and retrograde motions of the two inferior planets, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> appearances of all the five. Thus far did this new account of things render the appearances of the heavens more completely coherent than had been done by any of the former systems. It did this, too, by a more simple and intelligible, as well as more beautiful machinery. It represented the sun, the great enlightener of the universe, whose body was alone larger than all the planets taken together, as established immovable in the centre, shedding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> on all the worlds that circulated around him in one uniform direction, but in longer or shorter periods, according to their different distances. It took away the diurnal revolution of the firmament, whole rapidity, upon the old hypothesis, was beyond what even thought could conceive. It not only delivered the imagination from the embarrassment of epicycles, but from the difficulty of conceiving these two opposite motions going on at the same time, which the system of Ptolemy and Aristotle bestowed upon all the planets; I mean, their diurnal westward, and periodical eastward revolutions. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> revolution round its own axis took away the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for supposing the first, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> was easily conceived when by itself. The five planets, which seem, upon all other systems, to be objects of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> by themselves, unlike to every thing to which the imagination has been accustomed, when supposed to revolve along with the earth round the sun, were naturally apprehended to be objects of the same kind with the earth, habitable, opaque, and enlightened only by the rays of the sun. And thus this hypothesis, by classing them in the same species of things, with an object that is of all others the most familiar to us, took off that wonder and uncertainty which the strangeness and singularity of their appearance had excited; and thus far, too, better answered the great end of philosophy. Neither did the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and simplicity of this system alone recommend it to the imagination; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> and unexpectedness of that view of nature which it opened to the fancy, excited more wonder and surprise than the strangeness of those appearances, which it had been invented to render natural and familiar, and these sentiments still more endeared it. For though it is the end of philosophy to allay that wonder which either the unusual or seemingly disjointed appearances of nature excite, yet it never triumphs so much as when, in order to connect together a few, in themselves perhaps inconsiderable objects, the has, if I may say so, created another constitution of things, more natural indeed, and such as the imagination can more easily attend to, but more new, more contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> opinion and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, than any of those appearances themselves. As in the influence before us, in order to connect together some seeming irregularities in the motions of the planets, the most inconsiderable objects in the heavens, and of which the greater part of mankind have no occasion to take any notice during the whole course of their lives, she has, to talk in the hyperbolic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Tycho Brahe, moved the earth from its foundations, sloped the revolution of the firmament, made the sun stand still, and subverted the whole order of the universe. Such were the advantages of this new hypothesis, as they appeared to its author when he first invented it. But though that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a>, so natural to the learned, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> which they are so apt to take in exciting, by the novelty of their supposed discoveries, the amazement of mankind, may notwithstanding what one of his disciples tells us to the contrary, have had its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in prompting Copernicus to adopt this system; yet when he had completed his Treatise of Revolutions, and began coolly to consider what a strange doctrine he was about to offer to the world, he so much dreaded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of mankind against it, that, by a species of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINENCE">continence</a> of all others the most difficult to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, he detained it in his closet for thirty years together. At last, in the extremity of old age, he allowed it to be extorted from him, but died as soon as it was printed, and before it was published. Copernicus, the name of an astronomical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, invented by Mr Whitton, to exhibit the motion and phenomena of the planets, both primary and secondary. It is built upon the Copernican system, and for that reason called by his name.

COPHTI

Pages 278-279

COPTS, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> COPTI, a name given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, who are of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Jacobites. The critics are extremely divided about the origin and orthography of the word; some write it Cophi, others Cophites, Cophites, Copts, &c. Scaliger derives the name from Coptos, an anciently celebrated town of Egypt, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the Thebaid. Kircher refutes this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, and maintains, that the word originally signifies "cut" and "circumscribed;" and was given these people by the Mahometans, by way of reproach, because of their practice of circumcision: but P. Sollier, another Jesuit, refutes this opinion. Scaliger afterwards changed his opinion, and derived the word from Ανυπότης, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of Egypt, by retrenching the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>: but this opinion, too, P. Sollier disputes. John de Leo and others say, that the Egyptians anciently called their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> Elcbibth, or Cibth, from Cibth their first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, whence Coptite, &c. others say from Cobtim <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> king of Egypt. Vanleb derives the word Copt from Copt, son of Misfrain, grandson of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>. All these etymologies P. Sollier rejects, on this principle, that were they true, the Egyptians ought all equally to be called Cophi; whereas, in effect, none but the Christians, and among those none but the Jacobites, bear the name, the Melchites not being comprehended under it. Hence he chooses to derive the word from the name Jacobite, retrenching the first syllable; whence Cobite, Cobea, Copta, and Copta. The Copts have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> who resides at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, but he takes his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>; he has no archbishop under him, but 11 or 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. The rest of the clergy, whether <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> or regular, is composed of the orders of St Anthony, St Paul, and St Macarius, who have each their monasteries. Besides the orders of priests, deacons, and subdeacons, the Copts have likewise archimandrites, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> whereof they confer with all the prayers and ceremonies of a strict ordination. This makes a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> among the priests; and besides the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and authority it gives them with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, it comprehends the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> and functions of archpriests. By a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of 600 years standing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> elected bishop be not already archimandrite, that dignity must be conferred on him before episcopal ordination. The second person among the clergy, after the patriarch, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITULAR">titular</a> patriarch of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, who also resides at Cairo, because of the few Copts at Jerusalem; he is, in effect, little more than the bishop of Cairo: only he goes to Jerusalem every Easter, and visits some other places in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> near Egypt, which own his jurisdiction. To him belongs the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Coptic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, during the vacancy of the patriarchal see. To be elected patriarch, it is necessary the person have lived all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINENCE">continence</a>; it is he confers the bishoprics. To be elected bishop, the person must be in the celibate; or, if he has been married, it must not be above once. The priests and inferior ministers are allowed to be married before ordination; but are not obliged to it, as Ludolphus erroneously observes. They have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of deacons, and even confer the dignity frequently on children. None but the lowest rank among the people commence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>; whence arises that excessive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> found among them; yet the respect of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> towards the clergy is very extraordinary. Their office is longer than the Roman office, and never changes in anything: they have three liturgies, which they vary occasionally. The monastic life is in great esteem among the Copts: to be admitted into it, there is always required the consent of the bishop. The religious Copts make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of perpetual chastity; renounce the world, and live with great austerity in deserts: they are obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> in their clothes and their girdle, on a mat stretched on the ground; and to prostrate themselves every evening 150 times, with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> on the ground. They are all, both men and women, of the lowest class of the people; and live on alms. The nunneries are properly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>; and few enter but widows reduced to beggary. F. Roderic reduces the errors and opinions of the Copts to the following heads: 1. That they put away their wives, and espouse others while the first are living. 2. That they have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sacraments, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, the eucharist, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, ordination, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, fasting, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. 3. That they deny the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Son. 4. That they only allow of three ecumenical councils; that of Nice, Constantinople, and Ephesus. 5. That they only allow of one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and operation, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, after the union of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. For their errors in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, they may be reduced, 1. To the practice of circumcising their children before baptism, which has obtained among them from the 12th century. 2. To their ordaining deacons at five years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. 3. To their allowing of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> in the second degree. 4. To their forbearing to eat blood; to which some add their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of a baptism by fire, which they confer by applying a hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> to their forehead or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>. —Others palliate these errors, and show that many of them are rather abuses of particular persons than doctrines of the feet. This seems to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with regard to their polygamy, eating of blood, marrying in the second degree, and the baptism of fire; for circumcision, it is not practised as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, nor as of any divine appointment, but merely as a custom which they derive from the Ishmaelites; and which, perhaps, may have had its origin from a view to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and decency in those hot countries. The Copts, at different times, have made several reunions with the Latins; but always in appearance only, and under some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of their affairs. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Pope Paul IV. a Syrian was dispatched to Rome from the patriarch of Alexandria, with letters to that pope; wherein he acknowledged his authority, and promised obedience; desiring a person might be dispatched to Alexandria, to treat about a reunion of his church to that of Rome; pursuant to which, Pius IV., successor to Paul, chose F. Roderic, a Jesuit, whom he dispatched in 1561, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of apostolical nuncio. But the Jesuit, upon a conference with two Copts deputed for that purpose by the patriarch, was made to know, that the titles of father of fathers, pastor of pastors, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all churches, which the patriarch had bestowed on the pope in his letters, were no more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> matters of civility and compliment; and that it was in this manner the patriarch used to write to his friends: they added, that since the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHALCEDON">Chalcedon</a>, and the establishment of several patriarchs independent of one another, each was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and master of his own church. This was the answer the patriarch gave the pope, after he had received a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> remitted to him from Rome, by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Venetian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>.

COPHTIC

Pages 279-280
or Coptic, the language of the Copts, the ancient language of the Egyptians, mixed with... COPHIC a great deal of Greek, the characters it is written in being all Greek. It has a form and construction peculiar to itself: it has no inflections of the nouns or verbs; but expresses number, case, gender, person, mood, tense, and possessive pronouns, by letters and particles prefixed. F. Kircher is the first who published a grammar and vocabulary of the Coptic. There is not known any book extant in the Coptic, except translations of the Holy Scriptures, or of ecclesiastical offices; or others that have relation thereto, as dictionaries, &c. The ancient Coptic is now no longer found but in books; the language now used throughout the country is Arabic. The old Coptic, which Kircher maintains to be a mother tongue, and independent of all others, had been much altered by the Greeks: for besides that it has borrowed all its characters from the Greek, with a very little variation, a great number of the words are pure Greek. Vossius, indeed, affirms, that there was no Coptic language till after Egypt became subject to the Arabs. The language, according to him, is a mixture of Greek and Arabic: the very name thereof not being in the world till after the Arabs were masters of the country. But this, M. Simon observes, proves nothing; except that what was anciently called Egyptian, has since by the Arabs been called Coptic, by a corruption of speech. There are, it is true, Arabic words in the Coptic; yet this by no means proves but that there was a language before that time, either Coptic or Egyptian. Pietro de la Valle observes, that the Copts have entirely lost their ancient tongue; that it is now no longer understood among them; that they have nothing extant therein but some sacred books; and that they still say mass in it. All their other books have been translated into Arabic, which is their vulgar tongue; and this has occasioned the originals to be lost: it is added, that they rehearse the epistles and gospels in the mass twice; once in Arabic and once in Coptic. Indeed, if we believe F. Vanleeb, the Copts say the mass in Arabic, all but the epistles and gospels, which they rehearse both in that and Coptic. Coptic Bible. See Bible. Coptic Liturgies are three; one attributed to Basil, another to St Gregory, and the third to Cyril: they are translated into Arabic for the use of the priests and people.

COPIATA

Pages 280-280

under the western empire, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>-digger. In the first ages of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> there were clerks destined for this employment. In the year 357 Constantine made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> in favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>'s copiate, i.e. of those who had the care of interments; whereby he exempts them from the lustral contribution which all other traders paid. It was under him also that they first began to be called copiates, q.d. clerks destined for bodily labour, from κοπέω, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> κοπάω, σκίνδω, κεδό, ἑρίω, "I cut, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>," &c. Before that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they were called decani and lecticarii; perhaps because they were divided by decades or tens, each whereof had a bier or litter for the carriage of the dead bodies. Their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among the clerks was the next in order before the chanters. COPING of a wall, the top or cover of a wall, made sloping to carry off the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Coping over, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARPENTRY">Carpentry</a>, a sort of hanging over, not <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> to its upright, but bevelling on its under side till it end in an edge.

COPIST

Pages 280-280

in diplomatic science, signifies a transcriber <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> copier of deeds, books, &c.

COPPA

Pages 280-280

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a cop <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cock of grafs, hay, or corn, divided into titheable portions; as the tenth cock, &c. This word in strikethes denotes the gathering or laying up the corn in cops or heaps, as the method is for barley or oats, &c. not bound up, that it may be the more fairly and justly tithed: and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> they still retain the word, a cop or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of hay, straw, &c. COPPEL. See CUPEL.

COPPER

Pages 280-280

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, called by the alchemists Venus, on account of its facility of uniting with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of different metallic substances. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, when pure, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, and its specific gravity from 8.7 to 9.3, which depends not only on its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of purity, but also on its condensation by hammering. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

COPPERAS

Pages 280-280

a name given to the fictitious sulphate of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. COPPERPLATE. See Engraving.

COPPICE

Pages 280-280
or Copse, a little wood, consisting of under-woods, or such as may be raised either by sowing or planting.

COPTOS

Pages 280-280

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a famous trading town of the Thebais, inhabited by Egyptians and Arabs, some distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; others <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it in a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Nile, on which, however, it had a port. Here Isis, on hearing of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, cut one of her locks and put on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>; and hence the name Coptos, signifying privation. A <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> this of the antiquity of the place. And for this reason the Ifiaci, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> priests of Isis, were bald, according to Juvenal.

COPULATION

Pages 280-280

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, otherwise called coition. See Generation.

COPY

Pages 280-281

in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, a transcript of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, made for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and satisfaction of some of the parties concerned, or in order to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> thereof. Copy is also used for an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of any original <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; particularly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, draught, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, &c. Copy, among printers, denotes the manuscript or original of a book given to print from. Copy-Hold, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> for which a tenant has nothing to show but the copy of the rolls made by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. It is called a bare tenure; because the tenant holds the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the lord. However, it is not simply at the will of the lord, but according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> by which such estate is defeasible, and the tenant's heirs may inherit it; and a copy-holder, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he does his services, and does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the custom, cannot be ejected by the lord; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he be, he shall have trespass against him. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Tenure and Villenage. Copy-Holder, one who is admitted tenant of lands or tenements within a manor, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> out of mind, by use and custom of the manor, have been demised, and devised to such as will take them in fee-simple or fee-tail, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, years, or at will, according to the custom. Copy-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> custom of the manor by copy of court-roll; but is generally where the tenant has such estate either in fee or for three lives. Copy-Right, the right which an author may be supposed to have in his own original literary compositions; so that no other person, without his leave, may publish or make profit of the copies. When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> by the exertion of his rational powers has produced an original work, he has clearly a right to dispose of that identical work as he pleases; and any attempt to take it from him, or vary the disposition he has made of it, is an invasion of his right of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. Now the identity of a literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> consists entirely in the sentiment and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; the same conceptions, clothed in the same words, must necessarily be the same composition; and whatever method be taken of conveying that composition to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, or to the eye of another, by recital, by writing, or by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, in any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of copies, or at any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of time, it is always the identical work of the author which is so conveyed; and no other man (if hath been thought) can have a right to convey or transfer it without his consent, either tacitly or expressly given. This consent may perhaps be tacitly given when an author permits his work to be published without any reserve of right, and without stamping on it any marks of ownership; it is then a present to the public, like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, or the laying out a new highway: but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a bargain for a single <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, or a total <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> or gift of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPYRIGHT">copyright</a>; in the one case the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> hath been thought to continue in the original proprietor; in the other the whole property, with its exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, to be perpetually transferred to the grantee. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it is urged, that though the exclusive right of the manuscript, and all which it contains, belongs undoubtedly to the owner before it is printed or published; yet from the instant of publication, the exclusive right of an author or his assigns to the sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> immediately vanishes and evaporates; as being a right of too subtile and unsubstantial a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to become the subject of property at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, and only capable of being guarded by positive statute and special <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of the magistracy. The Roman law adjudged, that if one man wrote anything, though ever so elegantly, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> of another, the writing should belong to the original owner of the materials on which it was written: meaning certainly nothing more thereby than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> operation of writing, for which it directed the scribe to receive a satisfaction: especially as, in works of genius and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, such as a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> painted on another man's canvas, the same law gave the canvas to the painter. We find no other mention in the law of any property in the works of the understanding, though the sale of literary copies, for the purposes of recital or multiplication, is certainly as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> as the times of Terence, Martial, and Statius. Neither with us in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> hath there been (till very lately) any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> determination upon the right of authors at the common law. It was determined in the case of Miller v. Taylor in B. R. Pafch. 9 Geo. III. 1760, that an exclusive copy-right in authors subsisted by the common law. But afterwards, in the case of Donaldson v. Becket, before the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords, which was finally determined 22d February 1774, it was held, that no copy-right subsists in authors, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the several terms created by the statute 8 Ann. c. 19. This statute declares, that the author and his assigns shall have the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of printing and reprinting his works for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of 14 years, and no longer; and also protects that property by additional penalties and forfeitures; directing farther, that, if at the end of that term, the author himself be living, the right shall then return to him for another term of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>.

COQUES

Pages 281-281

Gonzalo, an esteemed painter of portraits and conversations, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1618, and was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Ryckaert; under whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> he applied himself diligently to cultivate those promising talents which he possessed; not only by practising the best rules administered to him by his instructor, but also by studying <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with singular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> admirer of Van Dyck; and fixing on the manner of that great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of so far succeeding, that next to him he was esteemed equal to any other painter of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. In the school of Ryckaert he had been accustomed to paint conversations, and he frequently composed subjects of fancy like <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENIERS">Teniers</a>, Oltade, and his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; and by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> he introduced a very agreeable style of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, in a kind of hitherto conversation, which seemed much more acceptable to persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> than the general manner of painting portraits, and procured him great reputation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. In that way he composed several fine pictures for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. and likewise several for the archduke Leopold, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>; which latter prince, as a mark of respect, presented Coques with a rich <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> chain, and a gold medal, on which the bust of that prince was impressed. He died in 1684. He had an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>; his portraits were well defined, with easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> attitudes; he disposed the figures in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> so as to avoid confusion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> embarrassment; he gave an extraordinary clearness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to his heads and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and his touch was free, firm, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, a circumstance very uncommon in works of a small size.

COQUIMBO

Pages 281-282

a port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>, in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated at the mouth of a river of the same name, which discharges itself into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 75° 10'. N. Lat. 30° 8'. COR Caroli, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, an extra-constellated <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> in the northern hemisphere, situated between the Coma Berenices and Ursa <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, so called by Dr Halley in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>. Cor-Hydrae, a fixed star of the first magnitude, in the constellation of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRA">Hydra</a>. Cor-Leonis, in Astronomy, a fixed star of the first magnitude in the constellation Leo. Cor-meille, a noted plant, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the highlands of Scotland. Its roots dried are the support of the highlanders in long journeys, amidst the barren hills deject of the supports of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, like the alimentary powders, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> for a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> repel the attacks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. Infused in liquor it is an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEVERAGE">beverage</a>, and, like the nepenthe of the Greeks, exhilarates the mind. From the similitude of found in the name, it seems to be the same with chara, the root discovered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of Caesar at Dyrrachium, which steeped in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> was such a relief to the famished <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">Or</a> we may reasonably believe it to have been the Caledonian food described by Dio, of which the quantity of a bean would prevent both hunger and thirst; and this, says the historian, they have ready for all occasions.

CORACIAS

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROLLER">Roller</a>, a genus of birds of the order of picae. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORACOBRACHIALIS

Pages 282-282

in Anatomy, the name of a muscle in the arm, serving to raise it upwards.

CORACOIDES

Pages 282-282

in Anatomy, a small short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of the scapula. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORACOMANTES

Pages 282-282

in antiquity, persons who foretold events from their observations on crows.

CORAL STONE

Pages 282-282

a name for a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a> which breaks in veins, and is found in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>. That of Rochlitz in Saxony is the most celebrated, and is found in globules which have a kind of crust about them.

CORALLINA

Pages 282-282
or Coral, in Zoology, a genus belonging to the order of vermes zoophyta. See Helminthology Index. CORAL FISHERY. Red coral is found in the Mediterranean, on the shores of Provence; from Cape de la Couronne to that of St Tropez; about the isles of Majorca and Minorca; on the south of Sicily; on the coasts of Africa; and, lastly, in the Ethiopic ocean, about Cape Negro.

CORALLINES

Pages 282-282

a genus belonging to the vermes zoophyta. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CORALLOENDRON. See Erythrina, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. CORALLOIDES (FRUTICES). See Eschara and Keratophyta.

CORAM

Pages 282-282
Captain Thomas, a gentleman remarkably distinguished by his humanity, was born about the year 1668, and spent the early part of his life in the station of master of a vessel trading to our colonies. Afterwards residing in the eastern part of the metropolis, among sea-faring people, where business often obliged him to come early into the city, and return late, he frequently saw young children exposed in the streets through the indigence or cruelty of their parents. This excited his compassion, and induced him to project the foundation of an hospital for foundlings. In this humane design he laboured with indefatigable diligence for seventeen years; and by his application procured a number of the nobility and gentry to patronize and carry the scheme into execution, and at length obtained the royal charter for it. He was also highly instrumental in promoting the trade of America, by procuring a bounty upon naval stores imported from our colonies. He was likewise eminently concerned in setting on foot the colonies of Georgia and Nova Scotia. His last charitable design, in which he lived to make some progress, was a scheme for uniting the North American Indians more closely to the British interest, by an establishment for the education of Indian girls. In short, he spent the greatest part of life in labouring for the public, and experienced a fate too common in those who devote their talents to such laudable purposes; being at last indebted for subsistence to the voluntary subscriptions of some public-spirited persons, at the head of whom was the late Frederic prince of Wales. Captain Coram died in 1751; and was interred, at his own desire, in a vault under the chapel of the Foundling Hospital.

CORANICH

Pages 282-283

among the Scotch and Irish, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of fingering at funerals, anciently prevalent in those countries, and still practised in several parts. Of this custom Mr Pennant gives the following account. "I had not the fortune to be present at any in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; but formerly assisted at one in the south of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, where it was performed in the fulness of horror. The cries are called by the Irish the ulogbne and bullulu; two words very expressive of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> uttered on these occasions; and being of Celtic stock, etymologists would swear to be the origin of the ulogbne of the Greeks and ululatus of the Latins. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> is very fond of using the last whenever any of his females are distressed; as are others of the Roman poets, and generally on occasions similar to this. It was my fortune to arrive at a certain town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that a person of some distinction departed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; my curiosity led me to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where the funeral seemed conducted in the purest classical form. Quodcumque aspicaret lucius, gemitufque sonabant, Formaque non taciti funeris intus erat. In short, the conclusion was set up by the friends in the same manner as Virgil describes that consequential of Dido's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; Lamentis, gemutique, et farnimeo ululatu Tecta fremunt. Immediately after this followed another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, fully described by Camden in his account of the manners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Irish; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> expostulations and reproaches given to the deceased for quitting this world, where she enjoyed so many blessings, so good a husband, and such fine children. This custom is also of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, for Euryalus's mother makes the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to her dead son. Tunc illa senecet Sera moe requies? potius reliquere solam, Crudelis? But when the time approached for carrying out the corps, the cry was redoubled, Tremulis ululatis aethera compleant; a numerous band of females waiting in the outer <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to attend the hearse, and to pay in chorus the last tribute of their voices. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of this sorrowing train, and the neglect of their persons, were admirably suited to the occasion; their robes were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and flowing, resembling the ancient pall; their feet naked, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and dishevelled: I might truly say, Ut qui conducl plorant in funera, dicunt Et faciunt prope plura dolentibus examino. The corpse was carried slowly along the verge of a most beautiful lake, the ululatus was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, and the the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> ended among the venerable ruins of an old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>."

CORAX

Pages 282-282

the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Corvus. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORBAN

Pages 283-283

in Jewish antiquity, were those offerings which had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in opposition to the minehah, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those which had not. It is derived from the word karab, which signifies "to approach;" because the victims were brought to the door of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a>. The corban were always looked upon as the most sacred offerings. The Jews are reproached with defeating, by means of the corban, the precept of the fifth commandment, which enjoins the respect due to parents. For when a child had no mind to relieve the wants of his father or mother, he would say to them, "It is a gift (corban) by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me;" i.e., "I have devoted that to God which you ask of me, and it is no longer mine to give." Corban is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> which the Mahometans perform at the foot of Mount Arrafat in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>. It consists in killing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sheep, and distributing them among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>.

CORBEILS

Pages 283-283

in Fortification, little baskets about a foot and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, eight inches wide at the bottom and twelve at the top; which being filled with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, are frequently set one against another upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> elsewhere, leaving certain port holes, from whence to fire upon the enemy under <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> without being seen by them.

CORBEL

Pages 283-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the representation of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>, sometimes seen on the heads of caryatides. The word is also used for the vase, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tambour, of the Corinthian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>; so called from its resemblance to a basket, or because it was first formed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of a basket. Corbel, or Corbil, is also used, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, for a short piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> placed in a wall, with its end sticking out six or eight inches, as occasion serves, in manner of a shouldering-piece. The under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the end thus sticking out is sometimes cut into the form of a boulting; sometimes of an ogee, and sometimes of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, &c., according to the workman's fancy; the upper side being plain and flat. Corbel is also used by some architects for a niche or hollow left in walls for images, figures, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> to stand in.

CORBET

Pages 283-283

RICHARD, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, and an eminent poet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EWELL">Ewell</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, toward the latter end of the 16th century; and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he was esteemed one of the most celebrated wits of the university.
