Entering into holy orders, he became a popular preacher, and was made chaplain to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I.: when, after several preferments in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, he was, in 1629, made bishop of Oxford; and, in 1632, was translated to the see of Norwich. He was very hospitable, and always a generous encourager of public designs. He died in 1635. There have been several editions of his poems published under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Poemata Stromata.

CORBEY

Pages 283-283

a town of Picardy in France, with a famous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of Benedictine monks. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOMME">Somme</a>, 10 miles east of Amiens, and 75 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 35. N. Lat. 49. 55.

CORCELET

Pages 283-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the fly-clasps which is analogous in its situation to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> in other animals. Many have called it the breast in these also, but improperly; because the breast of other animals is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the lungs and trachea, but these organs are in the fly-clasps distributed throughout the whole body. CORCHORUS: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandria clasps; and in the natural method ranking under the 37th order, Columnea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORCULUM

Pages 283-283

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> from cor "the heart," little heart; the essence of a seed, and principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the future plant, attached to and contained within the lobes. It consists of two parts, termed by Linnaeus Plumula and Rostellum. The former is the radicula of Grew and other naturalists. The corculum is in fact the embryo of the future vegetable; and is attached by two trunks of vessels to the lobes at their union. The first of its two parts mounts upward, and becomes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>. The other strikes into the ground, and is the rudiment of the root. The lobes and heart of the seed are distinctly visible in the bean, and other seeds of that clasps, especially after remaining some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The principle of life is seated either at the summit or base of the seed. From this circumstance are constructed the two first classes in Caesalpinus's method, containing trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> only.

CORCYRA

Pages 283-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, opposite to Thesprotia, a district of Epirus, called Scheria and Phaeacia by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. In Callimachus it is called Drepane; its most ancient name, according to the Scholiast, from the curvity of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. Famous for the shipwreck of Ulysses and the gardens of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCINOUS">Alcinous</a>. Now Corfu. Corcyra, a cognominal town of the island; formerly powerful, and capable of coping with mighty states; situated about the middle of the east side of the island, called The Town of the Phaeacians by Homer. Now Corfu, from the Κόρυφη of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, the name of the citadel. It was a colony of the Corinthians. Corcyreis, the people. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19. 48. Lat. 39. 50. Corcyra Nigra, an island in the Adriatic, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a> (Pliny); called Melena by the Greeks, to distinguish it from the island in the Ionian sea. The epithet Nigra was added, from its woods of tall trees with which it is almost covered. Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CURZOLA">Curzola</a>.

CORD

Pages 283-283
or Chord, an assemblage of several threads of hemp, cabled or twisted together by means of a wheel. See Cordage. The word comes from the Greek ξεσθην, which properly signifies an intestine or gut, of which cords may be made. See Chord. Magical Cord, an instrument in great use among the Laplanders, and by them supposed to be endowed with a number of virtues. It is a cord or rope with three knots tied in it. They use many magical rites and ceremonies in the tying of this cord; and, when thus prepared, it is supposed to have power over the winds; and they will sell, by means of it, a good wind, or at least the promise of one, to a ship. If they untie only one of these knots, a moderate gale succeeds; if two, it is much stronger; and if three, a storm is sure to follow. Cord of Wood, a certain quantity of wood for burning,

CORD-WOOD

Pages 284-284

is new wood, and such as, when brought by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, comes on board a vessel, in opposition to that which is floated.

CORDAGE

Pages 284-284

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in general for all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, whether small, middling, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. See ROPE. The naval cordage of the earlier ages was in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> only thongs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. These primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> were retained by the Caledonians in the third century. The nations to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the Baltic had them in the ninth or tenth centuries; and the inhabitants of the western isles of Scotland make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them at present; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the skin of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, or the raw and salted hide of a cow, into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> pieces, and fastening the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> to their horses with them, or even twisting them into strong ropes of 20 or 30 fathoms length. But these, in the south of our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and on the continent, were early superseded by the use of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> chains. The very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> and commercial <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of the Veneti, that were so intimately connected with the Belgae of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, used iron chains for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> in the days of Caesar. But in the more distant and refined countries of the south, both thongs and these had long given <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to the use of vegetable threads and the arts of combining them into strength. In this manner the Greeks appear to have used the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rushes of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and the Carthaginians the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. And as all the cordage of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> was made of these materials at their last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> on our island, so the art of manufacturing them would be necessarily introduced with the Roman settlements among the Britons. Under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Roman artists their thongs of leather would naturally be laid aside, and the junci, or rushes of the plains, worked up into cordage. And what remarkably coincides with this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is, that the remains of old cables and ropes are still distinguished among the British sailors by the name of old junk. The nations of Roman Britain, and the tribes of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALEDONIA">Caledonia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, had inherited, from their earliest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, many of the rudier arts of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. Their ships were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> open boats, framed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> timbers ribbed with hurdles and lined with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>. These were furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> and sails. The latter were formed of hides, as the tackle was of thongs. They were actually of hides among the Veneti as late as the days of Caesar; and they were never furled, but only bound to the mast. But these flight <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-boats, and their rude furniture, would soon be dismissed by the provincials for the more substantial vessels and more <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> sails of the Romans. The Roman sails, which were composed of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> in the days of Agricola, were afterwards made of hemp; and our own are therefore denominated cannabis or canvas by our mariners at present. And about the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> assuredly did the junk of the British cordage give way to the same materials; the use of hempen ropes upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and of hempen nets for hunting, being very common among the Romans in the first century.

CORDATED

Pages 284-284

an appellation frequently given by naturalists to things somewhat resembling a heart.

CORDED

Pages 284-284

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> corded, some authors take for a cross wound <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wrenched about with cords; others, with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, take it for a cross made of two pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>.

CORDELIER

Pages 284-284

a Franciscan, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> of the order of St Francis. The Cordeliers are clothed in thick grey cloth, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COWL">cowl</a>, a chaperon, and cloak of the same; having a girdle of rope or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> tied with three knots: whence the name.—They are otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a> Friars, their original name. The denomination Cordelier is said to have been first given them in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> against the infidels; wherein the Friars Minor having repulsed the barbarians, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> having inquired their name, it was answered, they were people cordelez, "tied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>." The Cordeliers are to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> professed Scotists.

CORDEMOI

Pages 284-284

GERADE, a learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and historian, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, made himself known to M. Boffuet, who placed him about the dauphin in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of reader. He instructed that young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fidelity; and in 1675 was received into the French academy. He wrote a general <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of France during the first races of the French kings, in two volumes; and five discourses on the distinction between Body and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">Soul</a>, which were printed together in 1702 in quarto. He died in 1684. M. Cordemoi followed the principles of Descartes. CORDIA: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order, Aperifolice. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORDIAL

Pages 284-284

in Medicine, whatever raises the spirits, and gives them a sudden strength and cheerfulness; as wine, spirits, the effluvia of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, fruit, and many other substances.

CORDING

Pages 283-284

so called because formerly measured with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>. The dimensions of a statute cord of wood are eight feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, four feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and four feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>.

CORDOBA

Pages 284-286
or Cordova, a city of Andalusia in Spain, situated on the river Guadalquivir, in a very extensive plain. The circumference is large; but it is not peopled in proportion to its extent, for there are Cordova. a great many orchards and gardens within the walls. There are many superb structures, palaces, churches, and religious houses; particularly the cathedral, which is very magnificent: It was formerly a mosque when the Moors possessed the town; for which reason it still retains the name of Mezquita, which has the same meaning. The cathedral is very rich in plate; four of the silver candlesticks cost 50l. a-piece. The revenue of the see amounts to 350l. per annum; but as the bishops cannot devise by will, all they die possessed of eleemosynas to the crown. The square called the Plaza Mayor is surrounded with very fine houses, under which are piazzas. The trade is flourishing on account of the river; and confluents of wine, silk, and Cordovan leather. In the neighbourhood of this place are a vast number of orange and lemon trees, which renders their fruits exceeding cheap. The best horses in Spain come from hence. Cordova was the ancient Corduba mentioned in the preceding article. After the fall of the Roman empire, it was subjected to the dominion of the Goths; but in the eighth century it was raised by the Moorish princes to a state of splendor unequalled in any other part of the world. In the year 755, Abdoullahman, only heir-male of the Omnidid line, having passed over from Africa at the head of a few desperate followers, found means to raise a rebellion in Spain; when, after a battle fought on the banks of the Guadalquivir, in which he overthrew the lieutenant of the Abbasid caliph of Damascus, he became king of all the Moorish possessions in the south of Spain, and in 759 fixed his royal residence at Cordova. Then began those flourishing ages of Arabian gallantry and magnificence which rendered the Moors of Spain superior to all their contemporaries in arts and arms, and made Cordova one of the most splendid cities of the world. Agriculture and commerce prospered under the happy sway of this hero; and the face of the country was changed from a scene of desolation, which the long wars and harsh government of the viceroys had brought on, into a most populous flourishing state, exceeding in riches, number of inhabitants, activity, and industry, any prior or subsequent era of the Spanish history. He added new fortifications to the town, built himself a magnificent palace with delicious gardens, laid causeways through the marshes, made excellent roads to open ready communication between the great towns, and in 786 began the great mosque, which he did not live to finish. During the course of two centuries, this court continued to be the resort of all professors of the polite arts, and of such as valued themselves upon their military and knightly accomplishments; whilst the rest of Europe was buried in ignorance, debased by brutality of manners, or distracted by superstitious disputes. England, weakened by its heptarchy, was too inconsiderable even to be mentioned in the political history of the times. France, though it had a gleam of reputation under Charlemagne, was still a barbarous unpolished nation; and Italy was in utter confusion; the frequent revolutions and change of masters rendering it impossible for learning, or any thing good to acquire a permanent footing in so unstable a soil: Greece, though still in possession of the arts and luxury of ancient Rome, had lost all vigour, and seemed absorbed in the most futile of all pursuits, viz. that of scholastic argument and religious subtleties. The residence of the Omnidid caliphs was long conspicuous for its supreme magnificence, and the crowds of learned men who were allured to it by the protection offered by its sovereigns, the beauty of the country, the wholesomeness of the climate, and the variety of pleasures that returned incessantly in one enchanting round. Cordova became the centre of politeness, industry, and genius. Tilts and tournaments, with other costly shows, were long the darling pastimes of a wealthy happy people; and this was the only kingdom in the west where geometry, astronomy, and physic were regularly studied and practised. Music was no less honoured; for we find, that in 844 a famous musician called Ali Zerib came to settle at Cordova, and formed several pupils, who were supposed to equal the most celebrated performers that were ever known even in the East. That architecture was greatly encouraged, we need no other proof than the great and expensive fabrics undertaken and completed by many of these Spanish monarchs. Whatever faults may be justly condemned in their manner by the connoisseur, accustomed to the chastest noble graces of the Grecian proportions, certainly nobody can behold what remains of these Moorish edifices, without being strongly impressed with a high idea of the genius of the artists, as well as the grandeur of the prince who carried their plans into execution. These sultans not only gave the most distinguished protection to arts and sciences, and to the persons learned in any of them, but were themselves eminently versed in various branches of knowledge. Alkahem II. collected so immense a quantity of manuscripts that before the end of his reign the royal library contained no less than 600,000 volumes, of which the very catalogue filled 40 huge folios. The university of Cordova was founded by him, and under such favourable auspices rose to the highest pitch of celebrity. Abdoullahman was succeeded by his son Hifsem, whose passion for glory and architecture was not in the least inferior to that of his father. He put the finishing hand to the mosque, which the plunder of the southern provinces of France enabled him to complete in the course of a few years. The bridge over the Guadalquivir was a work of Hifsem's after his own plan. Alkahem succeeded Hifsem. Abdoullahman II. was also passionately fond of building. He was the first that brought the supplies of water to Cordova by means of leaden pipes laid upon aqueducts of stone. The quantity was so considerable, that every part of the palace, the mosques, baths, squares, and public edifices, had all of them their fountains constantly playing. A great many of these works still subsist. He paved the whole city, and erected several mosques. After him reigned Mahomet Almundar, Abdallah, and Abdoullahman III., who surpassed all his predecessors in splendor, riches, and experience. His subjects vied with each other in profusion and magnificence. This monarch was succeeded by his son Alkahem II., who left a minor to succeed him, and the kingdom to be governed by the famous vizir Mahomet Abenamir, sur- COR named Almanzor, or "the defender," from his great victories and wise conduct. His descendants inherited from him the visirship, and a power as absolute as if they had been caliphs, until the weakness of the sovereigns encouraged, and the influence of the ministers provoked, the grandees to disturb the state with their jealousies and dissensions. These broils occasioned such a series of civil war and anarchy, as overthrew the throne of Cordova, and destroyed the whole race of Abdoulrahman. Thus the glorious edifice, founded by the valour and prudence of that conqueror, and cemented by similar virtues in many of his successors, sunk into nothing as soon as the sceptre devolved upon weak enervated princes, whose indolence and incapacity transferred the management of every thing to a visir. Many petty kingdoms sprung up out of the ruins of this mighty empire; and the Christians soon found opportunities of destroying, by separate attacks, that tremendous power, which when united had proved an overmatch for their utmost force. New Cordoba, a considerable town of South America, in the province of Tucuman, with a bishop's see, 175 miles from St Jago. W. Long. 62° 5'. S. Lat. 32° 10'.

CORDON

Pages 284-284

in Fortification, a row of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, made round on the outside, and set between the wall of the fortress which lies alone, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> which stands perpendicular, after such a manner, that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> may not be offensive to the eye; whence the cordons serve only as an ornament, ranging round about the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, being only used in fortifications of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; for in those made with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> the void space is filled up with pointed flares.

CORDUAN

Pages 286-286

a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHAROS">pharos</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of France, in Guienne, at the mouth of the river Girond. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> is extremely fine; and it is placed there to hinder vessels from running on the sand-banks at the mouth of the river. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 9'. N. Lat. 45° 36'.

CORDUBA

Pages 284-284

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Baetica, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the Baetis. Built by Marcellus, according to Strabo; but which Marcellus is not so clear. It was the first colony sent into those parts by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and named Patricia, because at first inhabited by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> men, both of the Romans and natives. It is mentioned by Sil. Italicus in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and hence it is probable the first Marcellus was the founder, and not the Marcellus engaged in the civil war between Caesar and Pompey. It was famous for the birth of the two Senecas and of Lucan (Martial), and for its rich produce in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> (Statius, Martial). Still retaining its name a little altered. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. Lat. 37°-45°.

CORDUS

Pages 286-286

Valerius, a learned botanist, was the son of Ericius Cordus, a physician and poet of Germany. Having learned the languages, he applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, in the prosecution of which he examined the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Germany, and travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; but being wounded in the leg by the kick of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, died at Rome in 1554. He wrote Remarks on Dioscorides, and other works.

CORDWAINERS

Pages 286-286
or Cordiners, the term whereby the statutes denominate shoemakers. The word is formed from the French cordonnier, which Menage derives from corduano, a kind of leather brought from Cordova, whereof they formerly made the upper leathers of their shoes. Others derive it from corde "rope," because anciently shoes were made of cords; as they still are in some parts of Spain, under the name of alpargatas. But the former etymology is better warranted; for, in effect, the French workmen who prepare the corduans are still called corduani- ners. In Paris they have two pious societies under the titles of freres cordoniens, "brothers shoemakers," established by authority towards the middle of the 17th century; the one under the protection of St Crispin*, the other of St Crispianus, two saints who had formerly honoured the profession. They live in community, and under fixed statutes and officers; by which they are directed both in their spiritual and secular concerns. The produce of their shoes goes into a common stock, to furnish necessaries for their support; the rest to be distributed among the poor.

COREA

Pages 286-287

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> lying to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, between 99° and 109° degrees of E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>., and between 32° and 46° of N. Lat. It is divided into 8 provinces, which contain 40 cities of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, 51 of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and 70 of the third. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the whole Corea is Han-ching, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> resides. The Jesuits say, the people are well made, of a sweet and tractable disposition, and fond of learning, music, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, and in general resemble the Chinese. Their houses are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, being covered with thatch; and they have no beds, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>. They have little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and therefore make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth in its room. Their trade consists in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, pencils, ginfeng, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>, fowls whose tails are three feet long, horses no more than three feet in height, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> skins, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">castor</a>, and mineral <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. In general it is a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, though abounding in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. It is tributary to China. M. Grolier relates an observation concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Corea, which, in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, furnishes a new <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the revolutions which the surface of our globe has undergone. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Chinese book affirms, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> where Kipe, the king of Corea, established his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, was built in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which forms at present a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the territories of Yong-ping-fou, a city of the first class in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Petcheli. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this (says he) be admitted as a fact, we may from thence conclude, that these territories formerly belonged to Corea; and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Lea-tong, which at present separates this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> from the province of Petcheli, did not then exist, and that it has been formed since; for it is not probable that the sovereign would have fixed his residence without the boundaries of his kingdom, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in a place where he was separated from it by a wide and extensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. This conjecture is confirmed by certain facts admitted by the Chinese. Thus when Yu, named the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, undertook to drain and carry off the waters which had inundated the low grounds of several provinces, he began by the river Hoang-ho, the overflowing of which caused the greatest devastation. He went in search of its source to the bottom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, from whence he directed its course across the provinces of Chen-fu, Chen-fu, Honan, and Petcheli. Towards its mouth, in order to weaken the rapidity of its waters, he divided them into <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> channels, through which he caused the river discharge itself into the eastern sea near the mountain of Kie-che-chan, which then formed a promontory. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the present, that is, about 3050 years, the river Hoang-ho has departed so much from its ancient course, that its mouth at present is about six degrees farther south. We must also remark, that the mountain Kie-che-chan, which was formerly united to the main <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Yong-ping-fou, stands at present in the sea at the distance of about 50 leagues to the south of that city. If the sea has been able to cover with its waters that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of territory which at present forms part of the gulf of Lea-tong, may we not be allowed to suppose that like inundations may have formed successively the whole of that gulf, the ancient existence of which seems so ill to agree with the residence of the kings of Corea in the territories of Yong-ping-fou? It is true, the Chinese history makes no mention of so considerable a physical revolution: but it is equally futile with regard to the 500 ly (50 leagues) extent of ground which is at present covered by the sea beyond the mountains of Kie-che-chan. Besides, of all the changes which the surface of our globe experiences, those only are mentioned in history which happen suddenly, and which consequently make more <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the minds of men. Corea chiefly produces wheat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and ginfeng, with a kind of palm tree which yields a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> capable of producing a yellow varnish little inferior to gilding. Hence also are exported castor and sable skins; also gold, silver, iron, and fossil salt; a kind of small brushes for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, made of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>'s tail, are likewise manufactured here, which are exported to China and highly esteemed there. The sea coasts abound in fish, and great numbers of whales are found there every year towards the north-east. Several of these, it is said, have in their bodies the harpoons of the French and Dutch, from whom they have escaped in the northern extremities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; which seems to indicate a passage from the European into the Asiatic seas round the continents of Europe and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. A considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the paper of Corea is annually imported into China; indeed the tribute due to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> is partly paid with it every year. It is made of cotton, and is as strong as cloth, being written upon with a small hair-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>; but must be done over with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> before it can be written upon in the European manner. It is not purchased by the Chinese for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, but for filling up the squares of their fan-windows; because, when oiled, it resists the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> better than that of China. It is used likewise as wrapping paper; and is serviceable to the tailors, who rub it between their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> until it becomes as soft and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> as the finest cotton cloth, instead of which it is often employed in lining clothes. It has also this singular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, that if it be too thick for the purpose intended, it may be easily split into two or three leaves, each of which is even stronger than the best paper of China. The Coreans are well made, ingenious, brave, and tractable; are fond of dancing; and show great docility in acquiring the sciences, to which they apply with great ardour, and which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> in a particular manner. The northern Coreans are larger sized and more robust than those of the south; have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for arms, and become excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. Their arms are crossbows and long sabres. Men of learning are distinguished from other classes of people by two plumes of feathers in their caps; and when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> present the Coreans with any books for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, they dress themselves in the richest attire, and burn perfumes before they treat concerning the price. The Coreans mourn three years, as in China, for a father or mother; but the time of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> is confined to three months. Their dead are not interred until three years after their decease; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> is performed, they place around the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> the clothes, chariot, and horses of the deceased, with whatever else he showed the greatest fondness for while alive; all which they leave to be carried off by the assistants. Their houses, as in China, consist only of one story, and are very ill built; in the country being composed of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and in cities generally of brick, but all thatched with straw; the walls of their cities are constructed after the Chinese manner, with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> turrets, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, and arched gates. Their writing, dress, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies, and creed, as well as the greater part of their customs, are borrowed from the Chinese. Their women, however, are less confined, and have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of appearing in public with the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, for which they are often ridiculed by their neighbours. They differ from the Chinese also in their ceremonies of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and in the manner of contracting it; the parties in this country taking the liberty to choose for themselves, without consulting the inclinations of their parents, or suffering them to throw any obstacles in their way.

COREIA

Pages 287-287

in antiquity, a festival in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Proserpine, named Core, Kogn, which, in the Molossian dialect signifies a beautiful woman.

CORELLI

Pages 287-288

Arcangelo, the famous Italian musician and composer, a native of Fusignano, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, was born in 1653. He entertained an early propensity for the violin; and as he advanced in years, laboured incessantly in the practice of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. About the year 1672, his curiosity led him to visit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, probably with a view to attend the improvements which were making in music under the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Mazarine, and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the establishment of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> academy; but notwithstanding the character which he brought with him, he was driven back to Rome by Lully, whose jealous temper could not brook so formidable a rival as this illustrious Italian. In the year 1680 he visited Germany, and met with a reception suitable to his merit from most of the German princes, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>; in whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he was retained, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. After about five years stay abroad, he returned again to Rome, and there pursued his studies with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> assiduity. The proficiency of Corelli on his favourite instrument the violin was so great, that the fame of it spread throughout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The style of his performance was learned, elegant, and pathetic; and his tone firm and even. Mr Geminiani, who was well acquainted with, and had studied it, used to resemble it to a sweet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>. A person who had heard him perform says, that, whilst he was playing on the violin, it was usual for his countenance to be disturbed, his eyes to become as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> as fire, and his eye-balls to roll as in an agony. Corelli was highly favoured by that great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and music, Cardinal Ottoboni. Crespelini says, that he regulated the musical academy held at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of his eminence every Monday afternoon. Here it was that Mr Handel became acquainted with him; and in this academy a serenata of Mr Handel, entitled "Il Trionfo del Tempo," was performed, the overture to which was in a style so new and singular, that Corelli was confounded in his first attempt to play it. During the residence of Corelli at Rome, besides those of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, many persons were ambitious of becoming his disciples, and learning the practice of the violin from the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> on that instrument the world had then heard of. Of these it is said the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Edgecumbe was one; and that the fine mezzotinto print of Corelli by Smith was scraped from a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> painted by Mr Hugh Howard at Rome for that nobleman. Corelli died at Rome in 1713; and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Rotunda, otherwise called the Pantheon. Corelli, in the first chapel on the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the entrance. Over the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> is a sepulchral monument to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, with a marble bust thereon, erected at the expense of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> William, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> palatine of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, under the care and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Cardinal Ottoboni. For many years after his decease, this excellent musician was commemorated by a solemn musical performance in the Pantheon, on the anniversary of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. In the year 1730 an eminent master, now living, was present at that solemnity, who relates that at the third and eighth of his concertos were performed by a numerous band, among whom were many who had been the pupils of the author. He adds, that these two pieces were performed in a slow, distinct, and firm manner, without graces, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they are wrote; and from hence concludes, that this was the manner in which they were played by the author himself. He died possessed of about 600l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. He was a passionate admirer of pictures, and lived in an uninterrupted friendship with Carlo Cignani and Carlo Marat; these two eminent painters were rivals for his favour; and for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of years presented him at times with pictures, as well of other masters as of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. The consequence was, that Corelli became possessed of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and valuable collection of original paintings; all which, together with the sum above-mentioned, he bequeathed to his dear friend and patron Cardinal Ottoboni, who reserving the pictures to himself, generously distributed the rest of his effects among the relations of the testator. Corelli is said to have been remarkable for the mildness of his temper and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> of his deportment; nevertheless, he was not infensible of the respect due to his skill and exquisite performance. Cibber, in the Apology for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, p. 340, relates, that when he was playing a solo at Cardinal Ottoboni's, he discovered the cardinal and another person engaged in discourse, upon which he laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his instrument; and being asked the reason, gave for answer, that he feared the music interrupted their conversation. The compositions of Corelli are celebrated for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> resulting from the union of all the parts; but the fineness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> is another distinguishing characteristic of them: the allegro in the 10th solo is as remarkable for spirit and force, as that in the 11th is for its enchanting delicacy: his jigs are in a style peculiarly his own: and that in the 5th solo was never equalled. In the gavot movements in the 2d and 4th operas, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> is distributed with great judgment among the several parts. In his minuets alone he seems to fail; Bononcini, Mr Handel, and Giuseppe Martini, have excelled him in this kind of airs. It is said there is in every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> a style both in speaking and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, which never becomes obsolete; a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of phraseology, so consonant and congenial to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> and principles of its respective <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, as to remain settled and unaltered. This, but with much greater latitude, may be said of music; and accordingly it may be observed of the compositions of Corelli, not only that they are equally intelligible to the learned and unlearned, but that the impressions made by them have been found to be as durable in general. His music is the language of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and, for a series of years, all that heard it became sensible of its effects: of this there cannot be a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> than that, amidst all the innovations which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of change had introduced, it continued to be performed, and was heard with delight, in churches, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, at public solemnities, and festivities, in all the cities of Europe for near 40 years. Men remembered, and would refer to pallia in it as to a classic author; and even at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the masters of the science do not hesitate to pronounce of the compositions of Corelli, that, of fine harmony and elegant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>, they are the most perfect exemplars.

COREOPSIS

Pages 288-288

TICKSEED SUNFLOWER: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORFE CASTLE

Pages 288-288

a borough-town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> in England. It takes its name from a strong castle, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, that stood there, but is now in ruins. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 8. N. Lat. 50. 33.

CORFU

Pages 288-289

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, at the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, formerly called Coreyra and Phocasia, famous for the gardens of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCINOUS">Alcinous</a>. It belongs at present to the Venetians; and forms the bulwark of Christendom against the Turks, who have often attempted to reduce it, but without success. It is well fortified, and has 50 castles; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the inhabitants is said to be about 53,000. The inhabitants are of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and the Venetians send them a governor and magistrates, which are changed every two years. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very fruitful, and produces a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of wine, olives, and several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, particularly figs, which are exceedingly good. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> is likewise called Corfu: see the following article. Corfu, a city of the island of that name, belonging to the Venetians. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, strongly fortified, and defended by a garrison of about 10,000 men; which, however, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of a late traveller, do not appear adequate to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the fortifications. A number of very excellent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cannon are mounted on the different forts, which, he observes, are so divided, that it would take treble the number of their garrison to defend them. However, the republic of Venice is generally at peace with the different European nations, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> power of the Turks being much decayed, they have little to apprehend; though to prevent any sudden surprise, the Venetians keep a formidable squadron in the harbour of Corfu, and the works have been much improved by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> General Paterion.—In the late <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> they had with the Turks, this town was attacked by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 80,000 men, and attempted to be stormed several times by the enemy; but the garrison, which consisted of 12,000 men, under the command of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Schulenburg, made so brave and gallant a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, that they always repulsed them, and obliged them to raise the siege, and abandon the place with considerable loss. For this piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> the republic has caused a magnificent statue to be erected in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the count, with an elegant Latin inscription, setting forth the many eminent services of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> achievements. The circumference of the city is about four miles; the number of inhabitants inhabitants on the whole island is computed at about 50,000, the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of whom are Greeks. This island is the residence of the governor general, whose jurisdiction extends over all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> subject to the republic of Venice, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a> seas, and is considered as one of the greatest honours they can confer on a subject. He is always a nobleman of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and has his appointment for three years only, in which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he makes a tolerable addition to his fortune, and on his return to Venice is generally advanced to the honours of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. In the city are many handsome Greek churches, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which is that of St Speridione, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. It is embellished with some excellent paintings, and most superbly ornamented. The body of the saint from whom it was named, is preserved entire in a rich shrine within the church. The Greeks are most of them such fanatics as to be continually offering their devotions at this shrine, believing that through the intercession of the saint they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> obtain all their wants; and that by offerings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> their sins will be forgiven them; by which means the church has amassed an immense <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>. The relic of the saint is deposited in a silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, richly decorated with precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. It is in an amazing state of preservation; he having died in the island of Cyprus upwards of 700 years ago; and after remaining 400 years there, was transported to this place.—Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> fleet, the Venetians have another of galleys, that are manned by convicts whose crimes are not of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as to merit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The chief diversions of this place in the winter are operas; they have always a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of comedians for the season from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> their time in walking upon the ramparts; few except the governor and great officers of state are permitted to keep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. The Corfu people perfectly resemble the Zanteots in their manners (see <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZANTE">Zante</a>); though it must be observed, in praise of the former, that affections are uncommon among them, their laws being too severe to permit such practices with impunity. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19° 48'. N. Lat. 39° 50'.

CORIA

Pages 289-289

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Leon and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, towards the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, with a bishop's see. It is seated on a little river called Alagon, in a very fertile plain. There is nothing remarkable but the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, except at a little distance a river without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and a bridge without a river. This was caused by an earthquake, which turned the river another way. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 46'. N. Lat. 39° 50'.

CORIANDRUM

Pages 289-289

coriander: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 45th order, Umbellatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORIARIA

Pages 289-289

Tanner's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Myrtle-leaved <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUMACH">Sumach</a>: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioica clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 54th order, Mifcellanea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This plant is much used in the south of France, where it grows naturally, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, whence its name of tanner's fumac. It also dyes a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>.

CORINTH

Pages 289-291

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of antiquity, for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the most illustrious of all the Greek cities. It is said to have been founded 1514 years before Christ, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISYPHUS">Sisyphus</a> the son of Molus, and grandfather of Ulysses. Various reasons are given for its name, but most authors derive it from Corinthus the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PELEUS">Peleus</a>. It was situated on the south <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the isthmus which joins the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, now the Morea, to the continent. It consisted of a citadel built upon an eminence, and thence named Acrocorinthus; besides which it had two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> subjacent to it, named Lechium and Cenchrea. The whole state extended scarce half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in length <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> breadth; but so advantageously were the above-mentioned ports situated, that they might have gained the Corinthians a superiority, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not a command, over all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, had not their advantageous situation inclined them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> rather than <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. For their citadel was almost impregnable; and commanding both the Ionian and Aegean seas, they could easily cut off all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> from one half of Greece with the other; for which reason this city was called one of the fetters of Greece. But as the genius of the Corinthians led them to commerce rather than martial exploits, their city became the finest in all Greece. It was adorned with the most sumptuous buildings, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, palaces, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, porticoes, &c. all of them enriched with a beautiful kind of columns, which from the city were called Corinthian. But though the Corinthians seldom or never engaged in a war with a view of enlarging but rather of defending their little state, they did not forget to cultivate a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> both in time of peace and of war. Hence many brave and experienced generals have been furnished by Corinth to the other Grecian cities, and it was not uncommon for the latter to prefer a Corinthian general to any of their own. This city <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to preserve its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> till the year before Christ 146, when it was pillaged and burnt by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It was at that time the strongest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the world; but the inhabitants were so disheartened by a preceding defeat, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of their general, that they had not presence of mind enough even to shut their gates. The Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> Mummius, was so much surprised at this, that at first he could scarce believe it; but afterwards fearing an ambuscade, he advanced with all possible caution. As he met with no resistance, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> had nothing to do but destroy Corinth. destroy the few inhabitants that had not fled, and plunder the city. Such of the men as had staid were all put to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and the women were sold for slaves. After this the city was ravaged by the greedy soldiers, and the spoils of it are said to have been immense. There were more vessels of all sorts of metal, more fine pictures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> done by the greatest masters, in Corinth, than in any other city in the world. All the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> who had any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> furnished themselves here with their richest moveables: here were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> the finest statues for temples and palaces, and all the liberal arts brought to their greatest perfection. Many ineffable pieces of the most famous painters and statuaries fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the ignorant soldiers, who either destroyed them, or parted with them for a trifle. Polybius the historian was an eye witness to this barbarism of the Romans. He had the mortification to see two of them playing at dice on a famous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of Ariadne, which was accounted one of the wonders of the world. The piece was a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, so exquisitely done, that it was proverbially said of any extraordinary performance, "It is as well done as the Bacchus of Ariadne." This masterly piece of painting, however, the soldiers willingly exchanged for a more convenient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> to play upon; but when the spoils of Corinth were put up to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, Attalus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a> offered for it 600,000 sesterces, near 500l. of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Mummius was surprised at such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price offered for a picture, and imagined there must be some magical virtue in it. He therefore interposed his authority, and carried it to Rome, notwithstanding the complaints of Attalus. Here this famous picture was lodged in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, where it was at last destroyed by fire, together with the temple. Another extraordinary instance of the stupidity of Mummius is, that when the pictures were put on board the transports, he told the masters of the vessels very seriously, that if any of the things were either lost or spoiled, he would oblige them to find others at their own cost; as if any other pieces could have supplied the loss of those ineffable originals, done by the greatest masters in Greece. When the city was thoroughly pillaged, fire was let to all the corners of it at the same time. The flames grew more violent as they drew near the centre, and at last uniting there made one prodigious conflagration. At this time the famous metallic mixture is said to have been made, which could never afterwards be imitated by art. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and bronzes, which the Corinthians had concealed, were melted, and ran <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the streets in streams, and when the flames were extinguished, a new metal was found, composed of several different ones, and greatly esteemed in after ages. The town lay desolate until Julius Caesar settled there a Roman colony; when, in moving the rubbish and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a>, many vases were found of bronzes or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> finely embossed. The price given for these curiosities excited industry in the new inhabitants. They left no burying-place unexamined; and Rome, it is said, was filled with the furniture of the sepulchres of Corinth. Strabo was at Corinth soon after its restoration by the Romans. He describes the site as follows, "A lofty mountain, in perpendicular height as much as Corinth, three stadia and a half (near half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>), the ascent 30 stadia (3½ miles), ends in a pointed summit called Acrocorinthus. Of this the portion to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> is the most steep: beneath which lies the city on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> at the foot of the Acrocorinthus. The circuit of the city alone has been 40 stadia (5 miles), and as much of it as was unhindered by the mountain has been walled about. Within the inclosure was comprehended also the Acrocorinthus, where the mountain was capable of receiving a wall; and as we ascended, the vestiges were plain; so that the whole circumference exceeded 8½ stadia (near 11 miles). On the other sides, the mountain is less steep, but rises very high, and is visible all around. Upon the summit is a small temple of Venus; and below it the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> Pirene, which does not overflow, but is always full of pellucid and potable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. They say it unites with some other hidden veins, and forms the spring at the mountain foot, running into the city, and affording a sufficient supply for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the inhabitants. In the city is plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, and in the Acrocorinthus, as they say, for we did not see any. There they relate the winged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> Pegasus was taken as he was drinking, by Bellerophon. Below Pirene is the Siphneum, some temple or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, the remains not inconsiderable. From the summit is beheld to the north <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELICON">Helicon</a>, lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> covered with snow; and below both, to the west, the Cretan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a> and the Megaris, and by Corinthia and Sicyonia opposite to Phocis. Beyond all these are the mountains called the Oneian, stretching as far as Boeotia and Citheron from the Scironian rocks on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>." Strabo <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> likewise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEON">Cleon</a> from thence. Cenchrea was then a village. Lechaeum had some inhabitants. New Corinth had flourished 217 years when it was visited by Paeanias. It had then a few antiquities, many temples and statues, especially about the Agora or market-place, and several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a> introduced water from a famous spring at Stymphalus in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>; and it had various fountains alike copious and ornamental. The stream of one issued from a dolphin, on which was a brazen <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>; of another, from the hoof of Pegasus, on whom Bellerophon was mounted. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, coming along the road leading from the marketplace toward Sicyon, was the Odeum and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, by which was a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>. The old Gymnasium was at a distance. Going from the marketplace toward Lechaeum was a gate, on which were placed Paeston and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a> in gilded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>. Pirene entered a fountain of white marble, from which the current passed in an open channel. They supposed the metal called Corinthian bronzes to have been immersed while <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot in this water. On the way up to the Acrocorinthus were temples, statues, and altars; and the gate next Tenea, a village with a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, sixty stadia, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles and a half distant, on the road to Mycenae. At Lechaeum was a temple and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a> image of Neptune. At Cenchrea were temples; and by the way from the city a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> of cypress trees, sepulchres, and monuments. Opposite was the Bath of Helen, water tepid and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, flowing plentifully from a rock into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Mummius had ruined Corinth, and the munificence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Athenian Atticus Herodes was displayed in an edifice with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> inferior to few of the most celebrated structures in Greece. The Roman colony was reserved to suffer the same calamity as the Greek city, and from a conqueror more terrible than Mummius, Alaric the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> destroyer of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and universal Greece. In a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> harassed with frequent wars, as the Peloponnesus has since been, the Acrocorinthus was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> too consequential to be neglected. It was besieged and taken in 1459 by Mahomet II.; the despots or lords of the Morea, brothers of the Greek emperor who was killed in defending Constantinople, refusing payment of the arrears of the tribute, which had been imposed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> Morat in 1447. The country became subject to the Turks, except such maritime places as were in the possession of the Venetians; and many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants were carried away to Constantinople. Corinth, with the Morea was yielded to the republic at the conclusion of the war in 1698, and again by it to the Turks in 1715. Corinth retains its old name, and is of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, standing on a high ground, beneath the Acrocorinthus, with an easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> toward the gulf of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPANTO">Lepanto</a>; the houses scattered or in parcels, except in the Bazar or market-place. Cypresses, among which tower the domes of mosques, with corn-fields, and gardens of lemon and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> trees, are interspersed. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is reputed bad in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and in autumn exceedingly unhealthy. Wheler relates, that from the top of the Acrocorinthus or citadel, he enjoyed one of the most agreeable prospects which this world can afford. He guessed the walls to be about two miles in compass, including mosques, with houses and churches mostly in ruins. An <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> was consumed in going up on horseback. It was a mile to the foot of the hill; and from thence the way was very steep with many traverses. The families living below were much infested by corsairs, and on every alarm flocked up to the castle. According to Dr Chandler, Corinth has preserved but few monuments of its Greek or Roman citizens. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> remains, he informs us, are at the southwest corner of the town, and above the bazar or market; 11 columns supporting their architraves, of the Doric order, fluted, and wanting in height near half the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> proportion to the diameter. Within them, toward the western end, is one taller, though not entire, which, it is likely, contributed to sustain the roof. They have been found to be stone, not marble; and appear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, perhaps from a crust formed on the outside. The ruin he judges to be of very remote antiquity, and a portion of a fabric erected not only before the Greek city was destroyed, but before the Doric order had attained to maturity. He suspects it to have been the Siphneum mentioned by Strabo. North of the Bazar stands a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of brickwork, a remnant, it may be conjectured, of a bath, or of the Gymnasium. The inhabitants are most of them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who are allowed liberty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> by the Turks. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 28° 13'. N. Lat. 38° 14'. Corinth, the Isthmus of, in the Morea, is a neck of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> which joins the Morea to Greece, and reaches from the gulf of Lepanto to that of Egina. Julius Caesar, Caligula, and Nero, attempted to cut a channel through it, but in vain; and they therefore afterwards built a wall across it, which they called Hexamilium, because it was six miles in length. This was demolished by Amurath II., and afterwards rebuilt by the Venetians, but was levelled a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time by Mahomet II.

CORINTHA

Pages 289-289

a Grecian lady, celebrated for her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and poetic talents, was born at Theissu, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, and was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Myrtis another Grecian lady. Her verses were so esteemed by the Greeks, that they gave her the name of the lyric muse. She lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>, about 495 years before Christ; and is said to have gained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of lyric <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> from that poet; but Paulusians observes that her beauty made the judges partial.

CORINTHIAN

Pages 291-291

in general, denotes something belonging to Corinth: thus we say, Corinthian brafs, Corinthian order, &c. CORINTHIAN Brafs. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">Brass</a> and Corinth. CORINTHIAN Order, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the fourth order of architecture, according to Scamozzi; but M. Le Clerc makes it the fifth, being the most noble and delicate of all the five. See Architecture, No. 47.

CORIO

Pages 291-291

Bernardine, an historian, born of an illustrious family at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, in the year 1460. He was secretary of state to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Storza appointed him to write the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Milan. He died in 1500. The best edition of his history is that of 1503, in folio. It is printed in Italian, and is very scarce.

CORIS

Pages 291-291

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.
