Coris is also used in the East Indies for a kind of shell which pays for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>.

CORISPERMUM

Pages 291-291

tickseed: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-MONANDRIA">monandria</a> clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 12th order, Holaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORITANI

Pages 291-291

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, occupying widely the inland parts, as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, Rutland, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a> (Camden).

CORK

Pages 291-295

the bark of a tree of the same name, Quercus Suber, Lin. See Quercus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. To take off the bark, an incision is made from the top to the bottom of the tree, and at each extremity another round the tree, perpendicular to the first. When the tree is 15 years old, it may be barked for eight years successively; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the bark improves with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the tree. When stripped from the tree, which does not therefore die, the bark is piled up in a pond <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ditch, and loaded with heavy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> to flatten it, and reduce it into tables: hence it is removed to be dried; and when sufficiently dry, put in bales for carriage. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> care be not taken to strip the bark Cork bark, it splits and peels off itself; being pushed up by another bark formed underneath. The cork-tree, as well as the uses to which the bark is applied, was known both to the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Pliny informs us that the Romans employed it to stop all kinds of vessels; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it for this purpose does not appear to have been very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> till the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of glass bottles, of which, according to Professor Beckman, there is no mention before the 15th century. Other vegetable productions have been sometimes employed instead of cork. The *Spondias Lutea*, a tree which grows in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, particularly in moist places, and which is there called *mombin* or *mombraín*, is sometimes brought to England for the purpose of stopping vessels. The roots of liquorice are applied to the same use, and on that account, this plant is much cultivated in Scyria, and exported to other countries. A tree called *nyssa*, which grows in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> America, has been found also to answer as a substitute for cork. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> use of cork is, to put in shoes, slippers, &c., and to stop bottles. The Spaniards burn it to make that kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> called *Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>*, which is used by painters. The Egyptians made coffins of cork; which being lined with a resinous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, preserved dead bodies uncorrupted. The Spaniards line <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> walls with it, which not only renders them very warm, but corrects the moisture of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. *Fossil Cork*, a name given to a kind of stone which is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of amianthus, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> fibres loosely interwoven, and somewhat resembling vegetable cork. It is the lightest of all stones; by fire it is fusible, and forms a black glass. It possesses the general qualities of amianthus. See that article. **Cork**, in Latin *comitatus Corcaegiensis*, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. It is the most populous and considerable county of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> next to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, containing near a million of acres, and being divided into 15 baronies. It is bounded on the north-east by the county of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a>; on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a>; by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a> on the north; and by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the south and south-east. Including Desmond it is 85 miles in length and 50 in breadth; but is very unequal both ways. Though a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is foggy, mountainous, and barren, yet by the industry of the inhabitants it is pretty well cultivated and improved, and contains several good <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and harbours. **Cork**, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Ireland, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the county of that name. It is an episcopal see, and is the largest and most populous of any in the kingdom, Dublin alone excepted. It is situated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEE">Lee</a>, 15 miles from its mouth. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade, the harbour here being one of the finest in the world. Though smaller vessels can come up to the quay, yet the larger generally ride at a place called Passage. This city, together with its liberties, makes a county. It was built or rather fortified by the Danes, in the ninth century. The greatest part of it stands on a marshy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> surrounded by the river Lee, which also runs through the city, and divides it into several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. On this account some have thought the air very moist and unwholesome. Complaints have also been made against the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> as impure; but, from comparing the bills of mortality with those of other cities, it appears that the city of Cork is far from being unhealthy. This hath been accounted for from the influx of the tide, by which a stagnation of air is prevented. The first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of Cork was bestowed by Henry III. and afterwards ratified by Edward I., Edward II., and Edward III. Edward IV. granted a new charter; and the city received many favours from the succeeding monarchs. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. gave the citizens a new and ample charter; and King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. what is called the Great Charter, by which, among others, a clause in King James's charter was enforced, making this city a county of itself. The fee of Cork is reputed worth 2700l. a-year. The charter consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, chanter, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, archdeacon, and twelve prebendaries. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is dedicated to St Barr or Finbarr; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> is divided into five deaneries. There is very little to be found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers concerning the foundation of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Cork; yet it is generally ascribed to St Barr in the seventh century. Many of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> have been great benefactors to it. Through length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the church became quite ruinous; but it hath lately been completely rebuilt, and is now an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> structure. To defray the expense, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> laid a tax on all coals consumed in the city of Cork. The deanery is reputed to be worth 400l. a-year. Cork is much improved and enlarged, several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> streets have been lately added, by filling up the canals that formerly ran through them, and are now built up with elegant houses: the parade is very spacious, and is adorned with an equestrian statue of King George II. It hath the largest export in the kingdom, particularly of beef, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, tallow, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, fish, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. It is partly situated on several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, formed by the river Lee, which are banked and quayed in, somewhat like the towns in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; and partly on rising grounds, on the north and south sides of the river. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> besieged and took it from King James's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in 1690; when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Grafton, who served as a volunteer, was slain in the attack. It contains about 8600 houses, and upwards of 70,000 inhabitants. It hath twelve companies of foot quartered in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>. Besides a stately cathedral, built from the foundation, between 1725 and 1735, by the produce of a duty upon coals, as above noticed, it is adorned with several handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> churches. It has also an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, a new and beautiful customhouse, a town-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, several fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and various other public structures. The city possesses an annual revenue of about 1300l. out of which the mayor enjoys for his salary and the support of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> 500l. The wealth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of Cork arise from its capacious and commodious haven, where almost any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ships may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> with ease and safety. According to some accounts, when there has been no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, 1200 vessels have resorted hither in a year. Ships from England, bound to all parts of the West Indies, take in here a great part of their provisions; and on the same account the haven of Cork is visited by those also of most other nations. The slaughtering season continues from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August to the latter end of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; in which space it has been computed, that they they kill and cure seldom fewer than 100,000 head of black cattle. The rest of their exports consists of butts of tallow, candles, hides raw and tanned, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, pork, calves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a>, and rabbit skins, tallow, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> for England, linen and woollen yarn, and worsted. The merchants of Cork carry on a very extensive trade to almost all parts of the known world; so that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is annually increasing. The produce of the customs some years since exceeded 62,000l. and the number of ships that they employ is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> to what it was forty years ago. The only thing that seemed to be wanting to the security of the port of Cork was supplied in the earl of Chesterfield's memorable administration, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a fort on the great island, to command the entrance of the haven. The outlets of Cork are cheerful and pleasant. The country around the city, on both sides of the river, is hilly and picturesque; and the harbour called the Cove, is one of the best in the world; the entrance is safe, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> of England might ride in it, secure from every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> that blows. Ships of burden, however, are obliged to unload at Passage, five miles and a half from Cork, the channel not admitting vessels of above 150 tons. Cork Jacket or Waistcoat, is an invention of one Mr Dubourg, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> very fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>, but subject to the cramp, which led him to consider of some method by which he might enjoy his favourite diversion with safety. The waistcoat is composed of four pieces of cork, two for the breasts and two for the back; each pretty near in length and breadth to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a waistcoat without flaps; the whole is covered with coarse canvass, with two holes to put the arms through; there is a space left between the two back-pieces, and the same betwixt each back and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>-piece, that they may fit the easier to the body. Thus the waistcoat is only open before, and may be fastened on the wearer with strings; or, if it should be thought more secure, with buckles and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> straps. This waistcoat does not weigh above 12 ounces, and may be made up for about five or six shillings' expense. Mr Dubourg tried his waistcoat in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, and found that it not only supported him on the water, but that two men could not sink him, though they used their utmost efforts for that purpose. If those who use the sea occasionally, and especially those who are obliged to be almost constantly there, were to have these waistcoats, it would be next to impossible that they should be drowned. It would also be of vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to those that, for the sake of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, bathe in the sea; and even the most delicate and timorous young lady might by the help of one of these jackets venture into a rough sea. See <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-AIR_JACKET">Air-Jacket</a>, and Bamboo-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">Habit</a>. Cormandel. See Coromandel. Cor-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">Mass</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, said to have been established at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a> during the dominion of Charles V. and renewed on St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the 24th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. After the celebration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mass, the procession, consisting of the several tradesmen of the town, begins. Each person has a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> of wax in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and after each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> comes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGEANT">pageant</a>, followed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>-saint, usually of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> silver, richly wrought and adorned. The companies are followed by music; and after the musicians, the friars in the habits of their order, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> priests, and then the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> magnificently adorned, and preceded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">Machines</a> likewise of various fantastic forms and devices, and as variously accoutred, form a part of the show on this occasion; which is described as one of the most superb and magnificent in the world, by an eye-witness, in 1735. Cormorant, a corruption of corvorant. See Pelicanus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index. Corn, the grain or seeds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> separated from the spica or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, and used for making <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. There are several species of corn, such as wheat, rye, and barley, millet and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, oats, maize and lentils, peas, and a number of other kinds; each of which has its usefulness and propriety. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in every part of it; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and some other cantons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, particularly the coasts of Barbary; and some parts of America cultivated by the Europeans, particularly New England, New France, and Acadia, are the places which produce corn. Other countries have maize and rice in lieu of it; and some parts of America, both in the islands and continents, simple roots, such as potatoes and mimiac.—Egypt was anciently the most fertile of all other countries in corn; as appears both from sacred and profane <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. It furnished a good part of the people subject to the Roman empire, and was called the dry nurse of Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, seem now in the place of Egypt, and with their superfluities support a good part of Europe. For the first discovery and culture of corn, authors are much divided; the common <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is, that in the first ages men lived on the spontaneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; as acorns, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> or malt produced by the beech; which, they say, took its name fagus, from the Greek φάγειν, I eat. It is added, that they had not either the use of corn, or the art of preparing or making it eatable. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> has the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of being the first that showed the use of corn, on which account she was placed among the gods; others gave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to Triptolemus; others share it between the two, making Ceres the first discoverer, and Triptolemus the first planter and cultivator of corn. Diodorus Siculus affirms the whole to Isis; on which Polydore <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> observes, he does not differ from the self; Isis and Ceres being in reality the same. The Athenians pretend it was among them the art began; and the Cretans, or Cadians, Sicilians, and Egyptians, lay claim to the same. Some think the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Sicilians best supported, that being the country of Ceres; and authors add, she did not teach the secret to the Athenians, till she had first instructed her own countrymen. Others say, Ceres passed first into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, thence into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, and, last of all, into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; many of the learned, however, maintain it was in Egypt the art of cultivating corn first began; and it is certain there was corn in Egypt and the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the time of Ceres. Corn is very different from fruits, with respect to the manner of its preservation; and is capable of being preserved in public granaries, for pressing occasions, and of being kept for several centuries.—A little time after the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a>, under Henry II. of France, in the year 1578, the duc d'Esperon laid up vast stores of corn in the citadel; which was preserved in good plight to the year 1707, when the French king and his retinue, passing that way, ate bread baked thereof. The chief thing that contributes to the preservation of corn is a crust which forms on its surface, by the germination of the grain next underneath, to the thickness of an inch and a half. On that at Metz people walked, without its giving the least way. At <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a> was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a> cut in a rock, wherein a heap of corn was preserved a hundred and ten years: it was covered with a crust a foot thick. For the preservation of corn, the first method is to let it remain in the spile; the only expedient for conveying it to the islands and provinces of America. The inhabitants of those countries <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> it in the ear, and raise it to maturity by that precaution; but this method of preserving it is attended with several inconveniences among us; corn is apt to rot or sprout, if any of the least moisture is in the heap; the rats likewise infect it, and our want of straw also obliges us to separate the grain from the ear. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is to turn out and winnow it frequently; or to pour it through a trough or mill-hopper, from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> to another; being thus moved and aired every fifteen days, for the first six months, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> require less labour for the future, if lodged in a dry place; but if, through neglect, mites should be allowed to slide into the heap, they will soon reduce the corn to a heap of dust: this must be avoided by moving the corn anew, and rubbing the places adjacent with oils and herbs, whose strong odour may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> them away; for which garlic and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a>-elder are very effectual; they may likewise be exposed to the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which immediately kills them. When the corn has been preserved from all impurities for the space of two years, and has exhaled all its fires, it may be kept for so or even one hundred years, by lodging it in pits covered with strong planks closely joined together; but the safer way is to cover the heap with quicklime, which should be dissolved by sprinkling it over with a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water; this causes the grains to shoot to the depth of two or three fingers; and incloses them with an incrustation, as above mentioned, through which neither air nor insects can penetrate. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Corn, or Maize. See ZEA, Botany Index. Corn-Butterfly, method of destroying it. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index. Corn-Crake. See RALLUS, Ornithology Index. Corn-Mill, a water-engine for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> of corn. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>. Corn, in Farriery. See Farriery Index. Corns, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, hard excrescences, consisting of indurations of the skin arising on the toes, and sometimes on the sides of the feet, where they are much exposed to the pressure of the shoes. By degrees they press themselves farther <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> between the muscular fibres on these parts, and by their irritation occasion <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> pain. Many cures have been prescribed, but the total removal of them is always found to be attended with great difficulty. It has been recommended to soften them with plasters, and then to pull them up by the roots, to apply caustic, &c., but the best cure is to bathe them frequently in warm water, and pare away as much as possible of the indurated skin without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> blood. Cornage, an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, the service whereof was to blow a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> when any invasion of the Scots Cornarists was perceived. This tenure was very frequent in the northern counties near the Picts wall; but by flat, Car. II. all tenures are converted into free and common locage.—An old rental calls cornage, newt-geldi, q. d. neat-geld. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> says, in old books it is called borngeld. Cornarists, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> history, the disciples of Theodore Cornhart, an enthusiastic secretary of the states of Holland. He wrote at the same time against the Catholics, Lutherans, and Calvinists. He maintained that every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> needed reformation; but he added, that no person had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to engage in accomplishing it without a million supported by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. He was also of opinion, that a person might be a good Christian without being a member of any visible church. Cornarius, or Haguenbot, John, a celebrated German physician, born at Zwickow in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>. His preceptor made him change his name of Haguenbot to that of Cornarius, under which he is most known. At twenty years of age he taught <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, and explained the Greek and Latin poets and orators to his scholars; and at twenty-three was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICENTIATE">licentiate</a> in medicine. He found fault with most of the remedies provided by the apothecaries; and observing, that the greatest part of the physicians taught their pupils only what is to be found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a>, Rhazes, and the other Arabian physicians, he carefully sought for the writings of the best physicians of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and employed about fifteen years in translating them into Latin, especially the works of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>, Aetius, Eginetus, and a part of those of Galen. Meanwhile he practised physic with reputation at Zwickow, Frankfort, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARBURG">Marburg</a>, Nordhausen, and Jena, where he died of an apoplexy in 1558, aged fifty-eight. He also wrote some medicinal treatises; published editions of some poems of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> on medicine and botany; and translated some of the works of the fathers, particularly those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, and a part of those of Epiphanius. Cornaro, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, a Venetian of noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, memorable for having lived healthful and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> to above one hundred years of age by a rigid course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>. By the ill conduct of some of his relations he was deprived of the dignity of a noble Venetian; and seeing himself excluded from all employments under the republic, he settled at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>. In his youth he was of a weak <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> reduced himself at about forty years of age to the brink of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, under a complication of disorders; at which extremity he was told that he had no other chance for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, but by becoming sober and temperate. Being wise enough to adopt this wholesome counsel, he reduced himself to a regimen of which there are very few examples. He allowed himself no more than twelve ounces of food and fourteen ounces of liquor each day; which became habitual to him, that when he was above seventy years of age, the experiment of adding two ounces to each by the advice of his friends, had like to have proved fatal to him. At eighty-three he wrote a treatise which has been translated into English, and often printed, entitled, "Sure and Certain Methods of attaining a Long and Healthful Life;" in which he relates his own story, and extols temperance to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of enthusiasm. At length the yolk of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a> became sufficient... sufficient for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, and sometimes for two, until he died with much ease and composure in 1666. The writer of the Spectator, No 115, confirms the fact from the authority of the Venetian <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> at that time, who was a descendant of the Cornaro family.

CORNAVII

Pages 295-295

(<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>), a people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> beginning in the very heart of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and extending to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>. Now <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, Salop, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a> and Cheshire (Camden).

CORNEA TUNICA

Pages 295-295

in Anatomy, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> coat of the eye; so called from its substance resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a>, in Latin cornu. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORNEILLE

Pages 295-295

PETTER, a celebrated French poet, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> in the year 1606. He was brought up to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, which he attended for some little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but formed with a genius too elevated for such a profession, and having no turn for business, he soon deserted it. An affair of gallantry occasioned his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> his first piece, entitled Melite; which had prodigious success. Encouraged by the applause of the public, he wrote the Cid, and the other tragedies that have immortalized his name. In his dramatic works he discovers a majesty, a strength and elevation of genius, scarce to be found in any other of the French poets; and, like our immortal Shakespeare, seems better acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> than with the rules of critics. Corneille was received into the French academy in 1647, and died <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of that academy in 1684, aged 78. Besides his dramatic pieces, he wrote a translation, in French <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, of the "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">Imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ," &c. The best edition of his works is that of 1682, in 4 vols 12mo. Corneille, Thomas, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the former, was a member of the French academy and of that of incipitins. He discovered in his youth a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> inclination to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; and at length published several dramatic pieces in 5 vols 12mo, some of which were applauded by the public, and acted with success. He also wrote, 1. A translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses, and some of Ovid's Epistles; 2. Remarks on Vauglas; 3. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> of Arts, 2 vols folio; and, 4. An Universal Geographical and Historical Dictionary, in 3 vols folio. Corneille, Michael, a celebrated painter, was born as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in the year 1642; and was instructed by his father, who was himself a painter of great merit. Having gained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> at the academy, young Corneille obtained a pension from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV.; and was sent to Rome, where that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> had founded a school for young artists of genius. Having studied there some time, he gave up his pension, and applied to the antique with great care. He is said to have equalled Carache in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, but in colouring he was deficient. Upon his return from Rome, he was chosen professor in the academy of Paris; and was employed by the above prince in all the great works he was carrying on at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a> and Trianon, where are still to be seen some noble efforts of his genius. CORNEL TREE. See CORNUS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORNELIA

Pages 295-296
daughter of Scipio Africanus, was the mother of Tiberius and Caius Gracchus. She was courted by a king, but the preferred being the wife of a Roman citizen to that of a monarch. Her virtues have been deservedly commended, as well as the wholesome principles she inculcated in her two sons. When a Campanian lady made once a show of her jewels at Cornelia's house, and entreated her to favour her with a sight of her own, Cornelia produced her two sons, saying, "These are the only jewels of which I can boast." CORNELIA Lex, de civitate, was enacted, in the year of Rome 670, by L. Corn. Sylla. It confirmed the Sulpician law, and required that the citizens of the eight newly elected tribes should be divided among the 35 ancient tribes.—Another, de judiciis, in 673, by the same. It ordained, that the praetor should always observe the same invariable method in judicial proceedings, and that the proceeds should not depend upon his will.—Another de sumptibus, by the same. It limited the expenses which generally attended funerals.—Another de religione, by the same, in 677. It restored to the college of priests the privilege of choosing the priests, which by the Domitian law had been lodged in the hands of the people.—Another, de municipiis, by the same; which revoked all the privileges which had been some time before granted to the several towns that had assisted Marius and Cinna in the civil wars.—Another de magistratibus, by the same; which gave the power of bearing honours, and being promoted before the legal age, to those who had followed the interest of Sylla; while the sons and partizans of his enemies, who had been proscribed, were deprived of the privilege of standing for any office in the state.—Another, de magistratibus, by the same, in 673. It ordained, that no person should exercise the same office within ten years distance, or be invested with two different magistracies in one year.—Another, de magistratibus, by the same, in 673. It divested the tribunes of the privilege of making laws, interfering, holding assemblies, and receiving appeals. All such as had been tribunes were incapable of holding any other office in the state by that law.—Another, de magistratibus, by the same, in 670. It made it treason to lend an army out of a province or engage in a war without orders, to influence the soldiers to spare or ransom a captive general of the enemy, to pardon the leaders of robbers or pirates, or for the absence of a Roman citizen to a foreign court without previous leave. The punishment was aquae et ignis interdictio.—Another by the same. It gave the power to a man accused of murder, either by poison, weapons, or false accusations, and the setting fire to buildings, to choose whether the jury that tried him should give their verdict clam or palam, viva voce, or by ballot. Another by the same, which made it aquae et ignis interdictio to such as were guilty of forgery, concealing and altering of wills, corruption, false accusations, and the debauching or counterfeiting of the public coin. All such as were accessory to this offence were deemed as guilty as the offender.—Another, de pecuniae repetundis; by which a man convicted of peculation or extortion in the provinces was condemned to suffer the aquae et ignis interdictio.—Another, by the same; which gave the power to such as were sent into the provinces with any government, of retaining their command and appointment without a renewal of it by the senate, as was before observed.—Another by the same; which ordained, that the lands of proscribed persons should be common, especially those about Volaterræ and Felsulæ in Etruria, which Sylla divided among his soldiers.—Another by C. Cornelius tribune... of the people, in 686. It ordained, that no person should be exempted from any law according to the general custom, unless 200 senators were present in the senate; and no person thus exempted could hinder the bill of his exemption from being carried to the people for their concurrence.—Another, by Naflia, in 582, to make war against Perseus, son of Philip king of Macedon, if he did not give proper satisfaction to the Roman people. CORNELIAN. See CARNELIAN.

CORNET

Pages 296-296

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> economy, denotes an officer in the cavalry who bears the ensign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> colours of a troop. The cornet is the third officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and commands in the absence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>. He takes his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> from his ensign, which is <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; and is supposed to be called by that name from cornu, because placed on the wings, which form a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or horns of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Others derive the name from coronet; alleging, that it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for these officers to wear coronets or garlands on their heads.

CORNEUS

Pages 296-296

the name by which Linnaeus calls a kind of tin ore, found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> columns, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> sides, and terminating in prisms.

CORNICHE

Pages 296-296

is also used, in general, for all little projections in masonry <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> joinery, everywhere there are no columns, as the corniche of a chimney, buffet, &c. CORNICHE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">Ring</a>, in a piece of ordnance, is that next from the muzzle ring, backward.

CORNICULARIUS

Pages 296-296

in antiquity, an officer in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, whose business was to aid and assist the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> tribune in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>. The cornicularius went the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a> in lieu of the tribune, visited the watch, and were nearly what the aids <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> are in the French army. The denomination cornicularius was given them from a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, called corniculum, which they used in giving orders to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>: though Salmatius derives it from corniculum, the crest of a head-piece; it being an observation of Pliny, that they wore <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> horns on their helmets; and that these were called cornicula. In the Notitia Imperii we find a kind of secretary or registrar of the same name. His business was to attend the judge, and enter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his sentiments and decisions. The critics derive the word, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, from corniculum, a little horn to put <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> in.

CORNICULUM

Pages 296-296

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Sabines, to the east of Crustumerium, towards the Anio. It was burnt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by Tarquin; but restored again after the expulsion of the kings, (Florus.) Now in ruins, called il Monte Genaro, (Holtenius).

CORNISH DIAMOND

Pages 296-296

a name given by many people to the crystals found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of tin in Cornwall. See CORNWALL.

CORNIX

Pages 296-296

the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of CORVUS. See CORVUS, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORNOLANUS

Pages 291-291

C. MARCIUS, a famous Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, took Coriolai a town of the Volsci, whence he had his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a>: at last, disquieting the people, he was banished Rome by the tribune Decius. He went to the Volsci, and persuading them to take up arms against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, they encamped within four miles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He would not listen to proposals of peace till he was prevailed upon by his wife Veturia, and his mother Volumnia, who were followed by all the Roman ladies in tears. He was put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the Volsci as a traitor that had made them quit their conquest; upon which the Roman ladies went into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>; and in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where his blood was spilled there was a temple consecrated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a> virtue.

CORNU

Pages 296-296

See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>. Cornu Ammonis, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, fossil shells, called also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> snake stones. They are found of all sizes, from the breadth of a sixpence to more than two feet in diameter, and some even larger; some of them rounded, others greatly compressed, and lodged in different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of stones and clays; some again are smooth, and others variously ridged, their thine and ridges being either straight, irregularly crooked, or undulated. See Snake Stones. Corno Cerii. See HARTSHORN.

CORNUCOPIA

Pages 296-296

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> out of which proceeded plenty of all things; by a particular privilege which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> granted his nurse, supposed to be the goat Amalthea. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> is thus interpreted: That in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a> there is a little territory shaped not unlike a bullock's horn, exceeding fertile, given by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, Amalthea, whom the poets feign to have been Jupiter's nurse. In <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a> the cornucopia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> horn of plenty, is represented under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> horn, out of which issue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. On medals, F. Joubert observes, the cornucopia is given to all deities. CORNUCOPIÆ, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order, Gramineæ. See BOTANY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORNUS

Pages 296-296

CORNEL TREE, CORNELIAN CHERRY, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Dog-wood: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 47th order, Stellate.

CORNUTIA

Pages 296-296

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the didynamia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 46th order, Perfonata. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORNWALL

Pages 296-298

the most westerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded by the English channel on the south, St George's channel on the west, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> channel on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and on the east by the river Tamar, which separates it from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. Its name is supposed by some to be compounded of corn, signifying "a rock" in the British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and Gauls <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Wauls, the name the Saxons gave to the Britons. Others, however, think it is derived from the Latin cornu, or the British corn, "a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>," on account of its running out into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> somewhat in the form of a horn. Hither the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Britons (as well as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>) retired on the intrusion of the Saxons, where they opposed their further conquests. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> they formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> that existed for many years after under different princes, amongst whom were Ambrosius Aurelius, and the justly celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>; nor were they subdued till the middle of the 7th century, from which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Cornwall was considered as subject to the West Saxon kings, who began their sovereignty in 519, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> it till 828, under 18 sovereigns, the last of whom was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Egbert, who subdued Cornwall subdued all the others; and by uniting them, formed the kingdom of England, when this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was included in the county of Devon, then the 9th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>; and that accounts for Alfred's not mentioning Cornwall, which, on forming the circuits after the Norman conquest, is included in the western circuit. In 1337, Edward III. created it into a dukedom, and invested with it Edward the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a>. But this, according to the express words of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, is limited to the first born son and heir, on which account Richard II. was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Cornwall by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>. So was Henry V. by his father Henry IV. Henry VI. delivered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> to his son Prince Edward, and Edward IV. created his son Edward V. duke of Cornwall, as did Henry VIII. his son, afterwards Henry VIII. upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Arthur. James I. created his son Henry duke of Cornwall, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> on his decease came to his brother <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>. The eldest sons of succeeding kings have enjoyed this title by inheritance. These not only appoint the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, but all writs, deeds, &c., are in their name, and not in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s; and they have also peculiar royalties and prerogatives distinct from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, for which they appoint the officers. This county is 80 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, 40 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and 250 in circumference; containing 960,000 acres, and 126,000 inhabitants. It is divided into 9 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>; has 27 market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUNCESTON">Launceston</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRURO">Truro</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>, Helston, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALTASH">Saltash</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BODMIN">Bodmin</a>, St Ives, Tregony, Camelstow, Fowey, St Germans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENRYN">Penryn</a>, Callington, St Austell, East Looe, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PADSTOW">Padstow</a>, St Columb, Penpance, Grampound, Liskeard, Lelwithick, St Mawes, St Michael, Newport, Market Jew, Stratton, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REDRUTH">Redruth</a>; 1230 villages, 191 parishes, 89 vicarages; provides 640 men to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, and pays 8 parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-tax. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Tamar, Fale Cober, Looe, Camel, Fowey, Haile, Lemara, Kenfe, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRE">Aire</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> capes or head lands are the Land's-end, the Lizard, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Cornwall, Deadman's-head, Rame-head, &c., and a clutter of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, 144 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, called the Scilly Isles, supposed formerly to have been joined to the main land, though now 30 miles distant; abounding with antiquities, particularly druidical. As Cornwall is surrounded by the sea on all sides except the east, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is somewhat different from that of the other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The reasons of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be easily understood from what is observed concerning the climate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. The summers in Cornwall are less hot, and the winters less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, than in other parts of England, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> are observed to be more backward. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> and sudden winds are also more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in this than in other counties of England. The county is rocky and mountainous; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are rich in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, especially tin and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. The valleys are very pleasant and fertile, yielding great plenty both of corn and pasture. The lands near the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> are manured and fertilized with sea-weed, and a kind of sand formed by the particles of broken shells as they are dashed against each other by the sea. Cattle of all sorts are smaller here than in the other counties of England; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> of the sheep, which are mostly without horns, is very fine, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, both of them and the black cattle, extremely delicate. The county is well supplied with fish from the sea and the many rivers with which it is watered. The most noted of Cornwall, the sea-fish is the pilchard; of which prodigious quantities are caught from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> to November, and exported to different parts, especially to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is said that a million have been sometimes taken at a single draught. The natives are remarkable for their strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, as well as their dexterity in wrestling, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the Cornish hogs is highly extolled. This county abounds in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of different metals and semimetals; but the principal produce is tin. The Phoenicians early visited these coasts for this article, some think 400 or 450 years before Christ; and the mines continued to be wrought with various success at different periods. In the time of King John they appear to have yielded no great emolument; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of working them being wholly in the king as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Cornwall, and the mines farmed by the Jews for 100 marks; and according to this proportion the 10th of it, 6l. 13s. 4d., is at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> paid by the crown to the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>. In the time of Richard king of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> and earl of Cornwall, the tin-mines were immensely rich; the Jews being farmed out to him by his brother Henry III., what <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> they had was at his disposal. The Spanish tin-mines being slopped by the Moors, and none discovered in Germany, the Malabar coast, or the Spanish West Indies, Cornwall and its earls had all the trade of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> for it. The Jews being banished the kingdom, 18 Edw. I., they were again neglected till the gentlemen of Blackmore, lords of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> tithings best stored at that time with tin, obtained of Edmund earl of Cornwall, son of Richard king of the Romans, a charter under his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, with more explicit grants of privileges, courts, pleas, parliaments, and the toll-tin or 1/10th of all the tin raised. At this time too the right of bounding or dividing tin-grounds into separate partitions for the encouragement of searching for it seems to have been first appointed, or at least adjusted. This charter was confirmed 33 Edward I., and the Cornish separated from the Devonshire tinners. Their laws, particularly recited in Plowden's Commentaries, p. 237, were further explained 50 Edw. III., confirmed and enlarged by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, 8 Rich. II., 3 Ed. IV., 1 Ed. VI., 1 and 2 P. and M., and 2 Eliz., and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> divided into four parts under one general warden to do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, from whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> lies an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the duke of Cornwall in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, or for want of a duke of Cornwall to the crown. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-warden appoints a vice-warden to determine all flannery disputes every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; he also constitutes four stewards, one for each of the precincts before mentioned, who hold their courts every three weeks, and decide by juries of six persons, with an appeal referred to the vice-warden, lord warden, and lord of the prince's council. In difficult <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the lord-warden, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, issues his precept to the four principal towns of the flannery districts, who each choose six members; and these twenty-four flannators constitute the parliament of tinners. Each flannator chooses an assistant, making a kind of standing council in a different apartment to give information to the prince. Whatever is enacted by the body of tinners must be signed by the flannators, the lord-warden, or his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, and by the duke or the king, and thenceforward has with regard to tin affairs all the authority of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the whole. whole legislature. Five towns are appointed in the most convenient parts of the county for the tinniers to bring their tin to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a year. These are Liskeard, Leftwitheil, Truro, Helston, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENZANCE">Penzance</a>, the last added by Charles II. for the convenience of the western tinniers. In the time of Henry VIII., there were but two coines at Midsummer and Michaelmas; two more at Christmas and Lady-day were added, for which the tinniers pay an acknowledgment called Pq8 groats, or 4d. for every hundred of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> tin then coined. The officers appointed by the duke <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSAY">assay</a> it; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> well purified stamp it by a hammer with the duchy seal, the arms of Richard earl of Cornwall, a lion rampant G. crowned O. within a bordure of bezants S; and this is a permission to the coiner to sell, and is called coining the tin. Every hundred of white tin so coined pays to the duke 4s. The tin of the whole county, which, in Carew's time, in the last century, amounted to 30,000l. or 40,000l. yearly, has for 24 years past amounted one year with another to 180,000l. or 190,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. Of this the duke of Cornwall receives for his 4s. duty on every hundred of white tin above 10,000l. yearly; the bounders or proprietors of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> about ¼th at a medium clear, or about 30,000l. yearly; the remainder goes to the adventurers in the mine, who are at all the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of working. Tin is found collected and fixed in lodes and floors, or in grains and bunches in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> rock, or loofe and detached in single separate <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> called floes or freans, or in a continued course of such stones called the beubeyl or living stream, or in an arenaceous pulverized state. It is most easily discovered by tracing the lodes by the scattered fragments of them called floes, by leave of the lord of the soil or the bounder. The tin being divided among the lords and adventurers, is stamped and worked at the mill; and being thus dressed is carried under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> tin to the melting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where it is melted by Welch pit-coal, and poured into blocks of 320lb. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and carried to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COINAGE">coinage</a> town. Mundic, a scarce metal or mineral ore, of a white, braffy, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, is found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities, intermixed with tin, copper, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and sometimes by itself. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">Iron</a> ore is found in Cornwall, but the working it does not answer. There is no richer copper, nor a greater variety anywhere than in this county. Silver, if really found here in the reigns of Edward I. and II., has been rarely found since, nor do the lead mines answer. Very late discoveries have proved that Cornwall has more <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> than was formerly imagined. What is called the Cornish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> is a figured crystal generally hexagonal and pyramidal, or columnar, or both, of a fine clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and of all our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> diamonds in this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> esteemed the best, and some of different colours, black, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, &c. The clearer these are, the better they will bear engraving for seals. In privileges and language Cornwall seems to be another kingdom. By 21 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> it was ordered that all duty on Cornish cloth exported should be remitted to every Englishman within the duchy of Cornwall. This was first granted by the Black Prince, in consideration of their paying 4s. for the coinage of every hundred of tin; whereas Devonshire pays no more than 8d. They have also by grant from Richard earl of Cornwall, confirmed 25 Henry III., freedom to take land out of the sea and carry it through the Cornwall country for manure; whereupon in the following reign, on an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> made, we find a complaint that Saltash had lately taken 12s. yearly for each barge that carried sand up the Tamar; whereas nothing ought to have been demanded. They still continue this ancient method of improving their land, carrying it ten miles up into the country, and great part of the way on horses backs. Mr Ray supposes the virtue of this sand depends chiefly on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> mixed with it, which is so copious that in many places salt is boiled up out of a lixivium made of the sea sand; and the reason why sand when it has lain long in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> proves less enriching and useful is, that the dews and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> evaporate great part of its salt. They had likewise a privilege of trading to all parts of the world, granted them by Charles I. in recompense of their loyalty. The number of boroughs in this small county was surprisingly increased by Edward VI., who added seven to the original six, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> two, Elizabeth five, making in all 21, lending 40 members besides the county two. Eight of these boroughs had an immediate or remote connection with the demesne lands of the duchy; the rest belonged to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, or powerful families, or were old boroughs, which had legal immunities granted to them by their princes or lords. The Cornish language is a dialect of that which till the Saxons came in was common to all Britain, and more anciently to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>; but the inhabitants of this island being dispersed before those conquests, and driven into Wales and Cornwall, and thence into Bretagne, the same language, for want of frequent intercourse, became differently pronounced and written, and in different degrees mixed with different languages. Hence came the Welsh, the Cornish and the Armorican dialects, whose radicals are so much alike that they are known and admitted by the inhabitants of either country; but the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> so varied that they cannot <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>. The Cornish is reckoned the most pleasing of the three. It was spoken so generally here <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the reign of Henry VIII. that Dr John Moreman, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Mynhein, is said to have been the first who taught his parishioners the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, the creed, and ten commandments in English, and at the Reformation the natives desired the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in English. The older people in some parishes retained their original language to the middle of the last century; and the last sermon was preached in it in 1678. When Mr Ray was here, 1662, he could find but one person who could write this language; and it is now so nearly extinct, that Mr Barrington, in 1768, could only find one old woman who could read in it, and she is since dead. CORODY. See Revenue.

COROLLA

Pages 298-299

among botanists, the most conspicuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a flower, surrounding the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, and composed of one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more flower-leaves, most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called petals, to distinguish them from the leaves of the plant; according as there is one, two, or three of these petals, the corolla is said to be monopetalous, dipetalous, tripetalous, &c. COROLLARY is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> drawn from something already advanced or demonstrated: thus, it being demonstrated that a triangle which has two equal sides, COROLISTÆ, a name by which Linnæus distinguishes those systematic botanists who have arranged vegetables from the regularity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and other circumstances, of the petals, or beautiful coloured leaves of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. The best systems of this kind are those of Rivinus and Tournefort. The former proceeds upon the regularity and number of the petals; the latter, with much more certainty, on their regularity and figure.

COROLLULA

Pages 299-299

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by botanists to express the little partial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> which make up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> ones.

COROMANDEL

Pages 299-301

the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on this side the Ganges in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Golconda, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADURA">Madura</a>, and on the west by Bijnagar. This coast so much resembles that of Orixa, that the Abbé Raynal chooses to consider them as one, and gives to both the general name of Coromandel. Here an excessive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> reigns from the beginning of May to the end of October. It begins at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in the morning, and continues till nine in the evening. During the night it is allayed by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-breeze from the south-east; and most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> this refreshing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALE">gale</a> begins at three in the afternoon. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is less inflamed during the rest of the year, though in all seasons it is very hot. It rains almost continually during the months of November and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. This immense tract is covered with a parched sand for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of two miles, and sometimes only one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> along the coast. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was at first neglected by the Europeans for many reasons. It was separated by inaccessible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> from Malabar, where these bold adventurers endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> themselves. Spices and aromatics, which were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objects of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, were not to be found there. In short, civil dissensions had banished from it tranquillity, fecundity, and industry. At that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the empire of Bijnagar, to which this vast country was subject, was falling to ruin. The governors of Vilapour, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARNATIC">Carnatic</a>, Golconda, and Orixa, threw off their dependence, and assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of kings. Those of Madura, Tanjore, Mylore, Gingi, and some others, likewise usurped the sovereign authority, though they retained their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> title of Naick. This revolution had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> happened when the Europeans appeared on the coast of Coromandel. The foreign trade was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> inconsiderable; it consisted only of diamonds from Golconda, which were carried to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALICUT">Calicut</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>, and from thence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, whence they were circulated through all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and Asia. Masulipatan, the richest and most populous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of these countries, was the only market that was known for linens; they were purchased at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fair annually held there by the Arabian and Malayan vessels that frequented that bay, and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> arrived from distant parts. The linens were exported to the same places with the diamonds. The fondness for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of Coromandel, which began to prevail here, inspired all the European nations trading to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> seas with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of forming settlements there. They were not discouraged either by the difficulty of conveying goods from the inland parts of the country, where there was no navigable river; by the total want of harbours, where the sea at one season of the year is not navigable; by the barrenness of the coasts, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> uncultivated and uninhabited; nor by the tyranny and fluctuating state of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. They thought that silver would be industriously sought after; that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a> would furnish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and Bengal corn for subsistence; that a prosperous voyage of nine months would be more than sufficient to complete their ladings; and that by fortifying themselves they should be secure against the attacks of the weak tyrants that oppressed these countries. The first European colonies were established near the shore. Some of them obtained a settlement by force; most of them were formed with the consent of the sovereigns; and all were confined to a very narrow tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The boundaries of each were marked out by a hedge of thorny <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, which was their only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time fortifications were raised; and the security derived from them, added to the lenity of the government, soon increased the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of colonists. The splendor and independence of these settlements several times raised the jealousy of the princes in whose dominions they were formed; but their attempts to demolish them proved abortive. Each colony increased in prosperity in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> that founded it. None of the companies that exercised an exclusive privilege beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope had any concern in the trade of diamonds.
