This was always left to private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and by degrees fell entirely into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English, or the Jews and Armenians that lived under their protection. At present this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> object of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and industry is much reduced. The revolutions that have happened in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> have prevented people from resorting to these rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and the anarchy in which this unhappy country is plunged leaves no room to hope that they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be again attended to. The whole of the commercial operations on the coast of Coromandel is confined to the purchase of cottons. The manufacturing of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cotton brought there differs so little from ours, that it would be neither interesting nor instructive to enter into a minute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it. The process used in making their printed cottons, which was at first servilely followed in Europe, has since been rendered more simple, and brought to greater perfection by our manufacturers. The painted cottons which are brought there we have not yet attempted to imitate. Those who imagine we have been prevented from undertaking this branch merely by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price of labour among us, are mistaken. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> has not given us the wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and drugs necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of those bright and indelible colours which constitute the principal merit of the Indian manufactures; nor has she furnished us with the waters that serve to fix them. The Indians do not universally observe the same method in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> their cottons; either because there are some niceties peculiar to certain provinces, or because different soils produce different drugs for different uses. We should tire the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> of our readers were we to trace the flow... flow and painful progress of the Indians in the art of painting their cottons. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to believe that they owe it to length of time, rather than to the fertility of their genius. What seems to authorize this conjecture is, that they have stopped in their improvements, and have not advanced a single step in the arts for many ages; whereas we have proceeded with amazing rapidity. Indeed, were we to consider only the want of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> in the Indians, we should be tempted to believe, that, from time immemorial, they have received the arts they cultivate from some more industrious nation; but when it is remembered that these arts have a peculiar dependence on the materials, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, colours, and productions of India, we cannot but be convinced that they are natives of that country. It may appear somewhat surprising that cottons painted with all sorts of colours should be sold at so moderate a price, that they are almost as cheap as those that have only two or three. But it must be observed, that the merchants of the country sell to all the companies a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of cottons at a time; and that the demand for cottons painted with various colours makes but a small article in their assortments, as they are not much esteemed in Europe. Though cottons of all sorts are in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> manufactured through the whole country of Indostan, which extends from Cape Comorin to the banks of the Ganges; it is observable, that the finest are made in the eastern part, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ones in the centre, and the coarse ones in the most western parts. Manufactures are established in the European colonies, and upon the coast; they are more frequent at the distance of five or six leagues from the sea, where cotton is more cultivated, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> are cheaper. The purchases made there are carried 30 or 40 leagues farther into the country. The Indian merchants settled in the European factories have always the management of this business. The quantity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the goods wanted are settled with these people; the price is fixed according to the patterns; and at the time a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> is made, a third or fourth part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> agreed on is advanced. This arrangement is owing to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> these merchants themselves are under of advancing money to the workmen by the partners or agents who are dispersed through the whole country; of keeping a watchful eye upon them, for fear of losing what they have advanced; and of gradually lessening the sum, by calling for the cottons as fast as they are worked off. Without these precautions, nothing could be depended on in an oppressive government, where the weaver cannot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on his own account, either because his circumstances will not permit, or because he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> not venture to discover them for fear of exactions. The companies that have either success or good management, constantly keep the stock of one year in advance in their settlements. By this method they are sure of having the quantity of goods they have occasion for, and of the quality they choose, at the most convenient time; not to mention that their workmen, and their merchants, who are kept in constant employment, never leave them. Such nations as want money and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> cannot begin their mercantile operations till the arrival of their ships. They have only five or six months at most to execute the orders sent from Europe. The goods are manufactured and examined in haste; and they are even obliged to take such as are known to be bad, and would be rejected at any other time. The necessity they are under of completing their cargoes, and fitting out their vessels before hurricanes come on, leaves no room for nicety of inspection. It would be a mistake to imagine that the country agents could be prevailed upon to order goods to be made on their account in hopes of selling them with a reasonable advantage to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with whom they are engaged. For, besides that the generality of them are not rich enough to embark in so large an undertaking, they would not be certain of finding their account in it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the company that employ them should be hindered by unforeseen accidents from sending the usual number of ships, these merchants would have no vent for their commodities. The Indians, the form of whose dyes requires different breadths and lengths from those of the cottons fabricated for our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, would not purchase them; and the other European companies would be provided, or certain of being provided, with whatever the extent of their trade required, and their money enabled them to purchase. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of procuring loans, which was contrived to remedy this inconvenience, never has nor can be useful. It has been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, time immemorial, in Indostan, for every citizen who borrows money to give a written <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> to his creditor. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> is of no force in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of judicature, unless it is signed by three witnesses, and bears the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> and the year when it was made, with the rate of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> agreed upon by the parties. If the borrower fails to fulfil his engagements, he may be arrested by the lender himself. He is never imprisoned, because there is no fear of his making his escape. He would not even eat, without obtaining leave of his creditor. The Indians make a three-fold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of interest; one kind they call vice; another neither vice nor virtue; and a third, they say, is virtue. The first is four per cent. a month; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> two; and the third one. The last is, in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of beneficence that only belongs to the most heroic minds. Yet, though the Europeans, who are forced to borrow, meet with this treatment, it is plain they cannot avail themselves of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> without being involved in ruin. The foreign trade of Coromandel is not in the hands of the natives. In the western part, indeed, there are Mohammedans known by the name of Chitias, who, at Naur and Porto-Nuovo, send out ships to Acehien, Merguy, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, and the eastern coast. Besides vessels of considerable burden employed in these voyages, they have smaller embarkations for the coaling trade for Ceylon and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>-fishery. The Indians of Malipatam turn their attention another way. They import from Bengal white calicoes, which they dye or print, and sell them again at the places from whence they had them, at 35 or 40 per cent. advantage. Excepting these transactions, which are of very little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, the whole trade is vested in the Europeans, who have no partners but a few Banians and Armenians settled in their colonies. The quantity of calicoes exported from Coromandel to the different ports of India may be computed at 3500 bales. Of these the French carry 800 to Malabar, Mocha, and and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of France; the English, 1200 to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>, Malabar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIPPINE_ISLANDS">Philippine <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; and the Dutch 1500 to their different settlements. Except 500 bales destined for Manila, each of the value of 100 guineas, the others are of such an ordinary kind that they do not exceed 30 guineas at prime cost; so that the whole number of bales does not amount to more than about 150,000. Coromandel furnishes Europe with 9500 bales; 800 of which are brought by the Danes, 2500 by the French, 3000 by the English, and 3200 by the Dutch. A considerable part of these calicoes are dyed blue, or striped blue and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> for the African trade. The others are fine muslins, printed calicoes, and handkerchiefs from Maffulipatan, or Paliacate. It is proved by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> that each of these bales costs only about £21 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; consequently they ought to bring in to the manufactory where they are wrought near £60,000. The payments are not entirely made in specie, either in Europe or Asia; we give in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, cloths, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, coral, and some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of less value. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Asia pays with spices, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, corn, and dates. All these articles taken together may amount to about £10,000; and from this calculation it follows, that Coromandel receives annually from Europe about £300,000 in money. The British, who have acquired the same superiority on this coast that they have elsewhere, have formed on it several settlements.

CORONA

Pages 305-305

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, near Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELICON">Helicon</a>, and the lake Copais, situated on an eminence; famous for the defeat of the Athenians and Boeotians by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGESILAUS">Agesilaus</a>. Another Corona of Thessaly; having Narthacium to the east, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMIA">Lamia</a> near the Sperchius to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>).

CORONARIAE

Pages 305-305

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the 10th order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, in Linnaeus's Fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Method. Under this name, instead of the more obvious one li-baccæ, Linnaeus collects a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of genera, most of which furnish very beautiful garden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, viz. albuca, cyanella, fritillaria, helonias, hyacinthus, hypoxis, lilium, melanthium, ornithogalum, scilla, tulipa, agave, aletris, aloe, anthericum, alphodelus, bromelia, burmannia, hemerocallis, polyanthes, tillandsia, veratrum, yucca.

CORONATION

Pages 305-305

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, particularly applied to the crowning of kings, upon their succeeding to the sovereignty. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">KING</a>.

CORONE

Pages 305-305

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Messenia, situated on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, giving name to the Sinus Coroneus, (Pliny); now Golfo di Corone. Pausanias takes it to be the Aepea of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>; but Strabo Thurio, and Pliny Pedafus, now Coron, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELVEDERE">Belvedere</a>, in the Morea. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 22. N. Lat. 36. 30.

CORONELLI

Pages 305-305

VINCENT, a famous geographer, born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. His skill in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> having brought him to the knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> d'Estrees, his eminence employed him in making globes for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. With this view Coronelli spent some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and left a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of globes there, which are esteemed. In 1685, he was made cosmographer to the republic of Venice; and four years after public professor of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>. He founded an academy of cosmography at Venice; and died in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in 1718. He published about 400 geographical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a>, an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of cosmography, several books on geography, and other works.

CORONER

Pages 305-306

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> officer in England, so called because he hath principally to do with pleas of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> such wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> is more immediately concerned. And in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the king's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> coroner in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and may, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he pleases, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the jurisdiction of a coroner in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the realm. But there are also particular coroners for every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in England; usually four, but sometimes six, and sometimes fewer. This officer is of equal authority with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>; and was ordained, together with him to keep the peace, when the earls gave up the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARDSHIP">wardship</a> of the county. He is chosen by all the freeholders of the county <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and by the statute of Westminster I. it was enacted, that none but lawful and discreet knights should be chosen; but it seems now sufficient if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> have lands enough to be made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, whether he be really knighted or not; for the coroner ought to have an estate sufficient to maintain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his office, and answer any fines that may be made upon him for his CORONER his misbehaviour; and if he hath not enough to answer, his fine shall be levied on the county, as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for electing an insufficient officer. Now, indeed, through the culpable neglect of gentlemen of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, this office has been suffered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into disrepute, and get into low and indigent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; so that although formerly no coroners would be paid for serving their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and they were by the aforesaid statute of Westminster i. expressly forbidden to take a reward under pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> forfeiture to the king, yet for many years past they have only desired to be chosen for the sake of their perquisites; being allowed fees for their attendance by the statute 3 Hen. VII. c. 1. which Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> complains of heavily, though since his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> those fees have been much enlarged. The coroner is chosen for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; but may be removed, either by being made sheriff or chosen verderor, which are offices incompatible with the other; and by the statute 25 Geo. II. c. 29. extirpation, neglect, or misbehaviour, are also made causes of removal. The office and power of a coroner are also, like those of the sheriff, either judicial or ministerial; but principally judicial. This is in great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> ascertained by statute 4 Edw. I. De officio coronatoris; and consists, first, in inquiring, when any person is slain, or dies suddenly, or in prison, concerning the manner of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. And this must be super vi et corpus; for if the body is not found, the coroner cannot fit. He must also fit at the very <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the death happened. And his inquiry is made by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> from four, five, or six, of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, over whom he is to preside. If any be found guilty by this inquest of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, he is to commit to prison for farther <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, and is also to inquire concerning their lands, goods, and chattels, which are forfeited thereby; but whether it be murder or not, he must inquire whether any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of death has accrued to the king, or the lord of the franchise, by this death; and must certify the whole of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> to the court of king's bench, or the next assizes. Another branch of his office is to inquire concerning shipwrecks; and certify whether wreck or not, and who is in possession of the goods. Concerning <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TREASURE_TROVE"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>-trove, he is also to inquire concerning the finders, and where it is, and whether any one be suspected of having found and concealed a treasure; "and that may well be perceived (<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> the old statute of Edw. I.), where one liveth riotously, haunting taverns, and hath done so of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time;" whereupon he might be attached and held to bail upon this suspicion only. The ministerial office of the coroner is only as the sheriff's substitute. For when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> exception can be taken to the sheriff, for suspicion of partiality (as that he is interested in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, or of kindred to either plaintiff or defendant), the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> must then be awarded to the coroner, instead of the sheriff, for execution of the king's writs. CORONET. See CROWN.

CORONET

Pages 306-306
or Coronet, of a horse, the lowest part of the palfrey, which runs round the coffin, and is distinguished by the hair joining and covering the upper part of the hoof.

CORONILLA

Pages 306-306

jointed-podded Colutea: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 32d order, Papilionaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORPORA CAVERNOSA

Pages 306-306

in Anatomy, two spongy bodies, called also corpora nervosa and corpus spongiosum. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CORPORA Pyramidalia, are two protuberances of the under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the cerebellum, about an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; so called from their resemblance to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>. See Anatomy Index. CORPORA Striata. See Anatomy Index.

CORPORAL

Pages 306-306

is also an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, signifying the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> spread under the chalice in the eucharist and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, to receive the fragments of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any chance to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. Some say it was Pope Eusebius who first enjoined the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the corporal; others ascribe it to St Sylvester. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to carry corporals, with some solemnity, to fires, and to heave them against the flames, in order to extinguish them. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> de Comines says, the pope made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XI. a present of the corporale whereon my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> lung mafs.

CORPORATION

Pages 306-309

a body politic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> incorporate, so called, because the persons or members are joined into one body, and are qualified to take, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, &c. Of corporations there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety subsisting, for the advancement of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, of learning, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; in order to preserve entire and for ever those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and immunities, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were granted only to those individuals of which the body corporate is composed, would upon their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> be utterly lost and extinct. To show the advantages of these incorporations, let us consider the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in either of our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, founded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> fundandum et orandum, for the encouragement and support of religion and learning. If this was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> voluntary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, the individuals which compose it might indeed read, pray, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, and perform scholastic exercises together, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as they could agree to do so; but they could neither frame nor receive any laws or rules of their conduct; none at least which would have any binding force, for want of a coercive power to create a sufficient obligation. Neither could they be capable of retaining any privileges or immunities: for, if such privileges be attacked, which of all this unconnected assembly has the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or ability to defend them? And, when they are dispersed by death or otherwise, how shall they transfer these advantages to another set of students, equally unconnected as themselves? So also, with regard to holding estates or other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, if <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> be granted for the purposes of religion or learning to 20 individuals not incorporated, there is no legal way of continuing the property to any other persons for the same purpose, but by endless conveyances from one to the other, as often as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> are changed. But when they are consolidated and united into a corporation, they and their successors are then considered as one person in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>: as one person, they have one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, which is collected from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the majority of the individuals: this one will may establish rules and orders for the regulation of the whole, which are a sort of municipal laws of this little republic; or rules and statutes may be prescribed to it at its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, which are then in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> laws: the privileges and immunities, the estates and possessions, of the corporation, when once vested in them, will be for ever vested, without any new conveyance to new successors; for all the individual members that have existed from the foundation to the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, or that shall ever hereafter exist, are but one person in law, a person that never dies: in like manner as the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> is still the same river, though the parts which compose it are changing every instant. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of originally inventing these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> constitutions entirely belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. They were introduced, as Plutarch says, by Numa; who finding, upon his accession, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> torn to pieces by the two rival factions of Sabines and Romans, thought it a prudent and politic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to subdivide these two into many smaller ones, by instituting separate <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> trade and profession. They were afterwards much considered by the civil law, in which they were called universitatis, as forming one whole out of many individuals; or collegia, from being gathered together: they were adopted also by the canon law, for the maintenance of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; and from them our spiritual corporations are derived. But our laws have considerably refined and improved upon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, according to the usual genius of the English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, particularly with regard to sole corporations, consisting of one person only, of which the Roman lawyers had no notion; their maxim being that, Tres faciunt collegium; though they held, that if a corporation, originally consisting of three persons, be reduced to one, Si universitas ad annum redit; it may still subsist as a corporation, Et si non universitas. As to the several sorts of corporations, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of them is into aggregate and sole. Corporations aggregate consist of many persons united together into one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and are kept up by a perpetual succession of members, so as to continue for ever: of which kind are the mayor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> of a city, the head and fellows of a college, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Corporations sole consist of one person only and his successors, in some particular station, who are incorporated by law, in order to give them some legal capacities and advantages, particularly that of perpetuity, which in their natural persons they could not have had. In this sense the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> is a sole corporation; so is a bishop; so are some deans and prebendaries, distinct from their several chapters; and so is every parson and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>. And the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, or at least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> will be very apparent, if we consider the case of a parson of a church. At the original endowment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches, the freehold of the church, the church-yard, the parsonage-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the glebe, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a> of the parish, were vested in the then parson by the bounty of the donor, as a temporal recompense to him for his spiritual care of the inhabitants, and with intent that the same emoluments should ever afterwards continue as a recompense for the same care. But how was this to be effected? The freehold was vested in the parson; and, if we suppose it vested in his natural capacity, on his death it might descend to his heir, and would be liable to his debts and incumbrances: or at best, the heir might be compelled, at some trouble and expense, to convey these rights to the succeeding incumbent. The law therefore has wisely ordained, that the parson, quatenus parson, shall never die, any more than the king; by making him and his successors a corporation. By which means all the original rights of the parsonage are preserved entire to the successor; for the present incumbent, and his predecessor who lived <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> centuries ago, are in law one and the same person; and what was given to the one was given to the other also. Another division of corporations, either sole or aggregate, is into ecclesiastical and lay. Ecclesiastical corporations are, where the members that compose it are entirely spiritual persons, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, certain deans and prebendaries, all archdeacons, parsons, and vicars, which are sole corporations; deans and chapters at present, and formerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> and convent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> and monks, and the like, bodies aggregate. These are erected for the furtherance of religion; and perpetuating the rights of the church.—Lay corporations are of two sorts, civil and eleemosynary. The civil are such as are erected for a variety of temporal purposes. The king, for instance, is made a corporation, to prevent in general the possibility of an interregnum or vacancy of the throne, and to preserve the possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> entire; for immediately upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a> of one king, his successor is in full possession of the regal rights and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. Other lay corporations are erected for the good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a town or particular district, as a mayor and commonality, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> and burgesses, or the like: some for the advancement and regulation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> and commerce; as the trading companies of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; and some for the better carrying on of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> special purposes; as church wardens, for conservation of the goods of the parish; the college of physicians and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of surgeons in London, for the improvement of the medical science; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> society for the advancement of natural knowledge; and the society of antiquarians for promoting the study of antiquities. The eleemosynary sort are such as are constituted for the perpetual distribution of the free alms or bounty of the founder of them to such persons as he has directed. Of this kind are all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> for the maintenance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, sick, and impotent; and all colleges, both in our universities and out of them: which colleges are founded for two pur- poses: 1. For the promotion of piety and learning by proper regulations and ordinances. 2. For imparting affluence to the members of those bodies, in order to enable them to prosecute their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> and studies with greater ease and affluence. And all these eleemosynary corporations are, strictly speaking, lay, and not ecclesiastical, even though composed of ecclesiastical persons, and although they in some things partake of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, privileges, and restrictions of ecclesiastical bodies. Having thus marshalled the several <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of corporations, let us next proceed to consider, 1. How corporations in general may be created. 2. What are their powers, capacities, and incapacities. And, 3. How they may be dissolved. I. Corporations, by the civil law, seem to have been created by the mere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> and voluntary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> of their members; provided such convention was not contrary to law, for then it was illicitum collegium. It does not appear that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s consent was necessary to be actually given to the foundation of them; but merely that the original founders of these voluntary and friendly societies (for they were little more than such) should not establish any meetings in opposition to the laws of the state. But in England the king's consent is absolutely necessary to the erection of any corporation, either impliedly or expressly given. The king's implied consent is to be found in corporations which exist by force of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, to which our former kings are supposed to have given their concurrence; common law being nothing else but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, arising from the universal agreement of the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. Of this sort are the king himself, all bishops, parsons, vicars, church-wardens, and some others; who by common law have ever been held (as far as our books can show us) to have been corporations, virtute officii; and this incorporation is so inseparably annexed to their offices, that we cannot frame a complete legal idea of any of these persons, but we must also have an idea of a corporation, capable to transmit his rights to his successors, at the same time. Another method of implication, whereby the king's consent is presumed, is as to all corporations by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, such as the city of London, and many others, which have existed as corporations, time whereof the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> runneth out to the contrary; and therefore are looked upon in law to be well created. For though the members thereof can show no legal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of incorporation, yet in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> antiquity the law presumes there once was one; and that by the variety of accidents, which a length of time may produce, the charter is lost or destroyed. The methods by which the king's consent is expressly given, are either by act of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> or charter. By act of parliament, of which the royal assent is a necessary ingredient, corporations may undoubtedly be created: but it is observable, that most of those statutes which are usually cited as having created corporations, do either confirm such as have been before created by the king; as in the case of the college of physicians, erected by charter to Hen. VIII., which charter was afterwards confirmed in parliament: or, they permit the king to erect a corporation in futuro with such and such powers; as is the case of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of England, and the society of the British fishery. So that the immediate creative act is usually performed by the king alone, in virtue of his royal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>. All the other methods therefore whereby corporations exist, by common law, by prescription, and by act of parliament, are for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> reducible to this of the king's letters patent, or charter of incorporation. The king's creation may be performed by the words creamus, ergimus, fundamus, incorporamus, or the like. Nay it is held, that if the king grants to a set of men to have gildam mercatorium, "a mercantile meeting or assembly," this is alone sufficient to incorporate and establish them for ever. The king (it is said) may grant to a subject the power of erecting corporations, though the contrary was formerly held; that is, he may permit the subject to name the persons and powers of the corporation at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; but it is really the king that erects, and the subject is but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>; for though none but the king can make a corporation, yet qui facit per alium, facit per se. In this manner the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> has power by charter to erect corporations; and has actually often exerted it in the erection of several matriculated companies, now subsisting, of tradesmen subservient to the students. When a corporation is erected, a name must be given to it; and by that name alone it must sue and be sued, and do all legal acts. II. After a corporation is so formed and named, it acquires many powers and rights, which we are next to consider. Some of these are necessarily and inseparably incident to every corporation; which incidents as soon as a corporation is duly erected, are tacitly annexed of course. As, 1. To have perpetual succession. This is the very end of its incorporation; for there cannot be a succession for ever without an incorporation; and therefore all aggregate corporations have a power necessarily implied of electing members in the room of such as go off. 2. To sue or be sued, implead or be impleaded, grant or receive, by its corporate name, and do all other acts as natural persons may. 3. To purchase lands and hold them, for the benefit of themselves and their successors: which two are consequential to the former. 4. To have a common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. For a corporation, being an invisible body, cannot manifest its intentions by any personal act or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> discourse: it otherwise acts and speaks only by its common seal. For though the particular members may express their private consents to any act by words or signing their names, yet this does not bind the corporation; it is the fixing of the seal, and that only, which unites the several assents of the individuals who compose the community, and makes one <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> assent of the whole. 5. To make by-laws or private statutes for the better government of the corporation; which are binding upon themselves, unless contrary to the laws of the land, and then they are void. But no trading company is with us allowed to make by-laws which may affect the king's prerogative or the common profit of the people, under penalty of 40l. unless they be approved by the chancellor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> justices, or the judges of assize in their circuits; and even though they be so approved, still, if contrary to law, they are void. These five powers are inseparably incident to every corporation, at least to every corporation Corporation aggregate; for two of them, though they may be practised, yet are very unnecessary to a corporation sole; viz. to have a corporate seal to testify his sole assent, and to make statutes for the regulation of his own conduct. Corporations have a capacity to purchase lands for themselves and successors; but they are excepted out of the statute of wills; so that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVISE">devise</a> of lands to a corporation by will is good; except for charitable uses, by stat. 43. Eliz. c. 4, which exception is again greatly narrowed by the stat. 9. Geo. II. c. 36. And also, by a great variety of statutes, their privilege even of purchasing from any living grantor is much abridged; so that now a corporation, either ecclesiastical or lay, must have a license from the king to purchase, before they can exert that capacity which is vested in them by the common law: nor is even this in all cases sufficient. These statutes are generally called the Statutes of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTMAIN">mortmain</a>. See Mortmain. The general duties of all bodies politic, considered in their corporate capacity, may, like those of natural persons, be reduced to this single one; that of acting up to the end or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, whatever it be, for which they were created by their founder. III. How corporations may be dissolved. Any particular member may be disfranchised, or lose his place in the corporation, by acting contrary to the laws of the society, or the laws of the land; or he may resign it by his own voluntary act. But the body politic may also itself be dissolved in several ways; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> is the civil death of the corporation; and in this case their lands and tenements shall revert to the person, or his heirs, who granted them to the corporation; for the law doth annex a condition to every such grant, that if the corporation be dissolved, the grantor shall have the lands again, because the cause of the grant faileth. The grant is indeed only during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the corporation; which may endure forever; but when that life is determined to be the dissolution of the body politic, the grantor takes it back by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a>, as in the case of every other grant for life. The debts of a corporation, either to or from it, are totally extinguished by its dissolution; so that the members thereof cannot recover, or be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with them, in their natural capacities: agreeable to that maxim of the civil law, Si quid universitatis debetur, singulis non debetur; nec, quod debet universitas, singulis debent. A corporation may be dissolved, 1. By act of parliament, which is boundless in its operations. 2. By the natural death of all its members, in cases of an aggregate corporation. 3. By surrender of its franchises into the hands of the king, which is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a>. 4. By forfeiture of its charter, through negligence or abuse of its franchises, in which case the law judges that the body politic has broken the conditions upon which it was incorporated, and therefore the incorporation is void. And the regular course is to bring an information in nature of a writ of quo warranto, to inquire by what warrant the members now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> their corporate power, having forfeited it by such and such proceedings. The exertion of this act of law, for the purposes of the state, in the reigns of King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> and King James II. particularly by seizing the charter of the city of London, gave great and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> offence; though perhaps, in strictness of law, the proceedings in most of them were sufficiently regular; but the judgment against that of London was reversed by act of parliament after the revolution; and by the same statute it is enacted, that the franchises of the city of London shall never more be forfeited for any cause whatsoever. And because by the common law corporations were dissolved, in case the mayor or head officer was not duly elected on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> appointed in the charter or established by prescription, it is now provided, that for the future no corporation shall be dissolved upon that account, and ample directions are given for appointing a new officer, in case there be no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, or a void one, made upon the charter or prescriptive day.

CORPORATION ACT

Pages 309-309

is that which prevents any person from being legally elected into any office relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> corporation, unless within a twelvemonth before he has received the sacrament of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a> according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England; and which enjoins him to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> and supremacy when he takes the oath of office; otherwise his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> is void.

CORPOREITY

Pages 309-309

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of that which is corporeal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> has body; or that which constitutes or denominates it such.—The corporeity of God was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of the Anthropomorphites. Some authors reproach Tertullian with admitting a corporeity in the Deity; but it is manifest, by body he means no more than substance.—The Mahometans reproach the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a> at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of the corporeity of God. Many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> believed the corporeity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>.

CORPS

Pages 309-309

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> borrowed from the French, signifying any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> that projects <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> advances beyond the naked of a wall; and which serves as a ground for some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> or the like. Corps de Bataille, is the main body of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> drawn up for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. Corps de Garde, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> in an army, sometimes under <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a>, sometimes in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, to receive a body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, who are relieved from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, and are to watch in their turns, for the security of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, station, &c.—The word is also used for the men who watch therein. It is usual to have, beside the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, a little corps de garde, at a good distance before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; to be the more readily advertised of the approach of the enemy.

CORPSE

Pages 309-309

a dead body. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any one, in taking up a dead body, steals the shroud, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other apparel, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be felony. Stealing only the corpse itself is not felony; but it is punishable as a misdemeanor by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>.

CORPULENCY

Pages 309-310

the state of a person too much loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fat. Corpulency is the occasion of various diseases, and particularly the apoplexy. It was held infamous among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Lacedemonians. Sennertus mentions a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that weighed 600 pounds, and a maid 36 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> who weighed 450. Bright of Malden, who died at the age of 29 years in 1750, weighed 616 pounds. Chiapin Vitelli, marquis of Cerona, a noted Spanish general in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, from an excessive excessive corpulency, is said to have reduced himself by drinking of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of leanness, that he could fold his skin several times round him. Castile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, in the form of a bolus, an electuary, pills, or dissolved in a gill or more of soft <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, from one to four drachms taken at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-time, is strongly recommended with a view of reducing corpulency, in a discourse on its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, causes, and cure, by Mal- colm Fleming, M.D., Lond. 1760. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORPUS

Pages 310-310

in Anatomy, is applied to several parts of the animal structure; as corpus callus, corpus savernum, &c. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Corpus is also used in matters of learning, for sev- eral works of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> collected and bound to- gether. Gratian made a collection of the canons of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, called corpus canonum. The corpus of the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> is composed of the digest, code, and institutes. We have also a corpus of the Greek poets; and ano- ther of the Latin poets. Corpus Christi, a festival of the church of England, kept on the next Thursday after Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, in- stituted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the eucharist; to which also one of the colleges of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> is dedicated.

CORPUSCLE

Pages 310-310

in Physics, a minute particle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> physical atom, being such as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> body is made up of. By this word is not meant the elementary particles, nor hypothetical principles of chemists; but such particles, whether of a simple or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> na- ture, whose parts <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be dissolved nor dissipated by ordinary degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>.

CORPUSCULAR PHILOSOPHY

Pages 310-310

is that way of philosophizing which endeavours to explain things, and to account for the phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, by the mo- tion, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, rest, position, &c. of the corpuscles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the minute particles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Mr Boyle sums up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> principles of the cor- puscular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, which now flourishes under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> in these particulars; 1. They suppose that there is but one catholic or universal matter, which is an extended, impenetrable, and divisible substance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all bodies, and ca- pable of all forms. 2. That this matter, in order to form the vast variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bodies, must have mo- tion in some or all its assignable parts; and that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> was given to matter by God the Creator of all things, and has all manner of directions and tendencies. 3. Matter must also be actually divided into parts, and each of these primitive particles, fragments, or atoms of matter must have its proper magnitude or size, as also its peculiar figure or shape. 4. They sup- pose also, that these differently sized and shaped par- ticles may have different orders and positions, where- of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety may arise in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of bodies.

CORRADINI DE SEZZA

Pages 310-310
Peter Marcellinus, a learned civilian and cardinal, born at Sezza, in 1658, acquired the esteem and confidence of Clement XI. and died at Rome in 1743. He was the author of a learned and curious work, entitled, "Verus Latium profanum et sacrum," 2 vols folio; and a history of Sezza, in 4to.

CORRADO

Pages 310-310

Sebastian, an Italian grammarian of the 16th century, taught the Greek and Latin tongues at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGGIO">Reggio</a>, where he formed an academy of polite li- terature; and at length removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>- der to be professor of those languages. He wrote sev- eral works, the most esteemed of which are, "Que- flora in qua Ciceronis vita referatur," an excellent performance; and, "de Lingua Latina." He died in 1556.

CORRECTION

Pages 310-312

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of retrench- ing the faults in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> which the corrector gives the first proofs, to point out and amend the faults, to be rectified by the compositor. The corrections are placed on the margin of each page, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> against the line where the faults are found. There are different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> used to express different corrections, as D or δ, dele, for any thing to be el- iminated or left out. When anything is to be inserted, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is marked in the line with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARET">caret</a> ^, and the insertion added in the margin. When a word, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>, &c. is to be altered, it is erased out of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, and that to be put in its room written in the margin; always observing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be several mistakes in the same line, that the corrections in the margin be separated by little bars, or strokes, |. If a space be omitted, its place is marked with a caret, and the margin with ×. If a space be wrong placed, as in the middle of a word, the two parts are connected with a caret, and the same character put in the margin. If a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, it is expressed on the margin with 9. If any thing be transposed, it is marked thus: The shortest are the fullest least; for the shortest follies are the least; and in the margin is added tr in a circle. If Roman characters are to be changed for Italic, or vice versa, a line is drawn under them thus, and Roman or Italic added in the margin; if to capi- tals, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> line. If a word or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> is entirely omitted, the place is marked with a caret, and in the margin is inserted the word out. If the letters of a word stand too far asunder, a line is drawn under them, and in the margin is put a crooked line or hook, thus . Correction <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, a place of confinement, where vagrants and persons guilty of crimes of an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, suffer <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> by being obliged to labour for a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as for months or years, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the crime. The benefit arising to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and the reformation of offenders, from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of punishment, have been variously esti- mated by different writers, according to the views which they have taken of the effects and consequences which are supposed to follow the confinement and re- straint to which the criminal is subjected. It has been regarded as one of the greatest defects of the laws of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, that, excepting the punishment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, there is no other which is accompanied with that degree of severity and terror to awe or restrain offenders from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of crimes. To this pur- pose are the following observations of Dr Paley. The laws of England, he says, "are not provided with any other punishment than that of death, sufficiently terri- ble to keep offenders in awe. Transportation which is the punishment <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in the order of severity, answers the purpose of example very imperfectly; not only be- cause exile is in reality a slight punishment to those who have neither <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, nor friends, nor regular means Correction of subsistence at home, but because the punishment, whatever it be, is unobserved and unknown. A transported convict may suffer under his sentence, but his sufferings are removed from the view of his countrymen; his misery is unseen; his condition strikes no terror into the minds of those for whose warning and admonition it was intended. This chasm in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of punishment produces also two farther imperfections in the administration of penal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; of which the first is, that the same punishment is extended to crimes of very different characters and malignancy; and the second, that punishments, separated by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, are assigned to crimes hardly distinguishable in their guilt and mischief. This defect, it has been supposed might be made up by the proper management of houses of correction. For as the object of punishment is not only the amendment of the offender, but is also intended to operate as an example to others, both these objects seem to be more certainly attained by the confinement and labour to which criminals are subjected in houses of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> than by any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of punishment provided by the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It is greatly to be regretted that the punishments inflicted by the laws of this country, whether imprisonment or exile, pain or infamy, have rarely the effect of producing any reformation of the criminal. On the contrary he often returns to the world more hardened in crime, and more determined in his wicked courses. Houses of correction might probably in this respect be attended with more beneficial consequences. This seems to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> house of correction, an account of which in this view <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not, it is hoped, be unacceptable to our readers. It is extracted from the Journal of the Travels of M. Thouin. The Amsterdam correction house, from the employment of the prisoners confined in it, is called the rapping-house, and is destined to the reception of those malefactors whose crimes do not amount to a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> offence. Their punishment cannot so properly be denominated solitary confinement as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEQUESTRATION">sequestration</a> from society during a limited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of years. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is situated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the suburbs to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The exterior has nothing remarkable, either with respect to form or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It is detached from the street by a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, which contains the keeper's lodge, together with apartments for the different servants belonging to the establishment. Over the gate, which opens from this court into the prison, are placed two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, representing two men in the act of sawing a piece of logwood. The inner court is in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, round which are arranged the apartments of the prisoners, together with the necessary warehouses. One part of the ground story is divided into different chambers; the other serves as a depot for the logwood, and the implements employed in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>. The keeper, whose countenance, contrary to the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of persons of his profession, was strongly indicative of urbanity and gentleness, introduced M. Thouin into an apartment where two prisoners were at work in sawing a large log of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPEACHY">Campeachy</a> wood. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> is composed of four blades joined together, with very strong, large, and sharp <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, which make a scissure in the wood of nearly two inches in breadth. The operation is repeated, till the pieces become too small to undergo the saw, when they are ground in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> peculiarly constructed for this purpose. This employment requires an extraordinary exertion of strength, and is at first a severe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> even to robust persons; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, and practice, soon render it easy; and the prisoners in a short time become competent to furnish, without painful exertion, their weekly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINGENT">contingent</a> of 200 lbs. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of sawed pieces. After completing this task, they even find time to fabricate a variety of little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in wood and straw, which they sell to those who visit the prison, or dispose of, by means of agents, in the town. M. Thouin next inspected three apartments of different dimensions, which opened into the inner court. The one was inhabited by four, the second by six, and the third by ten prisoners. The furniture of the rooms consisted in hammocks, with a mattress, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLANKET">blanket</a>, and a coverlid to each, tables, chairs, and stools, glafs, &c., earthen vessels, and various other articles of convenience. Everything in these apartments was distinguished by neatness and propriety; and notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants allotted to each was fully adequate to the dimensions of the rooms, the senses were not offended with any disagreeable scent, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> was in every respect as pure and wholesome as the surrounding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. In an obscure part of the building are a number of cells, in which formerly those prisoners who revolted against the proper subordination of the place, or ill-treated their comrades, were confined for a few days. But the keeper assured M. Thouin that these cells had not been made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for upwards of 10 years. They are dark gloomy dungeons, with only a small aperture for the admission of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and air. The suppression of this barbarous and coercive punishment does <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. The store-rooms are filled with various kinds of wood for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>; as the hematosylum campechianum, the morus tinctoria, the caesalpinia japonica, &c. They are all exotics, with the exception of the evonymus Europaeus. The warehouses were not of sufficient extent to contain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wood, which was deposited in piles in different parts of the court. The prisoners, amounting to 76 in number, were uniformly habited in coarse woollens; wear very good stockings, large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> shoes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flints, and caps or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>. They are, by the rules of the house, obliged to frequent ablutions, which greatly contribute to the preservation of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. There was only one sick person amongst them; and, what is not a little remarkable, almost all the prisoners had formerly lived in large commercial <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; very few villagers were amongst them. They had all been sentenced to imprisonment for theft; but it depends upon themselves, by reformation and good behaviour, to shorten the term of their confinement, which many of them frequently do. The keeper, whose humanity to the unfortunate persons committed to his care entitles him rather to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of their protector than their gaoler (and M. Thouin informs us, that the prisoners generally called him by no other name than father), afflicts them with his counsels and friendly admonitions. He registers every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, in a book appropriated to this purpose, both the instances of good and bad behaviour, which is annually submitted. Correction submitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the magistracy, who, from this report, abridge or prolong the term of confinement, according to the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> which each prisoner appears to merit. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">Cases</a> frequently happen where a malefactor, condemned to an imprisonment of eight years, by his good behaviour procures his enlargement at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of four; and so in proportion for a shorter term. But great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is paid to discriminate between actual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> and hypocritical artifice. The reward of good behaviour is not, however, confined to, or withheld till, the period of actual liberation. Their restoration to society is preceded by a progressive amelioration of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. Their work is gradually rendered less laborious, they are accommodated with separate apartments, and employed in the services of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy. The keeper even entrusts them with commissions beyond the precincts of the prison; and scarce a single instance has occurred of their abusing this indulgence. By this prudent management, a considerable saving is effected in the expense of the establishment, at the same time that it tends to wear away <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, and to initiate the prisoners by gradual advances into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> duties of social life. M. Thouin made particular inquiries whether it was customary for persons after their discharge to be confined a second and third time, as is but too often the case in many countries, for a repetition of their offence. He was informed, that such instances very rarely occur; but the case is not without precedent, as he observed in the person of a young Jew, who was then in the rapping-house for the third time. The case of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is somewhat extraordinary. During the period of his detention, he always conforms, with the most scrupulous observance, to the rules of the place, and gives general satisfaction by his exemplary conduct. But such, as he himself avowed to our traveller, is his constitutional propensity to thieving, that no sooner is the term of his imprisonment elapsed, than he returns with redoubled ardour to his lawless courses. It is not so much for the sake of plunder, as to gratify his irresistible impulse, that he follows this vicious life; and M. Thouin adds, that he recounted his different exploits with as much exultation and triumph as a veteran displays when rehearsing his warlike achievements. Another salutary regulation in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, from which the best consequences result, is the indulgence granted to the prisoners of receiving the visits of their wives and mistresses twice every week. Proper care, however, is taken to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against the introduction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; and the ladies, in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, purchase their admission by giving a trifling sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> at the gate, which becomes the perquisite of the aged prisoners, whose wants are of a different nature from their youthful comrades. Thus the pleasures of one class contribute to the comforts of the other; and the entrance money, trifling as it is, keeps away a crowd of idle vagabonds, who have no acquaintance with the prisoners. The ladies at their visits are permitted to eat and drink with their lovers; and when the conversation becomes too animated for a third person to be present, the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> obligingly take the hint, and leave them to enjoy a tête-à-tête.—By this prudent regulation, many hurtful consequences attendant on a total seclusion from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> society are guarded against. M. Thouin concludes his account with observing, that the rapping-house at Amsterdam bears a greater resemblance to a well-ordered manufactury than to a prison. It were to be wished, that all similar institutions were conducted upon a similar <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>.
