But it is probable that solitary confinement and less intercourse with their friends would have a better effect in reforming the habits of offenders than the indulgences which M. Thouin considers as so beneficial. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> whom we formerly quoted observes, that "of reforming punishments none promises so much success as that of solitary imprisonment, or the confinement of criminals in separate apartments. This improvement of the Amsterdam house of correction would augment the terror of the punishment, would seclude the criminal from the society of his fellow-prisoners, in which society the worst are sure to corrupt the better; would wean him from the knowledge of his companions, and from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of that turbulent pernicious life in which his vices had engaged him; would raise up in him reflections on the folly of his choice, and dispose his mind to such bitter and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENITENCE">penitence</a>, as might produce a lasting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the principles of his conduct." In addition to the confinement and labour which offenders undergo in houses of correction, some are subjected to whipping at certain stated intervals. The benefit arising from this mode of punishment, with regard to the reformation of the criminal, has been justly questioned. If any good effect is to be expected from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, it must be inflicted in private. It has been observed by one* who knew <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature well,* Fielding, that punishment which deprives a man of all sense of honour will never contribute to make him virtuous; and it is generally found that the folder who has once been whipped, becomes quite indifferent to propriety of conduct. Fasting, which is not attended with shame, promises to be a more effectual punishment of profligacy.

CORRECTOR

Pages 312-312

in Medicine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, an ingredient in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, which guards against or abates the force of another.

CORREGIDOR

the name of an officer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and countries subject to the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. He is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> judge of a town <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. CORREGIO. See Allegri.

CORRELATIVE

Pages 312-312

something opposed to another in a certain relation. Thus father and son are relatives. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a> and darkness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and rest, are correlative and opposite terms.

CORRIDOR

Pages 289-289
or Corridor, in Fortification, a road or way along the edge of the ditch, without-side; encompassing the whole fortification. The word comes from the Italian corridor, or the Spanish corridor. It is also called the covert-way, because covered with a glacis, or esplanade, serving it as a parapet.—The corridor is about 20 yards broad. Corridor is also used in architecture for a gallery or long aisle around a building, leading to several chambers at a distance from each other, sometimes wholly inclosed, and sometimes open on one side.

CORRIDOR-WAY

Pages 326-326
or CORRIDOR, in Fortification, a space of ground, level with the field on the edge of the ditch, three or four fathoms broad, ranging quite round the half moons and other works towards the country. It has a parapet raised on a level, together with its banquets and glacis. See FORTIFICATION.

CORRIGIOLA

Pages 312-312

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clais, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 45th order, Miscellanea. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORROSION

Pages 312-313

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of gnawing away, by degrees, the continuity of the parts of bodies. Corrosion, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, an action of bodies, by means of proper menstruums, that produces new <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a>, Corrosive combinations, and a change of their form, without converting them to fluidity. CORROSIVE SUBLIMATE <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">MERCURY</a>. See Chemistry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CORRUGATOR MUSCLE. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

CORROSIVES

Pages 313-313

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, are medicines which corrode whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body they are applied to. Such are burnt <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> precipitate of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, white vitriol, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> precipitate of mercury, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> infernalis, &c. CORRUPTICOLÆ, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> who rose out of the Monophysites in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> about the year 519, under their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> Severus, the pretended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. Their distinguishing doctrine, whence they derived their name, was, that the body of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ was corruptible; that the fathers had owned it; and that to deny it was to deny the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Julian of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>, another Eutychian, a refugee, as well as Severus, in Alexandria, maintained that the body of Jesus Christ had been always incorruptible; that to say it was corruptible, was to make a distinction between Jesus Christ and the Word, and by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to make two natures in Jesus Christ. The people of Alexandria were divided between the two opinions; and the partisans of Severus were called corrupticole, q.d. worshippers of something corruptible: sometimes they were denominated corruptibles; and the adherents of Julian incorruptibles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> phantasiafæ. The clergy and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> powers favoured the first; the monks and the people the latter.

CORRUPTION

Pages 313-313

the destruction, extinction, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least cessation for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, of the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of existence of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> body. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">Putrefaction</a>. Corruption of Blood, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, one of the consequences of an attainer; and is both upwards and downwards; so that an attainted person can neither inherit lands or other hereditaments from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, nor retain those he is already in possession of, nor transmit them by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to any heir; but the same shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESCHEAT">escheat</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the fee, subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s superior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of forfeiture; and the person attainted shall also obstruct all descents to his posterity, wherever they are obliged to derive a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> through him to a remoter ancestor. See Attainder. This is one of those notions which our laws have adopted from the feudal constitutions, at the time of the Norman conquest; as appears from its being unknown in those tenures which are indisputably Saxon, or gavel kind: wherein though by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Saxon laws, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is forfeited to the king, yet no corruption of blood, no impediment of descents, ensues; and on judgment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> felony, no escheat accrues to the lord. But by the law of England, derived as above, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s blood is so universally corrupted by attainer, that his sons can neither inherit to him nor to any other ancestor, at least on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their attainted father. This corruption of blood cannot be absolutely removed but by authority of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The king may excuse the public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of an offender; but cannot abolish the private right which has accrued, or may accrue, to individuals as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the criminal's attainer. He may remit a forfeiture in which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> is alone concerned; but he cannot wipe away the corruption of blood; for therein a third person hath an interest, the lord who claims by escheat. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> therefore a man hath a son, and is attainted, and afterwards pardoned by the king: this son can never inherit to his father, or father's ancestors; because his paternal blood, being once thoroughly corrupted by his father's attainder, must continue so: but if the son had been born after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, he might inherit; because, by the pardon, the father is made a new man, and may convey new inheritable blood to his after-born children. This corruption of blood, thus arising from feudal principles, but perhaps extended farther than even these principles <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> warrant, has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> looked upon as a peculiar hardship: because the oppressive parts of the feudal tenures being now in general abolished, it seems unreasonable to reserve one of their most inequitable consequences; namely, that the children should not only be reduced to present poverty (which, however severe, is sufficiently justified upon reasons of public policy), but also be laid under future difficulties of inheritance, on account of the guilt of their ancestors. And therefore in most (if not all) of the new felonies treated by parliament since the reign of Henry VIII. it is declared that they shall not extend to any corruption of blood: and by the statute 7 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> c. 21. (the operation of which is postponed by the statute 17 Geo. II. c. 39.) it is enacted, that after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the late pretender and his sons, no attainder for treason shall extend to the disinheritting any heir, nor the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of any person, other than the offender himself; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> have indeed carried the remedy farther than was required by the hardship above complained of; which is only the future obfliction of decents, where the pedigree happens to be deduced through the blood of an attainted ancestor.

CORSAIR

Pages 313-313

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> person who scours the seas, especially the Mediterranean, with a vessel armed for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or power, to plunder merchant vessels. The word comes from the Italian corsare, of corso, or a curfibus, by reason of their courses, or excursions.—The name is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given to the piratical cruisers of Barbary, who had their rise about the beginning of the 16th century. A corsair is distinguished from a privateer in this, that the latter does it under a commission, and only attacks the vessels of those at war with the state whence his commission is derived. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of a corsair is to be hanged, without <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMISSION">remission</a>; whereas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a> are to be treated as prisoners of war. All corsair vessels are good prizes.

CORSELET

Pages 313-313

a little cuirass: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, an armour or coat made to cover the whole body, anciently worn by the pike-men, usually placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> and flanks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, for the better resisting the enemy's assaults, and guarding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> placed behind them.

CORSICA

Pages 313-314

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Mediterranean, between 8° and 10° E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. and 41° and 43° N. Lat. On the south it is separated from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, by the strait of Bonifacio; to the east it has the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>; and to the west it is opposite the coasts of France and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is 150 miles COR Corsica, miles from north to south, and from 40 to 50 in breadth. It was known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks by the names of Callidita and Cynus, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by its present appellation. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> are many excellent harbours. It is mountainous, but fruitful valleys are interspersed; and it has some fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. With respect to products, Corsica has nothing peculiar to itself; but from the earliest times it has been famous for its swarms of bees, and produces vast quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, which, however, is reckoned bitter, on account of the box and yew with which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounds. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are rich in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and silver; a mine of the latter was opened in the year 1767, from which a quintal of mineral produced 18 ounces of silver. There are also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a> of Corsica is nearly equal to the oriental. Porphyries, jasper, talc, amethysts, emeralds, and other precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, are found scattered in the mountains; and the south coast abounds with beautiful coral. After many revolutions, this island was, for some centuries, under the dominion of the Genoese, whose tyranny was such, that the Corsicans were almost in a perpetual state of insurrection. In 1736, a German adventurer, Theodore baron Newhoff, brought some assistance to them, and, on his assurances of more powerful aid, they elected him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>; but, as he could not substantiate his promises, he was obliged to leave the island. He came to England, was thrown into the Fleet prison, released by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of insolvency (after having registered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Corsica for the benefit of his creditors) and suffered to die in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> indigence. The Genoese tired of the contest, sold the sovereignty to France, in 1767, and the celebrated Paoli, who had been elected to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> command, in 1755, was obliged to abandon the island in 1769. After the French revolution, in 1789, Corsica was admitted as an eighty-third department of France, at the particular request of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a>, of which Paoli was at the head. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, however, of some events which followed the revolution of 1792, Paoli revolted; the French, by the assistance of the English, were expelled from the island; and Corsica, on the 19th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1794, was declared annexed to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, according to a new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, which had been previously formed. In October 1796, however, the English found it expedient to evacuate the island, of which the French immediately took possession, and again united it to their republic, dividing it into two departments, Golo and Liamone; of the former of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTIA">Bastia</a> is the chief town, and of the latter <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AJACCIO">Ajaccio</a>.

CORSNED

Pages 314-314
or Morsel of Exorcration, a species of trial or purgation * anciently in use among us, and which probably arose from an abuse of revelation in the dark ages of superstition. It consisted of a piece of cheese or bread, about an ounce in weight, which was consecrated with a form of exorcism; deriving of the Almighty that it might cause convulsions and palsy, and find no passage if the man was really guilty; but might turn to health and nourishment if he was innocent; as the water of jealousy among the Jews was, by God's especial appointment, to cause the belly to swell, and the thigh to rot, if the woman was guilty of adultery. This consecrated was then given to the suspected person, who at the same time also received the holy sacrament: if indeed the consecrated was not, as some have suspected, the sacramental bread itself; till the subsequent invention of transubstantiation preserved it from profane uses with a more profound respect than formerly. Our historians assure us, that Godwin, earl of Kent, in the reign of King Edward the Confessor, abjuring the death of the king's brother, at last appealed to his consecrated, "per buccellam deglutirem abjuravit," which stuck in his throat and killed him. This custom has been long since gradually abolished, though the remembrance of it still subsists in certain phrases of abjuration retained among the common people: as, "I will take the sacrament upon it; May this morsel be my last;" and the like.

CORT

Pages 314-314

Cornelius, a celebrated engraver, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOORN">Hoorn</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in 1536. After having learned the first principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and engraving, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> to complete his studies, and visited all the places famous for the works of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> masters. At <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> he was courteously received by Titian; and engraved several plates from the pictures of that admirable painter. He at last settled at Rome, where he died in 1578, aged 42. According to Balan, he was "the best engraver with the burin <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> graver only that Holland ever produced. We find in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>," adds he, "correctness of drawing, and an exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>." He praises also the taste and lightness of touch with which he engraved landscapes, and that without the affluence of the point. It is no small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, that Agostino Carracci was his scholar, and imitated his style of engraving rather than that of any other <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. His engravings are very numerous (151 according to Abbé Marolles), and by no means uncommon. CORTES of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> purely Spanish, signifying the courts, i.e. the states or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the states, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. Cortez, or Cortez, Ferdinand, a Spanish general, famous for the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, and other victories over the natives of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; but infamous for the cruelties he committed upon the vanquished, without regard to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. It probably was on this account he was but coolly received on his return to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> master <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V.: It is even asserted that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> asked him who he was? to which Cortez replied: "I am the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who gave you more provinces than your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> have left you <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>." Died in 1544, aged 63. See Mexico.

CORTEX

Pages 314-315

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the rind <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coarse outer bark of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The organization of the outer and inner barks, which differ principally in the fineness of their texture, is particularly explained under the article PLANTS. Wounds of the bark, and its separations from the wood, whether naturally or artificially made, are easily cured, and made to unite again by proper care. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> sections be made in the rinds of the alh and sycamore of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, three sides cut, and the fourth uncut, and the whole be afterwards bound round with a pack-thread, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> all unite again, only leaving a scar in each of the three sides where it was cut. If several parts of the bark of either of these trees be cut off, and entirely separated from the tree; some shallower, leav- ving a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bark on, and others deeper, to the wood itself; these pieces being again put into their places, and bound on with a pack-thread, will not indeed unite, but a fresh bark will grow in their places, and thrust them away: but if they be first carefully laid on in the exact <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> in which they originally grew, and then the whole part beyond the wound on every side covered with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of diachylon, or the like, and this bound over with pack-thread to keep all firmly in their places, the pieces of bark, whether cut off shallower or deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the very wood of the tree, will firmly unite themselves to the places where they originally grew. This cure will be performed in about three weeks; but the outer rind of the separated pieces will not be plum, but somewhat shrivelled; the edges also will recede somewhat from their original <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; so that there remains a sort of scar all round. These experiments are best made in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> season; for in the autumn and winter, the sap arising but weakly, the parts that should unite wither before that is brought about. The success of these experiments has made some think that the whole branch of a tree separated and bound on again might unite with the rest. But the experiments that have been made in the most favourable manner for such a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> have all proved vain, the branch cut off withering always in a few days, however well united and carefully kept on. **Cortex Peruvianus.** See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CINCHONA">Cinchona</a>, Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Cortex Winteranus.** See Wintera, Botany Index.

CORTONA

Pages 315-315

Pietro da.** See Berretini. **Cortona,** a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, mentioned by many of the Roman historians. It was originally called Corton, and lay to the northward of the lake Trasymenus. It still remains the name of Cortona. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. o. N. Lat. 43. 15.

CORTONESE

Pages 315-315

Pietro Paolo.** See Gorbo. **CORTUSA,** Bear's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> Sanicle: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the pentandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 21st order, Precise. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **CORUNNA,** <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Groyne, a port-town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated on a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, about 32 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSTELLA">Compostella</a>, and 20 south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERROL">Ferrol</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. o. N. Lat. 43. o. **Corus,** Omer, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, or Chomer, in the Jewish antiquities, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> containing 10 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> or 75 gallons and five pints; as a measure of things liquid, and 32 pecks and 1 pint as a measure for things dry. The corus or omer was most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> a measure for things dry; and the greatest that was used among the Jews. It contained, according to the rabbins, 10 ephahs or 30 sata or seahs. Corus is the most usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in the historical writers, and omer or chomer among the prophets. Corus is also used in some of our old writers for eight bushels or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; decem coros tritici, five decem quartaria. **Coruscation,** a glittering or gleam of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> issuing from any thing. It is chiefly used for a flash of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> darting from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>. There is a method of producing <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> coruscations, or sparkling fiery meteors, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be visible not only in the dark but at noon-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and that from two liquors actually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. The method is this. Fifteen grains of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> phosphorus are to be melted in about a drachm of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; when this is cold, pour upon it about two ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of vitriol; let these be shaken together, and they will at first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and afterwards they will throw up fiery balls in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, which will adhere like so many stars to the sides of the glass, and continue <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> a considerable time; after this, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of oil of turpentine is poured in, without shaking the phial, the mixture will of itself take fire, and burn very furiously. The vessel should be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and open at the top.

CORYATE

Pages 315-316

Thomas, a very extraordinary personage, who seems to have made himself famous by his whimsical extravagancies, was the son of a clergyman, and born at Oldcombe in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> in 1577. He acquired Greek and Latin at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and coming to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was received into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> of Henry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> Coryate was not over witty himself, he got acquainted with the wits of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and served to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> their abilities, having more learning than judgment. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> peripatetic: for, in 1608, he took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> journey on foot; and after he returned, published his travels under the following strange <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>: Crudities hastily gobbled up in five months Travels in France, Savoy, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Rhetia, Helvetia, some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Germany, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, Lond. 1611, 4to. In 1612 he set out again with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to spend ten years in travelling: he went first to Constantinople; and after travelling over a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the East, died of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a> in the East Indies. Some of the accounts of his peregrinations are to be found in Purchas's Pilgrimages.

CORYBANTES

Pages 316-316

in antiquity, priests of Cybele, who danced and capered to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of flutes and drums. See CROTALUM. Catullus, in his poem called Atys, gives a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of them, representing them as madmen. Accordingly Maximus Tyrius says, that those possessed with the spirit of Corybantes, as soon as they heard the sound of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, were seized with an enthusiasm, and lost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their reason. And hence the Greeks use the word οὐρανοῦς, to corobantizes, to signify a person's being transported <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> possessed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>. See Enthusiasm. Some say that the Corybantes were all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>; and that it is on this account Catullus, in his Atys, always uses <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a> epithets and relatives in speaking of them. Diodorus Siculus remarks, that Corybas, son of Jason and Cybele, passing into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> with his uncle Dardanus, there instituted the worship of the mother of the gods, and gave his own name to the priests. Strabo relates it as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of some, that the Corybantes were children of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Calliope, and the same with the Cabiri. Others say the word had its origin from this, that the Corybantes always walked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> may be allowed) or tossing the head, ἀγκυρωτῶς βασιλεύειν.

CORYBANTICA

Pages 316-316

a festival held in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the Corybantes, who educated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> when he was concealed in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> from his father <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, who would have devoured him.

CORYCEUM

Pages 316-316

in antiquity, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the gymnasium where people unrefted. It was otherwise called apodyterion.

CORYCOMACHIA

Pages 316-316

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, was a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> in which they pushed forwards a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, suspended from the ceiling, and at its return either caught it with their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> suffered it to meet their body. Oribasius informs us it was recommended for extenuating too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> bodies.

CORYDALES

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> in the Fragmenta Methodi Naturalis of Linnaeus, containing the following genera, viz. epimedium, hypocoum, leontice, melanthus, pingulcula, and utricularia.

CORYLUS

Pages 316-316

the Hazle: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the moroccia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 50th order, Amentaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORYMBIFERAE

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the name of an order <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> adopted by Linnaeus after Ray and Vaillant, in the former editions of his Fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Method. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> in the later editions is changed for Diacoidae, another name borrowed from Ray's Method, but used in a somewhat different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>.

CORYMBIUM

Pages 316-316

in antiquity, an ornament of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> worn by the women. Its form was that of a corymbus. CORYMB: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The calyx is diphyllous, uniflorous, and prismatical; the corolla monopetalous and regular; there is one woolly seed below each floret.

CORYMBUS

Pages 316-316

properly signifies a cluster of ivy berries. Among botanists, it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of flowering in which the lesser <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> partial flower stalks are produced along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stalk on both sides; and though of unequal lengths, rise to the same height, so as to form a flat and even surface at the top. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORYNOCARPUS

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clas. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORYPHA

Pages 316-316

Mountain Palm, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Umbrella Tree: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the order of Palmae, belonging to the monocota clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORYPHENA

Pages 316-316

a genus of fishes belonging to the order of thoracici. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CORYPHÆUS, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tragedy, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> leader of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> that composed the chorus: (see Chorus).—The word is formed from the Greek κορυφή, "tip of the head." The coryphaeus spoke for all the rest, whenever the chorus took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a person of the drama, during the course of the acts. Hence coryphaeus had passed into a general name for the chief or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of any company, corporation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, &c. Thus Eustatus of Antioch is called the coryphaeus of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice; and Cicero calls Zeno the coryphaeus of the stoics.

CORYVREKAN

Pages 316-316

a dangerous whirlpool on the west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Scotland, between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Scarba and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> point of that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURA">Jura</a>. It is so named from a young Danish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who perished in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: its dreadful vortex extends above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in circuit. Many smaller whirlpools and rapid currents are found in this neighbourhood; dangerous to those who are strangers to the coast.

CORYZA

Pages 316-317

CORYZA, in Medicine, a catarrh of the nose. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CORZOLA

Pages 317-317
or CURSOLA, an island in the gulf of Venice, divided from Ragusa in Dalmatia by a narrow strait. E. Long. 18°. N. Lat. 42°. 35'.

COS

Pages 317-317
or Coos, in Ancient Geography, a noble island on the coast of Caria, in the Hither Asia, 15 miles to the west of Halicarnassus, 100 in compass, called Meropis; and hence Thucydides joins both names together, Cos Meropis; it had a cognominal town Cor, but originally called Alypalaea, mentioned by Homer; with a port locked or walled round, (Scylax, Mela). The island was fruitful, and yielded a generous wine, (Strabo). It boasted of Hippocrates and Apelles; each at the head of his several profession. It was the country of Philetas, an excellent elegiac poet, who flourished in the time of Philip and Alexander: the preceptor of Ptolemy Philadelphus: so thin and light that he was obliged to wear lead to prevent being blown away by a puff of wind (Aelian, Athenaeus); much commended by Propertius. The vases Coe, made of silk, were famous for their fineness and colour, (Horace, Propertius, Tibullus). In the suburbs of Cos stood the temple of Aesculapius, a noble structure, and extremely rich. Cos, the Whetstone, in href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History, a genus of vitreous stones, consisting of fragments of an indeterminate figure, sub-opaque, and granulated. Of this genus there are several species, some consisting of rougher, and others of smoother, or even of altogether impalpable particles; and used not only for whetstones, but also for mill-stones, and other like purposes. Cos turcica, Turkey-stone, a species of stones of the garnet kind, belonging to the siliceous class. It is of a dull white, and often of an unequal colour; some parts appearing more compact than others. Its specific gravity is 2.598: it strikes fire with steel, and effervesces with acids. Mr Kirwan found that 100 parts of it contain 25 of carbonate of lime, and no iron. Cronstedt is of opinion that there are probably two sorts of stones known by this name, as that described by Wallerius neither gives fire with steel nor effervesces with acids. It is used as a whetstone; and those of the finest grain are the best bones for the most delicate cutting tools, and even for razors, lancets, &c.

COSCINOMANCY

Pages 317-317

the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a> by means of a sieve. The word comes from κοσκίνιον, κρίνων, "a sieve," and παράδειξις, divination. The sieve being suspended, after rehearing a formula of words, it is taken between two fingers only; and the names of the parties suspected repeated: he at whose name the sieve turns, trembles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shakes, is reputed guilty of the evil in question. This must be a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> practice: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>, in his third Idyllion, mentions a woman very skilful in it. It was sometimes also practised by suspending the sieve by a thread, or fixing it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of sheers, giving it room to turn, and naming, as before, the parties suspected; in which last manner coscinomancy is still practised in some parts of England. It appears from Theocritus, that it was not only used to find out persons unknown, but also to discover the secrets of those that were known.

COSENAGE

Pages 317-317

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ that lies where the trefoil, that is, the tritavus, the father of the befall, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> grandfather, being seized in fee at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of certain lands or tenements, dies; a stranger enters and abates; then shall his heir have this writ of cozenage; the form of which see in Fitz. Nat. Br. fol. 221.

COSENING

Pages 317-317

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, an offence whereby any thing is done deceitfully, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> out of contracts, which cannot be fitly termed by any especial name. In the civil law it is called flellionatus. See Stellionate.

COSENZA

Pages 317-317

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16°. 35'. N. Lat. 39°. 15'. It is an archbishop's see.

COSHERING

Pages 317-317

in the feudal customs, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the lords to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> and feast themselves and their followers at their tenants houses. The word coshering may perhaps be derived from the old English word coße, a cot <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cottage.

COSMETIC

Pages 317-317

in Physic, any medicine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> which renders the skin soft and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, or helps to beautify and improve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>; as lip-salves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> creams, cerule, &c.

COSMICAL

Pages 317-317

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, expressing one of the poetical risings of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>: thus a star is said to rise comically when it rises with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with that point of the ecliptic in which the sun is at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and the comical setting is when a star sets in the west at the same time that the sun rises in the east.

COSMOGONY

Pages 317-317

in Physics, signifies the science of the formation of the universe. It is formed of νεφελος, the world, and γεγονει, I am born. In our conjectures about the formation of the world there are two principles which we ought never to lose sight of. 1. That of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>; for certainly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> could not give itself existence, it must have received it. 2. That of a Supreme Intelligence directing this creation, and the arrangement of the parts of matter, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which this world was formed. See Creation and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">Geology</a>.

COSMOGRAPHY

Pages 317-317

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the world; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the art which teaches the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, disposition, and relation of all the parts of the world, with the manner of representing them on a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>. The word comes from νεφελος, world, and γεγονει, I describe. Cosmography consists chiefly of two parts: <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, which shows the structure of the heavens, and the disposition of the stars; and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, which shows those of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>.

COSMOLABE

Pages 317-317

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, serving to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> distances both in the heavens and on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The Cosmolabe is in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> measure the same with the astrolabe. It is also called pantacism, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the universal instrument, by L. Morgard, in a treatise written expressly upon it, printed in 1612.

COSMOLOGY

Pages 317-318

the science of the world in general. This Wolfius calls general, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> transcendental cosmology, and has has written a treatise on the subject, wherein he endeavours to explain how the world arises from simple substances; and treats of the general principles, of the modifications of material things, of the elements of bodies, of the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, of the perfection of the world, and of the order and course of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>.

COSMOPOLITE

Pages 318-318
or Cosmopolitan, a term sometimes used to signify a person who has no fixed living or place of abode, or a man who is a stranger nowhere. The word comes from the Greek κόσμος, world, and πόλις, city.—One of the ancient philosophers being interrogated what countryman he was? answered, he was a cosmopolite, i.e. an inhabitant or citizen of the world.

COSSACKS

Pages 318-319

a name given to the people inhabiting the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Dnieper and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> and borders of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>. The word implies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> troops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. These people are divided into European and Asiatic Cossacks. The first consist of the Zaporog, who dwell below the cataract of the Dnieper, some on the side next to Russia, and others on the opposite side of that river; the Lower and Upper Cossacks; the Bielgorod Cossacks; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Don Cossacks. The Asiatic Cossacks are composed of the rest of the Don Cossacks, the Grebin Cossacks, the Yaik Cossacks, and the Western Calmucks, who retiring from those that inhabited the south borders of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> under Yauki Can, settled upon the Wolga, and are dependent upon Russia. The Cossacks were known by that name ever since the 948th year of Christ. They dwelt upon Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> now called Kabardy; and were reduced under the Russian dominion by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Miloslav in the year 1621. Many Russians, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>, and others, who could not live at home, have, at different times been admitted among the Cossacks: but the latter, attracted from these fugitives, must have been an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and well governed <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Towards the beginning of the 16th century, the Zaporog Cossacks fixed their habitations on the spacious plains that extend along the banks of the Dnieper. They had undergone considerable hardships from the incursions of the Tartars, for which they afterwards found means to avenge themselves in an ample manner. The Poles being sensible how serviceable the Cossacks might be in defending them from the ravages of the Tartars, and even of the Russians, proposed to them terms of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>. In 1562, they solemnly took them under their protection, and engaged to pay them an annual subsidy; in return for which the Cossacks were to keep on foot a sufficient body of troops for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the Polish dominions. With a view to bind them still more strongly by ties of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, the Poles gave them the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> between the rivers Dnieper and Neister, and the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. The Cossacks applied themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> industry to the cultivation of this fertile spot; so that in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was interspersed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and handsome villages. Besides, they continually harassed the Turks, and did them great damage by their incursions; and, in order to prevent the latter from pursuing them, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> making <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPRISALS">reprisals</a>, they posted themselves of several small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Dnieper, where they kept their magazines, &c. The hetman or general of the Cossacks was not in the least subordinate to the field marshal of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; but acted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with him as an ally, and not as a subject of that republic. But this alliance, though of such manifest advantage to both parties, was not of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. The Poles, seeing the vast improvements made by the Cossacks in the country they had given up to them, became envious of them, and actually made an attempt to bring them into subjection, as we have seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Poland. In 1648 the Cossacks gained great advantages over them, and next year came to an accommodation, in which they not only preserved their old immunities, but obtained additional privileges. The result of all was, that these Cossacks remained under the protection of Russia; and as their former country was entirely laid waste in the late wars, they settled in the Russian Ukraine, upon receiving formal assurances from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Russia, that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> should be made in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and that no taxes whatever should be laid upon them. The Cossacks, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, were always to keep in readiness a good body of troops for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Russia: but in the year 1708 Mazeppa, their hetman or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, went over from the Russians to the Swedes; upon which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> I. resolved to prevent such revolts for the future. To this end, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Poltava, he sent a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> into the above-mentioned little islands in the Dnieper, whither the Cossacks had fled with their wives and children, and all their effects; and ordered them all to be put to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> without distinction, and the plunder to be divided among his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. He likewise sent a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men into their country, and caused several thousands of the Cossacks to be carried to the coasts of the Baltic, where they were put to all sorts of hard labour; by which means he in a manner extirpated the whole nation. What distinguishes the Zaporog Cossacks from all other people is, that they never suffer any women in their settlements, as the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a> are said not to have suffered any men among them. The women of these Cossacks live in other islands of the Dnieper. They never marry, nor have any family; all their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> children are enrolled as soldiers, and the females are left with their mothers. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> often has children by his sister, and the father by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. They know no laws but those which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> has introduced, founded on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> wants; though they have among them some priests of the Greek persuasion. They serve in the armies as irregulars; and woe to those who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The country of these Cossacks, who are an afflame of ancient Roxolans, Sarmatians, and Tartars, is called the Ocraine or Ukraine. It lies upon the borders of Russia and Poland, Little Tartary, and Turkey, and was anciently a part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>. By virtue of the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> settled between Russia and Poland, in 1693, the latter remains in possession of all that part of the Ukraine which is situated on the west side of the Dnieper, and is now but poorly cultivated. That on the east side, inhabited by the Cossacks, is in a much better condition, and extends about two hundred and sixty miles in length, and as many in breadth. It is one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> fertile plain, watered by a great number of fine rivers, diversified with pleasant woods, and yields such plenty of all sorts of grain, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> Cossacks. honey and wax, as to supply a great part of the Russian empire with those commodities. Its pastures are exceeding rich, and its cattle very large; but the inhabitants are greatly plagued by locusts, which infest this fine country. The houses in the Ukraine are, like those of the Russians, mostly built with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. The Cossacks are tall and well made, generally hawked, and of a good mien. They are hardy, vigorous, brave, and extremely jealous of what is most valuable in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; fickle and wavering, but sociable, cheerful, and sprightly. They are a very powerful people, and their forces consist wholly of cavalry.—Their dialect is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of the Polish and Russian languages; but the latter is the most predominant. They were formerly Pagans or Mahometans; but upon their entering into the Polish service, they were baptized <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>; and now that they belong to Russia, they profess themselves members of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Each of their towns, with the district belonging to it, is governed by an officer called ottomann or attamann. The Don Cossacks, so called from their residence upon the banks of the river Don, greatly resemble those already described. In the year 1559, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a> Ivan Basilowicz was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Russia, they voluntarily put themselves under his protection, and are at this time on a pretty equal footing with the other Russian subjects. They have several towns and villages upon the banks of the Don; but are prevented from extending themselves farther up the country, by the scarcity of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and wood in many places. Their chief support is grazing and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, and occasionally robbing and plundering, for which they want neither capacity nor inclination. Every town is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> called tamann; and the tamanns, with their towns, are under the jurisdiction of two ottomans, who reside at Thierkatky. The troops of these Cossacks likewise consist entirely of cavalry. In this country all the towns and villages are fortified and encompassed with palisades, to defend them against the incursions of the Calmucks and Kuban Tartars, with whom they are continually at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The Cossacks, in general, are of great service to garrison towns by way of defence, or to pursue an enemy; but are not so good at regular attacks. The Sieth Cossacks, who are also called Haidamacks, have their particular hetman. They inhabit the Russian, Polish, and Turkish dominions, along the banks of the Dnieper. The Yaik Cossacks dwell on the south side of the river Yaik; and upon the success of the Russian arms in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Astrakhan, voluntarily submitted to them. In stature they greatly resemble the other Cossacks; though by their boorish manner of living, and intermarriages with the Tartars, they have not the shape and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> peculiar to the rest of their countrymen. Their natural dispositions and customs are, however, nearly the same. Husbandry, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, and feeding of cattle, are their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> employments; and, like the other tribes, they let slip no opportunity of making depredations on their neighbours. Their continual wars with the Kara-Kalpacs and the Kafatshaia-Horda oblige them to keep their towns and villages in a state of defence. They are indeed subject to Russian waiwodes, to whom they pay an annual tribute in corn, wax, honey, and cattle; but they have also their particular chiefs, who govern them according to their ancient customs. Though the generality of the Yaik Cossacks profess the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, yet a great many relics of Mahometanism and Paganism are still found among them. Being naturally bold and hardy, they make excellent soldiers; and they are not so turbulent as the other Cossacks. They live entirely at peace with the Calmucks and their other neighbours, and even maintain a commercial intercourse with them.

COSSE DE GENISTE

Pages 319-319

an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> instituted in 1244, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> IX. at his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with Margaret of Provence. The motto on the collar of this order was, Exaltat humiles.

COSSET

Pages 319-319

among farmers, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLT">colt</a>, calf, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lamb, brought up by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>.

COSTA

Pages 319-319

CHRISTOPHER, a celebrated botanist of the 16th century, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, of a Portuguese father, and went into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, to perfect himself in the knowledge of simples, where he was taken prisoner, but found means to make his escape, and after several voyages, practised physic at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGOS">Burgos</a>. He wrote, 1. A Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> drugs and medicines. 2. His Voyages to the Indies. 3. A book in praise of Women; and other works.

COSTA-RICA

Pages 319-319

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> in New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and in the audience of Guatemala, bounded on the north-east by the Northern ocean, on the south-west by the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the north-west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NICARAGUA">Nicaragua</a>, and on the south east by Veragua. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is not very fertile, though there is plenty of cattle. Cartagena is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

COSTAL

Pages 319-319

an appellation given by anatomists to several parts belonging to the sides; thus we meet with costal muscles, vertebrae, &c.

COSTANZO

Pages 319-319

ANGELO DI, an Italian historian and poet, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Catulopa, was born in 1507, of a noble and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and died about 1591. He wrote, 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Naples, from 1250 to 1489; the best edition of which is that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUILA">Aquila</a>, in 1582, in folio, very scarce. 2. Italian poems, which are esteemed, and have had several editions.

COSTARD

Pages 319-320

GEORGE, a clergyman of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England, and author of several learned works, was born about the year 1710. He was educated at Wadham <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.A. in 1733. The first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> situation in which he was placed was that of curate of Islip in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. In 1747 he published, in 8vo, Some Observations tending to illustrate the Book of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>. In 1750 he published Two Dissertations: I. On the meaning of the word Kefia, mentioned in Job, chap. xlii. ver. 11. II. On the Signification of the word Hermes. In 1752 he published in 8vo, at Oxford, Dissertations II. Critico-Sacrae, quorum prima explicatur Ezek. xiii. 18. Altera vero, 2 Reg. x. 22. In 1755 he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Dr Birch, which is preserved in the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a> respecting the meaning of the phrase sphera barbarica. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after this he undertook to publish a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of Dr Hyde's Historia Religionis veterum Perforum, corumque Magorum; and which was accordingly printed under his inspection and with his corrections, at the Clarendon press. rendon Press at Oxford, in 4to. In 1760, Mr Coifard's extensive learning having now recommended him to the notice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> Northington, he obtained, by the favour of that nobleman, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1764, the vicarage of Twickenham in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, in which situation he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. In 1767 he published, in one volume quarto, The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, with its application to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, History, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>; occasionally exemplified by the Globes. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was chiefly intended for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of students, and contains a full and distinct view of the several improvements made in geography and astronomy. Mr Coifard has shown, "by a gradual deduction, at what time, and by whom, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> discoveries have been made in geography and astronomy; how each discovery has paved the way to what followed; and by what easy steps, through the revolution of so many ages, these very useful sciences have advanced towards their present state of perfection. In 1778 he published, in 8vo, A Letter to Nathaniel Bristley Haldred, Esq., containing some Remarks on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">Preface</a> to the Code of Gentoo Laws. This appears to have been the last of his publications. It contains some criticisms which were intended to invalidate the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which Mr Haldred had conceived concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity of the Gentoo laws; and some arguments against a notion which had been adopted by several writers, drawn from the observation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> phenomena, that the world is far more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> than it is represented to be by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> chronology. Mr Coifard died on the 10th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1782. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of uncommon learning, and eminently skilled in Grecian and oriental literature. His private character was amiable, and he was much respected in the neighbourhood in which he lived for his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and benevolence. Besides the works already mentioned, he wrote some others; and was also the author of learned papers, inserted in the Philosophical Transactions, on astronomical and chronological subjects.

a supernatural detention of the feces, with an unusual dryness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> thereof, and thence a suppression of their evacuation. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

COSTMARY

Pages 320-320

the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of tanzy. See Tanacetum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

COSTS

Pages 320-320

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, imply the expenses of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> recovered by the plaintiff, together with damages. Costs were not allowed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, the appearance of the vanquished party being his only <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>; but they are given by statute*. Costs are allowed in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> for failing to make answer to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> exhibited, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> making an insufficient answer; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a first answer be certified by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to be insufficient, the defendant is to pay 40s.; 3l. for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> insufficient answer; 4l. for a third, &c. But if the answer be reported good, the plaintiff shall pay the defendant 40s. costs.

COSTUME

Pages 320-320

a rule <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> precept in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> is enjoined to make every person and thing sustain its proper character, and not only observe the story, but the circumstances, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and take care that the habits, arms, manners, proportion, and the like, exactly correspond.

COTBUS

Pages 320-320

a town of Germany in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSATIA">Lusatia</a>. It is a strong important <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and has been subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> ever since the year 1645. It is seated on the river Spree, 60 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and 55 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a>. Here are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, who have introduced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>; and this place is noted for excellent beer, pitch, and the cultivation of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° 29'. N. Lat. 51° 40'.

COTE

Pages 320-320

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in coursing, to express the advantage one greyhound has over another when he runs by the side of it, and putting before it, gives the hare a turn. See Coursing. Cotz-Gore, a kind of refuse <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, so clung <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> clotted together that it cannot be pulled asunder. By 13 Rich. II. stat. i. c. 9. it is provided, that neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENIZEN">denizen</a> or foreigner make any other refuse of wool, but cotz-gore and villein. So the printed statute has it; but in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> roll of that year it is cotz-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and villein. Cot, or cote, signifies as much as cottage in many places, and was so used by the Saxons according to Verstegan.

COTELERIUS

Pages 320-320

John Baptist, fellow of the Sorbonne, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s Greek professor, was born at Nîmes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a> in 1627. He made a collection of the fathers who lived in the apostolic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, which he published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in two volumes folio in 1672; all reviewed and corrected from several MSS. with a Latin translation and notes. He also published Monumenta Ecclesia Graecæ, in 3 vols; being a collection of Greek tracts out of the king's and M. Colbert's <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, and which had never been published before; to these he added a Latin translation and notes. He intended a farther prosecution of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; but his intense studies broke his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and deprived him of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in 1686.
