Besides his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> skill in languages and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> antiquities, Cotelerius was remarkable for his probity and candour.

COTERELLUS

Pages 320-320

Cotarius and Cotellus, according to Spelman and Du Fresne, are servile tenants; but in Doomsday and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> MSS. there appears a distinction, as well in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> as in their name; for the cotarius hath a free socage tenure, and paid a slated firm <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rent in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, with some occasional customary services; whereas the cotellus seems to have held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> villainage, and his person, illue, and goods, were disposable at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>.

COTERIE

Pages 320-321

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> adopted from the French trading associations <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> partnerships, where each person advances his quota of stock, and receives his proportion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>; and which retains its original meaning when applied to little assemblies or companies associated for mirth and good humour, where each one furnishes his quota. quota of pleasantry. Here they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> new words not understood elsewhere, but which it becomes fashionable for others to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; and they are thought ridiculous who are ignorant of them. It has been sometimes used to signify a club of ladies.

COTES

Pages 321-321

ROGER, an excellent mathematician of the 18th century. He early discovered an inclination to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; and at 17 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was admitted a pensioner of Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. In 1706, he was appointed professor of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> in the professorship founded by Dr Plume archdeacon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, being chosen the first in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> merit and learning. In the year 1713, at the request of Dr Richard Bentley, he published at Cambridge, in 4to, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton's Principia, with all the improvements which the author had annexed thereto; to which he prefixed an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>. He prepared several useful books for the public; and wrote A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of the great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOR">Meteor</a> which appeared on the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1716, published in the Philosophical Transactions. He lived but a little while to carry on the discourses for which he was eminently qualified; dying in the prime of his age in 1716, to the great regret of all the lovers of the sciences.

COTESWOLD

Pages 321-321

several sheep-cotes, and sheep feeding on hills. It come from the Saxon cote, i.e. cota, "a cottage," and wold, "a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where there is no wood."

COTHURNUS

Pages 321-321

BUSKIN, a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> patten raised on soles of cork, wore by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> in tragedy to make them appear taller and more like the heroes they represented; most of whom were supposed to be giants. It covered the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the leg, and was tied beneath the knee. Aeschylus is said to have invented the cothurnus. See BUSKIN.

COTICE

Pages 321-321
or Corise', in Heraldry, is the fourth part of the bend; which with us is seldom or ever borne but in couples, with a bend between them; whence probably the name; from the French cote, "side;" they being borne, as it were, a-side of the bend.—A bend thus bordered is said to be cotised, cotice. He bears fable on a bend cotised argent three cinquefoils.

COTILLON

Pages 321-321

the name of a well-known brisk dance, in which eight persons are employed. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is French, and signifies an under-petticoat.

COTRONE

Pages 321-321

a town in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> standing on the site of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Croton, though not occupying the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of ground: (See CROTON). It is fortified with single walls, and a castle erected by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. Its private buildings are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and forlorn, the streets dismal and narrow. Cheese and corn are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> commodities. For the flowage of corn, there are ranges of granaries in the suburbs; and the annual export is about 20,000 tomoti. The cheese is tolerably good; but has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of that hot acrid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all cheese made with goats <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. The wine is not unpleasant, and appears susceptible of improvement by better management in the making and keeping.

COTTAGE

Pages 321-321

COTTAGIUM, is properly a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for habitation without lands belonging to it; flat. 4 Edw I. But by a later statute 3 Eliz. c. 7, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may build a cottage unless he lay four acres of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> thereto; except it be in market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cities, or within a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, or for the habitation of labourers in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, sailors, foresters, shepherds, &c., and cottages erected by order of justices of peace for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> impotent people are excepted out of the statute. The four acres of land to make it a cottage within the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> are to be freehold, and land of inheritance; and four acres holden by copy, or for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> or lives, or for any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be sufficient to make a lawful cottage.

COTTON

Pages 324-324
Charles, a burlesque poet, was descended of a good family, and lived in the reign of Charles II. and James II. His most celebrated piece is Scarronides or Travellie of the first and fourth books of the Aeneid. But though, from the title, one would be apt to imagine it an imitation of Scarron's famous Travellie of the same author, yet upon examination, it would be found greatly to excel not only that, but every other attempt of the same kind that hath been hitherto made in any language. He has also translated several of Lucian's dialogues, in the same manner, under the title of the Scoffer Scoff'd;—and written another poem of a more serious kind, entitled the Wonders of the Peak. The exact period of either Mr Cotton's birth or his death, is nowhere recorded; but it is probable the latter happened about the time of the revolution. Neither is it better known what his circumstances were with respect to fortune; they appear, however, to have been easy, if one may judge from the turn of his writings, which is such as seems scarcely possible for any one to indulge whose mind was not perfectly at ease. Yet there is one anecdote told of him, which seems to show that his vein of humour could not restrain itself on any consideration, viz. that in consequence of a single couplet in his Virgil Travellie, wherein he has made mention of a peculiar kind of ruff worn by a grandmother of his who lived in the Peak, he lost an estate of 400l. per annum; the old lady, whose humour and testy disposition he could by no means have been a stranger to, being never able to forgive the liberty he had taken with her; and having her fortune wholly at her disposal, although she had before made him her sole heir, altered her will, and gave it away to an absolute stranger.

COTTUS

Pages 324-324
or Bull-head, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of thoracici. See Ichthyology Index.

COTULA

Pages 324-324

May-weed: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cotula, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cotyla, a liquid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. Fannius says, the cotyla was the same thing with the hemina, which was half a sextarius. At cotylas, quas si placeat, dixisse licet Heminas recipit geminas sextarias unum. Chorier observes, that the cotyla was used as a dry measure as well as a liquid one; from the authority of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>, who in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> mentions two cotylae of wine, and in another two cotylae of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. COTURNIX. See Tetrao, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index.

COTUS

Pages 320-320

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monandra clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the eighth order, Scitamineae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

COTYLEDON

Pages 324-324

Navel-wort: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandra class; and ranking under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order, Succulentae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

COTYLEDONES

Pages 324-324

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the perishable porous side lobes of the seed, which involve, and for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> furnish nourishment to, the embryo plant. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

COTYTTO

Pages 324-324

the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of all debauchery. Her festivals, called Cotytta, were celebrated by the Athenians, Corinthians, Thracians, &c. during the night. Her priests were called baptos, and nothing but debauchery and wantonness prevailed at the celebration. A festival of the same name was observed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, where the votaries of the goddess carried about boughs hung with cakes and fruit, which it was lawful for any person to pluck off. It was a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> to reveal whatever was seen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> done at these sacred festivals. It cost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPOLIS">Eupolis</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for an unseemly reflection upon them. The goddess Cotytto is supposed to be the same as Proserpine.

COUCH

Pages 324-324

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, denotes a lay, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, whether in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, wherewith the painter covers his canvas, wall, wainscot, or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to be painted. The word is also used for a lay or impression on anything, to make it firm and consistent, or to screen it from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Paintings are covered with a couch of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>; a canvas to be painted must first have two couches of size, before the colours be laid; two or three couches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> are laid on wood, before the couch of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> be applied: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>-gilders lay a couch of water and whites of eggs on the leather, before they apply the gold or silver-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>. The gold-wire-drawers also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the word couch for the gold or silver leaf wherewith they cover the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> to be gilded or silvered, before they draw it through the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> that is to give it its proper thickness. The gilders use couch for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of gold or silver leaves applied on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> in gilding or silvering. Each couch of gold is but one leaf, or two at most, and each of silver three to gild: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the gilding be hatched, there are required from eight to twelve couches; and only three or four if it be without hatching. To silver there are required from four to ten couches, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Couch-grass. See Triticum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

COUCHANT

Pages 324-324

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is understood of a lion, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other beast, when lying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, but with his head raised; which distinguishes the posture of couchant from dormant, wherein he is supposed quite stretched out and asleep.

COUCHE

Pages 324-324

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, denotes any thing lying along: thus chevron-couche, is a chevron lying side-wise, with the two ends on each side of the shield, which should properly rest on the base.

COUCHER

Pages 324-324

is also used for the general book in which any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> corporation <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> their particular acts. Anno 3 and 4 Edw. VI. c. 10. COUGHING of a CATARACT, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>. See Surgery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

COUGH

Pages 326-326

in Medicine. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cough, in Farriery. See FARRIERY Index. Cough, called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HULK">hulk</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> to which young bullocks are subject. In this disorder the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>-pipe and its branches are loaded with small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. Farmers <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> the disease incurable; but fumigations with mercurials, as cinnabar, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with foetids, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, prove serviceable.

COUGHAGE

Pages 326-326
or STINKING BEANS; a kind of kidney-beans imported from the East Indies, where they are used as a cure for the dropsy. The down growing on the outside of the pod is so pointed as, like a nettle, to sting the flesh, though not with so painful a sensation. This, by a corruption of the word, is called cowitch. See DOLICHOS, BOTANY Index.

COULTER

Pages 326-326

in Husbandry, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, fixed in the beam of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, and serving to cut the edge of each furrow. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a>.

COUNCIL

Pages 326-327
or COUNSEL, in a general sense, an assembly of divers considerable persons to concert measures relative to the state. In Britain, the law, in order to assist the king in the discharge of his duties, the maintenance of his dignity, and the exertion of his prerogative, hath assigned him a diversity of councils to advise with. 1. The first of these is the high court of parliament. See PARLIAMENT. 2. The peers of the realm are by their birth hereditary counsellors of the crown; and may be called together by the king, to impart their advice in all matters of importance to the realm, either in time of parliament, or, which hath been their principal use, when there is no parliament in being. Accordingly, Bracton, speaking of the nobility of his time, says, they might properly be called "consoles a confundendum;" reges enim tales fibi afficiant ad confundendum." And in the law-books it is laid down, that the peers are created for two reasons: 1. Ad confundendum, 2. Ad defendendum, regem: for which reasons the law gives them certain great and high privileges; such as freedom from arrests, &c., even when no parliament is sitting; because the law intends, that they are always afflicting the king with their counsel for the commonwealth, or keeping the realm in safety by their prowess and valour. Instances of conventions of the peers, to advise the king, have been in former times very frequent; though now fallen into disuse, by reason of the more regular meetings of parliament. Sir Edward Coke gives us an extract of a record, 5 Henry IV., concerning an exchange of lands between the king and the earl of Northumberland, wherein the value of each was agreed to be settled by advice of parliament (if any should be called before the feast of St Lucia), or otherwise by advice of the grand council of peers, which the king promises to assemble before the said feast, in case no parliament shall be called. Many other instances of this this kind of meeting are to be found under our ancient kings: though the formal method of convoking them had been so long left off, that when King Charles I. in 1640 issued out writs under the great seal to call a council of all the peers of England, to meet and attend his majesty at York, previous to the meeting of the long parliament, the earl of Clarendon mentions it as a new invention, not before heard of: that is, as he explains himself, so old, that it had not been practised in some hundreds of years. But though there had not for long time before been an instance, nor has there been any fine, of assembling them in so solemn a manner, yet in cases of emergency, our princes have at several times thought proper to call for, and consult as many of the nobility as could easily be brought together: as was particularly the case with King James II. after the landing of the prince of Orange; and with the prince of Orange himself before he called the convention parliament which afterwards called him to the throne. Besides this general meeting, it is usually looked upon to be the right of each particular peer of the realm, to demand an audience of the king, and to lay before him with decency and respect such matters as he shall judge of importance to the public weal. And therefore, in the reign of Edward II., it was made an article of impeachment in parliament against the two Hugh Spencers, father and son, for which they were banished the kingdom, "that they by their evil counsels would not suffer the great men of the realm, the king's good counsellors, to speak with the king, or to come near him; but only in presence and hearing of said Hugh the father and Hugh the son, or one of them, and at their will, and according to such things as pleased them." 3. A third council belonging to the king, are, according to Sir Edward Coke, his judges of the courts of law, for law-matters. And this appears frequently in the English statutes, particularly Edward III. c. 5, and in other books of law. So that when the king's council is mentioned generally, it must be defined, particularized, and understood, secundum subjectam materiam; "according to the subject matter;" and if the subject be of a legal nature, then by the king's council is understood his council for matters of law; namely, his judges. Therefore, when by statute Richard II. c. 5, it was made a high offence to import into England any papal bulls, or other processes from Rome; and it was enacted, that the offenders should be attached by their bodies and brought before the king and his council to answer for such offence; here, by the expression of king's council, were understood the king's judges of his courts of justice, the subject matter being legal: this being the general way of interpreting the word council. 4. But the principal council belonging to the king is his privy council, which is generally by way of eminence, called the council. For an account of its constitution and powers, see the article Privy-Council. Aulic Council. See Aulic. Common Council, in the city of London, is a court wherein are made all bye-laws which bind the citizens. It consists, like the parliament, of two houses; an upper, composed of the lord-mayor and aldermen; and a lower, of a number of common-council men, chosen by the several wards, as representatives of the body of the citizens. Council of War, an assembly of the principal officers of an army or fleet, occasionally called by the general or admiral to concert measures for their conduct with regard to sieges, retreats, engagements, &c. Council, in church history, an assembly of prelates and doctors, met for the regulating matters relating to the doctrine or discipline of the church. National Council, is an assembly of the prelates of nation under their primate or patriarch. Oecumenical or General Council, is an assembly which represents the whole body of the universal church. The Romans reckon eighteen of them; Bullinger, in his treatise de conciliis, six; Dr Prideaux, seven; and Bishop Beveridge has increased the number to eight, which, he says, are all the general councils which have ever been held since the time of the first Christian emperor. They are as follows: 1. The council of Nice, held in the reign of Constantine the Great, on account of the heresy of Arius. 2. The council of Constantinople, called under the reign and by the command of Theodosius the Great, for much the same end that the former council was summoned. 3. The council of Ephesus, convened by Theodosius the younger at the suit of Nestorius. 4. The council of Chalcedon, held in the reign of Martinus, which approved of the Eutychian heresy. 5. The second council of Constantinople, assembled by the emperor Justinian, condemned the three chapters taken out of the book of Theodorus of Mopsuestia, having first decided that it was lawful to anathematize the dead. Some authors tell us, that they likewise condemned the several errors of Origen about the Trinity, the plurality of worlds, and pre-existence of souls. 6. The third council of Constantinople, held by the command of Constantius Pogonatus the emperor, in which they received the definitions of the five first general councils, and particularly that against Origen and Theodorus of Mopsuestia. 7. The second Nicene council. 8. The fourth council of Constantinople, assembled when Louis II. was emperor of the West. The regulations which they made are contained in twenty-seven canons, the heads of which are set down by M. du Pin, to whom the reader is referred.

COUNSEL

Pages 327-328

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies advice <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> instruction how to behave in any difficult <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Counsel, or Advocate, in English courts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, are of two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> or degrees; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRISTERS">Barristers</a>, and Serjeants. See these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>; also Advocate. From both these degrees some are usually selected to be his majesty's counsel, learned in the law; the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of whom are called his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a>, and solicitor-general. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s counsel, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of serjeant, was Sir Francis <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, who was made to honoris causa, without either patent or fee; so that the first of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> order (who are now the sworn servants of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, with a standing salary) seems to have been Sir Francis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>; afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> keeper of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> to King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. These king's counsel answer, in some degree, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> of the revenue, advocati fisci, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. For they must not be employed in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> against the crown without special license; in which restriction they agree COUNSEL with the advocates of the fisc; but, in the imperial law, the prohibition was carried still farther, and perhaps was more for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of the sovereign; for, excepting some peculiar caules, the fiscal advocates were not permitted to be at all concerned in private suits between subject and subject. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> has of late years prevailed of granting letters patent of precedence to such barristers as the crown thinks proper to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> with that mark of distinction: whereby they are entitled to such <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and preaudience as are assigned in their respective patents; sometimes next after the king's attorney-general, but usually next after his majesty's counsel next being. These, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s attorney and solicitor general, rank promiscuously with the king's counsel; and, together with them, fit within the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of their respective courts: but receive no salaries, and are not sworn; and therefore are at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to be retained in caules against the crown. And all other sergeants and barristers indiscriminately, (except in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas, where only sergeants are admitted,) may take upon them the protection and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of any suitors, whether plaintiff or defendant; who are therefore called their clients; like the dependents on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman orators. These indeed practised gratis, for honour merely, or at most for the sake of gaining influence; and so likewise it is established with us, that a counsel can maintain no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> for his fees; which are given, not as locatio vel conducio, but as quiddam bonorarium; not as a salary or hire, but as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> gratuity, which a counsellor cannot demand without doing wrong to his reputation; as is also laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with regard to advocates in the civil law, whose bonorarium was directed, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, not to exceed in any case 10,000 sesterces, or about 80l. of English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. And in order to encourage due freedom of speech in the lawful defence of their clients, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to check the unseemly licentiousness of prostitute and illiberal men (a few of whom may sometimes infatuate themselves even into the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>), it hath been holden that a counsel is not answerable for any matter by him spoken, relative to the cause in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and suggested in the client's instructions; although it should reflect upon the reputation of another, and even prove absolutely groundless; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he mentions an untruth of his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, or even upon instructions, if it be impertinent to the cause in hand, he is then liable to an action from the party injured. And counsel guilty of deceit and collusion are punishable by the statute Westm. I. 3 Edw. I. c. 28. with imprisonment for a year and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and perpetual silence in the courts: a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> still sometimes inflicted for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> misdemeanors in practice.

COUNSELLOR

Pages 328-328

in general, a person who advises another: thus we say, a counsellor at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a privy counsellor, &c. COUNSELLOR at Law, a person retained by a client to plead his cause in a public <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of judicature. See ADVOCATE, BARRISTER, COUNSEL, and SERJEANT. Privy-Counsellor. See Privy-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a>.

COUNT

Pages 328-331

(Comes), a nobleman who possesses a domain erected into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. See Viscount. English and Scottish counts we distinguish by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earls; foreign ones still retain their proper name. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a count is a medium between that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> and a baron.—According to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, most plenipotentiaries and ambassadors assume the title of counts, though they have no county; as the count d'Avaux, &c. Anciently, all generals, counsellors, judges, and secretaries of cities under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, were called counts; the distinguishing character of a duke and count being this, that the latter had but one town under him, but the former had several. A count has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to bear on his arms a coronet, adorned with three precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and furmounted with three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pearls, whereof those in the middle and extremities of the coronet advance above the rest. Counts were originally lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s retinue, and had their name comites, à comitando, or à commeando: hence those who were always in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, or at the emperor's side, were called counts palatine, or comites à latere. See PALATINE. In the times of the commonwealth, comites among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> was a general name for all those who accompanied the proconsuls and proprietors into the provinces, there to serve the commonwealth; as the tribunes, praefects, scribes, &c. Under the emperors, comites were the officers of the palace. The origin of what we now call counts seems owing to Augustus, who took several senators to be his comiter, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DION">Dion</a> observes, i.e. to accompany him in his voyages and travels, and to assist him in the hearing of caules; which were thus judged with the same authority as in full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. Gallienus seems to have abolished this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, by forbidding the senators being found in the armies; and none of his successors re-established it. These counsellors of the emperor were really counts, comites, i.e. companions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; and they sometimes took the title thereof, but always with the addition of the emperor's name whom they accompanied: so that it was rather a mark of their office than a title of dignity.—Constantine was the first who converted it into a dignity; and under him it was that the name was first given absolutely. The name once established, was in a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> indifferently conferred, not only on those who followed the court, and accompanied the emperor, but also on most kinds of officers; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> whereof is given us by Du Cange. Eusebius tells us, that Constantine divided the counts into three classes; the first bore the title of illustres; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> that of clarissimi, and afterwards spectabiles; the third were called perfectissimi. Of the two first classes was the senate composed: those of the third had no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the senate, but enjoyed several other of the privileges of senators. There were counts who served on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, others at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; some in a civil, some in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, and some in a legal capacity: as comes avarii, comes sacrarum largitionum, comes sacri confessorii, comes curiae, comes capelle, comes archiatriorum, comes commerciorum, comes vexillationis, comes horrorum, comes opifiorum or annonae, comes domesticonum, comes equorum regiorum or comes stabuli, comes domorum, comes excubitorum, comes notariorum, comes legum or professor in jure, comes liminum or marcarum, comes portus Romae, comes patrimonii, &c. The Franks, Germans, &c., passing into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> and Germany, did not abolish the form of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; and as the governors of cities and provinces were called *counts*, *comites*, and *dukes*, *duces*, they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be called so. They commanded in time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and in time of peace they administered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Thus, in the time of Charlemagne, counts were the ordinary judges and governors of the cities. These counts of cities were beneath the dukes and counts who presided over provinces; the first being constituted in the particular cities under the jurisdiction of the latter. The counts of provinces were in nothing inferior to dukes, who themselves were only governors of provinces. Under the last of the second <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of French kings, they got their dignity rendered <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, and even usurped the sovereignty when Hugh Capet came to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; his authority was not sufficient to oppose their encroachments; and hence it is they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> the privilege of wearing coronets in their arms; they assumed it then, as enjoying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of sovereigns in their particular districts or counties. But, by degrees, most of the counties became reunited to the crown. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of count is now become very different from what it was anciently; being now no more than a title, which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> grants upon erecting a territory into a county, with a reserve of jurisdiction and sovereignty to himself. At first there was no clause in the patent of erection, intimating the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> of the county to the crown in default of heirs <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX. to prevent their being too numerous, ordained that duchies and counties, in default of heirs male, should return to the crown. The point of precedence between counts and marquises was formerly much controverted; the reason was, that there were counts who were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> of France, but no marquises; but the point was given up, and marquises took place; though anciently, when counts were governors of provinces, they were on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> even with dukes. William the Conqueror, as is observed by Camden, gave the dignity of counts in fee to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>; annexing it to this or that county or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and allotting for their maintenance a certain proportion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, arising from the prince's profits in the pleadings and forfeitures of the provinces. To this purpose he quotes an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> record, thus: Hen. II. Rex Anglie hic verbiis comitem creavit; scitis nos fecisse Hugonem Bigot comitem de Norf, &c. de tercio denario de <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a> et <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, sicut aliquis comes Angliae, &c. The Germans call a count, *graf*, or *graff*; which, according to a modern critic, properly signifies judge; and is derived from *gravio* or *grafio*, of *gravio*, I write. They have several kinds of these counts or grafts; as landgraves, marchgraves, burg-graves, and palgrave, or counts palatine. These last are of two kinds; the former are of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of princes, and have the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a>; the others have only the title of *count palatine* without the investiture of any palatinate. Some assert, that by publicly professing the imperial laws for twenty years, the person acquires the dignity of a count palatinate; and there are instances of professors in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> who have assumed the title accordingly; but there are others who question this right. **Count**, in Law, denotes the original <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> in a real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; as the declaration is in a personal one: the libellus of the civilians answers to both. Yet, count and declaration are sometimes confounded, and used for each other; as, count in debt, count in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>, &c. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">Counter</a>-Wheel**, in the striking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a clock, a wheel which moves round once in 12 or 24 hours. It is sometimes called the locking-wheel. See Clock-Making. **Counter**, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> which enters into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> words of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and generally implies opposition; but when applied to deeds, means an exact copy kept of the contrary party, and sometimes signed by both parties. **Counter-Changed**, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the intermixture or opposition of any metal with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. **Counter-Flory**, in Heraldry, is said of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>-de-luce are opposite to others. See Heraldry. **Counter-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">Drawing</a>**, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, is the copying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, or painting, by means of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>-cloth, an oiled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, or other transparent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, where the strokes appearing through are followed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, with or without colour. Sometimes it is done on glass, and with frames or nets divided into squares with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> or with thread, and also by means of instruments invented for the purpose, as the parallelogram. **Counter-Ermine**, in Heraldry, is the contrary of ermine, being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> field with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spots. **Counterfeits**, in Law, are persons that obtain any money or goods by counterfeit letters or false tokens, who being convicted before justices of assize or of the peace, &c., are to suffer such <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> as shall be thought fit to be inflicted under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, as imprisonment, pillory, &c. **Counter-Foil**, or **Counter-Stock**, in the exchequer, that part of a tally which is kept by an officer of the court. **Counter-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">Guard</a>**, in Fortification, is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> raised before the point of bastion, consisting of two long faces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the faces of the bastion, making a salient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>; they are sometimes of other shapes, or otherwise situated. **Counter-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>**, or **Counter-jour**, a light opposite to any thing, which makes it appear to disadvantage. A single counter-light is sufficient to take away all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of a fine painting. **Counter-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>**, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, a change of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> or wings of a battalion, by which means those that were in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> come to be in the rear. It also signifies returning, or marching back again. **Counter-Mine**, in War, a well and gallery drove and sunk till it meet the enemy's mine, to prevent its effect. **Counter-Paled**, in Heraldry, is when the escutcheon is divided into twelve pales paited per fesse, the two colours being counter-changed; so that the upper are of one colour and the lower of another. **Counter-Part**, in Music, denotes one part to be applied to another. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a> is said to be a counter-part to the treble. **Counter-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSANT">Passant</a>**, in Heraldry, is when two lions are in a coat of arms, and the one seems to go quite the contrary way from the other. Counter-Point, in Music, a term derived from the Latin preposition contra and the verb pingere; because the musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> by which the notes in each part are signified are placed in such a manner, each with respect to each, as to show how the parts answer one another. See Composition. Counter-Pointed (<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRE">Contre</a>-pointe), in Heraldry, is when two chevrons in one escutcheon meet in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, the one rising as usual from the base, and the other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> falling from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; so that they are counter to one another in the points. They may also be counter-pointed when they are founded upon the sides of the shield, and the points meet that way, called counter-pointed in fesse. Counterpoise, in the manege, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the action and seat of a horseman; so that in all the motions made by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, he does not incline his body more to one side than to the other, but continues in the middle of the saddle, being equally on his stirrups, in order to give the horse the proper and fashionable aids. Counter-potent (contre potence), in Heraldry, is reckoned a fur as well as vair and ermine; but composed of such pieces as represent the tops of crutches, called in French potences, and in old English potents. Counter-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, in rolling-press <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, a print taken off from another fresh printed; which by being passed through the press, gives the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the former, but inverted. To counter-prove, is also to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a design in black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> chalk, through the press, after having moistened with a sponge both that and the paper on which the counter-proof is to be taken. Counter-quartered (contre-ecartelé), in Heraldry, denotes the escutcheon, after being quartered, to have each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> again divided into two. Counter-Saliant, is when two beasts are borne in a coat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a> from each other directly the contrary way. Counter-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCARP">Scarp</a>, in Fortification, is properly the exterior talus or slope of the ditch; but it is often taken for the covered way and the glacis. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we say, the enemy have lodged themselves in the counter-scarp. Angle of the counter-scarp, is that made by two sides of the counter-scarp, meeting before the middle of the curtain. Counter-Signing, the signing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of a superior in quality of secretary. Thus charters are signed by the king, and counter-signed by a secretary of state, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>. Counter-Time, in the manege, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> or resistance of a horse that interrupts his cadence, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of his manege, occasioned either by a bad horseman or by the malice of a horse. Counter, is also the name of a counting-board in a shop, and of a piece of metal with a stamp on it, used in playing at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>. Counter of a Horse, that part of a horse's forehand which lies between the shoulders and under the neck. Counters in a ship are two. 1. The hollow arching from the gallery to the lower part of the straight piece of the stern, is called the upper-counter. 2. The lower counter is between the transom and the lower part of the gallery. Counter, is also the name of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">Poultry</a> and Woodstreet. Countors, Countours, or Counters, has been used for sergeants at law, retained to defend a cause, or to speak for their client in any course of law. It is of these Chaucer speaks: — A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> had he been, and a countour, Was nowhere such a worthy vavasour. They were anciently called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> contours. Countries, among the miners, a term or appellation they give to their works under ground. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">Country</a>, among geographers, is used indifferently to denote either a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, province, or lesser district. But its most frequent use is in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to town. Country-Dance is of English origin, though now transplanted into almost all the countries and courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. There is no established rule for the composition of tunes to this dance, because there is in music no kind of time whatever which may not be measured by the motions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>; and there are few long tunes of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> within the last century, that have not been applied to country-dances. County, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, originally signified the territory of a count or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a>, but now it is used in the same sense with shire; the one word coming from the French, the other from the Saxon.—In this view, a county is a circuit or portion of the realm; into fifty-two of which, the whole land, England and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, is divided for its better government and the more easy administration of justice. For the execution of the laws in the several counties excepting <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, Westmorland, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, every Michaelmas term officers are appointed, under the denomination of sheriffs. Other officers of the several counties are, a lord-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, who has the command of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> of the county; custodes rotulorum, justices of peace, bailiffs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a>, and coroner. Of the fifty-two counties, there are three of special note, which are therefore termed counties palatine, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, and Durham. See Palatine. County Corporate, is a title given to several cities, or ancient boroughs, on which our monarchs have thought fit to bestow extraordinary privileges; annexing to them a particular territory, land, or jurisdiction; and making them counties of themselves, to be governed by their own sheriffs and magistrates. County Court, in English Law, a court incident to the jurisdiction of the sheriff. It is not a court of record, but may hold pleas of debt or damages under the value of 40s. Over some of which causes these inferior courts have, by the express words of the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, a jurisdiction totally exclusive of the king's superior courts. For in order to be entitled to sue an action of trespass for goods before the king's justiciaries, the plaintiff is directed to make affidavit that the cause of action does really and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONA">bona</a> fide amount to 40s, which affidavit is now unaccountably disused, except in the court of exchequer. The statute tute also 43 Eliz. c. 6. which gives the judges in many personal actions, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> affords less damages than 40s. a power to certify the same and abridge the plaintiff of his full costs, was also meant to prevent vexation by litigious plaintiffs; who, for purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> oppression, might be inclined to institute such suits in the superior courts for injuries of a trifling value. The county court may also hold <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> of many real actions, and of all personal actions to any amount, by virtue of a special writ called justiciæ; which is a writ empowering the sheriff for the sake of dispatch to do the same justice in this county-court, as might otherwise be had at Westminster. The freeholders of the county are the real judges in this court, and the sheriff is the ministerial officer. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> conflux of freeholders, which are supposed always to attend at the county court (which Spelman calls forum plebeiae justitiae et theatrum comitivae potestatis), is the reason why all acts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> at the end of every session were wont to be there published by the sheriff; why all outlaws of absconding offenders are there proclaimed; and why all popular elections which the freeholders are to make, as formerly of sheriffs and conservators of the peace, and still of coroners, verderors, and knights of the shire, must ever be made in pleno comitatu, or in full county-court. By the statute 2 Edw. VI. c. 25. no county-court shall be adjourned longer than for one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, consisting of 28 days. And this was also the ancient usage, as appears from the laws of King Edward the elder; propositus (that is the sheriff) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> quartam circiter septimanam frequentem populi concionem celebrato; cuique jus dictio; lietique singulas dirimito. In those times the county-court was a court of great dignity and splendour, the bishop and the earldorman (or earl), with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> men of the shire, fitting therein to administer justice both in lay and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> causes. But its dignity was much impaired, when the bishop was prohibited, and the earl neglected to attend it. And, in modern times, as proceedings are removable from hence into the king's superior courts, by writ of pace or recordare, in the same manner as from hundred-courts and courts-baron; and as the same writ of false judgment may be had, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a writ of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, this has occasioned the same dispute of bringing actions therein.

COUPAR

Pages 331-331
or Cupar of Fife, a town in Scotland, capital of the county of Fife, about 10 miles west of St Andrew's: W. Long. 2. 40. N. Lat. 56. 20. It is situated on the north bank of the Eden, nearly in the center of the county; it boasts of great antiquity; the thanes of Fife, from the earliest times of which any account has been transmitted to us, held here their courts of justice; and in the rolls of parliament, assembled in the beginning of the reign of King David II. may be seen the names of commissioners from the royal borough of Cupar. It is governed by a provost, 3 bailies, a dean of guild, and 21 councillors. The revenue of the town amounts to 430l. sterling per annum. Cupar has the appearance of a neat, clean, well built, thriving town. The streets are well paved, and upwards of one third of the town is newly built. The church is a neat new building, and the spire is much admired for its light and elegant appearance. Adjoining to the town-house, the gentlemen of the county lately built a room for county meetings, and other apartments. The prisons are on the opposite side of the town-house. In Cupar, and the neighbouring country, a considerable quantity of coarse linens are manufactured; about 500,000 yards are annually stamped, the aggregate value of which is nearly 30,000l. sterling. Population of the town is about 3140. The parish of Cupar is an irregular square of 5 miles, divided into two parts by the river Eden, the banks of which are covered with numerous farm houses, and ornamented with elegant and stately villas. Carflogie, the seat of Colonel Clephane, is an ancient mansion. Garlie bank, the property of James Wemyss, Esq. of Wintham, is celebrated for the treaty concluded on the 13th of June 1559, between the duke de Chatelherault, on the part of the queen-regent, and the earl of Argyll commanding the forces of the congregation. The population of the parish (including the town of Cupar) in 1793, amounted to 3702; in 1801, there were 4463 inhabitants in the same district.

COUPED

Pages 331-331

is also used to signify such croffes, bars, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a>, chevrons, &c. as do not touch the sides of the escutcheon, but are, as it were, cut off from them.

COUPEE

Pages 331-331

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, wherein one leg is a little bent, and suspended from the ground; and with the other a motion is made forwards.

COUPLE CLOSS

Pages 331-331

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a chevron, never borne but in pairs, except there be a chevron between them, saith Guillim, though Bloom gives an instance to the contrary.

COUPLET

Pages 331-332

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a>, ode, song, &c. wherein an equal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, of verses, is found in each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; which divisions, in odes, are called *prophes*.—Couplet, by an abuse of the word, is frequently made to signify a couple of verses.

COURAGE

Pages 332-332

in *Ethics*, is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the mind, derived either from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> principle, or both, that enables men to encounter difficulties and dangers. See **Fortitude**.

COURANT

Pages 332-332

a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with *current*, and properly signifies running. See *Current*. *Courant*, is also a term in music and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>; being used to express both the tune <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and the dance. Without regard to the first, *courant*, or *courant*, is a piece of music in triple <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>: the air of the courant is ordinarily noted in triples of minims; the parts to be repeated twice. It begins and ends when he who beats the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> falls his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; in contradistinction from the saraband, which ordinarily ends when the hand is raised. With regard to dancing, the courant was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> of all the dances practised in England; it consists, essentially, of a time, a step, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>, and a coupee; though it also admits of other motions. Formerly they leaped their steps; in which point the courant differed from the low dance and pavades. There are simple courants and figured courants, all danced by two persons.

COURAP

Pages 332-332

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name for a distemper very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a> and other parts of the East Indies. It is a sort of herpes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> itch on the arm pits, groins, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>; the itching is almost perpetual; and the scratching is followed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pain and a discharge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> stick so to the skin as not easily to be separated without tearing off the crust. Courap is a general name for any sort of itch; but this distemper is thus called by way of eminence. It is so contagious that few escape it. For the cure, gentle and repeated purging is used, and externally the sublimate in a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is a good topic.

COURAYER

Pages 332-332
Peter Francis**, a Roman Catholic clergyman, distinguished by great moderation, charity, and temper, concerning religious affairs, as well as by learning; was born at Vernon in Normandy, 1681. While canon regular and librarian of the abbey of St Genevieve at Paris, he applied to our archbishop Wake for the resolution of some doubts, concerning the episcopal succession in England, and the validity of our ordinations: he was encouraged to this by the friendly correspondence which had passed between the archbishop and M. du Pin of the Sorbonne. The archbishop sent him exact copies of the proper records; and on these he built his "Defence of English Ordinations," which was published in Holland, in 1727. This exposed him to a prosecution in his own country; he therefore took refuge in England; where he was well received, and presented the same year by the university of Oxford with a doctor's degree. As it is somewhat uncommon for a Roman Catholic clergyman to be admitted to degrees in divinity by Protestant universities, the curious may be gratified with a sight of the diploma, and the doctor's letter of thanks, in "The present State of the Republic of Letters, for June 1728." In 1736, he translated into French, and published, "Father Paul's History of the Council of Trent," in 2 vols folio, and dedicated it to Queen Caroline; who augmented to 200l. a pension of 100l. a-year, which he had obtained before from the court. The learned Jer. Markland, in a letter to his friend Bowyer, September 1756, says, "Mr Clarke has given me F. Courayer's translation of the History of the Council of Trent; with whole preface I am so greatly pleased, that if he be no more a Papist in other tenets than he is in those he mentions (which are many, and of the most distinguishing clats), I dare say there are very few considerate Protestants who are not as good Catholics as he is." His works are many, and all in French: he translated Sleidan's "History of the Reformation." He died in 1776, after two days illness, at the age of 95; and was buried in the cloister of Westminster-abbey. In his will, dated Feb. 3, 1774, he declares, that he "dies a member of the Catholic church, but without approving of many of the opinions and superstitions which have been introduced into the Roman church, and taught in their schools and seminaries; and which they have insisted on as articles of faith, though to him they appear to be not only not founded in truth, but also to be highly improbable." And his practice was conformable to this declaration; for at London he constantly went to mass, and at Ealing in the country, whither he often retired, as constantly attended the service of the parish church; declaring at all times, that he "had great satisfaction in the prayers of the church of England." **COURBARIL.** See **Hymenea**.

COURIER

Pages 332-332
or **Currier**, (from the French *courir*, "to run") a messenger sent post, or express, to carry dispatches. The ancients too, had their couriers. We meet with two kinds: 1. Those who ran on foot, called by the Greeks *hemerodromi*, q. d. "couriers of a day;" Pliny, Corn. Nepos, and Caesar, mention some of these who would run 20, 30, 36, and in the circus even 40 leagues per day. 2. Riding couriers (*curiores equitantes*), who changed horses as the modern couriers do. Xenophon attributes the first couriers to Cyrus. Herodotus says they were very ordinary among the Persians, and that there was nothing in the world more swift than these kind of messengers. "That prince (says Xenophon) examined how far a horse would go in a day; and built stables, at such distances from each other, where he lodged horses, and persons to take care of them; and at each place kept a person always ready to take the packet, mount a fresh horse, and forward it to the next stage: and thus quite through his empire." But it does not appear that either the Greeks or Romans had any regular fixed couriers till the time of Augustus: under that prince they travelled in cars; though it would appear that they afterwards went on horseback. Under the western empire they were called *viatores*; and under that of Constantinople, *curiores*: whence the modern name. See **Post**.

COURLAND

Pages 332-333

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> situated between E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 21° 26' and between N. Lat. 56° 30' and 57° 30'. It is bounded by the river Dwina, which divides it from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; by Lithuania, on the east; by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAMOGITIA">Samogitia</a>, on the south; and by the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the west; being 120 miles long and 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. This duchy duchy was formerly independent, and elected their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>; but it is now subject to Russia.

COURSE

Pages 333-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> contained between the nearest meridian and that point of the compass upon which a ship sails in any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Course, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> range of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the same height, throughout the whole length of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; and not interrupted by any aperture. It forms a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> to the intermediate space between the body of the building and the wings. Course of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLINTH">Plinth</a>, is the continuity of a plinth of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of a building; to mark the separation of the stories. Course is also used for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> ordinarily spent in learning the principles of a science, or the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> and questions therein. Thus, a student is said to have finished his course in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, &c. Course is also used for the elements of an art exhibited and explained, either in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> or by actual experiment. Hence our courses of philosophy, anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, &c. probably to called as going throughout or running the whole length or course of the art, &c.

COURSES

Pages 333-333

a name by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sails of a ship are distinguished, viz., the main-sail, the fore-sail, and the mizen: the mizen stay-sail and fore-sail are also sometimes comprehended in this denomination; as are the main stay-sails of all brigs and schooners. See SAIL.

COURSING

Pages 333-334

among sportsmen. There are three several sorts of coursing with greyhounds: 1. At the hare; 2. At the fox; and, 3. At the deer. For the deer, there are two sorts of courses; the one in the paddock, the other either in the forest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the purlieu. For the paddock course, there must be the greyhound and the terrier, and the mongrel greyhound, whose business it is to drive away the deer before the greyhounds are shipped; a brace or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASH">leash</a> are the usual <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> shipped at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, seldom at the utmost more than two brace. In coursing the deer in the forest or purlieu, there are two ways in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>: the one is coursing from wood to wood; and the other, upon the lawns <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the keeper's lodge. In the coursing from wood to wood, the way is to throw in some young hounds into the wood to bring out the deer; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any deer come out that is not weighty, or a deer or antler which is buck, fore, or forrel, then you are not to ship your greyhounds, which are held at the end of the wood, where the keepers, who can guess very well on these occasions, expect that the deer <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> come out. If a proper deer come out, and it is suspected that the brace or leash of greyhounds shipped after him will not be able to kill him, it is proper to waylay him with a couple of fresh greyhounds. The coursing upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> is the most agreeable of all other ways. When the keeper has notice of this, he will lodge a deer for the course; and then, by coming under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, the greyhounds may be brought near enough to be shipped for a fair course. The best method of coursing the hare, is to go out and find a hare sitting; which is easily done in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, by walking across the lands, either stubble, fallow, or corn grounds, and calling the eye up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>: for in summer they frequent those places for fear of the ticks, which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the woods at that season; and in autumn the rains falling from the trees offend them. The rest of the year there is more trouble required; as the bushes and thickets must be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> to rout them, and oftentimes they will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> so close, that they will not stir till the pole almost touches them: the sportsmen are always pleased with this, as it promises a good course. If a hare lies near any close or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a>, and with her head that way, it is always to be expected that she will take to that immediately on being put up; all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> are therefore to ride up and put themselves between her and the covert before she is put up, that she may take the other way, and run upon open ground. When a hare is put up, it is always proper to give her ground, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, as it is called; that is, to let her run 12 score yards, or thereabouts, before the greyhounds are shipped at her; otherwise she is killed too soon, the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sport is thrown away, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of observing the several turnings and windings that the creature will make to get away is all lost. A good sportsman had rather see a hare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> herself after a fair course, than see her murdered by the greyhounds as soon as she is up. In coursing the fox, no other art is required, than standing close, and in a clear wind, on the outside of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> where it is expected he will come out; and when he is come out, he must have head enough allowed him, otherwise he will return back to the covert. The slowest greyhound will be able to overtake him, after all the odds of distance necessary; and the only danger is the spoiling the dog by the fox, which too frequently happens. For this reason, no greyhound of any value should be run at this course; but the strong, hard, bitter dogs, that will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> anything. The laws of coursing established by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, and other sportsmen of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of England, are these: 1. He that is chosen fowlerer or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>-loose of the dogs, shall receive the greyhounds matched to run together into his leash as soon as he comes into the field; he is to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> next to the hare-finder, or him who is to start the hare, until he come to the form; and no horseman or footman is to go before or sideways, but all straight behind, for the space of about 40 yards. 2. A hare ought never to be coursed with more than a brace of greyhounds. 3. The hare-finder is to give the hare three whistles before he puts her up from her form or seat, to the end that the dogs may be prepared and attend her starting. 4. If there be not a particular danger of losing the hare, she should have about twelve score yards law. 5. The dog that gives the first turn, if after that there be neither cote, flip, nor wrench, wins the wager. 6. A go-by, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the hare, is counted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to two turns. 7. If neither dog turns the hare, he that leads to the last covert wins. 8. If any dog turns the hare, serves himself, and turns her again, it is as much as a cote, and a cote is esteemed as much as two turns. 9. If all the course be equal, he that bears the hare shall win; and if he be not borne, the course shall shall then be judged dead. 10. If a dog take a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in his course, and yet perform his part, he may challenge the advantage of a turn more than he gave. 11.
