If a dog turn the hare, serve himself, and give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> cotes, and yet in the end shall stand still in the field, the other dog, if he turns home to the covert, although he gives no other, shall be adjudged to win the wager. 12. If by misfortune a dog be rid over in the course, that course shall be adjudged void, and he that did the mischief is to make reparation to the owner. 13. If a dog gives the first and last turn, and there be no other advantage betwixt them, he that gives the odd turn wins. 14. A cote when a greyhound goes endways by the side of his fellow, and gives the hare a turn. 15. A cote serves for two turns, and two trippings or jerkings for a cote; and if the hare turns not quite about, the only wrenchbeth, in the sportman's phrase. 16. If there be no cotes given by either of the greyhounds, but one serves the other at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a>, then he that gives the most turns wins the wager. 17. Sometimes a hare does not turn, but wrenches; for she does not turn except the turns as it were round. In these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, two wrenches stand for one turn. 18. He that comes in first at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the hare takes her up, and saves her from breaking; he cherishes the dogs, and cleanses their mouths from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>; he is adjudged to have the hare for his pains. 19. Finally, those who are judges of the leath, must give their judgment before they depart out of the field, or else it is not to stand as valid.

COURT

Pages 334-335

an appendage to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> habitation; consisting of a piece of ground inclosed with walls, but open upwards. Court is also used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> or sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> resides. Court, in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is defined to be a place wherein <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> is judicially administered. And as, by our excellent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, the sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a> of the laws is vested in the person of the king, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> follow that all courts of justice, which are the medium by which he administers the laws, are derived from the power of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. For whether created by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> or letters patent, or subsisting by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a> (the only methods by which any court of judicature can exist), the king's consent in the two former is expressly, and in the latter impliedly, given. In all these courts, the king is supposed in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of law to be always present; but as that is in fact impossible, he is there represented by his judges, whose power is only an emanation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>. For the more speedy, universal, and impartial administration of justice between subject and subject, the law hath appointed a prodigious variety of courts, some with a more limited, others with a more extensive jurisdiction; some constituted to inquire only, others to hear and determine; some to determine in the first instance, others upon <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> and by way of review. See Law, No. xciviii., xcix., c., calii., clvi., clviii., and the respective <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. One distinction may be here mentioned, that runs throughout them all; viz. that some of them are courts of record, others not of record. A court of record is that where the acts and judicial proceedings are enrolled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> for a perpetual memorial and testimony: which rolls are called the records of the court, and are of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and supereminent authority, that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is not to be called in question. For it is a settled rule and maxim, that nothing shall be averred against a record, nor shall any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>, or even <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, be admitted to the contrary. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the existence of a record be denied, it shall be tried by nothing but itself; that is, upon bare inspection whether there be any such record or not; else there would be no end of disputes. But if there appear any mistake of the clerk in making up such record, the court will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> him to amend it. All courts of record are the king's courts in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of his crown and royal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and therefore no other court hath authority to fine or imprison: so that the very erection of a new jurisdiction with power of fine or imprisonment, makes it instantly a court of record.—A court not of record is the court of a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; whom the law will not intrust with any discretionary power over the fortune or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of his fellow subjects. Such are the courts-baron incident to every <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, and other inferior jurisdictions; where the proceedings are not enrolled or recorded; but as well their existence as the truth of the matters therein contained shall, if disputed, be tried and determined by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. These courts can hold no plea of matters cognizable by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, unless under the value of 40s.; nor of any forcible injury whatsoever, nor having any proceeds to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> the person of the defendant. In every court there must be at least three constituent parts, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, reus, and judex: the actor, or plaintiff, who complains of an injury done; the reus, or defendant, who is called upon to make satisfaction for it; and the judex, or judicial power, which is to examine the truth of the fact, to determine the law arising upon that fact, and, if any injury appears to have been done, to ascertain, and by its officers to apply the remedy. It is also usual in the superior courts to have attorneys, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> or counsel, as assistants. See Attorney and Counsel. Court-Baron, in English Law, a court incident to every manor in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, to be held by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> within the said manor. This court-baron is of two natures: the one is a customary court, appertaining entirely to the copyholders, in which their estates are transferred by surrender and admittance, and other matters transacted relative to their tenures only. The other is a court of common law, and it is the court of the barons, by which name the freeholders were sometimes anciently called; for that it is held before the freeholders who owe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the manor, the steward being rather the registrar than the judge. These courts, though in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> distinct, are equally confounded together. The court we are now considering, viz. the freeholder's court, was composed of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s tenants, who were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> of each other, and were bound by their feudal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> to assist their lord in the dispensation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> justice. This was formerly held every three weeks; and its most important business is to determine, by writ of right, all controversies relating to the right of lands within the manor. It may also hold plea of any personal actions, of debt, trespass on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, or the like, where the debt or damages do not amount to 40s. Which is the same sum, or three marks, that bounded the jurisdiction. were, in some sort, brothers and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> with regard to each other. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">Cousin</a>, John, a celebrated French painter, who excelled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> on glass. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the Last Judgment, in the vestry of the Minims of the Wood of Vincennes, is much admired. He was also a good sculptor. He wrote several works on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>; and died after the year 1689.

COUSU

Pages 335-335

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, signifies a piece of another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> metal placed in the ordinary, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were sewed on, as the word imports. This is generally of colour upon colour, or metal upon metal, contrary to the general rule of heraldry.

COUTANCES

Pages 335-335

a port town of Normandy, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Coutantin, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 32. N. Lat. 49. 0. This town, anciently called Conflintia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cofedia, is pleasantly situated among meadows and rivulets about five miles distant from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. By the remains of a Roman aqueduct, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ruins, it appears to be a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. It is the see of a bishop, suffragan of Rome; and has a magnificent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, esteemed one of the finest pieces of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The trade of this town is very inconsiderable, and the fortifications are quite demolished. They have several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, and two parochial churches.

COUTHUTLAUGH

Pages 335-335

from the Saxon couth, "knowing;" and uthlaug, "outlaw;" he that willingly receives a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> outlawed, and cherishes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conceals him; for which offence he was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times subject to the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> with the outlaw himself.

COVENANT

Pages 325-325

in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, is much used in connection with other terms; as, 1. The Covenant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a> is that which is made between God and those who believe the gospel, whereby they declare their subjection to him, and he declares his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a> of them and favour to them. The gospel is sometimes denominated a covenant of grace, in opposition to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic <a </a>class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. 2. Covenant of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">Redemption</a> denotes a mutual stipulation, tacit <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> express, between Christ and the Father, relating to the redemption of sinners by him, previous to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> on Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> under the character of Mediator. 3. Covenant of Works signifies, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of some divines, any covenant whereby God requires perfect obedience from his creatures, in such a manner as to make no express provision for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> of offences to be committed against the precepts of it, on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> of such supposed offenders, but pronounces a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> upon them: such, they say, was the covenant made with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> in a state of innocence, and that made with Israel at Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>. Solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">League</a> and Covenant, was established in the year 1643, and formed a bond of union between Scotland and England. It was sworn and subscribed by many in both nations; who hereby solemnly abjured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">popery</a> and prelacy, and combined together for their mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. It was approved by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> at Westminster, and ratified by the general assembly of Scotland in 1645. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. disapproved of it when he surrendered himself to the Scots <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in 1646; but in 1650 Charles II. declared his approbation both of this and the national covenant by a solemn oath; and in August of the same year, made a farther <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> at Dunfermline to the same purpose, which was also renewed on occasion of his coronation at Scone in 1651. The covenant was ratified by parliament in this year; and the subscription of it required by every member, without which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the parliament was declared null and void. It produced a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of diljections in the subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and was voted illegal by parliament, and provision made against it. Stat. 14 Car. II. c. 4. Art of the Covenant, in Jewish antiquity. See ARK.

COVENTRY

Pages 325-326

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, in England, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 26. N. Lat. 52. 25. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and is supposed to derive its name from a convent formerly situated here. Leofric, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Mercia, who rebuilt the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> after it had been destroyed by the Danes, and was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the place about the year 1040, is said, upon some provocation, to have loaded them with heavy taxes. Being importuned by his lady, Godina, to remit them, he consented, upon condition that she should ride naked through the town, which he little imagined she would ever comply with. But he found himself mistaken: for she accepted the offer, and rode through the town with her long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> scattered all over her body; having first enjoined the citizens not to venture, on pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, to look out as she passed. It is said, however, that a certain taylor could not help peeping: and to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> there is an effigy of him at the window whence he looked. To commemorate this extraordinary transaction, and out of respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their patroness, the citizens make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> every year, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a naked woman on horseback. After Leofric's death, the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a> became lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and granted it many privileges. At length it was annexed to the earldom of Cornwall; and growing considerable, had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> immunities and privileges conferred upon it by several kings; particularly that of a mayor and two bailiffs by Edward III.; and Henry VI. made it, in conjunction with some other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, independent of the county of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>. But afterwards Edward VI. for their disloyalty, deprived them of their liberties, which were not restored till they had paid a fine of 500 marks. By a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from James I. an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a> is allotted to each <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a>, with the powers of the justices of the peace within the city and its liberties. The walls were ordered to be demolished at the Restoration; and now nothing remains of them but the gates, which are very lofty. Coventry is noted for the two parliaments which were held in it; the one called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Dunces, and the other of Devils. The former was so called on account of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the lawyers; and the attainders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, Warwick, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, procured the other the epithet of Devils. The town-house of Coventry is much admired for its painted windows, representing several kings and others that have been benefactors to the city. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> carried on here are temmies and ribbands. Coventry sends two members to parliament, and gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to an ancient family of the same name.—Coventry is a bishop's see. The bishopric is said to have been founded by Offa <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Mercia, in the year 656 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 657; and although it hath a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> name, yet, like Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, it is a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. It was so extremely wealthy, that King Offa, by the favour of Pope Adrian, constituted it an archiepiscopal see; but this title was laid aside on the death of that king. In 1075, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, the 34th bishop, removed the see to Chester. In 1102, Robert de Limsey, his immediate successor, removed it to Coventry; and Hugo Novant, the 41st bishop, removed it back to Lichfield, but with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> opposition from the monks of Coventry. The dispute was finally settled in a manner nearly similar to that which is mentioned between Bath and Wells. Here it was agreed that the bishop should be styled from both places, and that Coventry should have the precedence; that they should choose the bishop alternately; and that they should both make one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> to the bishop, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of Coventry should be the chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Matters <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> thus till the Reformation, when the priory of Coventry being dissolved by King Henry VIII., the style of the bishop continued as before. But an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament passed 33d of King Henry VIII., to make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and chapter of Lichfield one sole chapter to the bishop. This see hath given three saints to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> one lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, three lord treasurers, three presidents of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, one chancellor to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and one <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the wardrobe. The old church built by King Offa being taken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by Roger de Clinton, the 37th bishop, he built the beautiful fabric that now stands in 1148, and dedicated it to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> and St Chad. During the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> rebellion, the church suffered much; but soon after the Reformation, it was repaired and beautified. This diocese contains the whole counties of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a> (except two parishes of the former), the largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Warwickshire, and nearly one half of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, in which are 555 parishes, of which 250 are inappropriate. It hath four archdeaconries, viz. Stafford, Derby, Coventry, and Shrewsbury. It is valued in the king's books at £591.18s. 2½d. and is computed to be worth annually £2800l. The clergy's tenth is £590l. 16s. 11½d. To this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> belong a bishop, a dean, a precentor, a chancellor, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, four archdeacons, twenty-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> prebendaries, five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>-vicars, seven lay clerks or singing men, eight choristers, and other under officers and servants.

COVERT

Pages 335-336

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, denotes something like a piece of hanging, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a> falling over the top of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> or other ordinary, so as not to hide, but only to be a covering to it. COW. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cow-Burner. See Buprestis, Entomology Index. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-Cow. See Trichecus, Mammalia Index. Cow-itch, or Cowbage. See Couhage and Dolichos, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Cow's-Lip. See Primula, Botany Index. Coward, in Heraldry, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> given to a lion borne in an escutcheon with his tail doubled, or turned in between his legs. Cowel, Dr. John, a learned and eminent civilian, born about the year 1554. In 1607 he compiled a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, which gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> offence to Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> lawyers; so that they first accused him to James I, as afflicting that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> was in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> limited; and when they failed in that attempt, they complained of him to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons, as a betrayer of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the people, by afflicting that the king was not bound by the laws; for which he was committed to custody, and his book publicly burnt. He also published Institutes Juris Anglicani, in the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>'s Institutes; and died in the operation for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, in 1611. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COWES">Cowes</a>, a town and harbour on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>. It has no market, but is the best <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for trade in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; but as it lies low, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is accounted unhealthy. It is eight miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 25. N. Lat. 50. 45.

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is applied to the state and condition of a married woman, who is under the power of her husband, and therefore called femme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a>.

COVIN

Pages 326-326

a deceitful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> agreement between two or more to deceive or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> a third person: As, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a tenant for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> conspire with another, that this other shall recover the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> which the tenant holds in prejudice of him in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a>. Dr Skinner takes the word to be a corruption of the Latin convenium, and therefore writes it coven. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">CONSPIRACY</a>.

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, is when houses are built projecting over the ground-plot, and the turned projection arched with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, lathed and plastered.

COVINUS

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a kind of chariot, in which the Gauls and Britons used to fight in battles.

COWL

Pages 336-336
or COUT, a sort of monkish habit worn by the Bernardines and Benedictines. The word is formed from cucullus, by confounding the two first syllables into one, as being the same twice repeated.—There are two kinds of cowl: the one white, very large, worn in ceremony, and when they assist at the office; the other black, worn on ordinary occasions, in the streets, &c. F. Mabillon maintains the coul to be the same thing in its origin with the scapular. The author of the apology of the emperor Henry IV. distinguishes two forms of couls: the one is a gown reaching to the feet, having sleeves, and a capuchin, used in ceremonies; the other a kind of hood to work in, called also a scapular, because it only covers the head and shoulders.

COWLEY

Pages 336-338
ABRAHAM, an eminent poet, was born at London in 1618. His father, who was a grocer, dying before he was born, his mother procured him to be admitted a king's scholar at Westminster. His first inclination to poetry arose on his lighting on Spenser's Fairy Queen, when he was but just able to read; and this inclination so far improved in him, that at 13 he began to write several poems; a collection of which was published in 1613, when he was but 15. He has been represented as possessed of so bad a memory that his teachers could never bring him to retain the ordinary rules of grammar. But the fact was, as Dr Johnson notices, not that he could not learn or retain the rules; but that being able to perform his exercises without them, he spared himself the labour. In 1636 he was elected a scholar of Trinity college, Cambridge, and removed to that university. Here he went through all his exercises with a remarkable degree of reputation; and at the same time must have pursued his poetical turn with great eagerness, as it appears that the greatest part of his poems were written before he left that university. He had taken his degree of master of arts before 1643, when, in consequence of the turbulence of the times, he, among others, was ejected from the college; whereupon, retiring to Oxford, he entered himself of St John's College; and that very year, under the denomination of a scholar of Oxford, published a satire called the Puritan and the Papist. It is apparent, however, that he did not remain very long at Oxford; for his zeal to the royal cause engaging him in the service of the king, who was very lenient of his abilities, and by whom he was frequently employed, he attended his majesty in many of his journeys and expeditions, and gained not only that prince's esteem, but that of many other great personages, and in particular of Lord Falkland, one of the principal secretaries of state. During the heat of the civil war, he was settled in the earl of St Albans's family; and when the queen-mother was obliged to retire into France, he accompanied her thither, laboured strenuously in the affairs of the royal family, undertook several very dangerous journeys on their account, and was the principal instrument in maintaining an epistolary correspondence between the king and queen, whose letters he ciphered and deciphered with his own hand. His poems, entitled The Mistres, were published at London in 1647; and his comedy called The Guardian, afterwards altered and published under the title of Cutter of Coleman-street, in 1650. In 1656 it was thought proper by those on whom Mr Cowley depended that he should come over into England, and, under pretence of privacy and retirement, should give notice of the posture of affairs in this nation. Upon his return he published a new edition of all his poems, consisting of four parts; viz. I. Miscellanies. II. The Mistres, or Several Copies of Love-letters. III. Pindaric Odes, written in imitation of the style and manner of Pindar, IV. Davidis, a sacred poem of the troubles of David, in four books. Soon after his arrival, however, he was seized, in the search after another gentleman of considerable note in the king's party; but although it was through mistake that he was taken, yet when the republicans found all their attempts of every kind to bring him over to their party proved ineffectual, he was committed to a severe confinement, and it was even with considerable difficulty that he obtained his liberty; when, venturing back to France, he remained there, in his former situation, till near the time of the king's return. During his stay in England he wrote his Two Books of Plants, published first in 1662; to which he afterwards added four books more; and all fix, together with his other Latin poems, were printed at London in 1678. It appears by Mr Wood's Fasti Oxonienses, that our poet was created doctor of physic at Oxford, December 2. 1657. Soon after the Restoration he became possessed of a very competent estate, through the favour of his principal friends the duke of Buckingham and the earl of St Albans; and being now upwards of 40 years of age, he took up a resolution to pass the remainder of a life which had been a scene of tempest and tumult, in that situation which had ever been the object of his wishes, a studious retirement. His eagerness to get out of the bustle of a court and city made him less careful than he might have been in the choice of a healthful habitation in the country; by which means he found his solitude from the very beginning suit less with the constitution of his body than with his mind. His first rural residence was at Barn Elms, a place which, lying low, and being near a large river, was subject to a variety of breezes from land and water, and liable in the winter-time to great inconvenience from the dampness of the soil. The consequence of this Mr Cowley too soon experienced, by being seized with a dangerous and lingering fever. On his recovery from this he removed to Chertsey, a situation not much more healthy, where he had not been long before he was seized with another confining disease. Having languished under this for some months, he at length got the better of it, and seemed pretty well recovered from the bad symptoms, when one day in the heat of summer 1667, staying too long in the fields to give some directions to his labourers, he caught a most violent cold, which was attended with a defluxion and stoppage in his breast; and for want of timely care, by treating it as a common cold, and refusing advice till it was past remedy, he departed this life on the 28th of July in that year, being the 49th of his age; and on the 3d of August following, he Cowley was interred in Westminster-abbey, near the ashes of Chaucer, and his beloved Spenser. He was a man of a very amiable character, as well as an admirable genius. King Charles II. on the news of his death, declared "that Mr Cowley had not left a better man behind him in England." A monument was erected to his memory by George Villiers duke of Buckingham in 1675. Besides the work already mentioned, Mr Cowley wrote, among other things, A Proposition for the Advancement of Experimental Philolophy; A Discourse by way of Vifion concerning the Government of Oliver Cromwell; and Several Discourses by way of Essays in Prose and Verse. Mr Cowley had designed also a Discourse concerning Style, and a Review of the Principles of the Primitive Christian Church, but was prevented by death. A spurious piece, entitled The Iron Age, was published under Mr Cowley's name during his absence; and, in Mr Dryden's Miscellany Poems, we find A Poem on the Civil War, said to be written by our author, but not extant in any edition of his works. An edition of his works was published by Dr Spratt, afterwards bishop of Rochester, who also prefixed to it an account of the author's life. The reverend editor mentions, as very excellent of their kind, Mr Cowley's letters to his Friends; none of which, however, were published. The moral character of Mr Cowley appears, from every account of it, to have been very excellent. "He is represented by Dr Spratt (says Dr Johnson), as the most amiable of mankind; and this posthumous praise may be safely credited, as it has never been contradicted by envy or by faction." As a poet, his merits have been variously estimated. Lord Clarendon has said he made a flight above all men; Addison, in his account of the English poets, that he improved upon the Theban bard; the duke of Buckingham upon his tombstone, that he was the English Pindar, the Horace, the Virgil, the delight, the glory of his times. And with respect to the harshness of his numbers, the eloquent Spratt tells us, that if his verses in some places seem not as soft and flowing as one would have them, it was his choice and not his fault. "Such (says Mr Knox) is the applause lavished on a writer who is now seldom read. That he could ever be esteemed as a pindaric poet is a curious literary phenomenon. He totally mistook his own genius when he thought of imitating Pindar. He totally mistook the genius of Pindar, when he thought his own incoherent sentiments and numbers bore the least resemblance to the wild yet regular sublimity of the Theban. He neglected even those forms, thestrophe, antistrophe, and epode, which even imitative dulness can copy. Sublime imagery, vehement pathos, poetic fire, which constitute the essence of the Pindaric ode, are incompatible with witty conceits, accurate antitheses and vulgar expression. All these imply the coolness of deliberate composition, or the meanness of a little mind; both of them most repugnant to the truly Pindaric ode, in which all is rapturous and noble. Wit of any kind would be improperly displayed in such composition; but to increase the absurdity, the wit of Cowley is often false. That he had a taste for Latin poetry, and wrote in it with elegance, the well known epitaph on himself, upon his retirement, and an admirable imitation of Horace, are full proofs. But surely his rhetorical biographer makes use of the figure hyperbole, when he affirms that Cowley has excelled the Romans themselves. He was inferior to many a writer of less name in the Musae Anglicane. But still he had great merit; and I must confess I have read his Latin verses with more pleasure than any of his English can afford." Essays, vol. ii. p. 363—365. To Cowley's compositions in prose Mr Knox hath paid a very honourable testimony. He says, that in this department he is an elegant, a pleasing, a judicious writer; and that it is much to be lamented that he did not devote a greater part of his time to a kind of writing which appeared natural to him, and in which he excelled. Dr Joseph Warton observes, that it is no caricature of Cowley to represent him as being possessed of a strained affectation of striving to be witty upon all occasions. "It is painful (adds this excellent critic), to censure a writer of so amiable a mind, such integrity of manners, and such sweetness of temper. His fancy was brilliant, strong, and sprightly; but his taste false and unclassical, even though he had much learning." Dr Beattie has characterized Cowley in the following terms. "I know not whether any nation ever produced a more singular genius than Cowley. He abounds in tender thoughts, beautiful lines, and emphatical expressions. His wit is inexhaustible, and his learning extensive; but his taste is generally barbarous, and seems to have been formed upon such models as Donne, Martial, and the worst parts of Ovid: nor is it possible to read his longer poems with pleasure, while we retain any relish for the simplicity of ancient composition. If this author's ideas had been fewer, his conceits would have been less frequent; so that in one respect learning may be said to have hurt his genius. Yet it does not appear that Greek and Latin did him any harm; for his imitations of Anacreon are almost the only parts of him that are now remembered or read. His Davideis, and his translations of Pindar, are destitute of harmony, simplicity, and every other classical grace." But the works of this celebrated poet have been nowhere so amply criticized as in his Life by Dr Johnson. After a particular examination of the different pieces, the Doctor, in taking a general review of Cowley's poetry, observes, that he wrote with abundant fertility, but negligent or unskillful selection; with much thought, but with little imagery; that he is never pathetic, and rarely sublime, but always either ingenious or learned, either acute or profound." Of his prose he speaks with great approbation. "No author (says he) ever kept his verse and his prose at a greater distance from each other. His thoughts are natural, and his style has a smooth and placid equality, which has never yet obtained its due commendation. Nothing is far sought or hard laboured; but all is easy without feebleness, and familiar without grossness." Upon the whole, he concludes as follows: "It may be affirmed, without any encomiastic fervour, that he brought to his poetical labours a mind replete with learning, and that his passages are embellished. lished with all the ornaments which books could supply; that he was the first who imparted to English numbers the enthusiasm of the greater ode and the gaiety of the less; that he was qualified for sprightly fancies and for lofty flights: that he was among those who freed translation from servility, and, instead of following his author at a distance, walked by his side; and that though he had left versification yet improvable, he left likewise from time to time such specimens of excellence as enabled succeeding poets to improve it. So many of Cowley's productions being now esteemed scarcely worthy of a perusal, while others of them are distinguished by their beauty, Dr Hurd (the present bishop of Worcester), thought proper to make a selection of them, which he published in 1772, under the title of Select Works of Mr Abraham Cowley, in two volumes; with a preface and notes by the Editor.

COWPER

Pages 338-340

WILLIAM, a distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> poet, was born at Berkhamstead in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a> in the year 1732. His father, who was rector of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, was nephew to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> Cowper. Mr Cowper was educated at Westminster school; and in that celebrated seminary he acquired his classical knowledge. But it would appear from his poem, entitled "Tirocinium," that the impressions which he then received were not favourable to this system of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; and gave him a permanent dislike to public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. Through family <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> and lucrative <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of clerk to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords had been provided for him; he was, therefore entered at the Temple for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, in order to qualify him for it. In this situation his manners were amiable and decent; and though it is probable that he did not refuse to indulge in those pleasures which are usual among young men similarly situated, yet there seems no reason to suppose that he had any peculiar causes for self-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> disposition was timid and diffident; his spirits were constitutionally weak, even to the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> unfitness for worldly concerns; so that when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> came for assuming that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> to which he had been destined, he shrank with such terror from the idea of making his appearance before the most august <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, that, after a violent struggle with himself, he actually resigned the employment, and with it all his prospects in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. It appears to have been under the agitation of mind which this circumstance occasioned, and which threw him into a serious illness, that he was led to a deep consideration of his state in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> view; and from the system he had adopted, this course of reflection excited in him the most alarming and distressful apprehensions. In vain did his theological friends set before him those encouraging views which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a> is calculated to present, and which to many is the source of a confidence perhaps as excessive as their former fears; the natural disposition of his mind fitted it to receive all the horrors, without the consolations of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. We are told, that "the terror of eternal judgment overpowered and wholly disordered his faculties; and he remained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months in a continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of being instantly plunged into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> misery." In this shocking condition he became the subject of medical care, and he was placed in the receptacle for lunatics kept by Dr Cotton of St Albans, an amiable and worthy physician, and the author of some well known poems. At length he recovered a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of serenity; but his mind had acquired that indelible tinge of melancholy by which it was ever after characterized, and which rendered his whole life little more than a succession of intervals of comfort between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> paroxysms of settled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a>. It is unnecessary to follow him through all his scenes of retirement. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> of his time was spent at the house of his relation, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Cowper, at Cole-green; and part at Huntingdon, with his intimate friend the reverend Mr Unwin. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the latter, he removed with his widow to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OLNEY">Olney</a> in Buckinghamshire, which was thenceforth the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> place of his residence. The affectionate intimacy he enjoyed with this lady is strongly expressed in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, which have probably been understood by most readers as expressive of a conjugal union: —Witnes, dear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of my walks, Whole arm this twentieth winter I perceive Fast lock'd in mine, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> Confirm'd by long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of thy worth And well-tried virtues could alone inspire— Witnes a joy that thou hast doubled long. Task, Book I. At Olney he contracted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> friendship with the reverend Mr Newton, then minister there, and since rector of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Woolnoth, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, whose religious opinions were in unison with his own. When Mr Newton published his volume of Hymns, called "The Olney's Collection," it was enriched with some compositions from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of Cowper, distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> C. They bear internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of a cultivated underhanding, and an original genius. His time was now wholly dedicated to that literary leisure, in which the mind, left to its own operations, follows up that line of pursuit which is the most congenial to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and the most adapted to its powers. In his garden, in his library, and in his daily walks, he seems to have disciplined his muse to the picturesque and vivid habits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> always distinguish Cowper among our national poets. No writer, with the exception of Thomson, seems to have studied <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with more diligence, and to have copied her with more fidelity. An advantage which he has gained over other men, by his disdaining to study her "through the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> of books," as Dryden calls it; and by his pursuing her through her haunts, and watching her in all her attitudes, with the eye of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> as well as of a poet. As Mr Cowper had no relish for public concerns, it was not singular that he should have neglected the study of the law, on which he had entered. That knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> life, which is so requisite for the legal profession, would hardly be acquired on the banks of the Ouse, and in silent contemplations on the beauties of nature. In this retreat, he exchanged for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, the ambition and tumult of a forensic occupation; dedicating his mind to the cultivation of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and storing it with those images which he derived from the inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> of a rich and varied scenery, in a most beautiful and romantic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.—The first volume of his poems, which was published by Mr Newton in 1787, consists of of various pieces, on various subjects. It seems, that he had been affiduous in cultivating a turn for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and argumentative verification, on moral and ethical topics. Of this kind is The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> Talk, and several other pieces in the collection. He who objects to these poems as containing too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a neglect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> in the arrangement of his words, and the expressions too profuse, will condemn him on principles of criticism which are by no means <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the object and style of the subject be considered. Horace apologized for the style of his own satires, which are, strictly speaking, only ethical and moral discourses, by observing, that those topics required the pedellion and familiar diction, and a form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, not carried to the heights of poetry. But if the reader will forego the delight of smooth verification, and recollect that poetry does not altogether consist in even and polished metre, he will remark in these productions, no ordinary depth of thinking and of judgment, upon the most important objects of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> intercourse; and he will be occasionally struck with lines, not unworthy of Dryden for their strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> poems are well known. Of these, the verses supposed to be written by Alex. Selkirk, on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Juan Fernandez, are in the most popular estimation. There is great originality in the following stanza. I am out of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>'s reach; I must finish my journey alone; Never hear the sweet music of speech; I start at the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of my own." It would be absurd to give one general character of the pieces, that were published in this volume: yet, this is true concerning Mr Cowper's productions; that in all the varieties of his style, there may still be discerned the likeness and impressiveness of the same mind; the same unaffected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, which always rejects unreasonable ambitions and ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; the same easy vigour; the same serene and cheerful hope, derived from a steady and unshaken faith in the dogmas of Christianity. Mr Cowper, perhaps, does not derive praise from the choice and elegance of his words; but he has the higher praise of having chosen them without affectation. He appears to have used them as he found them; neither introducing fallacious refinements nor adhering to obsolete barbarisms. He understood the whole science of numbers, and he practised their different kinds with considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>; and, if his verses do not flow so softly as the delicacy of a modern <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> requires, that roughness, which is objected to in his poetry, is his choice, not his defect. But this sort of critics, who admire only what is exquisitely polished, like Cuyp's pictures, these lovers of "gentle nefs without finesse," ought to take into their estimate, that vast <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of thought which is so abundantly poured over the writings of Cowper, without which human discourse is only an idle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of sounds and syllables. The favourable reception which this volume experienced, produced another of superior merit. His principal performance was undoubtedly "The Talk," a poem. The occasion that gave birth to it was trivial. A lady had requested him to write a piece in blank <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and gave him for its subject a thing next to her, viz. the sofa. This he expanded into one of the finest moral poems our language has produced. It is written in blank verse as desired; and Cowper, though in that respect it resembles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>'s, it is nevertheless original and highly characteristic. It is not too flatly for familiar description, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> too depressed for sublime and elevated imagery. If it has any fault, it is that of being too much laden with idiomatic expression; a fault which the author, in the rapidity with which his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> and his utterance seem to have flowed, very naturally incurred. In this poem, his fancy ran with the most exquisite freedom. The poet enlarges upon his topics, and confirms his argument by every variety of illustration. He never however dwells upon them too long, and leaves off in such a manner, that it seems it was in his power to have said more. The arguments of the poem are various. The works of nature, the associations with which they exhibit themselves, the designs of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, and the passions of men. Of one advantage, the writer has amply availed himself. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> not being rigidly confined to any precise subject, he has indulged himself in all the laxity and freedom of a miscellaneous poem. Yet he has still adhered so faithfully to the general laws of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRUITY">congruity</a>, that whether he inspires the softer affections into his reader, or delights him with keen and playful raillery, or discourses on the ordinary manners of human nature, or holds up the bright pictures of religious consolation to his mind, he adopts, at pleasure, a diction just and appropriate, equal in elevation to the sacred effusions of pious rapture, and sufficiently easy and familiar for descriptions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> life; skilful alike in soaring without effort, and descending without meanness. He who desires to put into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of youth a poem, which not destitute of poetic embellishment, is free from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of a licentious tendency, will find in the Talk a book adapted to his purpose. It would be absurd and extravagant audacity to condemn those poetical productions in which love constitutes the leading feature. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> has in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> been the concernment of life, the theme of the poet, the plot of the stage. Yet there is a kind of amorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>, bordering on morbid enthusiasm, which the youthful mind too often imbibes from the glowing sentiments of the poets. Their genius describes, in the most splendid colours, the operations of a passion which requires rebuke rather than incentive, and lends to the most grovelling sensuality, the enchantments of a rich and creative imagination. But in the Talk of Cowper, there is no licentiousness of description. All is grave, majestic, and moral. A vein of sober thinking pervades every page, and, in finished poetry, describes the insufficiency and vanity of human pursuits. Not that he is always severe. He frequently enlivens the mind of his reader by sportive descriptions, and by representing in elevated <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, ludicrous objects and circumstances, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the mock heroic, so admired in Phillipp's Splendid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">Shilling</a>. The historical account he has given of chairs, in the first book of the Talk, is a striking specimen of his powers of verification, and of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for humour in this latter style. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is however the most detained by those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, in which the charms of rural life, and the endearments of domestic retirement are described. The Talk abounds with incidents, introduced as episodes, and interposing an agreeable relief to the grave and serious part of the poetry. His Crazy Kate is a description of the calamity of a disordered reason, admirably exact and affecting. "She begs an idle <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> of all the meets." What poet would have introduced so minute a circumstance into his representation! and yet that minuteness constitutes its happy effect. Of his talent for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> there cannot be a better specimen than his sketch of the melancholy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, probably sketched from what too faithful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> suggested of himself: Look where he comes—In this embower'd alcove Stand clofe concealed, and see a statue move; Lips <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a>, and eyes fixt, foot falling slow, Arms hanging idly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, hands clasped below, Interpret to the marking eye, distress, Such as its symptoms only can express. That tongue is silent now—that silent tongue Could argue once, could jeft or join the song, Could give advice, could censure or commend, Or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> the sorrows of a drooping friend. Renounc'd alike its office and its sport, Its brisker and its graver strains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> short; Both fall beneath a fever's secret sway, And like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> brook are past away. Retirement. His John Gilpin is universally known, and may be considered as a sporting piece of humour, which would have done <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to many writers, but can hardly be said to have added to Mr Cowper's reputation. His next work was a translation of the Iliad and Odyssey into Miltonic blank verse. It is an unjust piece of criticism to compare the version of Mr Pope to that of Mr Cowper. The merits of each are distinct and appropriate. Mr Pope has exhibited <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> as he would have sung had he been born in England. Mr Cowper has endeavoured to portray him, as he wrote in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, adhering frequently to the peculiarities of his original's idiom, and desiring to preserve his strength and energy, together with his harmony and smoothness. Mr Cowper died of a fever and lingering illness, at East <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEREHAM">Dereham</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, April 25, 1800.

COX

Pages 340-340

RICHARD, a learned prelate, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> pillar of the Reformation, was born at Whaddon in Buckinghamshire, of low parentage, in the year 1499. From Eaton school he obtained a scholarship in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, of which he became a fellow in 1519; he was thence invited to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Wolsey, and was there made one of the junior canons of Cardinal college. In 1525 he was incorporated bachelor; and the following year took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts in the same university. In this situation he became remarkable for his learning and poetical abilities; but his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the opinions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> rendered him hateful to his superiors, who stripped him of his preferment, and threw him into prison on a suspicion of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>. Being, however, soon released, he was chosen master of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> school, which flourished remarkably under his care. In 1537 he commenced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at Cambridge; in 1540 was made archdeacon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>; and the following year prebendary of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, on its being new founded by King Henry VIII. In 1546 he was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, Oxford. By the recommendation of Archbishop Cranmer and Bishop Goodrich, to the latter of whom he had been chaplain, he not only obtained the above preferments, but was chosen preceptor to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Edward, on whose accession to the throne he became a favourite at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, was sworn of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and made king's almoner. In 1547 he was elected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of Oxford; in 1548 canon of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>; and the next year dean of Westminster. About this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was appointed one of the commissioners to visit the university of Oxford; in which office his zeal for reformation was so excessive, that he destroyed a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of curious and valuable books, for no better reason than because they were written by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. On the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> he was stripped of all his preferments and committed to the Marshalsea. He was, however, soon released, and immediately left the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Having resided some time at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a> with his intimate friend <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Queen Mary he returned to England, and, with other divines, was appointed to revive the liturgy. He often preached before the queen; and in 1559 was preferred to the see of Ely, which he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to enjoy upwards of 21 years. He was, however, no favourite with the queen; the reason assigned for which was, his zealous opposition to her retaining the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a> and wax-candles on the altar of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> chapel; also his strenuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of the clergy, which her majesty always disapproved. He died on the 22d of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1581, aged 81. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of considerable learning, a zealous and rigid bulwark of the church of England, and an implacable enemy both to Papists and Puritans. In a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Archbishop Parker, he advises him to proceed vigorously in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECLAIMING">reclaiming</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> punishing the Puritans, and not to be discouraged at the frown of those court-favourites who protected them; assuring him that he might expect the blessing of God on his pious labours to free the church from their dangerous attempts, and to establish uniformity. This zealous reformer we find had not totally lost sight of the Popish texts, compel them to come in; but a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his implacability and self-importance appears in his letter to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Burleigh, in which he warmly expostulates with the council for interfering in behalf of the Puritans, or meddling in affairs of the church, admonishing them to keep their own sphere. Such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> from a bishop would make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> privy council stare. His works are, 1. Two Latin Orations on the Dispute between Dr Tresham and Peter Martyr, Lond. 1549, 4to. 2. Liturgy of the Church of England; in compiling, and afterwards correcting which, he was principally concerned. 3. The Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">Prayer</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> printed at the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s Psalms by Sternhold and Hopkins. 4. Translation of the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Epistle to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, in the new translation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> in the reign of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. 5. Resolutions of some Questions concerning the Sacrament in the Collection of Records at the end of Burnet's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Reformation. 6. Several Letters to the Queen and others, published in Strype's Annals of the Reformation. He is also said to have been concerned in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> concerning the divine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and to have assisted Lilye in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>.

COYPEL

Pages 340-341

Anthony, an excellent French painter, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1661. Noyel Coypel, his father, being chosen by M. Colbert to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the academy at Rome, he took his son with him into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where Anthony Coypel formed himself on the works of the greatest masters, and on his return to France was made first painter to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> employed him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> gallery of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and allowed him a pension. In 1714, he was director of the Academy of Painting and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a>. In 1715, he was made the first painter to the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, and was ennobled on account of his merit. He died in 1722. M. Coypel, his son, also excelled in the same art. COZENING; tricking, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> defrauding.—In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, it denotes an offence where anything is done deceitfully, whether belonging to contracts or not, which cannot be properly termed by any special name.

COZUMEL

Pages 341-341

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> near the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Yucatan, where Cortez landed and refreshed his troops before entering upon the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 89°. 0. and N. Lat. 13°. 0. CRAB. See Cancer, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Crab's Claws, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, are the tips of the claws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> crab broken off at the verge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, so much of the extremity of the claws only being allowed to be used in medicine as is tinged with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The blackness, however, is only superficial; they are of a grayish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> within, and when levigated furnish a white powder. Crab's claws are of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the alkaline absorbents; but they are superior to the generality of them, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, as they are found on a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> to contain a volatile urinous <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. Crab's Eyes, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, are a strong concretion in the head of the cray-fish. They are rounded on one side, and depressed and sinuated on the other, considerably heavy, moderately hard, and without smell. We have them from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Mulcovy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and many other places. What are usually met with in the shops are prepared by art. Crab's eyes are much used both in the shop medicines and extemporaneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, being accounted absorbent. Crab <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">Lice</a>, a troublesome kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>, which stick so fast with their claws to the skin as to render it difficult to dislodge them. They are called platulae, morpiones, petola, and pediculae: they usually infest the arm pits and pudenda. Cleanliness is the best preventative. But these vermin may be easily removed with the application of a little mercurial ointment. Crab, a sort of wooden pillar, whose lower end, being let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> through a ship's decks, rests upon a socket like the capstern; and having in its upper end, three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four holes, at different heights, through the middle of it, one above another, into which long bars are thrust, whose length is nearly equal to the breadth of the neck. It is employed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> in the cable, or to purchase any other weighty body which requires a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> power. This differs from a capstern, as not being furnished with a drum-head, and by having the bars to go entirely through it, reaching from one side of the deck to the other; whereas those of the capstern, which are superior in number, reach Crab-yaws, about eight inches or a foot into the drum-head, according to its size. See Capstern. Crab-Yaws, a name in Jamaica for a kind of ulcer on the soles of the feet, with hard callous lips, so hard that it is difficult to cut them. The ung. carul. fort., is their cure.

CRACATOA

Pages 341-341

the most southerly of a cluster of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> lying in the entrance of the straits of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUNDA">Sunda</a> in the East Indies. Its whole circumference does not exceed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles; and off its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-eastern extremity is a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> forming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook anchored when visiting this island on his last voyage. On the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the small island is a reef of rocks, within which is a tolerable shelter against all northerly winds, there being 27 fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the mid channel, and 18 near the reef. Between the two islands there is a narrow passage for boats. The shore that constitutes the west side of the road runs in a north-westery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, having a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of coral running into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> for a little way, so that it is difficult for boats to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> except at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> water; but the anchoring ground is very good and free from rocks. In the inland parts the ground is elevated, rising on all sides gradually from the sea, and is entirely covered with wood, excepting a few spots which are cleared by the inhabitants for sowing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is reckoned very healthy in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with the neighbouring countries, but it is very thinly inhabited. There are abundance of turtle on the coral reefs; but other refreshments are scarce, and sold at an exorbitant price. Water is not plentiful: Captain Cook was obliged to supply himself from a small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> opposite to the southern extremity of the small island above-mentioned. To the southward is a hot spring, whose waters are used as a bath by the inhabitants. The road where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">Resolution</a> anchored lies in S. Lat. 8°. 6. and by observation, in 105°. 36'. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. by the time-keeper in 104°. 48'. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the compass one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> W.
