On the full and change days it is high water at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> o'clock in the morning, and the tide rises three feet four inches perpendicular.

CRACKOW

Pages 341-342
or Cracow, a city of Poland, situated in a palatinate of the same name, E. Long. 20°. 16'. N. Lat. 50°. 8. It was formerly the capital of Poland, where the kings were elected and crowned, and was once almost the centre of the Polish dominions, but is now a frontier town; a proof how much the power of this republic has been contracted. Crackow stands in an extensive plain, watered by the Vistula, which is broad but shallow: the city and its suburbs occupy a vast tract of ground, but are so badly peopled, that they scarcely contain 16,000 inhabitants. The great square in the middle of the town is very spacious, and has several well-built houses, once richly furnished and well inhabited, but most of them now either untenanted or in a state of melancholy decay. Many of the streets are broad and handsome; but almost every building bears the most striking marks of ruined grandeur: the churches alone seem to have preserved their original splendour. The devastation of this unfortunate town was begun by the Swedes at the commencement of the present century, when it was besieged and taken by Charles XII. but Crackow, the mischiefs it suffered from that ravager of the north were far less destructive than those it experienced during the late dreadful commotions, when it underwent repeated sieges, and was alternately in possession of the Russians and Confederates. The effects of cannon, grape, and musket shot, are still discernible on the walls and houses. In a word, Crackow exhibits the remains of ancient magnificence, and looks like a great capital in ruins: from the number of fallen and falling houses one would imagine it had lately been sacked, and that the enemy had left it only yesterday. The town is surrounded with high walls of brick, strengthened by round and square towers of whimsical shapes, in the ancient style of fortification: these walls were built by Venceslaus king of Bohemia during the short period in which he reigned over Poland. The university of Crackow was formerly, and not unjustly, called the mother of Polish literature, as it principally supplied the other seminaries with professors and men of learning; but its lustre has been greatly obscured by the removal of the royal residence to Warsaw, and still more by the late intestine convulsions. In this city the art of printing was first introduced into Poland by Haller; and one of the earliest books was the Constitutions and Statutes compiled by Casimir the Great, and afterwards augmented by his successors. The characters are Gothic, the same which were universally used at the invention of printing: the great initial letters are wanting, which shows that they were probably painted and afterwards worn away. The year in which this compilation was printed is not positively known; but its publication was certainly anterior to 1496, as it does not contain the statutes passed by John Albert in that year. The most flourishing period of the university was under Sigismund Augustus in the 16th century, when several of the German reformers fled from the persecutions of the emperor Charles V. and found an asylum in this city. They gave to the world several versions of the sacred writings, and other theological publications, which diffused the reformed religion over great part of Poland. The protection which Sigismund Augustus afforded to men of learning of all denominations, and the universal toleration which he extended to every sect of Christians, created a suspicion that he was secretly inclined to the new church; and it was even reported that he intended to renounce the Catholic faith, and publicly profess the reformed religion. Towards the southern part of the town, near the Vistula, rises a small eminence or rock, upon the top of which is built the palace, surrounded with brick walls and old towers, which form a kind of citadel to the town. This palace owes its origin to Ladislaus Jagiellon; but little of the ancient structure now appears, as the greatest part was demolished by Charles XII. in 1701, when he entered this town in triumph after the battle of Klipow. It has been since repaired. The remains of the old palace consist of a few apartments, which are left in their ancient state as they existed in the last century. This palace was formerly the residence of the kings of Poland, who, from the time of Ladislaus Locketec, have been crowned at Crackow. The Polish and German historians differ concerning the time when the title of king was first claimed by the sovereigns of this country; but the most probable account is, according to Mr Coxe, that in 1295 Premillas assumed the regal title, and was inaugurated at Gnefna by the archbishop of that diocese. He was succeeded by Ladislaus Locketec, who offending the Poles by his capricious and tyrannical conduct, was deposed before he was crowned; and Venceslaus king of Bohemia, who had married Richa daughter of Premillas, being elected in his stead, was in 1300 consecrated at Gnefna. Ladislaus, after flying from his country and undergoing a series of calamitous adventures, was at length brought to a penit of his misconduct. Having regained the affection of his subjects, he was restored, in the lifetime of Venceslaus, to part of his dominions; and he recovered them all upon the demise of that monarch in the year 1305: he governed, however, for some years without the title of king; but at length in 1320 was crowned at Crackow, to which place he transferred the ceremony of the coronation; and afterwards enacted, that for the future his successors should be inaugurated in the cathedral of this city. Since that period all the sovereigns have been consecrated at Crackow, excepting the last king. Previous to his election a decree was issued by the diet of convocation, that the coronation should be solemnized for this turn at Warsaw, without prejudice in future to the ancient right of Crackow; a proviso calculated to satisfy the populace, but which will not probably prevent any future sovereign from being crowned at Warsaw, now become the capital of Poland and the residence of its kings. The diadem and other regalia used at the coronation are still kept in the palace of Crackow, under so many keys, and with such care, that it was impossible to obtain a sight of them. Adjoining to the palace stands the cathedral, also within the walls of the citadel. Here all the sovereigns, from the time of Ladislaus Locketec, have been interred, a few only excepted, viz. Louis and Ladislaus II. who were kings of Hungary as well as of Poland, and whose bodies were deposited in Hungary; Alexander, who died and was buried at Vilna; Henry of Valois, interred in France; and the late monarch Augustus III. The sepulchres of the kings of Poland are not distinguished by any peculiar magnificence; their figures are carved in marble of no extraordinary workmanship, and some are without inscriptions. The bishop of Crackow is the first in the kingdom, duke of Saveria, and very often a cardinal. His revenues are larger than those of his metropolitan the archbishop of Gnefna, and are computed to amount to 40,000 dollars per annum.

CRADLE

Pages 342-343

in engraving, is the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used in scraping mezzotintos, and preparing the plate. It is formed of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, resembling a chisel with one sloping side, upon which are cut hollow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> very near each other, and at equal distances. The acting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this tool is made circular, and the corners are rounded. Cradle rounded. After being properly tempered, it must be sharpened on the whetstone. There are various sizes of this instrument. Cradle, among shipwrights, a frame placed under the bottom of a ship, in order to conduct her smoothly and steadily into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> when she is going to be launched; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it supports her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> while she slides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sloping passage called the sway, which are for this purpose daubed with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> and tallow.

CRAFT

Pages 343-343

a general name for all sorts of vessels employed to load <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> discharge merchant ships, or to carry alongside or return the stores of men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Such are lighters, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOY">hoy</a>, barges, prams, &c. See those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>.

CRAIL

Pages 343-343
or CAREIL, a parliament town of Scotland, situated on the sea-coast of the county of Fife, about seven miles south-east of St Andrews. W. Long. 2° 30' N. Lat. 56° 17'.

CRAMBE

Pages 343-343
SEA-CABBAGE, SEA-BEACH KALE, or SEA-COLEWORT, a genus of plants belonging to the tetradynamia class, and in the natural method ranking under the 39th order, Siliqueae. See BOTANY Index. CRAMERIA: A genus of plants belonging to the tetrandria class. See BOTANY Index.

CRAMOND

Pages 343-343

OVER and NETHER, two villages about four miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; of which only the last deserves notice, as having been once a famous naval station of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It is situated at the influx of the river Almond into the Forth. Three Roman <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> meet at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which was called by them Alaterosa, and whither they brought their grain for the support of their troops. The village contains about 300 inhabitants. Here are the remains of a bath and satory; and many altars, medals, &c. have been dug up.

CRAMP

Pages 343-343

a spasmodic affection of the muscles of different parts of the body, as of those of the neck, arms, legs, &c. accompanied with a violent but transitory pain. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CRAMP-IRON

Pages 343-343
or Cramps, a piece of iron bent at each end, which serves to fasten together pieces of wood, stones, or other things.

CRAMPONEE

Pages 343-343

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, an epithet given to a crols which has at each end a cramp <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> piece coming from it; that from the arm in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> towards the sinister <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, that from the arm on that side downwards, that from the arm in base towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEXTER">dexter</a> side, and that from the dexter arm upwards.

CRANAGE

Pages 343-343

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of using a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRANE">crane</a> at a wharf, and also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> paid for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up wares out of a ship, &c. with a crane. CRANE. See ARDEA, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CRANE

Pages 343-343

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, a machine used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> for raising <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and other weights. See MECHANICS. CRANE'S <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">BILL</a>. See GERANIUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CRANGANOR

Pages 343-343

a Dutch <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> on the Malabar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> in the East Indies, seated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 75° 5'. N. Craniolet Lat. 10° 0'. See COCHIN. CRANIOPLARIA: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 40th order, Peronata.

CRANIUM

Pages 343-343

in Anatomy, an assemblage of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> which cover and enclose the brain and cerebrum, popularly called the skull. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The word comes from the Greek κρανος, of κρανος, galea, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>," because it serves to defend the brain like a head-piece. Perzon, again, derives κρανος, from the Celtic crean, because of its roundness.

CRANK

Pages 343-343

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. A ship is said to be crank-sided, when for want of a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ballast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cargo, she cannot bear her sails, or can bear but small sail for fear of overfetting.—She is said to be crank by the ground, when her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> is so narrow that she cannot be brought on ground without danger. Crank is also an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> brace which supports the lanthorns on the poop-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, &c.

CRANMER

Pages 343-347

THOMAS, a celebrated archbishop, reformer, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>, was the son of Thomas Cranmer, Esq. of Asheton in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, where our author was born in 1489. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 14, he was admitted a student of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, of which he afterwards became fellow; but marrying the relation of an innkeeper's wife, he lost his fellowship and quitted the college. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his wife he was re-admitted fellow of Jesus College. In 1523 he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and was made theological lecturer and examiner. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> being at Cambridge, he retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a relation at Waltham <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, where, meeting with Fox the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s almoner, and Gardiner the secretary, he gave his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> concerning King Henry's <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with Catherine much to the satisfaction of his majesty. This opinion was, that instead of disputing about the validity of the king's marriage with Catherine, they should reduce the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to this simple question, "Whether a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may marry his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s wife <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not?" When the king was told of it he said, "This fellow has got the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> low by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>." He then sent for him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, made him one of his chaplains, and ordered him to write in vindication of the divorce in agitation. This book having quieted the tender <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> of the king, he was desirous that all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> should be convinced of the illegality of his marriage with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Catherine; and for that purpose sent Cranmer to France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and Germany, to dispute the matter with the divines of those countries. At <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> Cranmer married a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife. Being returned to England, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1533 he was consecrated archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>; in May following he pronounced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of divorce between the king and queen; and soon after married the amorous monarch to Ann Boleyn. Being now at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, he exerted himself in the business of the Reformation. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> was translated into English, and monasteries dissolved principally by his means. In 1536 the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> conscience again required the affiance Cranmer, instance of our archbishop; in this year he divorced the king from Ann Boleyn. In 1537 he visited his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, and endeavoured to abolish the superstitious observation of holidays. In 1539 he and some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> fell under the king's displeasure, because they could not be brought to give their consent in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> that the monasteries should be suppressed for the king's sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. He also strenuously opposed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> for the six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in the house of lords, speaking three days against it; and upon the passing of that statute sent away his wife into Germany. In 1540 he was one of the commissioners for inspecting into matters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and explaining some of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> doctrines. The result of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> was the book entitled A necessary Erudition of any Christian man. After <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Cromwell's death (in whose behalf he had written to the king), he retired and lived in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> privacy, meddling not at all with state affairs. In 1541 he gave orders pursuant to the king's directions, for taking away superstitious shrines; and exchanging Bishopsham for Beckenham, united the latter to his diocese. In 1542 he procured the "Act for the advancement of true religion and the abolishment of the contrary," which moderated the rigour of the six articles. But the year following, some enemies preferring accusations against him, he had like to have been ruined, had not the king interposed in his behalf. His majesty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> afterwards to protect him from his enemies; and at his death appointed him one of the executors of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and one of the regents of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In 1556 he crowned young Edward, during whose short reign he promoted the reformation to the utmost of his power; and was particularly instrumental in composing, correcting, and establishing the liturgy by act of parliament. He had also a share in compiling the thirty-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> articles of religion. In 1553 he opposed the new settlement of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> upon Lady Jane Grey, and would no way be concerned in that affair (though at last, through many opportunities, he was prevailed upon to set his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to it); neither would he join in any of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a>'s ambitious projects. Upon Queen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s accession to the throne, he was committed to the Tower; partly for setting his hand to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of Lady Jane's succession, and partly for the public offer he had made a little before of justifying openly the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> proceedings of the late king. Some of his friends, foreseeing the storm that was likely to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon him, advised him to fly, but he absolutely refused. In the ensuing parliament, on November the 3rd, he was attainted, and at Guildhall found guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>; whereupon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his archbishopric were sequestrated. In April 1554, he and Ridley and Latimer were removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in order for a public disputation with the Papists; which was accordingly held there towards the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, with great noise, triumph, and impudent confidence on the Papists' side, and with as much gravity, learning, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, and convincing sufficiency on the side of the Protestant bishops. The 20th of April, two days after the end of these disputations, Cranmer and the two others were brought before the commissioners, and asked, Whether they would subscribe (to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>)? which they unanimously refusing, were condemned as heretics. From this sentence the archbishop appealed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> judgment of the Almighty; and wrote to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, giving them an account of the Cranmer disputation, and desiring the queen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> for his treason, which it seems was not yet remitted. By the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> which met this year, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> of the true and Catholic Doctrine of the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of our Saviour Christ was ordered to be burnt. Some of his friends petitioned the queen in his behalf; putting her in mind how he had once preserved her in her father's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> intercessions with him for her, so that she had reason to believe he loved her, and would speak the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> to her more than all the rest of the clergy. All endeavours in his behalf, however, were ineffectual; and the archbishop being degraded and most ignominiously treated, was at last flattered and terrified into an insincere recantation and renunciation of the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. But this triumph was not sufficient to gratify the pious vengeance of the Roman Mary. On the 24th of Feb. 1556, a writ was signed for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of Cranmer; and on the 24th March, which was the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, he was brought to St Mary's church, Oxford, and placed on a kind of stage over against the pulpit, where Dr Cole, provost of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETON">Eton</a>, was appointed to preach a sermon on the occasion. While Cole was haranguing, the unfortunate Cranmer expressed great inward confusion; often lifting up his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and eyes to heaven, and frequently pouring out floods of tears. At the end of the sermon, when Cole desired him to make an open profession of his faith, as he had promised him he would, he first prayed in the most fervent manner; then made an exhortation to the people present, not to set their minds upon the world, to obey the king and queen, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> each other, and to be charitable. After this he made a confession of his faith, beginning with the creed, and concluding with these words: "And I believe every word and sentence taught by our Saviour Jesus Christ, his apostles, and prophets, in the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>.—And now (added he) I come to the great thing that so much troubleth my conscience, more than any thing I ever did or said in my whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and that is the setting abroad a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> contrary to the truth, which I here now renounce as things written with my hand contrary to the truth which I thought in my heart; and written for fear of death, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> my life <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it might be: that is, all such bills and papers which I have written or signed with my hand since my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>, wherein I have written many things untrue. And forasmuch as my hand offended, writing contrary to my heart, my hand shall first be punished; for, may I come to the fire, it shall be first burned. As for the pope, I refuse him as Christ's enemy and antichrist, with all his false doctrine. And as for the sacrament, I believe as I have taught in my book against the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>." Thunderstruck as it were with this unexpected <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, the enraged Papish crowd admonished him not to dissemble. "Ah!" (replied he with tears) since I lived hitherto, I have been a hater of falsehood and a lover of simplicity, and never before this time have I dissembled." Whereupon they pulled him off the stage with the utmost fury, and hurried him to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his martyrdom over against Baliol college; where he put off his clothes in haste, and standing in his shirt, and without shoes, was fastened with a chain to the stake. Some pressing him to agree to his former recantation, he Cranmer, he answered, showing his hand, "This is the hand that wrote it, and therefore it shall first suffer <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>." Fire being applied to him, he stretched out his right hand into the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, and held it there unmoved (except that once with it he wiped his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>) till it was consumed; crying with a loud <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, "This hand hath offended;" and often repeating, "This unworthy right hand." At last the fire getting up, he soon expired, never stirring or crying out all the while; only keeping his eyes fixed to heaven, and repeating more than once, "Lord Jesus receive my spirit." Such was the end of the renowned Thomas Cranmer, in the 67th year of his age. It was noticed above, that after the passing of the act for the six articles, Archbishop Cranmer sent his wife into Germany. But after returned again to England; and Mr Strype informs us that "in the time of King Edward, when the marriage of the clergy was allowed, he brought her forth, and lived openly with her." Mr Gilpin says, "he left behind him a widow and children; but as he always kept his family in obscurity for prudential reasons, we know little about them. They had been kindly provided for by Henry VIII.; who, without any solicitation from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> himself, gave him a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> from the abbey of Walbeck in Nottinghamshire, which his family enjoyed after his decease. King Edward made some addition to his private fortune; and his heirs were restored in blood by an act of parliament in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. Archbishop Cranmer wrote a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books; many of them he published himself; and many of them still remain in MSS. viz. two folio volumes in the king's library, several letters in the Cotton collection, &c. Mr Gilpin remarks, That "the character of the archbishop hath been equally the subject of exaggerated praise and of undeserved censure." The most indefensible parts of the archbishop's character are the readings with which he sometimes concurred in the unjustifiable proceedings of Henry VIII. and the instances wherein he showed himself to be actuated by intolerant principles. "He first recommended himself to Henry by the zeal which he displayed in promoting the king's divorce from Queen Catherine. As to this, it may be allowed, that Dr Cranmer might think the marriage wrong; but though it possibly might be a point of conscience with the king, it could however be none with him; and there was manifestly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between advising not to do a thing, and advising to undo it when already done, at least in a matter of so disputable a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. On the other hand, to repudiate a woman with whom the king had cohabited near 20 years as his wife, and to illegitimate a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, bred up in the highest expectations, and now marriageable, were acts of such cruelty, that it seems to indicate a want of feeling to be in any degree <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a> to them. To this may be added, that the notoriety of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for Ann Boleyn, which all men believed to be, if not the first mover, at least the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of his pretended scruples, threw a very indelicate imputation on all who had any concern in the affair. No serious churchman, one would imagine, could be fond of the idea of administering to the king's passions. It is with concern, therefore, that we see a man of Dr Cranmer's integrity and simplicity of manners acting so much out of character as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> an affair of this kind, if not with his conscience, at least with all delicacy of sentiment; and to parade through Europe, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, defending everywhere the king's pious intentions. But the cause (continues Mr Gilpin) animated him. With the illegality of the king's marriage, he endeavoured virtually to establish the insufficiency of the pope's dispensation; and the latter was an argument so near his heart, that it seems to have added merit to the former. We cannot indeed account for his embarking so zealously in this business without supposing his principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> was to free his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from the tyranny of Rome; to which this step very evidently led. So desirable an end would in some degree, he might imagine, sanctify the means." Of two of the instances of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> in which Archbishop Cranmer was concerned, Mr Gilpin gives the following account. "Juan Bocher and George <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> were accused, though at different times; one for denying the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of Christ, the other for denying his divinity. They were both tried and condemned to the stake; and the archbishop not only consented to these acts of blood, but even persuaded the aversion of the young king into a compliance. 'Your majesty must distinguish (said he, informing his royal pupil's conscience) between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> opinions and such as are the essential articles of faith. These latter we must on no account suffer to be opposed.' Mr Gilpin justly observes, that 'nothing even plausible can be suggested in defence of the archbishop on this occasion, except only that the spirit of Popery was not yet wholly repressed.'" These instances of injustice and barbarity were indeed totally indefensible, and a great disgrace to Cranmer and to all who were concerned in them. It does not appear that he endeavoured to promote the death of Lambert; but, as Mr Gilpin observes, it were to be wished he had rid his hand of the disputation likewise. The public disputation, in which Cranmer bore some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, proved the means of bringing Lambert to the stake. One of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> transactions of Archbishop Cranmer's life, was the firm stand that he made against the act of the six articles. This act was so strongly supported by the king, that even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in parliament made little opposition to it. But Cranmer opposed it with great zeal and readiness. "The good archbishop (says Mr Gilpin) never appeared in a more truly Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than on this occasion. In the midst of so general a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a> (for there were numbers in the house who had hitherto shown great forwardness in reformation) he alone made a stand. Three days he maintained his ground, and baffled the arguments of all opposers. But argument was not their weapon, and the archbishop <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> himself obliged to sink under superior power. He may ordered him to leave the house. The primate refused: 'It was God's business (he said), and not man's. And when he could do no more, he boldly entered his protest. Such an instance of fortitude is sufficient to wipe off many of those courtly stains which have fallen on his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>.' His behaviour in the cause of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> was also entitled to great commendation. "The last Cranmer's act of this reign (says Mr Gilpin) was an act of blood, and gave the archbishop a noble opportunity of showing how well he had learned that great Christian lesson of forgiving an enemy. Almost without the shadow of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, Henry had given directions to have the duke of Norfolk attainted by an act of parliament. The king's mandate stood in lieu of guilt, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> passed the house with great ease. No man, except the bishop of Winchester, had been so great an enemy to the archbishop as the duke of Norfolk. He had always thwarted the primate's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, and often than once had practised against his life. How many would have seen with secret <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> the workings of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> against so rancorous an enemy? satisfied in having themselves no hand in his unjust fate! But the archbishop saw the affair in another light: he saw it with horror; and although the king had in a particular manner interested himself in this business, the primate opposed the bill with all his might; and when his opposition was vain, he left the house with indignation, and retired to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROYDON">Croydon</a>. He was indeed remarkable for the placability of his temper, and for showing kindness to those by whom he had been greatly injured. Hence it is mentioned in Shakespeare's Henry VIII. as a common saying concerning him: "Do my lord of Canterbury But one shrewd turn, and he's your friend for ever." Archbishop Cranmer was a great friend and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of learned foreigners, who had been persecuted for their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the principles of the reformation. Mr Gilpin says, "the suffering professors of Protestantism, who were scattered in great numbers about the various countries of Europe, were always sure of an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> with him. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Lambeth might be called a seminary of learned men; the greater part of whom persecution had driven from home. Here, among other celebrated reformers, Martyr, Bucer, Ales, Phage, found sanctuary. Martyr, Bucer, and Phage, were liberally pensioned by the archbishop till he could otherwise provide for them. It was his wish to fix them in the two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, where he hoped their great knowledge and spirit of inquiry would forward his designs of restoring learning; and he at length obtained professorships for them all. Bucer and Phage were settled at Cambridge; where they only showed what might have been expected from them, both dying within a few months after their arrival. But at Oxford Martyr acted a very conspicuous part, and contributed to introduce among the students there a very liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of thinking. Of the learning of Archbishop Cranmer, Mr Gilpin remarks, that "it was chiefly confined to his profession. He had applied himself in Cambridge to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Greek and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> languages; which though esteemed at that time as the mark of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, appeared to him the only sources of attaining a critical knowledge of the Scriptures. He had so accurately studied canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, that he was esteemed the best canonist in England; and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> was so extensive, and his collections from the Fathers so very voluminous, that there were few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> in which he was not accurately informed, and in which he could not give the opinions of the several ages of the church from the times of the apostles. He was a sensible writer, rather nervous than elegant. His writings were entirely confined to the great controversy which then subsisted, and contain the whole sum of the theological learning of those times. His library was filled with a very noble collection of books, and was open to all men of letters. Mr Gilpin, after remarking that Archbishop Cranmer preached often wherever he visited, says, "In his sermons to the people he was very plain and instructive; insisting chiefly on the essentials of Christianity. The subjects of his sermons, for the most part, were from whence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> is to be fetched, and on whom the confidence of man ought to lean. They insisted much on doctrines of faith and works; and taught what the fruits of faith were, and what place was to be given to works; they instructed men in the duties they owed their neighbour, and that every one was our neighbour, to whom we might any way do good; they declared what men ought to think of themselves after they had done all; and, lastly, what promises Christ hath made, and who they are to whom he will make them good. Thus he brought in the true preaching of the gospel, altogether different from the ordinary way of preaching in those days; which was to treat concerning saints, to tell legendary tales of them, and to report <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> wrought for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of transubstantiation and other popish corruptions. And such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of conviction accompanied his sermons, that the people departed from them with minds possessed of a great hatred of vice, and burning with a desire of virtue." He was a great economist of his time. Mr Gilpin says, "he rose <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> at five o'clock and continued in his study till nine. These early hours, he would say, were the only hours he could call his own. After breakfast he generally spent the remainder of the morning either in public or private business. His chapel-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> was eleven, and his dinner-hour twelve. After dinner he spent an hour either in conversation with his friends, in playing at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESS">chess</a>, or in, what he liked better, overlooking a chess-board. He then retired again to his study till his chapel-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> rang at five. After prayers, he generally walked till six, which was in those times the hour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>. His evening <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> was sparing. Often he ate nothing; and when that was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it was his usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, as he sat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, to draw on a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of gloves; which was as much as to say, that his hands had nothing to do. After supper, he spent an hour in walking and another in his study, retiring to his bedchamber about nine. This was his usual mode of living when he was most vacant, but very often his afternoons as well as his mornings were engaged in business. He generally, however, contrived, if possible, even in the buffet day, to devote some portion of his time to his books besides the morning. And Mr Fox tells us, he always accustomed himself to read and write in a standing posture; esteeming constant fitting very pernicious to a studious man." Mr Gilpin also observes, "that he was a very amiable <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in his family, and admirably preserved the difficult medium between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> and restraint. He had, according to the custom of the times, a very numerous retinue, among whom the most exact order was..." was observed. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> held a kind of court in the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of his palace; in which all family affairs were settled, servants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> were paid, complaints were heard, and faults examined. Delinquents were publicly rebuked, and after the third admonition discharged. His hospitality and charities were great and noble; equal to his station, greater often than his abilities. A plentiful table was among the virtues of those days. His was always bountifully covered. In an upper room was spread his own, where he seldom wanted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of the first distinction. Here a great many learned foreigners were daily entertained, and partook of his bounty. In his great hall a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> table was plentifully covered every day for guests and strangers of a lower <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>: at the upper end of which were three smaller tables, designed for his own officers and inferior gentlemen. Among other instances of the archbishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, we have one recorded which was truly noble. After the destruction of monasteries, and before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> were erected, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> saw no <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of greater misery than that of wounded and disbanded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. For the use of such miserable objects as were landed on the southern coasts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, the archbishop fitted up his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>-house of Beckesbourn in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>. He formed it indeed into a complete <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>; appointing a physician, a surgeon, nurses, and everything proper, as well for food as physic. Nor did his charity stop here. Each man, on his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, was furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to carry him home, in proportion to the distance of his abode." To conclude with the character given by Mr Hume: "Archbishop Cranmer was undoubtedly a man of merit; possessed of learning and capacity; and adorned with candour, sincerity, and beneficence, and all those virtues which were fitted to render him useful and amiable in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. His moral qualities procured him universal respect; and the courage of his martyrdom, though he fell short of the rigid inflexibility observed in many, made him the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of the Protestant party."

CRANNY

Pages 347-347

in glass-making, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> wherewith the necks of glasses are formed.

CRANTARA

Pages 347-347

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Britons, was a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> signal used for collecting the distant and scattered warriors to the standard of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> having immediate occasion for the assistance of his followers to repel some sudden invasion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> engage in some expedition, besides striking the shield and sounding the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> to give warning to those who were within hearing, he sent the crantara, or a stick burnt at the end and dipped in the blood of a goat, by a swift messenger, to the nearest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a>, where he delivered it without saying one word but the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of rendezvous. This crantara, which was well understood to denote destruction by fire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> to all who did not obey this summons, was carried with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rapidity from village to village; and the prince in a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> found himself surrounded by all his warriors ready to obey his commands.

CRANTOR

Pages 347-347

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and poet, was born at Solos in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>. He left his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where he was admired; went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and there studied with Polemon under Xenocrates. He was considered as one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> supporters of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>; and was the first who wrote commentaries upon <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>'s works. He flourished 270 years before Christ.

CRAP

Pages 347-347

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> transparent stuff, in manner of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>: made of raw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> gummed and twisted on the mill; woven without crofting, and much used in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>. Crapes are either craped, i.e. crispied, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> smooth; the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, expressing a closer mourning; the latter single, used for that less deep. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> is reserved for young people, or those devoted to virginity. The silk destined for the first is more twisted than that for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>; it being the greater or less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of twisting, especially of the warp, which produces the crisping given it when taken out of the loom, steeped in clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and rubbed with a piece of wax for the purpose. Crapes are all dyed raw. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of this stuff came originally from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>: but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> manufacture of it is said to be at Lyons. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> tells us, that St Bathilda, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of France, made fine crap (crepa) of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, to lay over the body of St Eloy. The Bollandists own they cannot find what this crepa was. Binet says, it was a frame to cover the body of the saint: but others, with reason, take it to be a transparent stuff, through which the body might be seen; and that this was the crepa whence our word crap was formed.

CRASHAW

Pages 347-348

RICHARD, who was in his lifetime honoured with the friendship of Cowley, and since his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the praise of Mr Pope, who condescended both to read his poems and to borrow from them, was the son of William Crashaw, an eminent divine, and educated at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">Charter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He was then sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and was afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>-house, where he was fellow; in both which colleges he was distinguished for his Latin and English <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. Afterwards he was ejected from his fellowship, together with many others, for denying the covenant in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the rebellion; and he changed his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, being by catholic artifices converted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome; not converted, but rather, as Pope says, outwitted. He went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in hopes of recommending himself to some preferment there; but being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> scholar, was incapable of executing the new <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> he had formed. There he fell into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distress, which Cowley the poet hearing of in 1646, very kindly fought him out, gave him all the assistance he could, and at last got him recommended to Henrietta <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of England, then residing at Paris. Obtaining from her letters of recommendation, he travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and by virtue of those letters became secretary to a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> at Rome, and at last one of the canons <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chaplains of the rich church of our lady at Loreto, some miles distance from thence, where he died and was buried about 1650. Before he left England he wrote certain poems, entitled, "Steps to the Temple;" because (says Wood) he led his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the temple of God, in St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s church near to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. There, as we learn from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to these poems, he lodged under Tertullian's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. There he made his nest more gladly than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s swallow near the house of God; where, like a primitive saint, he offered more prayers in the night than others usually offer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. There he penned the said poems called "Steps to the Temple for Happy Souls to Climb to Heaven by." To the said Steps are joined other poems called "The Delight of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>," wherein are several Latin poems: which though of a mere <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mixture, yet they are sweet as they are innocent. He hath also written Carmen Deo nostro, being hymns and other sacred poems, addressed to the countess of Denbigh. He was excellent in five languages besides his mother tongue, namely, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Greek, Latin, Italian, and Spanish.

CRASIS

Pages 348-348

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> whereby two different letters are either contracted into one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a diphthong. Such, e.g., is πις for φις; αλην for αληνα, &c.; τοξες for τοξες, &c., where οι and ει are contracted into οι, and η and ι into η; and οι and ει into οι.

CRASSAMENTUM

Pages 348-348

in Physic, the thick <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the blood, otherwise called eruor, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the serum or aqueous part.

CRASSULA

Pages 348-348

lesser orpine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Live-ever: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 13th order, Succulentae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CRASSUS

Pages 348-349

M. Licinius, a celebrated Roman, farnamed Rich on account of his opulence. At first he was very circumcribed in his circumstances, but by educating slaves and selling them at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price he soon enriched himself. The cruelties of Cinna obliged him to leave Rome, and he retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, where he remained concealed for eight months. After Cinna's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he passed into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and thence to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he served Sylla and ingratiated himself in his favour. When the gladiators with Spartacus at their head had spread an universal alarm in Italy and defeated some of the Roman generals, Crassus was sent against them. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was fought, in which Crassus slaughtered 12,000 of the slaves, and by this decisive blow soon put an end to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and was honoured with an ovatio at his return. He was soon after made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> with Pompey in the year of Rome 682, and in this high office he displayed his opulence by entertaining the populace at 10,000 tables. He was afterwards censor, and formed the first triumvirate with Pompey and Caesar. As his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> was more predominant than that of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, Crassus never imitated the ambitious conduct of his colleagues, but was satisfied with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, which seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> an inexhaustible source of wealth. With hopes of enlarging his possessions he set off from Rome, though the omens proved unfavourable, and everything seemed to threaten his ruin. He crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, and forgetful of the rich cities of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, he hastened to make himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>. He was betrayed in his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> by the delay of Artavasdes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, and the perfidy of Ariamnes. He was met in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plain by Surena the general of the forces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORODES">Orodes</a> king of Parthia, and a battle was fought in which 20,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were killed and 10,000 taken prisoners. The darkness of the night favoured the escape of the rest; and Crassus, forced by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> and turbulence of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and the treachery of his guides, trusted himself to the general of the enemy on pretence of proposing terms of accommodation, and he was killed. His head was cut off and sent to Orodes, who poured melted <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his throat, and insulted his misfortunes. Though he has been called avaricious, yet he showed himself always ready of lending <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to his friends without <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. He was fond of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and his knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and extensive. CRATÆGUS, wild-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> tree, Hawthorn, &c. A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the icosandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 36th order, Pomaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The oxyanthus, hawthorn, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">thorn</a>, grows naturally all over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It is sometimes cultivated as an ornamental tree, but it is chiefly propagated for the purpose of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a>. In order to propagate a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of quick, one method is generally practised; namely, first burying the haws, and taking them up to sow the October following; though, says Hanbury, there is another way more preferable; namely, to prepare the beds, and sow the haws soon after they are gathered. Whoever pursues the former method, having gathered what quantity of haws <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> answer his purpose, should in some bye-corner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-garden or nursery dig a hole or pit capacious enough to receive them; some of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> which came out of the hole, after the haws are put in it, should be laid upon them; and being thus carefully covered down, they may remain there till October. Then, having ground well dug, and cleared of the roots of all troublesome weeds, and the mould being fit for working, the beds should be made for the haws. Four feet is a very good width of these beds, as they may be easily reached over to be weeded; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the alleys between be each one foot and a half wide, they will be of a good size. The beds being marked out with a line, sufficient mould must be raked out to cover the haws an inch and a half deep. This being done, and the bottom of the beds being made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> and even the haws should be sown, and afterwards gently tapped down with the back of the spade; and then the fine mould, which had been raked out of the beds, must be thrown over them, covering them an inch and a half deep. In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> the plants will come up, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> following should be kept clear of weeds; though it does sometimes happen, that few of them will appear till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> spring after sowing. Sometimes the young plants are planted out from the feed-beds at one, two, or three years old; but the best plants are obtained by transplanting them into fresh mould the first or second year, letting them remain in the nursery two or three years longer. The practice of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> nurserymen is this: The strongest of the feed-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> plants having been drawn at two or three years old for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, they clear the beds entirely by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the remaining weak underling plants, and transplanting them into fresh beds in this manner, which they call bedding them: The ground having been trenched, and the tips of the plants as well as the lower fibres of their roots having been taken off with a sharp <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, they strain a line along one side of the bed; and by chopping with a spade by the side of the line, leave a cliff or drill of a depth proportioned to the length of the plants to be laid in; and drawing the loofe mould somewhat towards them, leave the side of the drill next to the line with a smooth polished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. Against this face the plants are set up, leaning towards the line, about three inches asunder, leaving their heads about an inch above the mould, and placing their roots at such a depth as to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their stems from two to three inches deeper than they stood in the seed-bed. The loose mould being returned and pressed gently to the roots with the foot, the line is removed, and another row planted in the same manner about a foot from the first.

CRATCHES

Pages 349-349

in the manege, a swelling on the pateform, under the fetlock, and sometimes under the hoof; for which reason it is distinguished into the finer cratches, which affect the finer, and those upon the coronet, called quitter-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>.

CRATER

Pages 349-349

Cup, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the southern hemisphere; whose stars, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>; in Tycho's, eight; in Hevelius's ten; in the Britannic catalogue, thirty-one. Crater is also used to signify the mouth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> opening of a volcano or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> mountain, from whence the fire is discharged. See Volcano.

CRATES

Pages 349-349

of Thebes, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> the Cynic. It is said that he threw all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, that he might the more freely apply himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. Others assert that he placed it into another person's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, with orders to give it to his children <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they should happen to be fools: For (said Crates), if they should be philosophers, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have no need of it: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it was to be given to the people. He flourished about 328 years before Christ. He ought not to be confounded with Crates, a famous Academic philosopher, the disciple and friend of Polemon. This last Crates had Arcesilaus and other celebrated philosophers for his disciples; and flourished about 300 years before Christ.

CRATEVA

Pages 349-349

the GARLIC <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">PEAR</a>: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dodecandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 25th order, Putamineae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CRATINUS

Pages 349-349

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> comic poet, of whom we should scarcely have known anything, had not Quintilian, Horace, and Persius, mentioned him, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPOLIS">Eupolis</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> masters of what we call the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>. It is gathered that he died in the 87th Olympiad. Suidas tells us that he wrote 21 plays, and that he was splendid and bright in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>.

CRATIPPUS

Pages 349-349

a celebrated Peripatetic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was a native of Mitylene, where he taught <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; but at length went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, where Brutus and the son of Cicero were his disciples. Pompey went to see him after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>, and proposed to him his difficulties in relation to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>; when Cratippus comforted him, and by forcible arguments answered his objections. He wrote some pieces about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>: and is supposed to be the same with him whom Tertullian, in his book De Anima, has ranked among the writers upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>.

CRATO

Pages 349-350

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALENTEJO">Alentejo</a>, with a rich priory. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commandery which the knights of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a> have in Portugal. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 12. N. Lat. 38. 50. Vol. VI. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. the feet of our Saviour. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> deligh of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRAYON">Crayon</a>; and although it consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of figures, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and union are well preserved.

CRAYON

Pages 350-355

a general name for all coloured <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, earths, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other minerals and substances, used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in pastel; whether they have been beaten and reduced to a paste, or are used in their primitive consistence, after sawing or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow slips. In this last manner are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> crayons made, of blood-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or red chalk; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> ones, of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> and black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. Crayons of all other colours are compositions of earths reduced to paste. Crayon-Painting. Whether the painter works with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-colours, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-colours, or crayons, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> object of his pursuit is still the same: a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. But each <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> has its peculiar rules and methods. Painting with crayons requires in many respects a treatment different from painting in oil-colours; because all colours used dry are in their nature of a much warmer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> than when wet with oils, &c. For this reason, in order to produce a rich <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, a much greater portion of what painters <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> cooling teints must be applied in crayon painting than would be judicious to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in oils. Without any danger of a mistake, it is to be supposed, the not being acquainted with this observation is one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cause why so many oil painters have no better success when they attempt crayon-painting. On the contrary, crayon painters being so much used to those teints which are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> nature when used wet, are apt to introduce them too much when they paint with oils, which is seldom productive of a good effect. We shall now endeavour to give the students some directions towards the attainment of excellence in this art. Of the Application of the Crayons, with some previous Dispositions. The student must provide himself with some strong blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, the thicker the better, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the grain is not too coarse or knotty, though it is almost impossible to get any entirely free from knots. The knots should be levelled with a penknife or razor, otherwise they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> prove exceedingly troublesome. After this is done, the paper must be pasted very smooth on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, previously strained on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> frame, the size according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>: on this the picture is to be executed; but it is most eligible not to paste the paper on till the whole subject is first dead coloured. The method of doing this is very easy, by laying the paper with the dead-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> on its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, upon a smooth board or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, when, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, the back side of the paper must be covered with paste; the frame, with the strained cloth, must then be laid on the pasted side of the paper; after which turn the painted side uppermost, and lay a piece of clean paper upon it, to prevent smearing it: this being done, it may be stroked gently over with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; by which means all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> between the cloth and the paper will be forced out. When the paste is perfectly dry, the student may proceed with the painting. The advantages arising from pasting the paper on the frame according to this method, after the picture is begun, are very great, as the crayons will adhere much better than any other way; which will enable the student to finish the picture with a firmer body of colour and greater lustre. When the painters want to make a very correct copy of a picture, they generally make use of tiffany or black <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>, strained tight on a frame, which they lay flat on the subject to be imitated, and with a piece of sketching chalk trace all the outlines on the tiffany. They then lay the canvas to be painted on flat upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, placing the tiffany with the chalked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> upon it, and with an handkerchief brush the whole over; this presents the exact outlines of the picture on the canvas. The crayon painter may also make use of this method when the subject of his imitation is in oils; but in copying a crayon-picture, he must have recourse to the following method, on account of the glaigs. The picture being placed upon the easel, let the outlines be drawn on the glaigs with a small camel's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> dipped in lake, ground thin with oils, which must be done with great exactness. After this is accomplished, take a sheet of paper of the same size and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it on the glaigs, stroking over all the lines with the hand, by which means the colour will adhere to the paper, which must be pierced with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>-holes pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to each other. The paper intended to be used for the painting must next be laid upon a table, and the pierced paper placed upon it; then with some fine-pounded charcoal, tied up in a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a>, rub over the pierced lines, which will give an exact outline; but great care must be taken not to brush this off till the whole is drawn over with sketching chalk, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> made of whiting and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>-pipe clay, rolled like the crayons, and pointed at each end.
