Besides these scattered remains of the ancient creeds, there are extant some perfect forms, as those of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, Caesarea, Antioch, &c. The most universal creeds are, the Apostolical, the Athanasian, and the Nicene creeds. See these articles. These three creeds are used in the public offices of the church of England; and subscription to them is required of all the established clergy. Subscription to these was also required of the dissenting teachers, by the toleration <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>; but from which they are now relieved by 19 Geo. III.

CREEK

Pages 361-361

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a haven, where anything is landed from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. So many landing places as there are in a harbour <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> port, so many creeks there are. It is also said to be a shore or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> whereon the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> beats, running in a small channel from any part of the sea; from the Latin crepidus. This word is used in the flat. 4 Hen. IV. c. 20. and 5 Eliz. c. 5. CREENGLES. See Cringle. CRÉPER, See Certhia, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CREEPER

Pages 361-361

in naval affairs, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> resembling a grappling, having a flank, and four hooks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> claws. It is used to throw into the bottom of any river or harbour, with a rope fastened to it, to hook and draw up anything from the bottom which may have been lost. See Plate CL.

CREIIO

Pages 371-371

in Antiquity, a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of days allowed the heir to consider whether he would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> as heir to the deceased <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not; after which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he did not act, he was excluded from the estate.

CRELLIUS

Pages 361-361

JOHN, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCINIAN">Socinian</a>, born in 1590, in a village near <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>. In 1612 he went into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, where the Unitarians had a school, in which he became professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and minister at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a>, where he died in 1632, aged 42. He was the author, 1. Of a famous Treatise against the Mystery of the Trinity; 2. Commentaries on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; and other works. All of them are scarce.

CREMA

Pages 361-361

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and bishop's see of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a district of the Milanese, called from it Cremafo; it stands almost in the middle between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 15. and N. Lat. 45. 20.

CREMASTER

Pages 361-361

in Anatomy, the names of a muscle of the testicle, of which there is one on each side. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CREMATION">CREMATION</a> is sometimes used for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, particularly when applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of burning the dead. This custom is well known to have prevailed among most eastern nations, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with their descendants after they had peopled the different parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Hence we find it prevailing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, till Christianity abolished it.

CREMONA

Pages 361-362

CREMONA, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a Roman colony, with municipal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, settled beyond the Po, below the confluence of the Addua, on the report of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> (Polybius): a town at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> still maintaining its name and flourishing state. It was an opulent and mercantile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; but suffered greatly in the civil wars of Augustus (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>). In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Vitellius, it was destroyed by the partizans of Vespasian; but was soon after rebuilt by the munificence of the citizens and exhortations of Vespasian, (Tacitus). Now <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Cremonese, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 30'. Lat. 45°.

CRENELLE

Pages 362-362
or IMBATTLED, in Heraldry, is used when any honourable ordinary is drawn, like the battlements on a wall to defend men from the enemies shot. This attribute belongs to the arms of such as have defended castles for their prince or country, or of such as are killed in architecture.

CRENOPHYLAX

Pages 362-362

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, who had the inspection of fountains.

CREODIBA

Pages 362-362

in the customs of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, a robbery and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> committed in a wood, where the body of the person killed was burnt in order to prevent any discovery of the crime. The word, says Wendelinus, is compounded of cruy and diven, that is, "wood-robbes."

CREOLES

Pages 362-362

a name originally given to the families descended from the Spaniards who first settled at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. These are much more numerous than the Spaniards properly so called, and the Mulattoes, which two other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of inhabitants they distinguish; and are excluded from all considerable employments. It is now used in a more extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and applied to all natives of the West Indies.

CREON

Pages 362-362

son of Menoeceus, was father to Jocasta, the wife and mother of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OEDIPUS">Oedipus</a>. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Laius, who had married Jocasta without knowing that she was his mother, and by her he had two sons, Polynices and Eteocles. These two sons mutually agreed after their father's death to reign in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> each a year alternately. Eteocles first ascended the throne by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of seniority; but when he was once in power he refused to resign at the appointed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> led against him an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Argives to support his right. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> was decided by a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> between the two brothers. They both killed one another, and Creon ascended the throne till Leodamus the son of Eteocles should be of sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> to assume the reins of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. In his regal capacity he commanded that the Argives, and more particularly Polynices, who was the cause of all the bloodshed, should remain unburied. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this was in any manner disobeyed, the offenders were to be buried alive. Antigone the sister of Polynices transgressed, and was accordingly punished. Haemon the son of Creon, who was passionately fond of Antigone, killed himself on her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, when his father refused to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>. Creon was afterwards killed by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>, who had made war with him because he refused <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> to the Argives.

CREPANCE

Pages 362-362

in the manege, a chop <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cratch in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s leg, given by the spunges of the shoes of one of the hinder feet croffing and striking against the other hinder foot. This cratch degenerates into an ulcer. CREPIDÆ, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a kind of slippers or shoes, which were always worn with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALLIUM">pallium</a>, as the calcei were with the toga.

CREPIS

Pages 362-362

HAWK-WEEED: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CREPITATION

Pages 362-362

that noise which some salts make over the fire in calcination, called also detonation. CREPITATION is also used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, for the noise made by the ends <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, when the surgeon moves a limb to assure himself by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> of the existence of a fracture.

CREPUNDIA

Pages 362-362

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express such things as were exposed along with children, as rings, jewels, &c., serving as tokens whereby they afterwards might be known.

CREPUSCULUM

Pages 362-362

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, twilight; the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> from the first dawn <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appearance of the morning to the rising of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; and again, between the setting of the sun and the last remains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPIAS">Papias</a> derives the word from creperus; which, he says, anciently signified uncertain, doubtful, q. d. a dubious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. The crepusculum is usually computed to begin and end when the sun is about 18 degrees below the horizon; for then the stars of the sixth magnitude disappear in the morning and appear in the evening. It is of longer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> in the solstices than in the equinoxes, and longer in an oblique than in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> sphere. The crepuscula are occasioned by the sun's rays refracted in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and reflected from the particles thereof to the eye. See TWILIGHT.

CRESCENT

Pages 362-363

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> in form of a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. The Ottomans bear simple, a crescent montant, argent. The crescent is frequently used as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in coat armour, to distinguish it for that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> junior family. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the crescent is the Turkish symbol; or rather is that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> Byzantium, which bore this device from all antiquity; as appears from medals struck in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Augustus, Trajan, &c. The crescent is sometimes montant, i.e., its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> look towards the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, which is its most ordinary representation; whence some contend, that the crescent, absolutely so called, implies that situation; though other authors blazon it montant, when the horns are towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEXTER">dexter</a> side of the escutcheon, in which position others call it inversifont. Crescents are said to be adsofed, when their backs or thickest parts are turned towards each other; their points looking to the sides of the shield. Crescent <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, is that whose points look towards the bottom; turned crescents are placed like those adsofed; the difference is, that all their points look to the dexter side of the shield: contoured crescents, on the contrary, look to the sinister side: affronted or appointed crescents, are contrary to the adsofed, the points looking towards each other. CRESCENT is also the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order, instituted by Renatus of Anjou, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, &c., in 1448; so called from the badge or symbol thereof, a crescent of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> enamelled. What gave occasion to this establishment was, that Renatus took for his device a crescent, with the word lox, "praise," which, in the style of rebus, makes lox in crescent, q.d. by advancing in virtue, one merits praise.

CRESCENTIA

Pages 363-363

the CALABASH TREE: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 25th order, Putaminæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The shells of calabashes are made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for various purposes. At Barbadoes, besides drinking-cups and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCH">punch</a>-bowls, there are made of them spoons, dippers, and other utensils for the slaves. Some of these shells are too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, as to be capable of holding 15 pints of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The pulp is seldom eaten, except by cattle in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of drought. The wood, which is hard and smooth, is made into stools, chairs, and other furniture.

CRESCIMBENI

Pages 363-363

JOHN <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">MARIA</a>, an Italian poet, was born at Macerata in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, 1663. His talents for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and eloquence developed themselves early. His verses at first had too much pomp and point; but residing in Rome, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the best Italian poets, brought him back to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. He not only reformed himself, but undertook to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in general. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> he projected the establishment of a new academy, under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>; the members of which at first did not exceed 14, but afterwards increased much. They called themselves the shepherds of Arcadia, and each took the name of some shepherd and some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. The founder of this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> was appointed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of it in 1690, and held this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> 38 years; namely, to the year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1728. Among a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of works, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> and prose, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> is, A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Italian Poetry, very much esteemed, and reprinted, in 1731, at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, in five volumes, 4to. This history is accompanied with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a>, containing anecdotes of Italian poets. He published also A History of the Academy of Arcadia, together with the Lives of the most illustrious Arcadians; and many other works.

CRESS

Pages 363-363
WATER CRESS, OR CRESSES. See Sisymbrium, Botany Index. Indian CRESS. See Tropæolum, Botany Index.

CRESSY

Pages 363-364

a port town of Picardy in France, about 44 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>, and 27 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBEVILLE">Abbeville</a>, remarkable on account of the victory obtained there over the French by Edward III. of England, in the year 1346. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° O. N. Lat. 50° 20'. Edward having encountered and overcome many difficulties in his expedition, was at last so closely followed and harried by the French <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, commanded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France in person, that he determined to make a stand at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and to give his pursuers a check. For this purpose he chose his ground with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> judgment, on the gentle declivity of a hill, with a thick wood in his rear. He ordered deep entrenchments to be made on each flank, and waited with firmness the approach of his enemies. The king of France, dreading nothing so much as the escape of the English, began the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> of his great army from Abbeville early in the morning, August 26, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> it several hours with great eagerness, till he received intelligence that the English had halted at Cressy, and were prepared to give him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. He was advised at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> not to engage that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, when his troops were much fatigued with their march, and in great disorder; and he was disposed to have taken this advice. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of these times was so imperfect, that the orders given for halting were not obeyed; and one corps of this mighty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a> impelling another, they continued advancing till they came into the presence of their enemies in much confusion. Edward had employed the forenoon of this important day in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up his army in the most excellent order, in three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. The first line, which consisted of 800 men at arms, 4000 English archers, and 600 Welsh foot, was commanded by his young, amiable, and heroic son, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, assisted by the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and several other noblemen. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> line, composed of 800 men at arms, 4000 halberdiers, and 2400 archers, was led by the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a>; the last line <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> body of reserve, in which were 700 men at arms, 5300 billmen, and 6000 archers, was ranged along the summit of the hill, and conducted by the king in person, attended by the lords Mowbray, Mortimer, and others. When the army was completely formed, Edward rode along the lines, and by his words and looks inspired his troops with the most ardent courage and strongest hopes of victory. He then commanded the cavalry to dismount, and the whole army to sit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon the grass, in their ranks, and refresh themselves with meat, drink, and rest. As soon as the French army came in view, they sprung from the ground, full of strength and spirit, and stood ready to receive them. The king of France, assisted by the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a>, the dukes of Lorraine and Savoy, and several other sovereign princes, with the flower of the French <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, laboured to restore some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of of order to his prodigious army, and drew it up also in three lines, but very indistinctly formed. The first line was commanded in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> by the king of Bohemia; the second by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Alençon, the king of France's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>; and the third by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> in person; and each of these lines contained a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of troops than the whole English army. The battle of Cressy was begun about three o'clock in the afternoon, August 26, by a great body of Genoese crossbowmen, in the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, who let fly their quarrels at too great a distance to do any execution, and were presently routed by a shower of arrows from the English archers. The earl of Alençon, after trampling to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> many of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> Genoese, advanced to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, and made a furious attack on that corps commanded by the prince of Wales. The earls of Arundel and Northampton advanced with the second line to sustain the prince, and Alençon was supported by as many troops as could crowd to his assistance. Here the battle raged for some time with uncommon fury; and the earl of Warwick, anxious for the fate of the day and the safety of the prince, sent a messenger to the king, intreating him to advance with the third line. Edward, who had taken his stand on a windmill on the top of the hill, from whence he had a full view of both armies, asked the messenger, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his son was unhorsed, or wounded, or killed? and being answered, that the prince was unhurt, and performed prodigies of valour. "Go then," said he, "and tell my son and his brave companions, that I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not deprive them of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of their victory." This flattering message being made known, inspired the prince and his troops with redoubled ardour; and the king of Bohemia, the earl of Alençon, and many other great men, being slain, the whole first and second lines of the French army were put to flight. Philip, undismayed at the slaughter of his troops, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of so many princes, advanced to the charge with the line under his immediate command. But this body soon shared the same fate with the other two; and Philip, after having been unhorsed, and wounded in the neck and thigh, was carried off the field by John de Hainault, and fled with no more than five knights and about 60 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, of all his mighty army, which at the beginning of the battle consisted of more than 120,000 men. Such was the famous victory of Cressy, the greatest ever gained by any king of England. After the battle, the king flew into the arms of the prince of Wales, and grasping him to his bosom, cried in an ecstacy of joy, "My dear son, you have this day shewed yourself worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> which you lately received, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> for which you have so bravely fought; persevere in your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> course." The prince, as modest as he was brave, sunk down on his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> covered with blushes, and begged his father's blessing. Edward continued with his army at Cressy three days, employed in numbering and burying the dead. The French had left on this bloody <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> the king of Bohemia, 11 other princes, 80 <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANNERETS">bannerets</a>, 1200 knights, 1500 gentlemen, 4000 men at arms, and 30,000 other soldiers.

CREST

Pages 364-364

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> placed above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> in an achievement. See Heraldry. CREST-fallen, a fault of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, when the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his neck, called the crest, hangs to one side; this they cure by placing it upright, clipping away the spare skin, and applying plasters to keep it in a proper position.

CRETE

Pages 364-367

one of the largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Mediterranean, lying between 22 and 27 degrees of east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 35 and 36 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. According to Strabo, this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is 287 miles in length; and according to Pliny, 270; and according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYLAX">Scylax</a>, 312. As to its breadth, it is not, as Pliny observes, above 55 miles where widest; whence it was styled, as Stephanus observes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> Island. It has the Archipelago to the north, the African <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to the south, the Carpathian sea to the east, and the Ionian to the west. Anciently it was known by the names of Aeria, Chthonia, Idea, Curete, Macaritis, &c., but its most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name was that of Crete. The Cretan mythologists, quoted by Diodorus Siculus, relate that the first inhabitants of the island were the Daityli Idei, who dwelt around Mount Ida; they were regarded as magicians, because they possessed a variety of knowledge, and were particularly skilled... Crete led in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, who distinguished himself highly in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and music, was their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>. They discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of fire, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and invented the art of working these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> in Be- recynthius, a mountain near Aptera. Those invaluable discoveries procured them divine honours. One of them, named <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, rendered himself famous by his courage and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> exploits. He instituted the Olympic games; though posterity, by a mistake arising from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the same name, have ascribed that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to the son of Alcmene; who, indeed, trod in the steps of his predecessor, and raised himself also to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>. The Dactyli Idaei were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CURETES">Curetes</a>. These last at first inhabited the forests and caves of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Afterwards they entered into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and contributed, by their institutions, to the civilization of mankind. They taught men to collect flocks of sheep, to tame the ferocity of wild animals for domestic purposes, and to invite bees into hives, that they might sate them of the fruit of their labours. They first prompted men to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, and taught the use of the bow. They were the inventors of swords and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> dances. The noise which they made, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> in armour, hindered <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> from hearing the cries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> Rhea had entrusted to them. With the assistance of the nymphs, they brought up that god in a cave in Mount Ida, feeding him with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of the goat Amalthea, and with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. To this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> affixes the origin of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITANS">Titans</a>; their abode near Gnoiuss, where stood the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Rhea; their travels over the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>; the nuptials of Jupiter and Juno, celebrated nigh the river Therenus in Crete; the gods, goddesses, and heroes, who descended from them. The most illustrious of those heroes were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHADAMANTHUS">Rhadamanthus</a>. They are said to have been the sons of Jupiter and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPA">Europa</a>, who was conveyed into the island on a bull. Minos becoming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, built several cities; the most considerable of which are—Gnoiuss, on that side of the island which faces <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Phocuss on the southern shore, and Cydon on the western, facing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>. He gave to his subjects a code of admirable laws, which he pretended to have received from his father Jupiter in the grotto of Mount Ida. Rhadamanthus distinguished himself by the impartiality of his judgments, and by the inflexible severity with which he inflicted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> on the impious and wicked. His empire extended over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> isles of the Archipelago, and the inhabitants of the adjacent coasts of Asia submitted to him on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation for probity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Mythologists have constituted him judge in the regions below, to determine the future state of the righteous and the wicked. They have conferred on him the same honours which were bestowed on Minos, the justest of kings. Thus far have been followed the Cretan traditions as they are related by Diodorus; but historians differ about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of them. There are a variety of opinions concerning the first inhabitants of Crete. Strabo, who has discussed them with great erudition, says, after several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> on the subject; "I am not fond of fables; yet I have detailed these at some length, because they are connected with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. Every discourse concerning the gods should examine the religious opinions of antiquity, and distinguish them from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were pleased to conceal their knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> under a veil. It is now impossible to unfold the meaning of their enigmas. But by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> the numerous allegories which they have left us, and by examining attentively their mutual relations and differences, genius may perhaps be able to unfold the truths which are couched under them." But leaving mythology for the more certain records and monuments of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, we find that Crete received its name from Ctes, the first of its monarchs. He was author of several useful inventions, which contributed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of his subjects. Prompted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, they endeavoured to perpetuate the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his favours, and to immortalize his name, by naming the island after him. In order to distinguish the true Cretans from strangers, they were named Eteocretes. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of colonies, from different parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, settled in the island. The agreeableness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, and the fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, invited them to fix their habitation there. The Lacedaemonians, Argives, and Athenians, were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> people who sent colonies into Crete. This is what makes <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> say, "Crete is an extensive island in the midst of the stormy main. The soil is rich and fertile. It contains an immense number of inhabitants. It is adorned with a hundred cities. Its inhabitants speak in various languages. We find there Achaeans, valiant Eteocretes, Cydonians, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORIANS">Dorians</a>, and godlike Pelaegians." The Eteocretes inhabited the northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the island; they built there the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Proetus, and erected a temple to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> Jove. Ctes was not the only monarch who reigned in the island of Crete. He had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of successors. But history affords little information concerning them: only the names of a few of them are preserved, and a small number of events which happened under the reign of some others, but blended and disfigured with an intermixture of fable. Among those monarchs we find two Jupiters, and two of the name of Minos. However, most writers confound them, and ascribe to one those transactions and exploits which should be shared between the two. This remark chiefly regards Minos, who was esteemed the wisest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> of antiquity. The office assigned him in the regions below is a clear and certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his having gained an exalted reputation by his justice. Greece, says <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, has with great propriety adopted the laws of Crete; for they are founded on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> basis of reason and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, and have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> tendency to render the people, who live in subjection to them, opulent and happy. One of those laws forbade "the Cretans ever to carry their fertility so far as to intoxicate themselves with wine." The following was very suitable to repulse the presumptuous ardour of youth: "Let young people not canvass the laws with an indiscreet curiosity; let them not examine whether the lawgiver has done <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wrong in promulgating them; but let them join unanimously in declaring them good, since they proceed from the gods. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any of the old men perceive something thing in them meriting amendment, let him mention it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, or discuss it with his equals, but never in the presence of the young people." That excellent code was engraven on tables of brass; and Talos, chief minister to Minos, visited all the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and cities in the island, three times a-year, to observe in what manner the laws were executed and obeyed. The king of Crete, well knowing that the marvellous is necessary to command the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> and enforce the obedience of the people, pretended that he had received those laws from his father Jupiter, in the grotto of Mount Ida. In the same manner, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, before promulgating his laws, repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>, and gave out they had received the sanction of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>. A like reason induced Numa to pretend an intimacy with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGERIA">Egeria</a>, and Mahomet to ascribe his doctrines and institutions to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> of the angel Gabriel. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to this account, others of the ancients describe Minos as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> impotently abandoned to the fury of his passions, and a barbarous conqueror. Falling passionately in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with the nymph Dictynna, who refused to gratify his wishes, he pursued her to the brink of the shore, and forced her to plunge into the sea, where she was saved by some fishermen, who received her in their nets. He was the first of the Greeks who appeared in the Mediterranean at the head of a naval armament. He conquered the Cyclades, expelled the Carianians, established Cretan colonies in those islands, and committed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of them to his son. Being informed, while he was at Paros, that his son <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol1.html#article-ANDROGEUS">Androgeus</a> was slain at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, he declared war against Egeus, and imposed on him a disgraceful tribute; from the payment of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a> delivered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He took arms against Nilus, king of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, made him prisoner by the treachery of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYLLA">Scylla</a>, and put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, together with Megarus, the son of Hippomane, who had brought some forces to his assistance. Daedalus, who had by some means incurred his displeasure, despairing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> from so severe and inflexible a prince, employed the resources of his inventive genius, in order to escape from his power. He fled to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, gained the protection of King Cocalus, and obtained an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Valerius Flaccus has described his flight in a very lively and picturesque manner. "Thus Daedalus, with the wings of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, ascended from Mount Ida. Beside him flew the comrade of his flight, with shorter wings. They appeared like a cloud rising in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Minos, seeing his vengeance thus eluded, glowed with impotent rage. In vain he followed with his eyes the secure flight of his enemies through the wide expanse of heaven. His guards returned to Gortyna with their quivers filled with arrows." The Cretan monarch did not, however, give up his prey. He equipped a fleet, pursued the fugitive to Sicily, and fell before the walls of Camicum. It is plain, that those actions cannot agree to the character of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> monarch, whose merits raised him to the office of determining, in the regions below, the unalterable fate of the righteous and the wicked. We may, therefore, reasonably conclude, that Minos the legislator is a different person from the conqueror; that it was the former who gained a lasting reputation by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and justice; and the latter who subdued most of the islands of the Archipelago, but being enslaved by his passions, tarnished his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> by his cruelty and merciless thirst for vengeance. The last king of Crete was Idomeneus. This prince, accompanied by Merion, conducted 24 ships to the assistance of Agamemnon. Homer informs us of the illustrious exploits by which he signalized himself before the walls of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. At his departure, he committed the government of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> to Leucus his adopted son, promising him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of his daughter Clytthera if he governed wisely in his absence. That ambitious young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> soon forgot the favours which had been so lavishly bestowed on him. Gaining a number of partisans, he in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> aspired to the immediate possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. His impatience would not wait till he should obtain it lawfully by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Flattering himself, from the long absence of the king, that he was perhaps fallen before Troy, he determined to mount the throne. Mida, wife to Idomeneus, and the princess Clytthera, were an obstacle to his wishes. But ambition knows no restraint, and tramples under foot the most sacred obligations. The base wretch having seduced the people from their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, and captivated the affections of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, sacrificed those unfortunate victims in the temple. When Idomeneus, crowned with laurels, landed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Crete, Leucus, who had now firmly established his power, attacked him with an armed force, and obliged him to reembark. A different account is also given of the banishment of Idomeneus. Servius says that he had vowed, in a storm, to sacrifice to the gods the first person that his eyes should behold on the Cretan shore; that his son having met him first after his arrival, he fulfilled his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a>, by sacrificing him; and that the island, being soon after depopulated by pestilence, the inhabitants looked upon that affliction as the effect of divine vengeance, and expelled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARRICIDE">parricide</a>; who, retiring to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, founded Salentum, on the Messapian coast. But that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> appears entirely groundless. History mentions no son of Idomeneus. If he had a son of his own blood, why did he adopt Leucus? Why did he intrust to him the government of the island, when he promised him his daughter in marriage? The more probable opinion is, that the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> was introduced into the island by his ships, when he returned from the siege of Troy, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> asserts; and that Leucus artfully made use of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> to expel his lawful sovereign from the island. But it appears that the usurper did not long enjoy the fruit of his crimes. Soon after the departure of Idomeneus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> was abolished, and the government of Crete became republican. The republic of Crete has been celebrated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> of Plato, served Lycurgus as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> for that which he established in Lacedemon, and was beheld by all Greece with respect and admiration. Strabo has thought it not unworthy of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, and has consecrated the leading features of its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> to lasting fame in his immortal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. It was indeed a system of legislature, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> tendency was to call forth the buds of virtue in the heart of infancy; to open and expand them in youth; to inspire man, as he reached maturity, with the love of his country, of glory, glory, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; and to comfort and support the infirmities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> with the respect and esteem due to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> and wisdom of that period of life. It laboured to form affectionate friends, patriotic citizens, and worthy magistrates. It made no use, however, of a multitude of acts and statutes to produce those inestimable advantages. They flowed all from one source: the public education of youth, judiciously directed. The virtuous examples set before youth in the course of that education, the illustrious deeds which were recited to them with high applause, the honours conferred on valour and on noble actions, the opprobrium invariably <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> on vice; these were the only means which the Cretan lawgiver made use of to form a warlike, humane, and virtuous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. The Cretan government, soon after the expulsion of Idomenus, became aristocratical. The power was divided between the nobles and the people. Yet as the chief employments were occupied by the nobles, they directed the administration of affairs. Ten magistrates were annually elected, by a majority of voices, in the national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. These were named Coi/moi; and their public office and character were the same with those of the Ephori at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>. They were the generals of the republic in time of war, and directed all affairs of any importance. They had the right of choosing certain old men for counsellors. Those old men, to the number of twenty-eight, composed the Cretan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. They were chosen from among such as had discharged the office of Coi/moi, or had distinguished themselves by extraordinary merit and blameless probity. Those senators <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in office during life, possessed a weighty influence, and were consulted in every affair of any importance. This body was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> opposed by the wisdom of the legislator against the ambition of the ten chief rulers. He had imposed another restraint on their power, by limiting the period of their administration to one year. His foresight went still farther. The suffrages of the people might be obtained by bribery or personal influence, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> their choice might sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on a man unworthy of so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> an office. When that happened, he who had been undeservedly advanced to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of Coi/mos was degraded, either in a national assembly, or simply by the voices of his colleagues. This, doubtless, is what Plato alludes to, when he says, "Neither the commonwealth, which approaches too near to a monarchical constitution, nor that which affects a licentious liberty, is founded on the solid basis of a just medium between anarchy and despotism. O Cretans! O Lacedemonians! by establishing yours on firmer foundations, you have avoided those fatal extremes." Such were the distribution of power and the administration of public affairs in the Cretan government. Its simplicity was admirable. A people who were blessed with the sacred enjoyment of liberty, but possessed not sufficient knowledge and discernment to direct themselves, elected magistrates, to whom they delegated their authority. Those magistrates, thus arrayed with sovereign power, chose senators to assist and direct their deliberations. These counsellors could neither enact nor decide of themselves; but they held their office for life; and that circumstance contributed to strengthen their influence and to increase their experience. The magistrates were animated by the most powerful motives to distinguish themselves when in office, by unrestrained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> in the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. On one side, they were restrained by the fear of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>; on the other, actuated by the hope of becoming one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> members of the national <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>.

CREUSA

Pages 371-371

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Creon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Corinth. As she was going to marry Jason, who had divorced Medea, she put on a poisoned garment, which immediately set her body on fire, and she expired in the most excruciating torments. She had received this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> as a gift from Medea, who wished to take that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> of Jason. Some call her Glaucé. (Ovid, de Art. Am. i. 335.) A daughter of Priam, king of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> by Hecuba. She married Æneas, by whom she had, among other children, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASCANIUS">Ascanius</a>. When Troy was taken, she fled in the night with her husband; but they were separated in the midst of the confusion and tumult, and Æneas could not recover her, nor hear where she was. Some say the Cybele saved her, and carried her to her temple, of which she became priestess. Pauz. x. 26.—Virg. Æn. iii. 592.

CREUX

Pages 371-371

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, much used by the French; though not yet, that we know of, realized among us: but the want of a word of equal import in English, as it has frequently put us under a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of using this in the course of the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; so it pleads strongly for its admission into our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>.

CREUX ORIGINALLY

Pages 371-371

x originally signifies a hollow, cavity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pit, out of which something has been scooped or dug; hence it is used to denote that kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> and graving where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> and figures are cut and formed within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the plate or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> engraven on. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to relievo; where the lines and figures are embossed, and appear prominent above the face of the matter.

CREVIER

Pages 371-371

John Baptist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, a Parisian, was trained under the celebrated Rollin, and afterwards became professor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, in 1741, he took upon him to finish his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. He published other works, and was greatly serviceable to the cause of virtue and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> as well as letters. His death happened in 1765, at a very advanced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Besides the continuation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, he published, 1. An edition of Livius, cum Notis, in 6 vols 4to, 1748; and afterwards another edition, better adapted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his pupils, in 6 vols small 8vo. 2. La Histoire des Empereurs de Romains jusqu'à Constantin, 1749. 12 tom. 12mo. 3. Histoire de l'Université de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 7 tom. 12mo. 4. Rhetorique Francoise, a just and useful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. 5. Observations sur l'Esprit des Lois. Here he ventured out of his depth; he should have kept within the precincts of the belles lettres.

CREW

Pages 371-371

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of sailors belonging to a ship, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other vessel. The sailors that are to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> and manage a ship are regulated by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lasts it may carry; each last making two tons. The crew of a Dutch ship, from 40 to 50 lasts, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sailors and a swabber; from 50 to 60 lasts, the crew consists of eight men and a swabber; and thus increases at the rate of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> for every ten lasts; so that a ship of 100 lasts has 12 men, &c. English and French crews are usually stronger than Dutch; but always in about the same proportion. In a ship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> there are several particular crews, or gangs, as the boatwain's crew, the carpenter's crew, the gunner's crew, &c.

CRIBBAGE

Pages 372-372

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, to be learnt only by practice.

CRIBRATION

Pages 372-372

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, the passing any substance through a sieve <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scarf, in order to separate the finer particles from the groffer. CRIBROSUM OS. in Anatomy, called also os ethmoides. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CRICELASIA

Pages 372-372

the driving a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hoop. Driving a hoop was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GYMNASTICS">gymnastics</a>: this hoop was as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as the breadth of the person who used it. It was commended for rendering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> pliable, and for strengthening the nerves. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CRICETUS">CRICETUS</a>. See Mus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CRICHTON

Pages 372-377

James, a Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, who lived in the 16th century, and who, on account of his extraordinary endowments both of body and mind, obtained the appellation of "the admirable Crichton;" by which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> he has been distinguished to the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of this celebrated person's birth is said, by the generality of writers, to have been in 1551; but according to some he was born in August 1560. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> likewise between the biographers of this extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, with regard to his family, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and situation of his father. By some it is asserted, that James Crichton's father was Robert Crichton of Clunie, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>; and that this Robert Crichton commanded <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Langside in the year 1568. But it is said by others, that this gentleman was of Elchock in the same county, and that he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> advocate of Scotland in Queen Mary's reign from 1561 to 1573; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which time he held that office in conjunction with Spens of Condie. The mother of James Crichton was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> Stuart, the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir James Stuart of Beath, who was a descendant of Robert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a> the third son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Robert the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, by Elizabeth Muir <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> More, as she is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called; so that when the admirable Crichton boasted (as he did abroad), that he was sprung from Scottish kings, he said nothing but what was agreeable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. James Crichton is said to have received his grammatical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Perth, and to have studied <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> in the university of St Andrew's. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> in that university was Mr John Rutherford, a professor at that time famous for his learning, and who distinguished himself by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> four books on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s logic and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on his poetics. According to Aldus Manutius, who calls Crichton first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> to the king, he was also instructed, along with his majesty, by Buchanan, Hepburn, and Robertson, as well as by Rutherford; and he had scarcely arrived at the 20th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, when he had run through the whole circle of the sciences, and could speak and write to perfection in ten different languages. Nor was this all; for he had likewise improved himself to the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in riding, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> and singing, and in playing upon all sorts of instruments. Crichton, being thus accomplished, went abroad upon his travels, and is said to have gone to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; of his transactions at which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the following account is given. He caused placards to be fixed on all the gates of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, halls, and colleges belonging to the university, and on all the pillars and posts before the houses of the most renowned men for literature in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, inviting all those who were well versed in any art or science, to dispute with him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Navarre, that day six weeks, by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of the clock in the morning, where he would attend them, and be ready to answer to whatever should be propounded to him in any art or science, and in any of these 12 languages, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Syrian, Arabic, Greek, Latin, Spanish, French, Italian, English, Dutch, Flemish, and Sclavonian; and this either in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> or prose, at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the disputant. During this whole time, instead of closely applying to his studies, he regarded nothing but hunting, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAWKING">hawking</a>, tilting, vaulting, riding of a well managed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, toiling the pike, handling the musket, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> feats; or else he employed himself in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> games, such as balls, concerts of music vocal and instrumental, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, dice, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENNIS">tennis</a>, and the like diversions of youth. This conduct so provoked the students of the university, that, beneath the placard which was fixed on the Navarre gate, they caused the following words to be written: "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you would meet with this monster of perfection, to make search for him either in the tavern or bawdy-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, is the readiest way to find him." Nevertheless, when the day appointed arrived, Crichton appeared in the college of Navarre, and acquitted himself beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> in the disputation, which lasted from nine o'clock in the morning till six at night. At length, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, after extolling him highly for the many rare and excellent endowments which God and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> had bestowed upon him, rose from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and accompanied by four of the most eminent professors of the university, gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> and a purse full of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, as a testimony of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and favour. The whole ended with the repeated acclamations and huzzas of the spectators; and henceforward our young disputant was called, "the admirable Crichton." It is added, that he was so little fatigued with the dispute, that he went on the very next day to the Louvre, where he had a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> of tilting (an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> then in much request), and in the presence of some of the princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of France, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many ladies, carried away the ring 15 times successively. About two years after this we find him at Rome, where he affixed a placard upon all the eminent places of the city, in the following terms; Nos Jacobus Crichtonus Scotus, cuicumque rei propofitio ex improvviso respondimus. In a city which abounded in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, this bold challenge, to answer to any question that could be propounded to him without his being previously advertised of it, could not escape the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> of a palquinade. It is said, however, that being nowise discouraged, he appeared at the time and place appointed; and that, in the presence of the pope, many cardinals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, doctors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and professors in all the sciences, he displayed such wonderful proofs of his universal knowledge, that he excited no less surprize than he had done at Paris. Boccaccini, who was then at Rome, gives something of a different relation Crichton. relation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. According to this author, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASQUINADE">pasquinade</a> against Crichton, which was to the following effect, "And he that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> see it, let him go to the sign of the Falcon and it shall be shown," made such an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon him, that he left a place where he had been so grossly affronted as to be put upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with jugglers and mountebanks. From Rome he went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; where he contracted an intimate friendship with Aldus Manutius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAURENTIUS">Laurentius</a> Maffa, Speron Speroni, Johannes Donatus, and various other learned persons, to whom he presented several poems in commendation of the city and university. At length he was introduced to the doge and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, in whose presence he made a speech, which was accompanied with such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of eloquence, and such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of person and manner, that he received the thanks of that illustrious body, and nothing was talked of through the whole city but this rara in terris <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIS">avis</a>, this prodigy of nature. He held, likewise, disputations on the subjects of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, philosophy, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, before the most eminent professors, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> multitudes of people. His reputation was so great, that the desire of seeing and hearing him brought together a vast concourse of persons from different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> to Venice. It may be collected from Manutius, that the time in which Crichton exhibited these demonstrations of his abilities was in the year 1580. During his residence at Venice, he fell into a bad state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for the space of four months. However, before he was perfectly recovered, he went, by the advice of his friends, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, the university of which city was at that time in great reputation. The next day after his arrival, there was a meeting of all the learned men of the place, at the house of Jacobus Aloysius Cornelius; when Crichton opened the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> with an extemporary poem in praise of the city, the university, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> who had honoured him with their presence. After this, he disputed for six hours with the most celebrated professors on various subjects of learning; and he exposed, in particular, the errors of Aristotle and his commentators, with so much solidity and acuteness, and at the same time with so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, that he excited universal admiration. In conclusion, he delivered extempore an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> in praise of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, which was conducted with such ingenuity and elegance, that his hearers were astonished. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of Crichton's talents was on the 14th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1581. Soon after he appointed a day for another disputation to be held at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the bishop of Padua; not for the purpose of affording higher proofs of his abilities, for that could not possibly be done, but in compliance with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> solicitations of some persons who were not present at the former assembly. However, several circumstances occurred which prevented this meeting from taking place. Such is the account of Manutius; but Imperialis relates, that he was informed by his father, who was present upon the occasion, that Crichton was opposed by Archangelus Mercenarius, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; and that he acquitted himself so well as to obtain the approbation of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> company, and even of his antagonist himself. Amidst the discourses which were occasioned by our young Scotsman's exploits, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> applause that were bestowed upon his genius and attainments, there were not wanting some who endeavoured to detract from his merit. For ever, therefore, to confound these invidious impugners of his talents, he caused a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> to be fixed on the gates of St John and St Paul's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, wherein he offered to prove before the university, that the errors of Aristotle, and of all his followers, were almost innumerable; and that the latter had failed both in explaining their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s meaning, and in treating on theological subjects. He promised likewise to refute the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> of certain mathematical professors; to dispute in all the sciences, and to answer to whatever should be proposed to him or objected against him. All this he engaged to do, either in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> logical way, or by numbers and mathematical figures, or in 100 sorts of verses, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of his opponents. According to Manutius, Crichton sustained this contest, without fatigue, for three days; during which time he supported his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, and maintained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, with such spirit and energy, that from an unusual concourse of people, he obtained acclamations and praises, than which none more magnificent were ever heard by men. From Padua, Crichton set out for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>; where there happened to be at the time a gladiator, who had foiled in his travels the most famous fencers in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and had lately killed three who had entered the lists with him in this city. The duke of Mantua was much grieved at having granted this man his protection, as he found it to be attended with such fatal consequences. Crichton, being informed of his highness's concern, offered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, not only to drive the murderer from Mantua, but from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and to fight him for 1500 pistoles. Though the duke was unwilling to expose such an accomplished gentleman to so great a hazard; yet, relying upon the report he had heard of his warlike achievements, he agreed to the proposal; and the time and place being appointed, the whole court attended to behold the performance. At the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> Crichton stood only upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; while the Italian made his attack with such eagerness and fury, that, having overacted himself, he began to grow weary. Crichton now seized the opportunity of attacking his antagonist in return; which he did with so much dexterity and vigour, that he ran him through the body in three different places, of which wounds he immediately died. The acclamations of the spectators were loud and extraordinary upon this occasion; and it was acknowledged by all of them, that they had never seen Art grace Nature, or Nature second the precepts of Art, in so lively a manner as they had beheld these two things accomplished on that day. To <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, Crichton bestowed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of his victory upon the widows of the three persons who had lost their lives in fighting with the gladiator.
