To the man who has acquired a taste so acute and accomplished, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> wrong or improper must be highly disagreeable: if, in any instance, the overbearing power of passion sway him from his duty, he returns to it upon the first reflection with redoubled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> never to be swayed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>: he has now an additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> to virtue, a conviction derived from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> depends on regularity and order, and that a disregard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> or propriety never fails to be punished with shame and remorse. For the rules of criticism applicable to the fine arts, and derived from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature, see Architecture, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">Beauty</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRUITY">Congruity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">Comparison</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">Grandeur</a>, &c.

CRITO

Pages 388-388

an Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, flourished 400 years before Christ. He was one of the most zealous disciples of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, and supplied him with whatever he wanted. He had several scholars who proved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men, and he composed some dialogues which are lost.

CRITOLAUS

Pages 388-388

a citizen of Tegea in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. He with two brothers fought against the three sons of Demonitratus of Pheuneus, to put an end to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between their respective nations. The brothers of Critolaus were both killed, and he alone remained to withstand his three bold antagonists. He conquered them; and when at his return his sister deplored the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of one of his antagonists, to whom she was betrothed, he killed her in a fit of resentment. The offence deserved <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>; but he was pardoned on account of the services he had rendered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He was afterwards general of the Acheans; and it is said that he poisoned himself because he had been conquered at Thermopylae by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, about 146 years before the Augustan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

CRIZZELLING

Pages 388-388

in the glass trade, a kind of roughness arising on the surface of some kinds of glass. This was the fault of a peculiar sort of glass made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a> and some other places, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> flints, a crystallized sand, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of nitre, tartar, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>. The glass thus made is very beautiful, but, from the too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of the salts in the mixture, is subject to crizzel; that is, the salts in the mixture, from their too great proportion, are subject, either from the adventitious nitre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> from without, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from warm liquors put in them, to be either increased in quantity or dissolved, and thereby induce a coarseness or roughness irrecoverably clouding the transparency of the glass. This is what was called crizzelling; but by using an Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> pebble, and abating the proportions of the salts, the manufacture is now carried on with advantage, and the glass made with these salts is whiter than the finest Venetian, and is subject to no faults.

CROATIA

Pages 388-389

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Illyricum, is bounded on the east by Sclavonia and Bosnia, on the south and west by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORLACHIA">Morlachia</a>, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Drave, which separates it from a part of Sclavonia. It is about 80 miles in length and 70 in breadth, and was once divided between the Hungarians and Turks; but now the greatest part of it is subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. The Croats derive their origin from the Slavians; and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is a dialect of the Slavonian, approaching very near to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is divided into two parts, viz. that under, and that beyond, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">Save</a>. In the late wars between the empress <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, no less than 50,000 men were raised out of this small territory. Both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and foot are good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, especially the former. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, where cultivated, is fruitful in wine and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, &c., but being a frontier country, and much exposed to inroads, it is not so well cultivated as otherwise might be. CROCODILE. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACERTA">Lacerta</a>, Repetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fossil Crocodile, one of the greatest curiosities in the fossil world which the late ages have produced. It is the skeleton of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> crocodile, almost entire, found at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> depth underground, bedded in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. This was in the possession of Linkius, who wrote many pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and particularly an accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of this curious fossil. It was found in the side of a large mountain in the middle part of Germany, and in a stratum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> fossil stone, somewhat like our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> slate, but of a coarser texture, the same with that in which the fossil fishes in many parts of the world are found. This skeleton had the back and ribs very plain, and was of a much deeper black than the rest of the stone; as is also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in the fossil fishes which are preserved in this manner. The part of the stone where the head lay was not found; this being broken off <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> at the shoulders, but that irregularly; so that in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, a part of the back of the head was visible in its natural form. The two shoulder-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> were very fair, and three of the feet were well preserved: the legs were of their natural shape and size, and the feet preserved even to the extremities of the five toes of each. Crocodile (crocodilus), in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a captious and sophistical kind of argumentation, contrived to seduce the unwary, and draw them specially into a snare. It has its name crocodile from the following occasion, invented by the poets. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> woman, begging a crocodile that had caught her son walking by the riverside to spare and restore him, was answered, that he would restore him, provided she should give a true answer to a question he should propose: the question was, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">Will</a> I restore thy son <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not? To this the poor wo- Crocus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, suspecting a deceit, sorrowfully answered, Thou wilt not: and demanded to have him restored, because the had answered truly. Thou liest, says the crocodile; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> I restore him thou hast not answered truly: I cannot therefore restore him without making thy answer false. Under this head may be reduced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> called mentientes or insolubiles; which destroy themselves. Such is that of the Cretan poet: Omnes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> unum Cretenes semper mentiuntur: "all the Cretans, to a man, always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a>." Either, then, the poet lies when he affirms that the Cretans all lie, or the Cretans do not all lie.

CROCUS

Pages 389-390

saffron: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 6th order Enfata. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Crocus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, denotes any metal calcined to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Crocus Metallorum, an emetic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a> and nitre. See Chemistry Index. CRÈSUS, the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Lydia, remarkable for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, his conquests, his temporary prosperity, and the sad reverse of his fortune. He subdued the Phrygians, Mylians, Paphlagonians, Thracians, and Carian; amassed together immense riches; and became one of the most powerful and magnificent princes in the world. He drew the learned to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in conversing with them. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THALES">Thales</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>, Pittacus of Mytilene, Bias of Priene, Cleobulus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINDUS">Lindus</a>, and most of the other "wise men," as they are emphatically styled, who lived in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, as well as Æsop the fabulist, and the elegant Greek poets of the times, were bountifully received at the court of Croesus. There is still on record a memorable conversation between that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and Solon, which seemed to predict the subsequent events of his reign, and which had a late but important influence on the character and fortune of the Lydian king. Croesus having entertained his Athenian guest, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fashion, for several days, before he asked him any questions, ostentatiously showed him the magnificence of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and particularly the riches of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. After all had been displayed to the best advantage, the king complimented Solon upon his curiosity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of knowledge; and asked him as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who had seen many countries, and reflected with much judgment upon what he had seen, Whom of all men he esteemed most happy? By the particular occasion, as well as the triumphant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> with which the question was proposed, the king made it evident that he expected flattery rather than information. But Solon's character had not been enervated by the debilitating air of a court; and he replied with a manly freedom, "Tellus, the Athenian." Croesus, who had scarcely learned to distinguish, even in imagination, between wealth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, inquired with a tone of surprize, why this preference to Tellus? "Tellus," rejoined Solon, "was not conspicuous for his riches or his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, being only a simple citizen of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; but he was defended from parents who deserved the first honours of the republic. He was equally fortunate in his children, who obtained universal esteem by their probity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a>, and every useful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the mind or body: and as to himself, he died fighting gallantly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which his valour rendered victorious in a doubtful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>; on which account the Athenians buried him on the spot where he fell, and distinguished him by every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> can confer on illustrious merit." Croesus had little encouragement, after this answer, to ask Solon, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, Whom, next to Tellus, he deemed most happy? Such, however, is the illusion of vanity, that he still ventured to make this demand; and still, as we are informed by the most circumstantial of historians, entertained hopes of being favourably answered. But Solon replied with the same freedom as before, "The brothers Cleobis and Biton, two youths of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, whose strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> were crowned with repeated victory at the Olympic games; who deserved the affection of their parents, the gratitude of their country, the admiration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and who, having ended their lives with peculiar felicity, were commemorated by the most signal monuments of immortal fame." "And is the happiness of a king, then," said Croesus, "so little regarded, O Grecian stranger, that you prefer to it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> condition of an Athenian or Argive citizen?" The reply of Solon sufficiently justified his reputation for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of man," said he, "consists of 70 years, which make 25,550 days; an immense <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; yet in the longest life, the events of any one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be found exactly alike to those of another. The affairs of men are liable to perpetual vicissitudes: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a> who presides over our fate is envious of too much prosperity; and all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> life, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not condemned to calamity, is at least liable to accident. Whoever has uninterruptedly enjoyed a prosperous tide of success may justly be called fortunate; but he cannot before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> be entitled to the epithet of happy." The events which soon followed this conversation, prove how little satisfaction is derived from the possession of a throne. Victorious in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, unrivalled in wealth, supreme in power, Croesus felt and acknowledged his unhappiness. The warmest affections of his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> centered in his son Atys, a youth of the most promising hopes, who had often fought and conquered by his side. The strength of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> was accompanied with an excess of paternal care, and the anxiety of his waking hours disturbed the tranquillity of his rest. He dreamed that his beloved son was slain by a dart; and the solicitude with which he watched his safety, preventing the youth from his usual occupations and amusements, and thereby rendering him too eager to enjoy them, most probably exposed him to the much-dreaded misfortune. Reluctantly permitted to engage in a party of hunting, the juvenile ardour of Atys, increased by the impatience of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> restraint, made him neglect the precautions necessary in that manly amusement. He was slain by a dart aimed at a wild boar of monstrous size, which had long spread terror over the country of the Mylians. The weapon came from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of Adraustus, a Phrygian prince and fugitive, whom Croesus had purified from the involuntary guilt of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s blood, and long distinguished by peculiar marks of bounty. To the grateful protection of the Phrygian, Croesus recommended, at parting, the safety of his beloved son. A mournful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> of Lydians brought to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a> the dead body of Atys. The ill-fated murderer followed behind. When they approached the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> presence, Adraustes stepped forward and entreated Croesus to put him to death; thinking life no longer to be endured after killing, first his own brother, and then the son of his benefactor. But the Lydian king, notwithstanding the excess of his affliction, acknowledged the innocence of Adraustes, and the power of fate. "Stranger, your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> is blameless, being committed without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. I know that my son was destined to a premature death." Adraustes, though pardoned by Croesus, could not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> himself. When the mourners were removed, he privately returned, and perished by his own hand on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Atys. Two years Croesus remained disconsolate for the loss of his son; and might have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to indulge his unavailing affliction during the remainder of life, had not the growing greatness of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, which threatened the safety of his dominions, roused him from his dream of misery. (See Lydia.)—He marched against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, but was defeated; and retreating to his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> Sardis, was there besieged. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> was taken by assault; and as a Persian folder was going to kill Croesus, that prince's only surviving son, who had hitherto been dumb, terrified at his danger, cried, "Stop, folder, and touch not Croesus." But though delivered by this extraordinary accident from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> rage of the folder, he seemed to be reserved for a harder fate. Dragged into the presence of his conqueror, he was loaded with irons; and the stern, unrelenting Cyrus, of whose humane temper of mind we have so beautiful, but so flattering, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> in the philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> of Xenophon, ordered him, with the melancholy train of his Lydian attendants, to be committed to the flames. An immense pile of wood and other combustibles was erected in the most spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city. The miserable victims, bound hand and foot, were placed on the top of the pyre. Cyrus, surrounded by his generals, witnessed the dreadful spectacle, either from an abominable principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> he had bound himself by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> to sacrifice Croesus as the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his Lydian victory, or from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of curiosity, equally cruel and impious, to try whether Croesus, who had so magnificently adorned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> and enriched the ministers of the gods, would be helped in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of need by the miraculous interposition of his much honoured protectors. Meanwhile the unfortunate Lydian, oppressed and confounded by the intolerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of his present calamity compared with the security and splendor of his former state, recollected his memorable conversation with the Athenian sage, and uttered with a deep groan the name of Solon. Cyrus asked by an interpreter, "Whose name he invoked?" "His," replied Croesus, emboldened by the prospect of certain death, "whole words ought ever to speak to the heart of kings." This reply not being satisfactory, he was commanded to explain at full length the subject of his thoughts. Accordingly he related the important discourse which had passed between himself and the Athenian, of which it was the great moral, That no man could be called happy till his death. The words of a dying man are fitted to make a strong <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the heart. Those of Croesus deeply affected the mind of Cyrus. The Persian considered the speech of Solon as addressed to himself. He repented of his intended cruelty towards the unfortunate prince, who had formerly enjoyed all the pomp of prosperity; and dreading the concealed vengeance that might lurk in the bosom of fate, gave orders that the pyre should be extinguished. But the workmen who had been employed to prepare it, had performed their task with so much care, that the order could not speedily be obeyed. At that moment, Croesus calling on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, whose favourite shrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> had experienced his generous munificence, and whose perfidious oracle had made him so ungrateful a return; the god, it is said, sent a plentiful shower to extinguish the pyre. This event, which saved the life, and which sufficiently attested the piety, of Croesus, strongly recommended him to the credulity of his conqueror. It seemed impossible to pay too much respect to a man who was evidently the favourite of heaven. Cyrus gave orders that he should be seated by his side, and thenceforth treated as a king; a revolution of fortune equally sudden and unexpected. But the mind of Croesus had undergone a still more important revolution: for, tutored in the useful school of adversity, he learned to think with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, to govern his own passions by the dictates of reason, and to repay by wholesome advice the generous behaviour of his Persian <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. The first advantage which he derived from the change in Cyrus's disposition towards him, was the permission of sending his fetters to the temple of the Delphian Apollo, whose flattering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> had encouraged him to wage war with the Persians. "Behold," were his messengers instructed to say, "the trophies of our promised succours! behold the monuments of the unerring veracity of the god!" The Pythia heard their reproach with a smile of contemptuous indignation, and answered it with that solemn gravity which she was so carefully taught to assume: "The gods themselves cannot avoid their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a>, much less avert, however they may retard, the determined fates of men. Croesus has suffered, and justly suffered, for the crime of his ancestor Gyges; who, entrusted as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the guards, with the person of Candaules, the last king of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, was seduced by an impious woman to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> his master, to defile his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and to usurp his royal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. For this complicated guilt of Gyges the misfortunes of Croesus have atoned; but know, that through the favour of Apollo, these misfortunes have happened three years later than the fates ordained." The Pythia then proceeded to explain her answers concerning the event of the war against Cyrus, and proved, to the conviction of the Lydians, that her words, if properly understood, portended the destruction, not of the Persian, but of the Lydian empire. Croesus heard with resignation the report of his messengers, and acknowledged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the Delphian oracle, which maintained and increased the lustre of its ancient fame. This fallen monarch survived Cyrus. The manner of his death is not known.

CROFT

Pages 390-390

a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> adjoining to a dwelling-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and inclosed for pasture <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> arable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, or any other purpose.—In some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> deeds, crofta occurs as the Latin word for a "croft;" but cum tofis et creftis is more frequent. Croft is translated in Abbo Floriacensis, by praedium, a "<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>."

CROISADE

Pages 390-393
or Crusade, a name given to the expeditions expeditions of the Christians against the infidels for the conquest of Palestine. These expeditions commenced in the year 1096. The foundation of them was a superstitious veneration for those places where our Saviour performed his miracles, and accomplished the work of man's redemption. Jerusalem had been taken, and Palestine conquered, by Omar the successor of Abu Becr*, who succeeded Mahomet himself. This proved a considerable interruption to the pilgrims, who flocked from all quarters to perform their devotions at the holy sepulchre. They had, however, still been allowed this liberty, on paying a small tribute to the Saracen caliphs, who were not much inclined to molest them. But, in 1065, this city changed its matters. The Turks took it from the Saracens; and being much more fierce and barbarous than the former, the pilgrims now found they could no longer perform their devotions with the same safety they did before. An opinion was about this time also prevalent in Europe, which made these pilgrimages much more frequent than formerly. It was somehow or other imagined, that the thousand years mentioned in the 20th chapter of the Revelations, were fulfilled; that Christ was soon to make his appearance in Palestine, to judge the world; and consequently that journeys to that country were in the highest degree meritorious, and even absolutely necessary. The multitudes of pilgrims which now flocked to Palestine, meeting with a very rough reception from the Turks, filled all Europe with complaints against those infidels who profaned the holy city by their presence, and derided the sacred mysteries of Christianity even in the place where they were fulfilled. Pope Gregory VII. had formed a design of uniting all the princes of Christendom against the Mahometans; but his exorbitant encroachments upon the civil power of princes had created him so many enemies, and rendered his schemes so suspicious, that he was not able to make great progress in the undertaking. The work was referred for a meaner instrument. Peter, commonly called the bermi, a native of Amiens in Picardy, had made the pilgrimage to Jerusalem; and being deeply affected with the dangers to which that act of piety now exposed the pilgrims, as well as with the opprobrium under which the eastern Christians now laboured, formed the bold, and, in all appearance, impracticable design of leading into Asia, from the farthest extremities of the west, armies sufficient to subdue those potent and warlike nations that now held the Holy Land in slavery. He propounded his scheme to Martin II. who then filled the papal chair; but he, though sensible enough of the advantages which must accrue to himself from such an undertaking, resolved not to interpose his authority till he saw a greater probability of success. He summoned, at Placentia, a council consisting of 4000 ecclesiastics and 30,000 seculars. As no hall could be found large enough to contain such a multitude, the assembly was held in a plain. Here the Pope himself, as well as Peter, harangued the people, representing the dismal situation of their brethren in the east, and the indignity offered to the Christian name in allowing the holy city to remain in the hands of the infidels. These speeches were so agreeable to those who heard them, that the whole multitude suddenly and violently declared for the war, and solemnly devoted themselves to perform this service, which they believed to be so meritorious in the sight of God. But though Italy seemed to have embraced the design with ardour, Martin yet thought it necessary, in order to insure perfect success, to engage the greater and more warlike nations in the same enterprise. Having therefore exhorted Peter to visit the chief cities and sovereigns of Christendom, he summoned another council at Clermont in Auvergne. The fame of this great and pious design being now universally diffused, procured the attendance of the greatest prelates, nobles, and princes; and when the Pope and the hermit renewed their pathetic exhortations, the whole assembly, as if impelled by an immediate inspiration, exclaimed with one voice, "It is the will of God! it is the will of God!" These words were deemed so memorable, and so much the effect of a divine impulse, that they were employed as the signal of rendezvous and battle in all future exploits of these adventurers. Men of all ranks now flew to arms with the utmost ardour, and a crois was affixed to their right shoulder by all who enlisted in this holy enterprise. At this time Europe was sunk in the most profound ignorance and superstition. The ecclesiastics had gained the greatest ascendancy over the human mind; and the people, who committed the most horrid crimes and disorders, knew of no other expiation than the observances imposed on them by their spiritual pastors. But amidst the abject superstition which now prevailed, the military spirit had also universally diffused itself; and, though not supported by art or discipline, was become the general passion of the nations governed by the feudal class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law. All the great lords policed the right of peace and war. They were engaged in continual hostilities with one another: the open country was become a scene of outrage and disorder: the cities, still mean and poor, were neither guarded by walls nor protected by privileges. Every man was obliged to depend for safety on his own force, or his private alliances; and valour was the only excellence which was held in esteem, or gave one man the pre-eminence above another. When all the particular superstitions, therefore, were here united in one great object, the ardour for private hostilities took the same direction; "and all Europe (as the princess Anna Comnena expresses herself), torn from its foundations, seemed ready to precipitate itself in one united body upon Asia." All orders of men, now deeming the croisades the only road to heaven, were impatient to open the way with their swords to the holy city. Nobles, artisans, peasants, even priests, enrolled their names; and to decline this service was branded with the reproach of impiety or cowardice. The nobles who enlisted themselves were moved, by the romantic spirit of the age, to hope for opulent establishments in the east, the chief seat of arts and commerce at that time. In pursuit of these chimerical projects, they sold at the lowest price their ancient castles and inheritances, which had now lost all value in their eyes. The infirm and aged contributed to the expedition by presents and money; and many of them, not satisfied with this, attended tended it in person, being determined, if possible, to breathe their last in sight of that city where their Saviour had died for them. Women themselves, concealing their sex under the disguise of armour, attended the camp; and commonly forgot their duty still more, by prostituting themselves to the army. The greatest criminals were forward in a service which they considered as an expiation for all crimes; and the most enormous disorders were, during the course of these expeditions, committed by men inured to wickedness, encouraged by example, and impelled by necessity. The multitude of adventurers soon became so great, that their more sagacious leaders became apprehensive lest the greatness of the armament would be the cause of its own disappointment. For this reason they permitted an undisciplined multitude, computed at 300,000 men, to go before them under the command of Peter the hermit, and Gautier or Walter, surnamed the moneyer, from his being a folder of fortune. They took the road towards Constantinople through Hungary and Bulgaria; and, trusting that heaven, by supernatural assistance, would supply all their necessities, they made no provision for subsistence in their march. They soon found themselves obliged to obtain by plunder what they vainly expected from miracles; and the enraged inhabitants of the countries through which they passed, attacked the disorderly multitude, and slaughtered them without resistance. The more disciplined armies followed after; and, passing the straits of Constantinople, they were mustered in the plains of Asia, and amounted in the whole to 700,000 men. The rage for conquering the Holy Land did not cease with this expedition. It continued for very near two centuries, and eight different croisades were set on foot, one after another. The first was in the year 1096, as already observed. The princes engaged in it were, Hugo, count of Vermandois, brother to Philip I., king of France; Robert, duke of Normandy; Robert, earl of Flanders; Raymond, earl of Toulouse and St Giles; Godfrey of Bouillon, duke of Lorraine, with his brothers Baldwin and Eustace; Stephen, earl of Chartres and Blois; Hugo, count of St Paul; with a great number of other lords. The general rendezvous was at Constantinople. In this expedition, the famous Godfrey besieged and took the city of Nice. The city of Jerusalem was taken by the confederated army, and Godfrey chosen king. The Christians gained the famous battle of Alcalon against the sultan of Egypt; which put an end to the first croisade. The second croisade, in the year 1144, was headed by the emperor Conrad III. and Louis VII., king of France. The emperor's army was either destroyed by the enemy, or perished through the treachery of Manuel the Greek emperor; and the second army, through the unfaithfulness of the Christians of Syria, was forced to break up the siege of Damascus. The third croisade, in the year 1188, immediately followed the taking of Jerusalem by Saladin the sultan of Egypt. The princes engaged in this expedition were, the emperor Frederic Barbarossa; Frederic duke of Swabia, his second son; Leopold duke of Austria; Berthold duke of Moravia; Herman marquis of Baden; the counts of Nassau, Thuringia, Mifler, and Holland; and above 60 other princes of the empire; with the bishops of Beaufort, Cambrai, Munster, Osnabruck, Miflen, Paffau, Viburg, and several others. In this expedition, the emperor Frederic defeated the sultan of Iconium; his son Frederic, joined by Guy Lusignan king of Jerusalem, in vain endeavoured to take Acre or Ptolemais. During which transactions, Philip Augustus king of France, and Richard I., king of England, joined the croisade; by which means the Christian army consisted of 300,000 fighting men; but great disputes happening between the kings of France and England, the former quitted the Holy Land, and Richard concluded a peace with Saladin. The fourth croisade was undertaken, in the year 1195, by the emperor Henry VI., after Saladin's death. In this expedition the Christians gained several battles against the infidels, took a great many towns, and were in the way of succours, when the death of the emperor obliged them to quit the Holy Land, and return into Germany. The fifth croisade was published, by order of Pope Innocent III., in 1198. Those engaged in it made fruitless efforts for the recovery of the Holy Land; for, though John de Neuville, who commanded the fleet equipped in Flanders, arrived at Ptolemais a little after Simon of Montfort, Reynard of Dampierre, and others; yet the plague destroying many of them, and the rest either returning, or engaging in the petty quarrels of the Christian princes, there was nothing done; so that the sultan of Aleppo easily defeated their troops in 1204. The sixth croisade began in 1228; in which the Christians took the town of Damietta, but were forced to surrender it again. The next year the emperor Frederic made peace with the sultan for 10 years. About 1242, Richard earl of Cornwall, and brother to Henry III., king of England, arrived in Palestine at the head of the English croisade; but finding it most advantageous to conclude a peace, he reembarked, and steered towards Italy. In 1244, the Karasimans being driven out of Persia by the Tartars, broke into Palestine, and gave the Christians a general defeat near Gaza. The seventh croisade was headed by St Lewis, in the year 1249, who took the town of Damietta; but a sickness happening in the Christian army, the king endeavoured a retreat; in which being pursued by the infidels, most of his army were miserably butchered, and himself and the nobility taken prisoners. Then a truce was agreed upon for 10 years, and the king and lords set at liberty. The eighth croisade, in 1270, was headed by the same prince, who made himself master of the port and castle of Carthage in Africa; but dying in a short time, he left his army in a very ill condition. Soon after, the king of Sicily coming up with a good fleet, and raising Philip the Bold, son and successor of Lewis the king of Tunis, after several engagements with the Christians, in which he was always worsted, desired peace, which was granted upon conditions advantageous to the Christians; after which both princes embarked for their own kingdoms. Prince Edward of England, who arrived at Tunis at the time of this treaty, sailed towards Ptolemais, where he landed with a small body of Croifade of 300 English and French, and hindered Bendocdar from laying siege to Ptolemais; but being obliged to quit the Holy Land to take possession of the crown of England, this croifade ended without contributing anything to the recovery of the Holy Land. In 1291, the town of Acre, or Ptolemais, was taken and plundered by the soldan of Egypt, and the Christians quite driven out of Syria. There has been no croifade since that time, though several popes have attempted to stir up the Christians to such an undertaking; particularly Nicholas IV. in 1292, and Clement V. in 1311. Though these croifades were effects of the most absurd superstition, they tended greatly to promote the good of Europe. Multitudes indeed were destroyed. M. Voltaire computes the people who perished in the different expeditions at upwards of two millions. Many there were, however, who returned; and these having conversed so long with people who lived in a much more magnificent way than themselves, began to entertain some taste for a refined and polished way of life. Thus the barbarism in which Europe had been so long immersed, began to wear off soon after this time. The princes also who remained at home, found means to avail themselves of the frenzy of the people. By the absence of such numbers of restless and martial adventurers peace was established in their dominions. They also took the opportunity of annexing to their crown many considerable fiefs, either by purchase, or by the extinction of the heirs; and thus the mischiefs which must always attend feudal governments were considerably lessened. With regard to the bad success of the croifaders, it was scarce possible that any other thing could happen them. The emperors of Constantinople, instead of afflicting, did all in their power to disconcert their schemes. They were jealous, and not without reason, of such an inundation of barbarians. Yet, had they considered their true interest, they would rather have assisted them, or at least stood neuter, than entered into alliances with the Turks. They followed the latter method, however, and were often of very great difference to the western adventurers, which at last occasioned the loss of their city*. But the worst enemies the croifaders had, were their own internal feuds and dissensions. They neither could agree while marching together in armies with a view to conquest, nor could they unite their conquests under one government after they had made them. They set up three small states, one at Jerusalem, another at Antioch, and another at Edessa. These states, instead of afflicting, made war upon each other, and on the Greek emperors; and thus became an easy prey to the common enemy. The horrid cruelties they committed also were such as must have inspired the Turks with the most invincible hatred against them, and made them retort with the greatest obstinacy. They were such as could have been committed only by barbarians inflamed with religious enthusiasm. When Jerusalem was taken, not only the numerous garrison were put to the sword, but the inhabitants were massacred without mercy and without distinction. No age or sex was spared, even children at the breast were barbarously murdered. According to Voltaire, some Christians, who had been suffered by the Turks to live in that city, led the conquerors into the most private caves where women had concealed themselves with their children, and not one of them was suffered to escape. What eminently shows the enthusiasm with which these conquerors were animated, is their behaviour after this terrible slaughter. They marched over heaps of dead bodies towards the holy sepulchre; and while their hands were yet polluted with the blood of so many innocent persons, sang anthems to the common Saviour of mankind. Nay, so far did their religious enthusiasm overcome their fury, that these ferocious conquerors now burst into tears. If the absurdity and wickedness of this conduct can be exceeded by anything, it must be by what follows. In the year 1294, the frenzy of croifading seized the children, who are ever ready to imitate what they see their parents engage themselves in. Their childish folly was encouraged by the monks and schoolmasters; and thousands of these innocents were conducted from the houses of their parents on the faith of these words, "Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou perfected praise." Their base conductors sold a part of them to the Turks, and the rest perished miserably.

CROISERS

Pages 393-393

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order founded in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> discovery of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> by the empress Helena. They are dispersed in several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, particularly in the Low Countries, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, those in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> being at present suppressed. These religious follow the rule of St Augustine. They had in England the name of erowbed friars.

CROISES

Pages 393-393
or Croixes, in English antiquity, pilgrims bound for the Holy Land, or such as had been there; so called from a badge they wore in imitation of a cross. The knights of St John of Jerusalem, created for the defence and protection of pilgrims, were particularly called croixes.

CROIX

Pages 393-394

Francis Petit de la, secretary and interpreter to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France in the Turkish and Arabic languages, died November 4, 1695, in his 73rd year; after having executed this employment for the space of 44 years. And it appears, that he executed it with as much integrity as abilities; for, when the Algerines sought for peace of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV., conditions were offered, by which they were required to reimburse to this monarch 600,000 francs. The terms being thought exorbitant, they had recourse to stratagem; and they offered a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum to La Croix, who was the interpreter of all that passed, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would put into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> "crowns of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>," instead of "French crowns;" which would have made to the Algerines a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of more than 100,000 livres.* But the integrity of the interpreter triumphed over the temptation; which however was the greater, as it was next to impossible he should be discovered. Besides the Turkish and the Arabic, the Persian and the Tartarian, he also understood the Ethiopian and Armenian languages. He is well known to the learned world by many works. He translated the "<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of France" into the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. He digested the three volumes of "Voyages into the East Indies" of M. Thévenot. He made an accurate catalogue of all the Turkish and Persian books which are in the king's library. He composed two complete Dictionaries for the French and Turkish languages: and, when he was dying, he was about to present the world with the history of Jenghis Khan. He undertook this history. Cromarty, history by the order of M. Colbert: for this minister, altogether intent upon aggrandizing his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, was accustomed every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> to call together, either in the king's library <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his own, certain of the learned, whom, according as they excelled in their several departments in literature, he constantly set to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. This history, which cost La Croix more than ten years labour, is useful, not only to the learned who are curious to know past events, or to geographers who had hitherto been greatly ignorant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, but likewise to all who trade to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, or other eastern parts of the world. There is a good map of northern <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> drawn by M. de l'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a>, accompanying the work; which M. Petit de la Croix, the author's son, not only revised, but, to render it more curious, added to it an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of the lives of all those authors from whom it was extracted. It was translated into English, and published at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1722, 8vo.

CROMARTY

Pages 394-394

Frith of, is one of the finest bays in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; hence called by Buchanan Portus Salutis. It is divided from the Moray frith by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cromarty, and washes the southern shore of the county of Ross. It is about 16 miles in length, and sometimes three in breadth. The entrance is between two promontories <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> headlands, called the Sutors of Cromarty, which are about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half distant: there is the finest anchorage ground after passing the Sutors, for several miles up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, with deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on both sides, almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the shore, where in most places the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is so smooth, that supposing a vessel to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> (a thing scarcely probable), she might run <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a> without sustaining much damage. Such is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> room in the bay, and such is the capacity, that almost the whole British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> here in safety.

CROMLECH

Pages 394-395

in British antiquities, are huge, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, flat <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, raised upon other stones let up on end for that purpose. They are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLESEY">Anglesey</a>; under which article a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> one is described. See Plate CLXIV. These monuments are spoken of largely by Mr Rowland, by Dr Borlase, and by Wormius, under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARA">Ara</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> altar. Mr Rowland, however, is divided in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; for he partly inclines to the notion of their having been altars, partly to their having been sepulchres: he supposes them to have been originally tombs, but that in after times sacrifices were performed upon them to the heroes deposited within. Mr Keiller preserves an account of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Harold having been interred beneath a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of this kind in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and Mr Wright discovered in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> a skeleton deposited under one of them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> similarity of the monuments throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Mr Pennant observes, convinces the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to have been spread in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, perhaps with some slight deviations. Many of these monuments are both British and Danish; for we find them where the Danes never penetrated. The cromlech, or cromleh, chiefly differs from the Kiss-waen, in not being closed up at the end and sides, that Cromwell, that is, in not so much partaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>-like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; it is also generally of larger dimensions, and sometimes consists of a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stones: the terms cromlech and kilt-waen are however indiscriminately used for the same monument. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> cromlech is by some derived from the Armorice word crum, "crooked or bowing," and leb "<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>," alluding to the reverence which persons paid to them by bowing. Rowland derives it from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> words carem-luach, signifying a "devoted or consecrated stone." They are called by the vulgar coine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>, or Arthur's quoits, it being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> as well as Cornwall to ascribe all great or wonderful objects to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Arthur, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of those countries.

CROMWELL

Pages 398-398

Richard, eldest son of Oliver Cromwell, was by his father appointed successor to the protectorship, but very soon deposed by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>*. They* See Bri- discharged his debts, took all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> stuff, plate, &c., gave him a protection for six months, and so he retired. He was by no means qualified to support the station gained by the aspiring talents of his father. He was of a moderate temper, and untainted with that fanatical spirit which his father had so successfully cultivated. On the Restoration he went abroad; but returned in 1680 under the assumed name of Clark, and settled at Chehun in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, where he lived privately, and died in 1712, aged 86.

CRONENBURG

Pages 398-398

a town of Germany, in the circle of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and in the landgraviate of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>-Cassel, with a strong castle. It is seated at the foot of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, on a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and is surrounded with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> wall. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 15. N. Lat. 50. 15.

CRONIUS

Pages 398-399

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of the Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> Hecatombaion; which was the first Cronlot, first of their year, and answered to the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>.—There were feasts called Croniones celebrated at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> in this month, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, answering to the Saturnalia of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. CRONSLOT. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRONSTADT">Cronstadt</a>.

CRONSTADT

Pages 399-399

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of Russia, where the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> is stationed. It stands upon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Retufari in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>; and was founded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> I., as being provided with the safest harbour in these parts, and as forming a strong bulwark by sea for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the new <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. The only passage by which ships of burden can approach <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a> lies on the south side of Retufari, through a narrow channel; one side whereof is commanded by Cronstadt, and the opposite by Cronlot and the citadel. Cronlot, which stands upon a small island of sand, is a circular wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and surrounded with fortifications of wood that jut into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It contains a garrison of 100 men. The citadel is another small wooden fortress, constructed also upon an adjacent sand-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, and capable of holding about 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. All <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessels must sail between Cronstadt and these two fortresses, exposed to the fire of the opposite batteries; for the other parts of the gulf are only from one to eleven feet in depth. All these fortifications were, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, esteemed places of considerable strength; but now they derive their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> more from their past importance than from any resistance they could make against the attack of a powerful fleet. Cronstadt is built upon the south-eastern extremity of the island, and is defended towards the sea by wooden piers projecting into the water, and towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> by ramparts and bastions. It is a very fragmenting <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and occupies, like all the Russian <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, a larger space of ground than the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of habitations seems to require; the houses are mostly of wood, excepting a few fronting the harbour, which are of brick fluecoed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. Among the latter are the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for sailors, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, and the academy for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARINES">marines</a> and officers of the navy. That seminary usually contains between three and four hundred cadets, who are clothed, maintained, and taught at the expense of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. They are admitted at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of five, and are suffered to remain until they reach their seventeenth year. They learn accounts, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, fortification, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; and have masters in the French, German, English, and Swedish languages. They are trained to naval affairs, and make an annual cruise in the Baltic as far as Revel.—Cronstadt has a separate haven appropriated to the men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and another to merchant ships. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> to the haven for merchant ships is a canal and several dry docks, begun in 1719 by Peter I. for the purpose of refitting the men of war. This useful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was neglected under his successors, and was not completed until the reign of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. It has been still further beautified and improved by the present emperors; and is now applied for building as well as careening ships of the line. At the extremity of these docks is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reservoir 568 feet in length, which contains water sufficient, and half the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> over, to supply all the docks; which is pumped into it by means of a fire engine, the diameter of whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> is six feet. The length of this work, from the beginning of the canal to the end of the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCK">dock</a>, is 4221 feet. The sides of the docks are faced with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and the bottom is paved with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>. They are 40 feet deep and 150 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and are capable of containing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> men of war upon the stocks.

CRONSTAT

Pages 399-399

a town of Transylvania, near the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a>, subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25° O. N. Lat. 47° O.

CROSIER

Pages 399-399
or Crozier, a shepherd's crook; a symbol of pastoral authority, consisting of a gold or silver staff, crooked at the top, carried occasionally before bishops and abbots, and held in the hand when they give the solemn benedictions. The custom of bearing a pastoral staff before bishops is very ancient, as appears from the life of St Cæsarea of Arles, who lived about the year 500. Among the Greeks none but the patriarchs had a right to the crozier. The croisers were at first no more than simple wooden staves in form of a T, used to rest and lean upon. By degrees they were made longer; and at length arrived at the form we now see them of. Regular abbots are allowed to officiate with a mitre and crozier. Crosier, in Astronomy, four stars in the southern hemisphere, in the form of a cross, serving those who sail in south latitudes to find the antarctic pole.

CROSLLET

Pages 399-399

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is when a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> is crossed again at a small distance from each of the ends. Upton says it is not so often borne by itself in arms as other crosses are, but often in diminutives, that is, in small crolets scattered about the field. See Heraldry.

CROSS

Pages 399-402

a gibbet made with two pieces of wood placed crosswise, whether they cross with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> at the top like a T, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the middle of their length like a X. The cross to which our Saviour was fastened, and on which he died, was of the former kind; being thus represented by old monuments, coins, and crosses; and St Jerome compares it to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>, or praying with his arms extended. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the cross was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the Syrians, Egyptians, Persians, Africans, Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and Jews. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the cross was the most dreadful of all others, both for the shame and pain of it; and so scandalous, that it was inflicted as the last mark of detestation upon the vilest of people. It was the punishment of robbers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a>, provided that they were slaves too; but otherwise, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were free, and had the privileges of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Rome, this was then thought a profanation of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and too infamous a punishment for such a one, let his crimes be what they would. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic <a </a>class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> ordained, that the persons executed should not be left upon the tree after sunset, because he that is hanged in this manner is accursed of God, Deut. xxi. 22. The Jews believe, that the souls of those who remain upon the gibbet, and without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>, enjoy no peace, and receive no benefit from the prayers of other people; but wander up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> till their bodies are buried: which agrees with the notions that the Greeks and Romans had of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as may be seen in Hom. Iliad 4. and Virg. Aeneid. 6. The form of a crofs being such as has been already described, the body of the criminal was fastened to the upright piece by nailing the feet to it, and on the other transverse piece generally by nailing the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on each side. Now, because these parts of the body, being the instruments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, are provided by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with a much greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of nerves than others have occasion for; and because all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> is performed by the spirit contained in these nerves; it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> follow, as Stanhope observes, that wherever they abound, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of pain must needs in proportion be more quick and tender. The Jews confess, that indeed they crucified people in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, but deny that they inflicted this punishment upon any one alive. They first put them to death, and then fastened them to the cross either by the hands or neck. But there are indisputable proofs of their crucifying men frequently alive. The worshippers of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAAL">Baal</a>-panor and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Ai were hung up alive; as were also the defendants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, who were put into the hands of the Gibonites, 2 Sam. xxii. 9. Before crucifixion the criminal was generally scourged with cords: sometimes little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, or pieces of bones, were tied to these scourges, so that the condemned person might suffer more severely. It was also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, that he who was to be crucified should bear his own cross to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of execution. After this manner we find Christ was compelled to bear his own cross; and as he sunk under the burden, Simon the Cyrenian was constrained to bear it after him and with him. But whereas it is generally supposed that our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> bore the whole cross, i.e., the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and transverse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> both, this seems to be a thing impossible; and therefore Lipsius (in his treatise De Supplicio Crucis) has set the matter in a true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, when he tells us that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> only carried the transverse beam; because the long beam, or the body of the cross, was either fixed in the ground before, or made ready to be set up as soon as the prisoner came; and from hence he observes, that painters are very much mistaken in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of our Saviour carrying the whole cross. There were several ways of crucifying; sometimes the criminal was fastened with cords to a tree, sometimes he was crucified with his head downwards. This way St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> chose out of respect to his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Jesus Christ, not thinking himself worthy to be crucified like him; though the common way of crucifying was by fastening the criminal with nails, one through each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and one through both feet, or one through each of them: for this was not always performed in the same manner; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> sometimes representing Jesus Christ crucified with four nails, and sometimes with three. The criminal was fixed to the cross quite naked; and in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the Saviour of the world was not used with any greater tenderness than others upon whom the punishment was inflicted. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> divided his clothes among them, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> lots for his tunic, which is an under garment worn over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> like a shirt. The text of the gospel shows clearly, that Jesus Christ was fastened to the cross with nails; and the Psalmist (xxii. 16.) had foretold long before, that they should pierce his hands and his feet; but there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disputes concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these nails. The Greeks represent our Saviour as fastened to the cross with four nails; in which particular Gregory of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a> agrees with them, one at each hand and foot. But several are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that our Saviour's hands and feet were pierced with three nails only, viz. one at each hand, and one through both his feet: and the custom of the Latins is rather for this last opinion; for the generality of the old crucifixes made in the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> have only three nails. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NONNUS">Nonnus</a> thinks that our Saviour's arms were besides bound fast to the cross with chains; and St Hilary speaks of the cords where-with he was tied to it. Sometimes they who were fastened upon the cross lived a good while in that condition. St Andrew is believed to have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> three days alive upon it. Eusebius speaks of certain martyrs in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> who were kept upon the cross till they were starved to death. Pilate was amazed at Jesus Christ dying so soon; because naturally he must have lived longer, if it had not been in his power to have laid down his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and to take it up again. The thighs of the two thieves who were crucified together with our Saviour were broken, in order to hasten their death, that their bodies might not remain upon the cross on the Sabbath-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> (John xix. 31, 32, 33.), and to comply with the law of Moses, which forbids the bodies to be left there after sunset. But among other nations they were suffered to remain upon the cross a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Sometimes they were devoured alive by birds and beasts of prey. Guards were appointed to observe that none of their friends or relations should take them down and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> them. The story of the Egyptian matron and the folder who was set to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the cross, is very well known. The Roman soldiers who had crucified Jesus Christ and the two thieves continued near the cross till the bodies were taken down and buried. Crosses were usually, in former times, erected on the tops of houses, by which tenants pretended to claim the privileges of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPLARS">Templars</a> Hospitallers, to defend themselves against their rightful lords. This was condemned by the statute Wil. II. c. 37: It was usual also, in those days, to set up crosses in places where the corpse of any of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> rested as it was carried to be buried, that a transiuntibus pro ejus animo diperceatur. Crosses, &c., are forbidden to be brought into England by 13 Eliz. c. 2, on pain of a premunire, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">Invention</a> of the Cross, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> feast solemnized on the third of May, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of St Helena's (the mother of Constantine) finding the true cross of Christ deep in the ground on Mount Calvary; where she erected a church for the preservation of part of it; the rest being brought to Rome and deposited in the church of the Holy Cross of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. Theodoret mentions the finding of three crosses; that of Jesus Christ and those of the two thieves; and that they distinguished between them by means of a sick woman, who was immediately healed by touching the true cross. The place is said to have been pointed out to her by St Quiriacus, then a Jew, afterwards converted and canonized. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXALTATION">Exaltation</a> of the Cross, an ancient feast, held on the 14th of September, in memory of this, that Heraclius restored to Mount Calvary the true cross in 642, which had been carried off 14 years before by Colossus king of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, upon his taking Jerusalem from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Phocas. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of the cross appears to have been practised in the ancient church; inasmuch as the heathens, particularly Julian, reproach the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> with it. And we do not find that their apologists disclaimed the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. Momay, indeed, asserted, that this had been done by St Cyril, but could not support his allegation at the conference of Fontainebleau. St Helena is said to have reduced the adoration of the cross to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> principle, since she adored in the wood, not the wood itself, which had been directed idolatry and heathenism, but him who had been nailed to this wood. With such modifications some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> have been induced to admit the adoration of the cross. John Hus allowed of the phrase, provided it were expressly added, that the adoration was relative to the person of Christ. But however <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> may seem to triumph by virtue of such distinction and mitigations, it is well known they have no great place in their own practice. Imbert, the good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of Gafcony, was severely prosecuted in 1683 for telling the people, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of adoring the cross, practised in that church on Good Friday, they were not to adore the wood, but Christ, who was crucified on it. The curate of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> told them the contrary: it was the wood! the wood! they were to adore. Imbert replied, it was Christ, not the wood: for which he was cited before the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOURDEAUX">Bourdeaux</a>, suspended from his functions, and threatened with chains and perpetual imprisonment. It little availed him to cite the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>'s distinction; it was answered that the church allowed it not. Cross-Bearer (port-croix, cruciger), in the Roman church, the chaplain of an archbishop or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a>, who bears a cross before him on solemn occasions.
