The pope has the cross borne before him everywhere; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> anywhere out of Rome; and primates, metropolitans, and those who have a right to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALLIUM">pallium</a>, throughout their respective jurisdictions. Gregory XI. forbade all patriarchs and prelates to have it borne in presence of cardinals. A prelate bears a single cross, a patriarch a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> cross, and the pope a triple one on his arms. Cross-Bearers also denote certain officers in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, who make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> before the inquisitors or their vicars to defend the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, though with the loss of fortune and life. Their business is to provide the inquisitors with necessaries. They were formerly of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time some of their constitutions were changed, and they were called of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> of St Dominic. Pectoral Cross, is a cross of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or silver, or other precious materials, often enriched with diamonds, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, archbishops, &c., and regular abbeys, wear hanging from the neck. Order of the Cross, or Croisade, an order of ladies instituted in 1668 by the empress Eleonora de Gonzaga, wife of the emperor Leopold; on occasion of the miraculous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> cross wherein were inclosed two pieces of the true cross, out of the ashes of part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. It seems the fire had burnt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> wherein it was inclosed, and melted the crystal, yet the wood remained untouched. Maids of the Cross, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of young women instituted in 1265 at Roye in Picardy, and since dispersed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. They instruct young persons of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. Some take the three vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience; others retain their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. They are under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a superior. Cross, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is defined by Guillelmus, an ordinary composed of fourfold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; whereof two are perpendicular, and the other two transverse; so we must conceive of them, though they be not drawn throughout, but meet by couples, in four right angles, near the fesse point of the escutcheon. See Heraldry. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> was first bestowed on such as had performed, or at least undertaken, some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> for Christ, and the Christian profession; and is held by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> charge in all heraldry. What brought it into such frequent use, was the ancient expeditions into the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a>; and the holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> pilgrims, after their pilgrimage, taking the cross for their cognizance; and the ensign of that war being the cross. In those wars, says Mackenzie, the Scots carried St Andrew's cross; the French a cross argent; the English a cross or; the Germans, fesse; the Italians, azure; the Spaniards, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULES">gules</a>. St George's Cross, or the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> cross, in a field argent, is now the standard of England; that saint being the reputed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of this nation. Nor is it only in crosses that the variety is so great; the like is found in many other bearings, and particularly in lions, and the parts of them; whereof Columbiere gives us no less than 96 varieties. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a> mentions but 46 several crosses; Sylvanus Morgan, 26; Upton, 30; Johannes de Bado Aureo, 12; and to others, whom it is needless to mention. Upton owns he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> not presume to ascertain all the various crosses used in arms, for that they are at present almost innumerable; and therefore he only takes notice of such as he had seen used in his own time. Cross, in mining, two nicks cut on the superficies of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, thus +, which the miners make when they take the ground to dig for ore. This cross gives the miners three days liberty to make and set on <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. As many of these crosses as the miner makes to many acres of ground he may have in the vein, provided he set on stones within three days after making his cross or crosses. But if he make but one cross, and a stranger by makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and a stranger makes the third, every one is served with the next near, according as they have first or last, sooner or later, made their crosses upon the ground. Cross, in coins, a name given to the right side or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, the other being called the pile or reverse. It has been a common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, that the reverse was meant by the cross; because at this time, with us, it is marked with figures disposed in that form: but the stamping the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in these kingdoms on the right side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, was preceded by a general custom of striking on that part the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a cross; while the other, called the pile, contained the arms, or some other device. Cross, instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, &c., is derived from the Saxon practice of affixing the sign of the cross, whether they could write or not. Cross, in surveying, is an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> which consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> circle, divided into four equal parts by two lines crossing each other in the centre. At each extremity of the lines is fixed a perpendicular sight, with Crofs. Small holes below each slit, for the better discovering of distant objects. The crofs is mounted on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> or stand, to fix it in the ground, and it is found to be a very useful instrument for measuring small pieces of land, and taking offsets, &c. Cross-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">Bar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">Shot</a>, a bullet with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> bar passing through it, and standing six or eight inches out at both sides. It is used at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> for destroying the enemy's rigging. Cross-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">Bill</a>. See Loxia, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cross-Bill, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, is an original bill, by which the defendant prays relief against the plaintiff. Cross-Bows. See Bows and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">Archery</a>. Cross-grained Stuff, in joinery. Wood is said to be cross-grained, when a bough or branch has shot out of it; for the grain of the branch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> forward, runs athwart that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>. In wood well grown this defect is scarce perceptible, except in working; but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>-boards these boughs make knots. If the bough grew up with the young trunk, instead of a knot is found a curling in the stuff, very sensible under the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>. Cross-Jack, pronounced cro-jack, a sail extended on the lower yard of the mizen-mast, which is hence called the cross-jack yard. This sail, however, has generally been found of little service, and is therefore very seldom used. Cross-Piece, a rail of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> extended over the windlass of a merchant ship from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>-heads to the beltry. It is stuck full of wooden pins, which are used to fasten the running rigging as occasion requires. See Windlass. Cross-Staff, or Fore-staff, is a mathematical instrument of hard wood, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> staff of about three feet long, having each of its faces divided like a line of tangents, and having four cross pieces of unequal lengths to fit on the staff, the halves of these being as the radii to the tangent lines on the faces of the staff.—The instrument was formerly used in taking the altitudes of the celestial bodies at sea. Cross-Timing, in Husbandry, a method of harrowing land, consisting in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARROW">harrow</a> up the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> it went down before, and down that which it was drawn up. Cross-Trees, certain pieces of timber, supported by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> and trestle-trees, at the upper ends of the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, athwart which they are laid to sustain the frame of the top. Cross-Tree Yard, is a yard standing square, just under the mizen-top, and to it the mizen-top is fastened below. See Cross-Jack. Cross-Wort. See Valantia, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Ordeal of the Cross, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> frequently practised in the days of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. See Ordeal. Cross, an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, famous only for copying, in the reigns of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. and Charles II. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> there is a story current, more to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of his skill than of his probity. He is said to have been employed by Charles I. to copy the celebrated Madonna of Raphael in St Mark's church at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; and that, having obtained leave of the slate for that purpose, he executed his piece so well as to bring away the original and leave his copy in the place of it. The deception was not detected until it was too late to recover the loss; and this piece was bought in Oliver Cromwell's time by the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> for his master, who placed it in the Escorial.

CROSSEN

Pages 402-402

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a> in Germany, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a principality of the same name. It is situated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Bobar and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding in wine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the Oder which is fortified. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 15° 20' N. Lat. 52° 5'.

CROSSOSTYLUS

Pages 402-402

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a> class.

CROTALARIA

Pages 402-402

Rattle-wort: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 32d order, Papilionaceae.

CROTALO

Pages 402-402

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> music, like that described in the next article. The Turks were the first, among the moderns, who introduced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it for their troops. It is now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and other territories on the continent. It has only one tone; but its effect in marking <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> may be distinctly heard through the noise of forty drums. This is the same instrument with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> cymbalum.

CROTALUM

Pages 402-402

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kind of castagnetta, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, found on medals, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the priests of Cybele. The crotalum differed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISTRUM">sistrum</a>; though authors frequently confound the two. It consisted of two little <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> plates or rods, which were shaken in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and in striking against each other made a noise. It was sometimes also made of a reed split lengthwise; one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> whereof they struck against the other; and as this made a noise somewhat like that of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRANE">crane</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, they called that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> crotalifiria, a player on the crotala: and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a> calls a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> talker a crotalum. Clemens Alexandrinus attributes the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> to the Sicilians; and forbids the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> thereof to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, because of the indecent motions and gestures that accompany it.

CROTALUS

Pages 402-404
or Rattle-snake, in Zoology, a genus belonging to the order of amphibia serpentes. See Ophiology Index. The following is the account given by Mr Catesby of the crotalus horridus, or American rattle-snake. This grows sometimes to the length of eight feet, and weighs between eight and nine pounds. The colour of the head is brown; the eye red; the upper part of the body of a yellowish-brown colour, transversely marked with irregular broad black bands. The rattle is of a brown colour, composed of several horny, membranous cells, of an undulated pyramidal figure. These are articulated within one another in such a manner that the point of the first cell reaches as far as the basis of the protuberant ring of the third, and so on; which articulation, being very loose, gives liberty to the parts of the cells that are inclosed within the outward rings to strike against the sides of them, and so to cause the rattling noise which is heard when the snake shakes its tail. This is the most inactive and slow-moving of all the snakes, and is never the aggressor except in what it preys upon. The above gentleman is of opinion that no remedy is yet discovered for the bite of this animal. He had frequently access to see Indians bitten by it, and always thought that those who recovered were cured more through through the force of nature, or by reason of the lightness of the bite, than by the remedies used. He tells us, that the Indians know their destiny the moment they are bitten; and if the bite happens to be on any of the large veins, they apply no remedies, as knowing them to be entirely useless. He believes the reports of the fascinating power of this serpent, though he never had an opportunity of seeing it. See the articles Poison and Serpent. Crotalys Træ in antiquity, a kind of morris dancers, admitted to entertainments, in order to divert the company with their dancing and playing on an instrument called crotalum, whence they had their name. Crotchet, in Music, one of the notes or characters of time, equal to half a minim, and double of a quaver. Crotchets are also marks or characters, serving to inclose a word or sentence which is distinguished from the rest, being generally in this form [ ]. Croto, or Croton, in Ancient Geography, a noble city of the Brutii, built by the Achaeans, 150 stadia to the north of Lacinium, and in the neighbourhood of Metapontum. It was twelve miles in compass before the arrival of Pyrrhus in Italy; but after the devastation produced by that war, scarce half of it was inhabited. The citadel on one side hung over the sea, on the other towards the land. It was naturally strong from its situation, but afterwards walled round; on which side it was taken by Dionysius by stratagem, by means of the rocks behind it. Pythagoras, after his long peregrinations in search of knowledge, fixed his residence in this place, which some authors think his native one, at least that of his parents, supposing him to have been born in the isle of Samos, and not at some town of that name in Italy. This incomparable sage spent the latter part of his life in training up disciples to the rigid exercise of sublime and moral virtue, and instructing the Crotonites in the true arts of government, such as alone can insure happiness, glory, and independence. Under the influence of this philosophy, the Crotonites inured their bodies to frugality and hardships, and their minds to self-denial and patriotic disinterestedness. Their virtues were the admiration of Greece, where it was a current proverb, that the last of the Crotonites was the first of the Greeks. In one Olympiad, seven of the victors in the games were citizens of Croton; and the name of Milo is almost as famous as that of Hercules. The vigour of the men and beauty of the women were ascribed to the climate, which was believed to be endowed with qualities peculiarly favourable to the human system. Their physicians were in high repute; and among those, Alcmeon and Democides rendered themselves most conspicuous. Alcmeon was the first who dared to amputate a limb, in order to save the life of a patient; and also the first writer who thought of inculcating moral precepts under the amusing cloak of apologues. This invention is more commonly attributed to Æsop, as he was remarkably ingenious in this species of composition. Democides was famous for his attachment to his native soil. Though careful and enriched by the king of Persia, whose queen he had snatched from the jaws of death, he abandoned wealth and honours, and by stratagem escaped to the humble comforts of a private life at Croton.—The Pythagoreans are said to have discovered that disposition of the solar system, which, with some modifications, has been revived by Copernicus, and is now universally received, as being most agreeable to nature and experiment. Theano, the wife of Pythagoras, and many other women, emulated the virtues of their husbands. In those fortunate days the state of Croton was most flourishing. Its walls inclosed a circumference of 12 miles. Of all the colonies sent out from Greece, this alone furnished succour to the mother-country when invaded by the Perians. By its avenging arms the Sybarites were punished for their shameful degeneracy; but victory proved fatal to the conquerors, for riches, and all their pernicious attendants, infatuated themselves into Croton, and soon contaminated the purity of its principles. Indeed, the very constitution of human nature militates against any long continuance in such rigid practices of virtue; and therefore it is no wonder if the Crotonites fell by degrees into the irregularities they once abhorred. Not long after the Locrians, who were less corrupted, defeated them on the banks of the Sagra, and reduced the republic to distress and penury. This restored the remaining Crotonites to their pristine vigour of mind, and enabled them to make a brave, though unsuccessful resistance, when attacked by Dionysius of Syracuse. They suffered much in the war with Pyrrhus, and, by repeated misfortunes, decreased in strength and numbers, from age to age, down to that of Hannibal, when they could not muster 20,000 inhabitants. This small population being incapable of manning the extensive works erected in the days of prosperity, Croton was taken by the Carthaginians, and its citizens transported to Locri. The Romans sent a colony hither 200 years before Christ. In the Gothic war, this city rendered itself conspicuous by its fidelity to Justinian, and Totila besieged it long in vain. Croton, Wild Ricinus: A genus of plants, belonging to the monoeccia class; and in the natural method ranking under the 38th order, Trivce. See Botany Index. Crotona, a town of Italy, in the kingdom of Naples, seated on the gulf of Taranto, with a bishop's see and citadel. E. Long. 17° 27'. N. Lat. 39° 10'. Crotophaga, a genus of birds belonging to the order of picæ. See Ornithology Index. Crotoy, a town of France, in Picardy, and in Ponthieu. The fortifications are demolished. It is situated at the mouth of the river Somme. E. Long. 1° 45'. N. Lat. 50° 15'. Crouched Friars. See Croisiers. Croup, in Medicine. See Medicine Index. Croup of a Horse, in the manege, the extremity of the reins above the hips. Croupade, in the manege, a leap, in which the horse pulls up his hind legs, as if he drew them up to his belly. Crouté, Sour Croute, or Kroute. As this preparation of cabbage has been found of sovereign efficacy as a preservative in long voyages from the fear of scurvy, it may not be unacceptable to give a concise account. account of the process for making it, according to the information communicated by an ingenious German gentleman. The soundest and most solid cabbage are selected for this use, and cut very small, commonly with an instrument made for this purpose, not unlike the plain which is used in this country for slicing cucumbers. A knife is used when the preparation is made with great nicety. The cabbage thus minced is put into a barrel in layers, hand high, and over each is thrown a handful of salt and caraway seeds; in this manner it is rammed down with a rammer stratum super stratum, till the barrel be full; when a cover is put over it and pressed down with a heavy weight. After standing some time in this state it begins to ferment; and it is not till the fermentation has entirely subsided that the head is fitted to it, and the barrel is finally shut up and preserved for use. There is not a drop of vinegar employed in this preparation. The Germans write this preparation in the following manner: *Sauer kraut*, or *sauer kohl*; that is, in their language, "four herb, or four cabbage."

CROUSAZ

Pages 404-404

John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> de, a learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and mathematician, was born in 1663. Having made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of Des Cartes, he travelled to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and France; was successively professor in several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>; and at length was chosen governor to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Frederic of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a> Cassel, nephew to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. He wrote many works; the most esteemed of which are, 1. His Logic, the best edition of which is that of 1741, in 6 vols 8vo. 2. A Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">Beauty</a>. 3. A Treatise on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">Education</a> of Children, 2 vols 12mo. 4. Several Treatises on Philosophical and Mathematical Subjects, &c. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a> in 1748. CROW. See Corvus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Crow, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>, with a claw at one end and a sharp point at the other; used for heaving <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> purchasing great weights. Crow's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">Bill</a>, among surgeons, a kind of forceps for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> bullets and other foreign bodies out of wounds. Crow's Feet, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> of iron, having four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, each about three or four inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, so made, that whatever way they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> there is still a point up; they are thrown upon breaches, or in passes where the enemy's cavalry are to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, proving very troublesome, by running into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s feet and laming them. Crow's Foot, on ship board, a complication of small cords spreading out from a long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, like the smaller parts which extend from the back-bone of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>. It is used to suspend the canvings; or to keep the top-sails from striking violently, and fretting against the tops. Crow-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">Net</a>, is an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> for catching wild-fowl in the winter season, and may be used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. This net is made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> thread, or fine packthread; the meshes should be two inches wide, the length about ten yards, and the depth three; it must be verged on the side with good strong <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, and stretched out very stiff on long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> prepared for that purpose. When you are come to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where you would spread your net, open it, and lay it out at its full length and breadth; then fasten the lower end of the net all along the ground, so as only to move it up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; the upper end of the net must stand extended on the long cord; the further end thereof being staked first to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> by a strong cord about five yards distant from the net. Place this cord in an even line with the lower edge of the net. The other end must be at least 25 yards distant to reach into some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> shelter, by the means of which you may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> concealed from the fowl, otherwise no good success can be expected. The net must be placed in such exact order that it might give way to play on the fowl on the least pull of the cord, which must be done smartly, lest the fowl should prove too quick for you. This net may be used for pigeons, crows, or other birds, on corn-fields newly sown; as also in stubble-fields, provided the stubble conceals the net from the birds.

CROWD

Pages 404-404

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people assembled in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> scarce big enough to hold them all. To Crowd, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is to carry an extraordinary force of sail upon a ship, in order to accelerate her course on some important occasion; as in pursuit of, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flight from an enemy; to escape any immediate danger, &c.

CROWLAND

Pages 404-404

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, seated in the fens, in a dirty foil, and had formerly an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. There is no coming at it but by narrow causeways, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not admit a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a>. It has three streets, separated from each other by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-courses, whose banks are supported by piles, and set with willow trees. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> trade is in fish and fowl, which are in great plenty in the adjacent pools and marshes. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 10. N. Lat. 52. 40.

CROWN

Pages 404-407

an ornament worn on the head by kings, sovereign princes, and noblemen, as a mark of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. In scripture there is frequent mention of crowns, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them seems to have been very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the Hebrews. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> wore a crown, which was a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> placed upon the forehead, and tied with a ribbon of hyacinth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> azure blue. It seems also as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> private priests, and even common Israelites, wore also a sort of crown, since God commands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> not to take off his crown, nor affume the marks of one in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>. This crown was no more than a ribbon or fillet, with which the Jews and several people in the east girt their heads. And indeed the first crowns were no more than a bandelet drawn round the head, and tied behind, as we still see it represented on medals round the heads of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, the Ptolemies, and kings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. Afterwards they consisted of two bandelets; by degrees they took branches of trees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds; at length they added <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, insomuch that Claudius Saturninus says, there was not any plant whereof crowns had not been made. The woods and groves were searched to find different crowns for the several deities; and they were used not only on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and images of the gods, by the priests in sacrificing, and by kings and emperors, but also on altars, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, doors of housetops, sacred victims, ships, &c. The Roman emperors had four kinds of crowns; still seen on medals, viz. a crown of laurels, a radial or radiating crown, a crown adorned with pearls and precious Crown, ous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and the fourth a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, something like the mortier. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had also various kinds of crowns, which they distributed as rewards of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> achievements; as, 1. The oval crown, made of myrtle, and bestowed upon generals, who were entitled to the honours of the lesser triumph, called ovation. 2. The naval or rostral crown, composed of a circle of gold, with ornaments representing beaks of ships, and given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> who first grappled, or the soldier who first boarded, an enemy's ship. 3. The crown called in Latin vallaris, caerulescens, a circle of gold raised with jewels or palisades; the reward of him who first forced the enemy's entrenchments. 4. The mural crown, a circle of gold indented and embattled; given to him who first mounted the wall of a besieged <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and there lodged a standard. 5. The civic crown, made of the branch of a green oak, and given him who had saved the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of a citizen. 6. The triumphal crown, consisting at first of wreaths of laurel, but afterwards made of gold; proper to such generals as had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a triumph. 7. The crown called obfessionalis, or grammata, made of garlands growing on the place; the reward of a general who had delivered a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> from a siege. 8. The radial crown, given to princes at their translation among the gods. We meet also with the corona aurea, often bestowed on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> without any other additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>; athletic crowns, and crowns of laurel, destined to crown victors at the public games, poets, orators, &c. All these crowns were marks of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> to the wearers; and upon competitions with rivals for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and dignities, often determined the preference in their favour. See Plate CLXIV. For an account of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> crowns, see <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>. Crown is also used to signify the possessions and dignity of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. The crown of England, according to Sir William Blackstone, is, by common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and constitutional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>; and this in a manner peculiar to itself; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of inheritance may from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time be changed or limited by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, under which limitations the crown still continues hereditary. See Succession. Pleas of the Crown. See Pleas. Crown, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, is a general name, for coins, both foreign and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>, of or near the value of five shillings <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. In its limited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, crown is only applicable to that popular English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> which bears the name and which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to sixty English pence or five shillings, or to six livres French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. But, in its extensive sense, it takes in several others; as the French ecu, which we call the French crown, struck in 1641 for sixty sols, or three livres; also the pata- gon, dollar, ducatoon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIXDOLLAR">rixdollar</a>, and piastre or piece of eight. Crown, in an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> sense, is used for the clerical tonsure; which is the mark or character of the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>. This is a little circle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> shaved off from the crown of the head; more or less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the orders received: That of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> clerk is the smallest; that of priests and monks the largest. The clerical crown was anciently a round lift of hair, shaved off around the head, representing a real crown: this is easily observable in several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> statues, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> of St Dominic and St Francis still retain it. Crown, among jewellers, the upper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the rose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>, which all centres in the point at the top, and is bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> ribs. Crown-Office, an office belonging to the king's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, of which the king's coroner or attorney is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. In this office, the attorney general and clerk of the crown feversly exhibit informations for crimes and misdemeanours at common law, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of batteries, conspiracies, libelling, &c., on which the offender is liable to pay a fine to the king. Crown-Glass, denotes the finest sort of window-glass. See Glass. Crown-Seals. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Crown-Wheel of a Watch, the upper wheel next the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>, which by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> drives the balance, and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> pendulums is called the swing-wheel. Crown Imperial. See Fritillaria, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Crown Work, in Fortification, is an out-work running into the field; designed to keep off the enemy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> some hill or advantageous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, and cover the other works of the place. The crown-work consists of two demi-bastions at the extremes, and an entire bastion in the middle, with curtains. Crown, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a name given to two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>, the southern and the northern. Crown, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> included between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> or concentric peripheries of unequal circles. Crown-Poat, is a post in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> standing upright in the middle between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> rafters; and from which proceed struts or braces to the middle of each rafter. It is otherwise called a king post, or king's-piece, or joggle-piece.

CROWNE

Pages 407-407

John, a celebrated dramatic writer, born in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a>, where his father was a minister. Being impatient of the gloomy restraint of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he came to England, where he was reduced to enter into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of an old lady; of which he was soon as weary as he had been of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. He then had recourse to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, which quickly procured him favour at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>: but this kind of subsistence proving precarious, he ventured to solicit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. for some establishment. Charles promised to provide for him, but insisted first on having another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>; and suggested to him the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of a Spanish play, from which Crowne produced the comedy of Sir Courty Nice: but the sudden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> on the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the rehearsal, plunged him at once from his pleasing expectations into disappointment and distress, and left him no resource but his wits. He died some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> about the year 1703; and left behind him 17 tragedies and comedies, some of which are acted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> excellence lay in comedy; yet his tragedies are far from being contemptible. His plots are for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>; his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are in general strongly coloured and highly finished; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> lively and spirited, attentively diversified, and well adapted to the several speakers. So that on the whole he may assuredly be allowed to stand at least in the third <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of our dramatic writers.

CROWNING

Pages 408-408

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, denotes the finishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a knot made at the end of a rope. It is performed by interweaving the ends of the different strands artfully amongst each other, so as that they may not become loosened <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> untwisted. They are useful in all kinds of stoppers.

CROXAL

Pages 408-408

SAMUEL, an ingenious English divine, who in his youth wrote the celebrated poem entitled The Fair Circassian. He had the livings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, and the united parishes of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Somerset, and St Mary Mounthaw, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; both which he held till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1751. He published many other poems and translations, with an entire English edition of Alop's Fables. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to Whig principles, he enjoyed some other preferments, and was chaplain in ordinary to George II.

CROYDON

Pages 408-408

a town in Surry in England. Its situation is low, near the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>-head of the river Wandel, and it is in a manner surrounded with hills. It is pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and is chiefly noted for being the seat of the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. It has a large handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and a free school. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. s. N. Lat. 51. 22.

CRUCIAL INCISION

Pages 408-408

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an incision made in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>.

CRUCIANELLA

Pages 408-408

PETTY Madder: A genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the tetrandria clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 47th order, Stellatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CRUCIBLE

Pages 408-408

a chemical vessel made of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and so tempered and baked as to endure the greatest fire. They are used to melt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> minerals, ores, &c.

CRUCIFIX

Pages 408-408

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> upon which the body of Christ is fastened in effigy, used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> to excite in their minds a strong idea of our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. They esteem it an essential circumstance of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship performed at the altar; and on Good Friday they perform the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of adoring it, which is done in these words, O crux ave, spes unica; "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">Hail</a>, thou cross, our only hope." The officiating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> uncovers the crucifix, elevates it with both his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and says, Ecce lignum crucis; "Behold the wood of the cross." The people answer, in quo salus mundi pendit; "on which the Saviour of the world suffered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>." Then the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> bow with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reverence, and devoutly kiss the holy wood.

CRUCIFIXION

Pages 408-408

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> by nailing the criminal to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. See Cross.

CRUCIFORM

Pages 408-408

in general, something disposed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-ways; but more especially used by botanists, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> consisting of four petals disposed in the form of a cross.

CRUCITA

Pages 408-408

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>: A genus of the digynia order, belonging to the tetrandria clasps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those the order of which is doubtful. The interior calyx is tetraphyllous, the exterior calyx triphyllous; there is no corolla, and only one seed.

CRUDE

Pages 408-408

an epithet given to something that has not passed the fire <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> had a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of coction.

CRUDITY

Pages 408-408

among physicians, is applied to undigested substances in the stomach; to humours in the body which are unconcocted, and not prepared for expulsion; and to the excrements.

CRUISE

Pages 408-408

from the German krauts, "aerots," signifies to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> to and fro, to sail up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> within a certain space of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, called the cruising latitude, in quest of vessels, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fleets of an enemy, &c.

CRUISERS

Pages 408-408

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, are small men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to and fro in the Channel, and elsewhere, to secure our merchant ships and vessels from the enemy's small frigates and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a>. They are generally such as sail well, and are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> well manned: and indeed the safety of the trade in the Channel, and up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the foundings, and other places, absolutely requires the constant keeping out such ships at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

CRUMENTATA

Pages 408-408

among zoologists, animals furnished with a pouch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bag, wherein to receive their young in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of danger; as the opossum. See Delphus.

CRUOR

Pages 408-408

sometimes signifies the blood in general; sometimes only the venous blood; and sometimes extravasated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coagulated blood: but is most frequently used for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> globules of the blood; in contradistinction to the limpid or serous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>.

CRUPPER

Pages 408-408

in the manege, the buttocks of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; the rump: also a thong of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> put under a horse's tail, and drawn up by thongs to the buckle behind the saddle, so as to keep him from casting the saddle forwards on his neck. CRURÆUS, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Crureus, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSCULUS">Musculus</a>, in Anatomy, a fleshy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, covering almost all the foreside of the femoris, between the two vasti, which likewise cover the edges of this muscle on each side. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

CRURAL

Pages 408-408

in Anatomy, an epithet given to the artery which conveys the blood to the crura <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> legs, and to the vein by which this blood returns towards the heart. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CRUSADO

Pages 408-408

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, struck under Alphonso V. about the year 1457, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when Pope Calixtus sent thither the bull for a crusade against the infidels. This coin has a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> on one side and the arms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> on the other.

CRUSCA

Pages 408-409

an Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifying bran, is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> amongst us to denote that celebrated academy called Della Crusca, established at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> for purifying and perfecting the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. See Academy, No. 11. The academy took its name from its office, and the end proposed by it; which is, to refine the language, and as it were to separate the bran from it. Accordingly, its device is a sieve; and its motto, Il più bel fiore ne coglie; that is, "It gathers the finest flour thereof." In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apartment where the academy CRU Cruft academy meets, M. Moneonis informs us, that every thing bears an allusion to the name and device; the feats are in form of a baker's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>; their backs like a shovel for moving of corn; the cushions of gray fatin, in form of sacks or wallets; and the branches where the lights are placed resembling sacks. The vocabulary Della Crufta is an excellent Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, composed by this academy.

CRUSTA LACTEA

Pages 409-409

in Medicine, the same with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHOR">Achor</a>. CRUSTACEOUS fish, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, are those covered with shells, consisting of several pieces <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scales; as those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, lobsters, &c. These are usually softer than the shells of the testaceous kind, which consist of a single piece, and generally much thicker and stronger than the former; such as those of the oyster, scallop, cockle, &c. Dr Woodward observes, in his Natural History, that of all the shells found in beds of all the different matters dug out of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, there are scarce any of the crustaceous kind; the reason he gives for it is, that they being much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the rest, must have floated on the surface at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the deluge, when all the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> were formed; and there have corrupted and perished.

CRUTH

Pages 409-409
or CROWTH, a kind of musical instrument formerly in use among the common people in Wales. It is of the fidicinal kind, somewhat resembling a violin, 12 inches in length, and an inch and a half in thickness. It has six strings supported by a bridge, and is played on with a bow: the bridge differs from that of a violin, in that it is flat and not convex on the top; a circumstance from which it is to be inferred, that the strings are to be struck at the same time, so as to afford a succession of concords. The bridge is not placed at right angles with the sides of the instrument, but in an oblique direction; and, which is further to be remarked, one of the feet of the bridge goes through one of the sound-holes, which are circular, and rests on the inside of the back; the other foot, which is proportionally shorter, resting on the belly before the other sound-hole. Of the strings the four first are conducted from the bridge down the finger board, as in a common violin; but the fifth and sixth, which are about an inch longer than the others, leave the small end of the neck about an inch to the right. The whole six are wound up either by wooden pegs in the form of the letter T, or by iron pins, which are turned with a wrest like those of a harp or spinet. Of the tuning, it is to be remarked, that the fifth and sixth strings are the unison and octave of G; the fourth and fifth, the same of C; and the second and first, the same of D; so that the second pair of strings are a fourth, and the third a fifth, to the first. See Plate CLXIV. Concerning the antiquity of this instrument, there is but little written evidence to carry it further back than the time of Leland; nevertheless the opinion of its high antiquity is so strong among the inhabitants of the country where it was used, as to afford a probable ground of conjecture, that the cruth might be the prototype of the whole fidicinal species of musical instruments. Another evidence of its antiquity, but which tends also to prove that it was not peculiar to Wales, arises from a discovery lately made and communicated to the society of antiquarians, respecting the abbey-church of Melrose in Scotland, supposed to have been built about the time of Edward II. It seems that among the outside ornaments of that church there is the representation of a cruth, very little different from the description above given. The instrument is now disused, inasmuch that Sir John Hawkins, from whom we extract, tells us, that there is but one person in the whole principality of North Wales that can play upon it; and as he was at that time near 60 years of age, the succession of performers is probably near an end.

CRUX

Pages 409-411
or St Croix, one of the Caribbee s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands, situated about 60 miles south-east of Porto Rico, and subject to Denmark. From being a perfect desert, it has begun to flourish exceedingly, being made a free port, and receiving great encouragement from government. W. Long. 64° O. N. Lat. 17° 30'. La Cruz, an excellent harbour on the north-west coast of America, which was discovered by the Spaniards in 1779. They were introduced into it by a passage which they called Bucarelli's entrance, and which they placed in 55° 18' N. Lat. and 139° 15' W. Long. from the meridian of Paris. The latitude of this passage as laid down by the Spaniards seems to be correct; but the editor of Peroule's voyage concludes, from the survey made by Captain Cook on the coasts adjacent to the entrance of Bucarelli, that this entrance is about 135° 20' to the west of Paris, or near 133° west of Greenwich. The Spaniards were not long in the harbour of La Cruz before they received a visit from the inhabitants in its neighbourhood. Bartering took place. The Indians gave their peltry, and various trifles, for glass beads, bits of old iron, &c. By this traffic the Spaniards were enabled to gain a sufficiently exact knowledge of their genius, of their offensive and defensive arms, of their manufactures, &c. Their colour is a clear olive; many among them have, however, a perfectly white skin: their countenance is well proportioned in all its parts. They are robust, courageous, arrogant, and warlike. They clothe themselves in one or two undressed skins (with the fur apparently); these are the skins of otters, of sea-wolves, of benades (a species of deer), of bears, or other animals. Their dresses cover them from the neck to the middle of the leg; some, however, among them wear boots of smooth skin, resembling English boots, only that those of the Indians open before, and are laced tight with a string. They wear hats woven from the fine bark of trees, which is formed into the shape of a funnel or a cone. At the wrists they have bracelets of copper or iron, or for want of these metals the fins of whales; and round the neck, necklaces of small fragments of bones of fishes and other animals, and even copper collars of the bigness of two fingers. They wear in their ears pendants of mother-of-pearl, or flat pieces of copper, on which is embossed a resin of a topaz colour, and which are accompanied with jet beads. Their hair is long and thick, and they make use of a comb to hold it together in a small queue from the middle to the extremity; a narrow ribbon of coarse linen, woven for this purpose, serves as a ligament. They wear also as a covering a kind of scarf, woven in a particular manner, something more than a yard... La Cruz, and a half long, and about half a yard broad, round which hangs a fringe something more than half a quarter of a yard deep, of which the thread is regularly twisted. The women give proofs of their modesty and decency by their dress. Their physiognomy is agreeable, their colour fresh, their cheeks vermillioned, and their hair long; they plait it together in one long braid. They wear a long robe of a smooth skin tied round the loins, like that of a nun; it covers them from the neck as low as the feet; the sleeves reach down to the wrists. Upon this robe they put divers skins of otters or other animals to defend themselves from the inclemency of the weather. All the married women have a large opening in the under lip, and this opening orifice is filled up by a piece of wood cut in an oval shape, of which the smallest diameter is almost an inch; the more a woman is advanced in years the more this curious ornament is extended; it renders them frightful, the old women especially, whose lip, deprived of its wonted spring, and dragged by the weight of this extraordinary jewel, necessarily hangs in a very disagreeable manner. The girls wear only a copper needle, which crosses the lip in the place where the ornament is intended hereafter to be placed. These Indians in war make use of cuirasses and shoulder pieces of a manufacture like that of the whalebone flays among the Europeans. Narrow boards or scantlings form, in some sort, the woof of the texture, and threads are the warp: in this manner the whole is very flexible, and leaves a free use to the arms for the handling of weapons. They wear round the neck a coarse and large gorget which covers them as high as below the eyes, and their head is defended by a morion, or skull-piece, usually made of the head of some ferocious animal. From the waist downwards, they wear a kind of apron, of the same contexture as their cuirass. Lastly, a fine skin hangs from their shoulders down to the knee. With this armour, they are invulnerable to the arrows of their enemies; but thus armed, they cannot change position with so much agility as if they were less burdened. Their offensive arms are arrows; bows, of which the strings are woven like the large cords of our best musical instruments; lances, four yards in length, tongued with iron; knives, of the same metal, longer than European bayonets, a weapon however not very common among them; little axes of flint, or of a green stone, so hard that they cleave the most compact wood without injury to their edge. The pronunciation of their language is extremely difficult; they speak from the throat, with a movement of the tongue against the palate. The little use the women make of their inferior lip greatly injures the distinctiveness of their language. The Spaniards could neither pronounce nor write the words which they heard. From the vivacity of spirit in these Indians, and from their attention amply to furnish the market established in the harbour, it may be concluded that they are pretty laborious. They continually brought stuffs well woven and shaded with various colours, the skins of land and sea wolves, of otters, bears, and other smaller animals; of these some were raw, and others dressed. There were to be found at this market also coverlets of coarse cloth, shaded with white and brown colours, very well woven, but in small quantities: large ribbons of the same linen which might match with that of the Spanish officers' mattresses; skeins of thread such as this cloth was made of; wooden plates or bowls neatly worked; small boats, or canoes, painted in various colours, the figures of which represented heads with all their parts; frogs in wood, nicely imitated, which opened like tobacco boxes, and which they employed to keep their trinkets in; boxes made of small planks, of a cubical form, being three quarters of a yard on each side, with figures well drawn, or carved on the outside, representing various animals; the covers fabricated like Flanders clogs, with rabbed edges, formed so as to fit into the body of the box; animals in wood, as well those of the earth as of the air; figures of men of the same material, with skull-caps representing the heads of various fierce animals; snares and nets for fishing; copper collars for the neck, and bracelets of iron for the wrist, but which they would not part with except at a very high price; beak-like instruments, from which they drew sounds as from a German flute. The principal officers took such of these merchandises as were most agreeable to them, and left the remainder to the ships crews. As the Indians discovered that the Spaniards were very dainty in their fish, they did not let them want for choice: the greatest abundance was in salmon, and a species of sole or turbot three yards and a quarter long, broad and thick in proportion; cod and pilchards were also brought to market, and fishes resembling trout. From all this it may be inferred, that this gulf is full of fish; the banks too are covered with shells. The quantity of mother-of-pearl that these Indians cut to pieces for making ear-rings awakened the curiosity of the Spaniards: they tried to discover whether these people had not in their possession, or whether their country did not produce pearls, or some precious stones: their researches were fruitless, they only found some stones which they judged to be metallic, and which they carried on board, not having the necessary means for extracting the metal they might contain. The inhabitants of La Cruz feed upon fish, fresh or dry, boiled or roasted; herbs and roots which their mountains yield them, and particularly that which in Spain is called sea parsley; and, lastly, upon the flesh of animals which they take in hunting: the productions of the chase are undoubtedly abundant, seeing the number of dogs they keep for this purpose. They appeared to the Spaniards to worship the sun, the earliest and most natural of all idolatrous worship; and they paid a decent respect to the remains of their dead. Don Maurelle, one of the Spanish officers, in an expedition round the gulf, found in two islands three dead bodies laid in boxes of a similar form to those which have been described above, though considerably larger, and decked in their furs. These biers were placed in a little hut upon a platform, or raised floor, made of the branches of trees. The country is very hilly; the mountains are lofty, and their slope extends almost everywhere to the sea. The soil is lime-stone; it is nevertheless covered with an impenetrable forest of tall fir trees, very large and very straight. As these trees cannot strike very deep into the earth, the violence of the wind often tears them up by Crymodes the roots: they rot and become a light mould, upon which grows a bully thicket; and in this are found nettles, chamomile, wild celery, anife, a species of cabbage, celandine, elder, wormwood, forrel; and without doubt there are other plants along the rivers. The Spaniards saw ducks, gulls, divers, kites, ravens, geese, storks, gold-finches, and other little birds unknown to them. The commerce between the Spaniards and the Indians was quite undisturbed; and so defrauded were the latter to obtain iron, cloths, and other stuffs, that they sold their children for broken iron hoops and other wares. The Spaniards in this manner bought three young lads, one from five to six years old, another of four, and the third from nine to ten, not to make slaves, but Christians of them; they hoped besides to derive useful information from them as to the nature of the country and its inhabitants. These youths were so contented in being with the Spaniards, that they hid themselves when their parents came on board, from the apprehension of being again restored to them. Two young girls were also purchased with the same view; one very ugly, seven years of age; the other younger, better made, but fickle, and almost at the gates of death. At the full and change of the moon, the sea rises in the harbour of La Cruz seventeen feet three inches English; it is then high water at a quarter after 12 at noon; the lowest tides are fourteen feet three inches; the night tides exceed by one foot nine inches those of the day.

CRYMODES

Pages 411-411

among physicians, a kind of fever attended with a shivering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and inflammation of the internal parts of the body.

CRYPTA

Pages 411-411

in Anatomy: A name given by Ruyssch to glands situated on the back of the tongue, and to glands of the intestines.

CRYPTOGAMIA

Pages 411-411

(from κρύπτω, occultus, "concealed," and νύμφη, nupia, "nuptials"), the 24th class in the Linnaean system, comprehending those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> whose fructification is concealed, either through minuteness, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> within the fruit. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CRYPTOGRAPHY

Pages 411-411

the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in cipher, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with sympathetic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>. Among the methods which Ovid teaches young women to deceive their guardians, when they write to their lovers, he mentions that of writing with new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and of making the writing legible by means of coal dust or foot; from which it appears, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of sympathetic ink was known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. Tuta quoque eft, falliique oculos, è <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LATTE">latte</a> recenti Litera : carbonis pulvere tange; leger. De Arte Amandi, lib. iii.

CRYSTAL

Pages 411-414

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> siliceous genus. It always appears, where there has been no interruption to its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a>, in hexagonal prisms pointed at both ends. It is found of different kinds and colours. 1. Opaque or semi-transparent, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. 2. Opaque and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, or of a carnelian colour, from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORAN">Oran</a> in Barbary. 3. Opaque and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, from the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. 4. Clear. The specific gravity of these kinds of crystals is from 2650 to 2700. Professor Bergman extracted from them about six parts of argilla and one of calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> per hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; but Mr Gerhard found some so pure as to contain neither. 5. Clear and blackish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; the smoky topaz, or rauchtopaz of the Germans. It is found at Egan in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and at Lovisa in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>. These crystals are said to become clear by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> them in tallow. 6. Clear and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and sold instead of topazes. 7. Clear and violet-coloured; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMETHYST">amethyst</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, Bohemia, and Dannemore in Upland. The most transparent of these are called false diamonds, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, Alençon diamonds, &c. 8. Colourless rock crystal, properly so called, found in Bohemia, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Jemland, and many other places. 9. Pyramidal crystal with one or two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. These have no prismatic shape, but either stand upon a base in cavities of quartz veins, have only a single <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>, pyramid, and are of various colours; or they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in clayey earths, and have both pyramids, but no prism. They are found at Blackenburg upon the Hartz, and at Morseroth in the Silverland in Transylvania. The coloured transparent crystals derive their tinge from an exceedingly small portion of metallic oxide, but lose them entirely when strongly heated. They are called false gems; viz. the red from Oran in Barbary, false rubies; the yellow from Saxony, false topazes; the green from Dauphiny, very rare, false emeralds or prases; the violet from Vil in Catalonia, false amethysts; the blue from Puy in Valais in France, false sapphires. There are likewise opal or rainbow crystals, the various colours of which are thrown out in zones across the surface. They make a very fine appearance, though they never shine like the oriental opal. M. Fourcroy makes a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the crystals and quartz, by affirming that the former are unalterable in the fire, in which they neither lose their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, transparency nor colour; while the quartz loses the same qualities, and is reduced by it to a white and opaque earth. He classes the rock crystals, I. According to their form, viz. 1. Inflated hexagonal crystals ending in pyramids of six faces, which have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> refraction, or show two images of the same object when looked through. 2. Hexagonal crystals united, having one or two points. 3. Tetraedral, dodecaedral, flattened crystals; and which, though hexagonal, have nevertheless their planes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>. 4. Crystals in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses, from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Madagascar, which have a simple refraction. II. With regard to their colour, as being either diaphanous, reddish, smoky, or blackish. III. With regard to accidental changes, some are hollow; some contain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> within one or more cavities; some are cased one within the other; some are of a round form, as the pebbles of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; some have a crust of metallic calcareous or of pyrites; some are found crystallized in the inside of a cavity; while some seem to contain amianthus or albitus; and others contain flints. The same author reckons among crystals the oriental topaz, the hyacinth, the oriental sapphire, and the amethyst. M. Daubenton has always looked upon this last as a quartz of a crystal. When the rock crystals are semitransparent or intermixed with opaque veins, they are called by the Swedish lapidaries milk-crystals. When they are found in the form of round pebbles, which is occasioned by their being tossed about and rubbed against one another by floods or by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, they are called by the English lapidaries pebble-crystals. They come from the Indies, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, and other places. According to Bomare, the rock-crystals are generally formed upon or among quartz, which shows their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a>, and are to be found in all parts of the world. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of them is brought from Mount Saint Gothard in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. Large pieces of these, weighing from 5 to 800 pounds, were found there at Grimselberg; another of about 1200 pounds weight was found some years ago at Fribach in the Valais; and a piece six feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, four wide, and equally thick, was found in the island of Madagascar, where these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions are of the most extraordinary size and perfection. In the imperial collection at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, there is a pyramidal crystal vase two ells in height, cut wholly out of one piece. It is usual with the largest crystals of the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> to be full of cracks and flaws, and to be so constructed internally as to show all the prismatic colours; but the above-mentioned ones were quite free from these blemishes, and resembled columns of the purest glass, only much clearer than any glass can be made. Crystal is also found in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>.
