I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a circle be described touching a conic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTION">section</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off from the diameter that passes through

YET LET US INQUIRE WHAT

Pages 367-371

t let us inquire what means the Cretan lawgiver used to form virtuous citizens. All the Cretans were subjected to the power of their magistrates; and divided into two classes, the adults and the youth. Men arrived at maturity were admitted into the first. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> consisted of all the young men who were not below the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of seventeen. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of adults ate together in public halls. There rulers, magistrates, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and rich, feasted together, partook, without distinction, of the same simple fare. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bowl, filled with wine and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which went round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> from one to another, was the only drink, that they were allowed. None but the old men had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to call for more wine. Doubtless, that people, celebrated for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, were not strangers to the power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; for a woman was appointed to preside at each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. She openly distributed the most exquisite meats to those who had distinguished themselves by their valour <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wisdom. That judicious preference was so far from exciting envy or jealousy, that it only prompted every person to deserve it by brave and prudent conduct. Near where the citizens sat, two tables were laid, which they named Hospitable; all strangers and travellers were entertained at these; and there was also a particular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> set apart by the public, in which they might spend the night. To supply the public expenses, every citizen was obliged to bring a tenth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his annual income into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> magistrates were to take care that every person contributed his proportion. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, says <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, one part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, of the produce of the flocks, of the revenues of the state, and of the taxes and customs, is sacred to the gods: the other is distributed among the members of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>; so that men, women, and children, all subsist at the public expense. After dinner, the magistrates and senators usually spent some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in deliberating on the affairs of the state; they next recounted the noble deeds which had been done in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, celebrated the courage of their most distinguished warriors, and animated the youth to heroic valour. Those assemblies were the first school of the youth. At the age of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, the boy was permitted to handle the bow;—from that time he was admitted into the society of the adults, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the age of seventeen. There, sitting on the ground, and clothed in a plain and coarse dress, he served the old men, and listened, with respectful silence, to their advices. His young heart was inflamed with the recital of noble deeds in arms, and glowed with ardour to imitate them. He acquired habits of sobriety and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>. And being constantly witness of illustrious examples of moderation, wisdom, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a>; the seeds of virtue were thus sown and fostered in his heart before he attained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of reason. He was early accustomed to arms and to fatigue, that he might learn to endure excessive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, to clamber and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> among hills and precipices, and to bear manfully the blows and wounds which he might receive amid the gymnastic exercises or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was not confined to the gymnastic exercises; he was also taught to sing the laws, which were written in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, with a certain <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>; in order that the charms of music might dispose him to learn them with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and might impress them more deeply on his heart, and that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he should ever transgress them, he might not have the excuse of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> to offer. He next learned hymns in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the gods, and poems composed in praise of heroes. When he reached his seventeenth year, he retired from the society of the adults, and became a member of that of the young men. Here his education was still carried on. He exercised himself in hunting, wrestling, and fighting with his companions. The lyre played tunes of martial music; and he learned to follow exactly the sounds and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the musician. Those sports and exercises were sometimes attended with danger; because arms of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> were sometimes used in them. One dance, in which the youth aspired most ardently to excel, was the Pyrrhic, originally invented in Crete. The performers in that dance were arrayed in complete armour—they wore a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> short coat, which did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> below the knee, and was bound with a girdle going twice round the waist: on their feet and legs were buckles; above these they bore their arms, and performed various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> evolutions to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of musical instruments. "The Lacedemonians and Cretans (says Libanius) cultivated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> with amazing ardour; they considered that their laws had directed them to practise it for the most important purposes; and it was scarce less dishonourable for a Lacedemonian or Cretan to neglect the military dances, than to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> in battle." Those Cretans who were opulent and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-born, were permitted to form <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of young men of their own age. They often strove, with emulation, who should form the most numerous ones. The father of the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who formed one of those societies usually presided in it. He had a right to educate those warlike youth, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> them in running and in hunting, to confer rewards and inflict punishments. Friendship was in high estimation among the Cretans; but, says Strabo, the manner in which they conducted the intercourse of friendship was pretty extraordinary. Instead of mild persuasion, they made use of violence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the objects of their affections. He who conceived an affection for a young man of his own age, and wished to attach him to himself by indissoluble bonds, formed a scheme for carrying him off by violence. Three days before putting it into execution, he communicated it to his comrade. They could not then interfere to prevent it; because if they had, they would have appeared to think the young man unworthy of such an exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>. At the appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> they assembled to protect their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>. If the ravisher appeared to them not unworthy of the object of his affection, they made at first a faint resistance in obedience to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>—but, at last, joyfully favoured his enterprise; if, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, they thought him unworthy of the object of his choice, they made such resistance as to prevent him from executing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. The feigned resistance continued till the ravisher had conducted his friend into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of that society to which he belonged. They did not regard him who possessed superior beauty and gracefulness of person as the most amiable; but him who had most distinguished himself by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and valour. The ravisher loaded his young friend with favours, and conducted him wherever he desired; they were accompanied by those who had favoured the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a>: he carried him from feast to feast, procured him the pleasures of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> and good cheer; and after using all possible means to gain his heart for the course of two months, brought him back to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; and was obliged to give him up to his parents. But first he presented him with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of armour, an ox, and a drinking cup; which were the usual and legal presents on such occasions. Sometimes his generosity went still farther; and he made more expensive presents; to defray the expense of which his comrades contributed. The young man sacrificed the ox to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and gave an entertainment to those who had assisted when he was carried off. He then declared his sentiments concerning a connection with his ravisher, and told whether or not it was agreeable to him. If he had reason to complain of the treatment which he had received, the law allowed him to forsake a friend so unworthy of the name, and to demand his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. It would have been disgraceful, adds Strabo, to a young man who was handsome and well born, to be rejected by his friends on account of the depravity of his manners. Those who had been carried off received public honours. Theirs were the first places in the halls and at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. They were permitted to wear, during the rest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, those ornaments which they owed to the tenderness of friendship; and that mark of distinction testified to all who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them, that they had been the objects of some fond attachment. When the youth had finished their exercises, and attained the legal age, they became members of the class of adults; being then considered as men, they were permitted to vote in the national assemblies, and were entitled to stand candidates for any public office. They were then obliged to marry: but did not take home their wives till such time as they were capable of managing their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> concerns. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> (says Strabo) had considered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> as the greatest blessing that cities can enjoy. Liberty alone can secure the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the citizens of any state. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">Slavery</a> either robs them of it, or renders it precarious. The first care of nations should therefore be to preserve their liberty. Concord strengthens and supports her empire; she flourishes wherever the seeds of dissension are extinguished. Almost all those hostilities which prevail among nations or individuals <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> either from an inordinate desire of wealth or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>. Introduce, instead of those baneful principles, frugality, moderation, and equality of conditions; you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> thus banish envy, hatred, injustice, and haughty disdain." This was what the Cretan lawgiver happily effected. And the community, which was regulated by his wise institutions, rose to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, opulence, and power; and was honoured with the panegyrics of the most celebrated philosophers. lophers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; but the highest honour it ever obtained, was that of serving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> for the admirable form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> which he established at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>. The republic of Crete continued to flourish till the age of Julius Caesar. No other state has enjoyed so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. The legislature, regarding liberty as the only sure basis of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, had instituted a system of laws, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> tendency of which was, to inspire men with an ardent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for liberty, and with such virtue and valour as are necessary to support and defend it. All the citizens were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; all of them were skilled in the art of war. The valiant youth of other nations flocked to Crete, to learn the exercises, manoeuvres, and evolutions, of the military art. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOPOEMEN">Philopoemen</a> (says Plutarch) being impatient of idleness, and eager to acquire skill in arms, embarked for Crete. After spending a considerable time in the noblest exercises among that brave people, who were skilled in the art of war, and accustomed to an austere and temperate life, he returned to the Achaeans. The knowledge which he had acquired made him so eminent among them, that he was immediately appointed general of their cavalry." On the other hand, the legislator, being persuaded that conquests are generally unjust and criminal, that they often exhaust the strength of the victorious nation, and almost always corrupt its manners, endeavoured to preserve the Cretans from the ambition of conquest. The fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> abundantly supplied their wants. They needed not that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> should introduce among them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of foreign countries, along with which luxury and her train of attendant vices would also be introduced; and he knew how to inspire them with an indifference for such acquisitions without expressly forbidding them. The gymnastic exercises, which occupied the leisure of the gallant youth; the pleasures of the chase; the ardour of friendship; the public shows, at which all the different orders of the community, both men and women, used to assemble; the love of equality, order, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with which he inflamed every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; the wise institutions, which united a whole nation so closely that they composed but one family;—all these ties attached the Cretans to their native island; and finding at home that happiness which was the object of their wishes, they never thought of wandering abroad in search of an imaginary glory, or of extending their empire over other nations. Therefore, from the period at which that state assumed a republican form till the time when they were attacked by the arms of Rome, the nation was not once known to send a hostile force into the territories of any of their neighbours. This instance of moderation is unparalleled in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; no other nation can divide the glory of it with the Cretans. Individuals indeed might leave their country to engage in foreign armies. Those princes and states who knew their valour and skill in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">archery</a> eagerly sought to take them into their pay; all the neighbouring monarchs were desirous of having in their armies a body of Cretan archers. Over the whole world none were more celebrated than they for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> the bow. "The arrows of Gortynia (says Claudian), aimed from a trusty bow, are sure to wound, and never miss the destined mark." Though the multitude of independent cities which flourished in Crete did not unite their arms to subjugate the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and drench them with the blood of their inhabitants; yet they were not so wise as to live in peace among themselves. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCORD">Discord</a> often stalked among them with her flaming torch. The most powerful wished to enslave the rest. Sometimes Gnothus and Gortynia marched with social banners against their neighbours, levelled their fortresses, and subjected them to their power; at other times they attacked each other with hostile violence, and saw their bravest youth perish amid the horrors of civil war. Lyctos and Cydon opposed an invincible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to their ambition, and preserved their own liberty. The last of the cities had acquired such strength and influence, that she held the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> between the rival powers of the island. These wars destroyed a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the cities, and drenched the native country of Jupiter with blood. To what source must we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> those intestine dissensions? One part of the island was occupied by the Eteocretes, the original inhabitants; the rest was peopled with colonies from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, Sparta, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>. Perhaps the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> grudges which had subsisted among those strangers, being still unextinguished in their breasts, were easily rekindled by accident or circumstances, and inflamed with new fury. We may also suppose, that the most powerful among them, exulting in their superiority, would endeavour to take advantage of the weakness of the rest, and disregard all laws but those of force: besides, the glowing ardour of the youth, trained to military exercises, was ever ready to fly to arms. Such, probably, were the causes which fomented discord and hostility among a people living under the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, customs, and laws.—Whatever these might be, the Cretans being persuaded that the firm union of their soldiers was essential to victory, arrayed the bravest youths of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in splendid robes, and caused them to sacrifice to friendship before engaging in battle. In some countries it would be very proper to oblige the generals on such occasions, to sacrifice to concord. If such a sacrifice were performed with sincerity, it might preserve their glory untainted, and prevent such deluges of blood from being wasted without producing any advantages to the state. Their passion for war did not extinguish in the breasts of the Cretans that exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> which is the mother and nurse of the fine arts. "The Cretans (says Sozomen) gave an illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of their munificence to genius, by making <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> a present of a thousand pieces of silver; and to perpetuate the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of generosity, they recorded it by an inscription on a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>." In Crete, adds <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, men are still more devious of cultivating their understandings than of exercising their bodily powers. Often when dissensions arose, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of wisdom and the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> recalled them to reason and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THALES">Thales</a> of Gortynia, the preceptor of Lycurgus, was one of their most celebrated philosophers. Being both a poet and legislator, he made a happy use of his abilities and knowledge to extinguish among his countrymen the kindling sparks of discord. "His poems were moral discourses in verse, which recalled the people to concord and submission to the laws. Using a regular measure, he recommended the authority of his subject by the infusing and powerful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> of sentiment. So powerful were the effects of his verses, which addressed at once the ears, the heart, and the understanding of his hearers, that their rage was gradually softened. Next, opening their hearts to the love of peace, the advantages of which he described in glowing colours, they forgot their intestine dissensions, and ranged themselves around the standard of concord." That sage is said to have invented tunes for the military dances and for the Cretan Pyrrhic. Men who felt so strongly the influence of poetry and music could scarcely be enemies to pleasure. Accordingly they had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of distinguishing their fortunate days with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flint <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, their unfortunate days with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. At the end of the year they counted the number of their white stones, and reckoned that they had lived only so many days as were distinguished for having been fortunate. They did not think <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> existence, without the enjoyment of pleasure, worthy of the name of life. For this reason, they caused to be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> on their tombs: "He lived so many days; he continued in existence so long." A passion for glory is easily awakened in a feeling and generous breast. The Cretans eagerly repaired to the famous solemnities of Greece, and were often crowned at the Olympic, Nemean, and Pythian games; others of them were favorites of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, and verified the predictions of prophets, or celebrated the glorious deeds of their heroes. Several of them distinguished themselves by historical compositions. At the most ancient games, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> is said to have been bestowed on the poet who sung the noblest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>: Chrysothemis of Crete sung and gained the prize. The ravages of time have deprived us of almost all their works; and if <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a> had not preserved the memory of some of their crowns, we should not know even the names of the conquerors who wore them. The temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> at Ephesus, built by the Cretan Ctesiphon and his son Metagenes, was not proof against the frantic hand of the incendiary. Those ingenious architects had built it on the principles of the Ionic order; to the coarseness of the materials, the elegance of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, the symmetry of the parts, and the majesty and perfection of the whole, they had added solidity and strength, without which the rest must have been of small value. Their names have descended to posterity, but the pillars of that monument which has perpetuated their memory have been defaced or destroyed. Scarce a vestige remains of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> which was esteemed one of the seven wonders of the world. Nations are effaced from the earth like the monuments of their power, and after the revolution of several ages we can scarcely trace in their posterity any remains of their ancient character. Some of them exist longer, others shorter; but we may almost always calculate the period of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> by the excellence of their laws, and the fidelity with which they support and obey them. The republic of Crete, being established on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> basis, knew no foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for a period of ten centuries. She bravely repelled the attacks of those princes who attempted to enslave her. At length the time arrived when the warlike and victorious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> aspired to the empire of the world, and would suffer none but their subjects or slaves to inhabit within the reach of their arms. Florus does not scruple to acknowledge, that the Romans had no other motives for invading Crete but the ambitious desire of subduing the renowned native country of Jupiter. "If any person wish to know the reasons which induced us to attack Crete (says he), the true reason was our desire to subdue so celebrated an island. The Cretans had appeared to favour <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a>, and the Romans thought proper to declare war against them on that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a>. Mark Antony, father of the triumvir, attacked them with strong hopes of success; but was severely punished for his presumption and imprudence. The Cretans took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of his fleet, hung up his soldiers and sailors on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> amid the sails and cordage, and returned in triumph into their harbours." The Romans never forgot nor forgave a defeat. As soon as the Macedonian war was brought to a happy conclusion, they again took arms against the Cretans to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> their ignominy and loss. Quintus Metellus was sent to Crete with a powerful armament. He met with an obstinate and vigorous resistance. Panarus and Laethines, two experienced leaders, collected a body of 20,000 young warriors, all eager for battle, and of determined courage, employed their arms and arrows successfully against the Romans, and protracted the fate of Crete for three years. Those conquerors could not make themselves masters of the island before destroying its bravest warriors. They lost a great number of troops, and bought a bloody victory at the price of many a danger and much fatigue. However, their usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> at length prevailed. The first care of the conqueror was to abolish the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, and to establish in their room those of Numa. Strabo, that enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, complains of this act of severity; and informs us, that in his days the original laws of Crete were no longer in force, because the Romans compelled the conquered provinces to adopt their civil code. To secure themselves still more fully in the possession of the island, they sent a powerful colony to Gnoissus. From that era to the present time, that is, for a period of 1900 years, the Cretans have no longer formed a separate nation, or made any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> among the states and kingdoms of the world: their noble and ingenuous manners, their arts and sciences, their valour and their virtues, are no more. They have lost these with the loss of liberty. So true is it that man is not born for himself; and that, when deprived of that aid which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> has designed to strengthen and support his weaknesses, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of genius and the ardent glow of valour are extinguished in his breast; he becomes incapable of vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, and sinks below the natural virtue and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of the species. The island of Crete, joined with the small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, on the Libyan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, formed a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. It was at first governed by a proconsul; a quæstor and an assistant were afterwards sent there; at last, as Suetonius informs us, it was put under the government of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>. This island was one of the first places in the world that were favoured with the light of the gospel. St Paul introduced the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> into Crete; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> Titus, whom he left there to cherish and cultivate that precious plant, became the first bishop of the island. In the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Leo, it had twelve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, who were all subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Constantinople. Constantine separated Crete from Cyrene in the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> which he made of the provinces of the empire. Leaving three sons, Constansius, Constantine, and Constans, he assigned Thrace and the eastern provinces to the first; to the second, the empire of the west; the island of Crete, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and Illyria, to the third. When Michael Balbus sat on the throne of Constantinople, the rebellion of Thomas, which lasted three years, caused him to neglect the other parts of the empire. The Agarenians (a people of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>), who had conquered the finest provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, seized that opportunity. They fitted out a considerable fleet, plundered the Cyclades, attacked the island of Crete, and made themselves masters of it without opposition. In order to secure their conquest, they built a fortress which they named Khandak, "intrenchment." From that citadel the barbarians made incursions into the interior parts of the island, carrying havoc and devastation wherever they appeared. By repeated attacks, they subdued all the cities in Crete except Cydon. Michael made some ineffectual efforts to expel them from Crete. The emperor Basilus, the Macedonian, was not more successful. They defeated him in a bloody battle; but being vanquished by one of his generals, they were subjected to the payment of an annual tribute. At the end of ten years, the Arabians refused the tribute. It was referred for Nicephorus Phocas, who was afterwards emperor, to deliver this fine island from the yoke of the infidels. He landed on the island with a numerous army, boldly attacked them, and routed them in various engagements. The Saracens, no longer daring to meet so formidable a general in the field, fled for protection to their fortresses. Phocas being plentifully supplied with all the warlike <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> necessary for a siege, levelled their walls, and alarmed their hearts with terror. He took their cities and fortresses, and drove them into Khandaq their <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> and last resource. In the course of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months he subdued the whole island, took their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> Curup and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> Aremas prisoners, and reunited to the empire a province which had been 127 years in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the infidels. It remained under the dominion of the Romans till the time when Baldwin <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, being raised to the throne, liberally rewarded the services of Boniface marquis of Montferrat, by making him king of Thessalonica, and adding the island of Crete to his kingdom. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, being more covetous of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> than glory, sold it to the Venetians in the year 1194; under whom it assumed the name of Candia. See the sequel of its history under that article.
